Name: retrieval_gating_hypothesis
Title: The Retrieval Gate: Why LLMs Store Facts They Cannot Say, and How to Reopen Them
Short Hypothesis: Knowledge failures in LLMs are often not storage failures but *retrieval-gating* failures: the fact is encoded in intermediate representations but a query-dependent attention 'gate' fails to route it to the output. We hypothesize a small, identifiable set of attention heads acts as a query-conditioned router whose failure explains the internal-vs-external knowledge gap, and that intervening on this router recovers hidden knowledge without editing where the fact is stored.
Related Work: Prior work localizes factual associations to mid-layer MLPs (ROME; Knowledge Neurons) and shows localization does not predict editability (Hase et al. 2023). Recent work shows retrieval is distributed, redundant, and non-contiguous (Hochman et al. 2026), that query-specific neuron selection depends on attention (Query Localization, 2024), and that LLMs harbor 'hidden knowledge' inaccessible to generation despite 1000 samples (Inside-Out, 2025). Fakepedia (2023) studies grounding vs. parametric recall. None of these isolate a *causal, query-conditioned routing mechanism* that gates whether stored knowledge reaches the output, nor demonstrate a targeted attention intervention that reopens hidden knowledge. We reframe the storage/retrieval debate: rather than asking *where* knowledge lives, we ask *what decides whether it is expressed on a given query*, and provide a mechanism-level causal account plus a lightweight intervention.
Abstract: Large language models often 'know' a fact internally yet fail to produce it, a gap of up to 40% between internal and external knowledge. Existing explanations focus on where facts are stored (mid-layer MLPs) but leave open why storage sometimes fails to influence the answer. We propose the Retrieval Gate hypothesis: expression of stored knowledge is controlled by a small set of query-conditioned attention heads that route entity/attribute information to the final position, and knowledge failures are frequently *gating* failures rather than *storage* failures. We test this by (1) constructing paired 'hidden-knowledge' probes where linear readouts recover a fact from intermediate activations even when the model answers incorrectly; (2) using activation patching and attention-head causal tracing to identify which components differ between expressed and hidden cases across matched queries; (3) testing whether a compact, transferable set of 'gate' heads predicts expression across facts and query paraphrases; and (4) performing targeted interventions—amplifying gate-head attention to the subject token or patching gate-head outputs—to reopen hidden knowledge without editing MLP weights. We evaluate on GPT-J, Llama-3-8B, and Qwen3-8B using recovery rate of hidden facts, specificity (no collateral corruption of unrelated facts), and cross-query transfer. Confirming the hypothesis would unify puzzling findings (localization-editing mismatch, distributed redundant retrieval, hidden knowledge) under a single routing mechanism and yield a cheap, non-destructive alternative to weight editing for surfacing what models already know.
Experiments: Experiment 1 (H1 - hidden-knowledge set exists): Tests the premise that a non-trivial share of factual failures are retrieval-gating, not storage, failures - the fact is recoverable from intermediate representations though the model does not generate it. Data: three existing factual-QA sets used as-is and merged - PopQA (14,282 questions, 16 relations), the T-REx slice of LAMA (~34k subject-relation-object triples, 41 relations), and EntityQuestions (24 relations, ~176k questions); we sample 12,000 facts stratified by relation and by Wikidata-pageview popularity decile, fewer than the full pool because caching per-layer activations and training a probe at every layer is the compute bottleneck and 12k still gives >=300 facts per relation. Split 60/20/20 into probe-train / probe-val / test with no entity shared across splits. Model: Llama-3-8B (8B params, decoder-only), all base weights frozen; only a per-layer L2 logistic-regression content probe on the last-token residual stream is trainable, seeds 0/1/2. Systems compared: greedy-generation correctness vs. best-layer content probe, plus a random-label control probe and a probe trained on shuffled activations. Decisive metric: the hidden-set fraction = share of generation failures where the held-out content probe reaches top-1 accuracy >=0.7, reported first; supporting: per-layer probe AUROC, and control-probe accuracy (must sit near chance ~1/|answer-vocab|). Convincing: >=15% of failures are hidden while the control stays at chance. Undecidable band: a hidden fraction of 8-15% (control at chance) is real but possibly too small to carry the mechanism story - we would report it as a bounded phenomenon and run H2 only on the recoverable subset. Negative: <8% hidden, or the control probe matching the real probe, means apparent recovery is probe overfitting rather than stored-but-ungated knowledge, falsifying the retrieval-gating premise.

Experiment 2 (H2 - attention heads, not MLPs, carry the expressed/hidden gap): Tests that the component whose state differs between an expressed and a hidden run is attention (routing), not MLP (storage). Data: expressed-vs-hidden pairs matched on relation and popularity decile, drawn from the Experiment 1 test split; target 1,500 pairs (fewer than all hidden facts because activation patching costs one forward pass per component per pair; 1,500 gives ~90 pairs/relation). Model: Llama-3-8B, frozen; activation patching (no training) of the residual stream, per-layer MLP output, and per-head attention output from the expressed run into the hidden run at subject and last-token positions; 3 random re-pairings define a matched null. Systems compared: attention-head patches vs. MLP patches vs. full-residual patches vs. a random-source-run control. Decisive metric: fraction of patched components that flip the hidden run to the gold answer, reported separately for attention heads and MLPs (attention:MLP flip ratio first); supporting: total Delta log-prob of the gold token. Convincing: attention-head patches flip >=2x as many cases as MLP patches (e.g. >=30% vs <=15%), with a compact subset of heads accounting for most flips. Undecidable band: an attention:MLP flip ratio of 1.2-2.0x cannot separate routing-dominant from mixed - we would call gating partial and not claim attention dominance. Negative: MLP patches flip as many or more cases (ratio <=1.2x) means the gap lives in storage, not routing, falsifying H2.

Experiment 3 (H2 - a small, transferable, query-conditioned gate-head set): Tests that a small top-k head set (k<=10) predicts expression and generalizes across held-out facts and query paraphrases. Data: heads ranked by aggregated Experiment 2 causal contribution over probe-train pairs; evaluation on held-out test facts plus 5 paraphrases per fact (cloze, WH-question, indirect, templated, natural) from a template bank kept only when a natural-language-inference filter scores bidirectional entailment >=0.9, yielding ~6,000 (fact, paraphrase) items. Model: Llama-3-8B, frozen; gate-head features = attention mass the top-k heads place on subject/attribute tokens; a trainable linear classifier maps features to expression success, seeds 0/1/2. Systems compared: top-k gate-head features (k in {3,5,10,20}) vs. all-head features vs. an MLP-activation baseline vs. a random-head control. Decisive metric: AUROC of gate-head features predicting correct generation on held-out facts (first); supporting: AUROC across paraphrases and the k at which AUROC saturates. Convincing: k<=10 heads reach AUROC >=0.75 held-out and >=0.70 across paraphrases, within 0.03 of the all-head AUROC. Undecidable band: AUROC 0.60-0.75, or needing k>20 to reach it, means routing is real but diffuse - we would report a distributed gate and drop the 'small set' clause. Negative: AUROC <=0.60 or no better than the random-head control falsifies the compact-router claim.

Experiment 4 (H3 - reopening the gate recovers hidden facts without editing storage): Tests that intervening on gate heads recovers hidden facts more selectively than weight editing. Data: held-out hidden facts from the Experiment 1 test split, target 800 (fewer than all hidden facts because each is evaluated under a full specificity/fluency sweep). Model: Llama-3-8B, frozen except the ROME comparator; interventions are (a) scaling top-k gate-head attention toward subject tokens (scalar alpha swept 1-6), (b) patching gate-head outputs from a generic recall-prompting context, (c) a ROME MLP weight edit as the storage-editing comparator, (d) a random-head scaling control; seeds 0/1/2. Systems compared: (a),(b) vs. ROME vs. random control. Decisive metric: net recovered hidden facts per unit collateral = recovery rate / accuracy drop on 100 matched unrelated facts (first); supporting: raw recovery rate and held-out-text perplexity change. Convincing: gate-head interventions recover >=40% of hidden facts with <5% unrelated-accuracy drop and <2% perplexity rise, beating ROME on recovered-per-collateral by >=1.5x. Undecidable band: recovery 20-40%, or a 1.0-1.5x advantage over ROME, is inconclusive on selectivity - we would report the intervention as viable but not clearly better than editing. Negative: recovery <20%, or collateral no better than ROME, means gate manipulation does not causally reopen storage-independent knowledge, falsifying H3.

Experiment 5 (H2 - expression is a function of the query-to-gate mapping): Tests that whether a fixed fact is expressed tracks gate-head activation across query phrasings, not MLP content. Data: 500 facts with mixed cross-format expression, each rendered in the 5 validated paraphrase formats from Experiment 3 (2,500 items). Model: Llama-3-8B, frozen; measure gate-head activation and MLP activation per (fact, format), seeds 0/1/2 for the regression splits. Systems compared: within-fact expression variance explained by gate-head features vs. by MLP activations, via nested logistic regression (Delta pseudo-R^2). Decisive metric: Delta pseudo-R^2 that gate-head features add over MLP features in explaining per-format expression (first); supporting: within-fact expression variance across formats. Convincing: gate-head features add Delta R^2 >=0.15 and account for the majority of within-fact cross-format expression variance. Undecidable band: Delta R^2 0.05-0.15 leaves query-conditioning weakly supported - report as suggestive only. Negative: Delta R^2 <0.05, or MLP features explaining expression as well as gate features, means expression is not governed by the query-to-gate mapping.

Experiment 6 (H1-H3 generality - architecture-general gating): Tests that the hidden set, attention dominance, compact gate, and reopening result hold beyond one model. Data: reuse the Experiment 1 sampling pipeline (12,000 facts) per model. Model: repeat Experiments 1-4 on GPT-J-6B and Qwen3-8B, all frozen, identical seeds and hyperparameters. Systems compared: Llama-3-8B vs. GPT-J-6B vs. Qwen3-8B on each decisive metric. Decisive metric: sign-consistency across models of the Experiment 2 attention:MLP flip ratio and the Experiment 4 recovered-per-collateral advantage (first); supporting: per-model hidden fraction and gate-head AUROC. Convincing: all three models show attention:MLP flip ratio >=1.5x and gate-head AUROC >=0.70. Undecidable band: the pattern holding in 2 of 3 models is partial generality - report scope limited to those architectures. Negative: the direction reversing in the majority of models means gating is model-specific, not general.
Risk Factors and Limitations: Linear-probe recovery may reflect probe overfitting rather than genuine hidden knowledge; mitigated by held-out probe evaluation and comparing to random-label control probes.

The set of gate heads may not be small or transferable; distributed/redundant retrieval (Hochman et al.) suggests routing could be diffuse, which would partially falsify the compact-gate claim but still yield an informative negative result.
Interventions that reopen hidden knowledge may also increase confident hallucination on facts the model does not actually store; specificity controls are essential and could limit practical utility.
Distinguishing gating failures from subtle storage differences is hard; matched-pair design and MLP-patching controls reduce but may not fully eliminate confounds.
Findings on 6-8B models may not scale to larger frontier models an academic lab cannot run.

novelty.reasoning: Core claims: (1) hidden-knowledge failures are often retrieval-gating rather than storage failures; (2) a small query-conditioned set of attention heads acts as a router/gate for factual expression; (3) this gate is causally identifiable and transferable across facts/paraphrases; (4) targeted attention intervention can reopen hidden facts with less collateral than weight editing. Relative to prior work, the ingredients are known, but the specific causal framing and selective intervention are a plausible non-trivial delta. The novelty is mostly in the mechanism + intervention, not in the phenomenon.
revision_notes: State the exact falsifiable novelty claim: 'a compact, query-conditioned gate-head set causally mediates expression of internally recoverable facts.'
Differentiate explicitly from 'attention routes facts' papers by specifying what is new: compactness, transfer across facts, and causal reopening of hidden knowledge.
Clarify whether the contribution is a new mechanism, a new dataset of matched hidden/expressed pairs, or a new intervention; right now it is all three, which blurs the novelty center.
Add a crisp comparison table against Inside-Out, ROME, Knowledge Neurons, and query-localization work showing the actual delta.

impact.reasoning: The problem is real: why models can internally recover facts yet fail to say them matters for interpretability, hallucination/reliability, and editing. If true, it would affect how researchers think about knowledge failures and could offer a practical, non-destructive alternative to weight editing. The so-what is decent: practitioners may use gate interventions to surface latent knowledge and researchers may shift from storage-centric to routing-centric explanations.

review.reasoning: The hypothesis is testable, but the proposal overstates certainty in a hard-to-disentangle setting. The main weakness is confounding: probe recovery, attention causality, and storage-vs-routing are not cleanly separable yet. Experimental ideas are reasonable and feasible, but several controls are underspecified, and the intervention could simply amplify existing logits or induce artifacts rather than reveal a genuine gate mechanism. The core contribution could still be strong if executed carefully, but the current writeup needs tighter scope and more rigorous discriminative tests.

Name: format_bound_knowledge
Title: Format-Bound Knowledge: Why LLMs Store the Same Fact in Multiple Query-Specific Copies and Fail to Transfer Between Them
Short Hypothesis: The same factual knowledge is stored not once but as several redundant, format-specific representations tied to the surface form of the query that taught it (e.g., cloze vs. question vs. comparative vs. procedural use). Retrieval failures often arise from a 'format mismatch': a query in one format cannot access a fact whose representation is bound to another format. We hypothesize these format-specific copies are (a) causally dissociable via activation patching, (b) linearly identifiable as distinct residual-stream directions for the same fact, and (c) that a single learned 'format-bridge' steering vector can transfer access across formats without weight editing.
Related Work: Prior work localizes facts to mid-layer MLPs (ROME, Knowledge Neurons) and separates recall from reasoning circuits by layer/head (Disentangling Recall and Reasoning, 2025; LiReFs, 2025; Decoupling Knowledge and Reasoning, 2025). Procedural-vs-declarative studies (Meta-Cognitive Analysis, 2024; Procedural Knowledge Drives Reasoning, 2024) and SynthWorlds (2025) show declarative and procedural knowledge behave differently but treat each fact as a single store accessed differently. Knowledge-neuron work on multi-hop recall (2024) and RL-improves-traversal (2025) note query representations diverge while fact representations stay similar. None ask whether a *single fact is stored as multiple format-bound copies* whose non-interchangeability causes retrieval failure, nor demonstrate a format-bridge intervention. We reframe the storage/retrieval debate: instead of 'one store, many queries,' we test 'many format-specific stores of the same fact,' a distinct and testable structural claim.
Abstract: Large language models frequently answer a fact correctly when it is phrased one way but fail when it is phrased another, even without any reasoning steps. Standard accounts treat each fact as a single stored association accessed by different queries. We propose an alternative structural hypothesis: LLMs store the same fact as multiple redundant, format-specific representations, each bound to the surface form under which the fact was most often encountered (cloze completions, direct questions, comparative judgments, and procedural usage). Retrieval failures then arise from format mismatch: a query in one format activates a pathway to a copy that is missing or weak, while another copy holds the fact intact. We test this with a controlled multi-format probe set: for each fact we build four semantically equivalent query formats and identify facts answered correctly in some formats but not others. Using activation patching across formats and linear probing of the residual stream, we test whether (1) format-specific representations are causally dissociable, (2) the same fact yields distinct, format-predictive linear directions, and (3) patching or steering activations from a successful format into a failing one restores access. We further learn a single low-rank 'format-bridge' steering vector per format pair and test cross-fact, cross-format transfer, comparing recovery rate, specificity, and fluency against ROME weight editing. Experiments span GPT-J-6B, Llama-3-8B, and Qwen2.5-7B. Confirming the hypothesis would replace the 'one fact, many queries' picture with a 'many format-bound copies' account, unifying puzzling paraphrase-sensitivity and internal-vs-external knowledge gaps and yielding a cheap non-destructive way to unlock format-inaccessible knowledge.
Experiments: Experiment 1 (H1 - multi-format fact set with per-format correctness): Builds the substrate for the one-store-vs-many-copies test by rendering each fact in four formats and recording per-format correctness. Data: facts from PopQA (14,282 questions, 16 relations), the T-REx slice of LAMA (~34k triples, 41 relations), and EntityQuestions (24 relations, ~176k questions); we sample 8,000 facts stratified by relation and popularity decile, fewer than the full pool because each fact is expanded into 4 formats (32,000 items) and re-scored on 3 models. Each fact is rendered as (a) cloze completion, (b) direct WH-question, (c) true/false verification, (d) comparative multiple-choice; format equivalence is filtered by a GPT-4o meaning-preservation judgment plus a 200-item human spot-check (kept if judge agreement >=0.9 and human agreement >=0.85). Split 70/30 fact-disjoint into analysis/test. Model: Llama-3-8B (8B, decoder-only), frozen; greedy decoding, per-format correctness logged, seed 0 for generation. Systems compared: the four formats against each other, per fact. Decisive metric: per-format accuracy and the coverage of facts correct in >=1 format (first); supporting: pairwise format-agreement rates. Convincing: >=60% of facts are correct in at least one format and formats disagree on >=20% of facts, giving a usable format-bound pool. Undecidable band: format-disagreement of 10-20% is a thin substrate - proceed but flag low power for H1-H4. Negative: <10% disagreement means formats behave interchangeably, undercutting the format-boundedness premise before any mechanism test.

Experiment 2 (H1 - format-mismatch prevalence: one store vs. many copies): Tests whether a single format-independent store explains the data or whether a real fact-by-format interaction remains. Data: the 32,000 (fact, format) correctness records from Experiment 1's analysis split. Model: Llama-3-8B, frozen; the model here is the data source, and the statistical model is a logistic regression predicting correctness from per-fact difficulty and per-format bias, versus an augmented model adding a fact-by-format interaction; 3 cross-validation folds. Systems compared: null single-store logistic model vs. interaction model, likelihood-ratio tested. Decisive metric: fraction of facts correct in some-but-not-all formats (the format-bound set) that survives the null, i.e. the interaction's Delta pseudo-R^2 over the null (first); supporting: likelihood-ratio p-value and the raw format-bound fraction. Convincing: format-bound fraction >=20% with interaction Delta R^2 >=0.10 and LR p<0.001 - inconsistent with a single format-independent store. Undecidable band: Delta R^2 0.03-0.10 signals a graded rather than discrete-copy picture - we would report format-boundedness as a continuum, weakening the strong copy claim. Negative: Delta R^2 <0.03 (interaction not significant) means one noisy store fits the data, falsifying H1.

Experiment 3 (H2 - format-specific copies are causally dissociable via patching): Tests whether the fact signal that succeeds in format S can be transplanted to restore a failing format F. Data: matched pairs (same fact, success format S, failure format F) from the format-bound set, target 1,500 pairs (fewer than the full set because patching is one forward pass per component per pair). Model: Llama-3-8B, frozen; activation patching of residual-stream, MLP, and attention-head activations from S into F at subject and last-token positions across all layers; random-source-run null. Systems compared: S-into-F patches vs. random-source patches, per component/layer. Decisive metric: fraction of F failures flipped to correct by patching from S (first); supporting: which layers/components carry the transferable signal. Convincing: >=35% of failures flip under S-patching vs <=10% under the random control, localized to a coherent layer band - copies are causally linked and transplantable. Undecidable band: 15-35% flip rate means copies are partially linked - report partial dissociability. Negative: <15% flip, near the random control, means the format representations are missing or fully independent, so no single transferable fact signal exists.

Experiment 4 (H3 - distinct linear fact directions per format): Tests whether the fact-carrying direction shifts systematically with format. Data: residual-stream activations for the format-bound facts across their four formats (analysis split, ~6,000 facts x 4). Model: Llama-3-8B, frozen; trainable linear probes decode (a) fact identity and (b) query format from the last-token residual stream, with held-out facts and label-shuffle controls, seeds 0/1/2. Systems compared: cosine similarity of the fact-direction across formats for format-bound vs. format-robust facts; probe on real vs. shuffled labels. Decisive metric: mean cross-format cosine similarity of the decoded fact direction for format-bound facts (first, lower = more copy-like); supporting: format-classifier AUROC and fact-decode accuracy. Convincing: format-bound facts show cross-format fact-direction cosine <=0.5 while format-robust facts stay >=0.8, and the format classifier reaches AUROC >=0.85 - distinct, linearly identifiable copies. Undecidable band: cosine 0.5-0.8 for format-bound facts indicates overlapping-but-shifted directions - report a graded geometry. Negative: cosine >0.8 (indistinguishable from format-robust facts) or shuffle-level probes means there are no distinct format-specific directions, falsifying H3.

Experiment 5 (H4 - a single format-bridge steering vector transfers access without weight editing): Tests whether one low-rank vector per ordered format pair restores access in the failing format. Data: for each ordered pair S->F, a training split of (success-in-S, failure-in-F) states and a fact-disjoint held-out set of failing-F queries; target 600 held-out failures per major pair. Model: Llama-3-8B, frozen; the bridge is the mean activation difference between S-success and F-failure states, rank<=8, added at the Experiment 3 best layer; alpha swept 1-6, seeds 0/1/2. Systems compared: bridge vector vs. a random-direction control vs. no intervention. Decisive metric: recovered-facts-per-unit-collateral = recovery rate / accuracy drop on 200 unrelated facts (first); supporting: raw recovery rate, held-out perplexity change, and cross-fact/cross-format transfer of one vector. Convincing: >=40% recovery with <5% unrelated-accuracy drop and <2% perplexity rise, and one vector transfers to held-out facts of the same pair at >=25% recovery. Undecidable band: recovery 20-40%, or transfer only within-fact, means bridges are largely fact-specific - report limited but real transfer. Negative: recovery <20% or no better than the random control means no single bridge vector transfers access, falsifying H4.

Experiment 6 (H4 - bridge vs. weight editing): Tests whether the training-free bridge matches or beats weight editing on selectivity and cost. Data: the held-out failing-F queries from Experiment 5 (target 600 per pair). Model: Llama-3-8B; ROME and MEMIT edit the failing format's fact (weights modified) vs. the frozen-weight bridge; seeds 0/1/2. Systems compared: bridge vs. ROME vs. MEMIT. Decisive metric: recovered-facts-per-unit-collateral (first); supporting: wall-clock/compute per recovered fact and perplexity change. Convincing: bridge matches or exceeds ROME/MEMIT recovered-per-collateral at >=5x lower compute per fact. Undecidable band: bridge within +/-20% of editing on recovered-per-collateral - report parity, a still-useful training-free alternative. Negative: bridge recovered-per-collateral <0.8x editing means weight editing is the better lever, limiting H4's practical claim though leaving the mechanism intact.

Experiment 7 (H1 origin - format-boundedness traces to format-skewed pretraining exposure): Tests whether a fact's format-boundedness correlates with the format distribution of its supporting pretraining occurrences. Data: format-bound vs. format-robust facts scored on a model with searchable pretraining data; occurrences retrieved by pretraining-data search over the Pile/C4 shards, target 2,000 facts with >=5 retrievable supporting passages each. Model: Pythia-1.4B (open training data), frozen; format of each occurrence auto-labeled (cloze/QA/comparative/procedural) by pattern + classifier. Systems compared: format-entropy of a fact's occurrences for format-bound vs. format-robust facts. Decisive metric: regression coefficient (and AUROC) of occurrence format-skew predicting a fact's format-boundedness (first); supporting: partial correlation controlling for total occurrence count. Convincing: format-skew predicts format-boundedness at AUROC >=0.65 after controlling for frequency. Undecidable band: AUROC 0.55-0.65 is a weak trend - report as suggestive of a training-exposure origin. Negative: AUROC <=0.55 means exposure skew does not explain boundedness on this model, and we note it may still differ on the 6-8B models.

Experiment 8 (H1-H4 generality - architecture-general format-boundedness): Tests that prevalence, dissociability, distinct directions, and the bridge hold beyond one model. Data: reuse the Experiment 1 pipeline (8,000 facts x 4 formats) per model. Model: repeat Experiments 2-5 on GPT-J-6B and Qwen2.5-7B, frozen, identical seeds/hyperparameters. Systems compared: Llama-3-8B vs. GPT-J-6B vs. Qwen2.5-7B on each decisive metric. Decisive metric: sign-consistency across models of the Experiment 2 interaction Delta R^2, Experiment 3 flip rate, and Experiment 5 recovery (first); supporting: per-model format-bound fraction. Convincing: all three models show significant format-fact interaction, S-into-F flip >=25%, and bridge recovery >=25%. Undecidable band: the pattern in 2 of 3 models is partial generality - scope the claim to those architectures. Negative: reversal in the majority of models means format-boundedness is model-specific.
Risk Factors and Limitations: Format 'equivalence' is imperfect; comparative/verification formats may impose extra task demands beyond retrieval, confounding format-boundedness with task difficulty. Mitigated by regression controls and by focusing patching on subject-token fact signals rather than answer formatting.
The 'one store vs many copies' distinction may be a continuum rather than discrete copies; a graded result would still be informative but weakens the strong hypothesis.

Linear probe format-signatures could reflect query encoding rather than distinct fact copies; the patching experiment (which manipulates fact-carrying activations, not query tokens) is the decisive causal test.
A single format-bridge vector may not transfer across facts if bridges are fact-specific, limiting practical utility though still scientifically informative.
Steering could induce confident hallucination on facts not actually stored in any format; strict specificity controls are required.
Pretraining-origin analysis is only feasible on small open-data models and may not generalize to the 6-8B evaluation models.

novelty.reasoning: Core claims: (1) facts are stored as multiple format-bound copies rather than one fact with multiple query pathways; (2) these copies are causally dissociable by patching; (3) they appear as distinct linear residual-stream directions; (4) a learned format-bridge steering vector can transfer access across formats without weight editing. The setting is new enough: prior work on paraphrase consistency and multilingual factual consistency shows format/query failures, but not this exact structural claim across query formats. However, the observation itself is adjacent to known inconsistency phenomena, and the bridge method is a near-transplant of cross-lingual steering. The most novel part is the structural 'many copies' hypothesis, but it is also the most vulnerable to the standard null that query encodings differ while the underlying fact store is shared.
revision_notes: State explicitly what would falsify the proposal: e.g. if patching transfers but probes do not separate, or if format effects disappear after controlling for query difficulty/encoding.

Sharpen the delta vs prior work into one sentence: 'Unlike paraphrase-consistency and cross-lingual steering, we test whether formats induce causally separable fact representations within a single model.'
Reduce claims about 'distinct linear directions' unless the paper can prove them beyond probe artifacts; present as an empirical signature, not the core novelty.
Add a direct comparison to the one-store-many-queries null and to multilingual steering as the closest methodological baseline.

impact.reasoning: The phenomenon under study is factual retrieval inconsistency across query formats. People who care: interpretability, robustness, knowledge editing, and factuality researchers. Strongest one-line case: if facts are format-bound, then improving QA requires format-aware retrieval/intervention rather than treating knowledge as a single invariant store. This is a real research problem, but still mostly methodological and somewhat niche; the result would be valuable as a phenomenon if true, yet it is not obviously direction-shifting for the broader ML field. So what? If confirmed, serious researchers in factual consistency and model editing would likely care and cite it; if refuted, the field mostly keeps the existing one-store account and focus on query encoding.

review.reasoning: The hypothesis is interesting but currently overstated and undercontrolled. Main logical gap: format mismatch could be explained by query-encoding differences, task difficulty, or answer-space changes rather than multiple stored copies. The core claim is only falsifiable if the experiments cleanly separate representation storage from query processing. Related work is directionally present but not yet specific enough to isolate the exact delta from paraphrase consistency, multilingual steering, and multi-hop query-vs-fact representation work. Experimental plan is ambitious and testable, but several controls are missing: matched difficulty across formats, answer-space and frequency controls, strong random/targeted controls for patching and steering, and analyses to distinguish probe separability from representational artifact. If executed carefully, this could be a solid interpretability/knowledge-retrieval paper, but not yet submission-ready as written.

Name: retrieval_competition
Title: Retrieval Competition: How Interference Between Co-Activated Candidates Determines Whether Stored Knowledge Reaches the Answer
Short Hypothesis: When an LLM processes a factual query, it co-activates a *set* of competing candidate answers in the residual stream, and the final answer is decided by a winner-take-all competition whose outcome is largely insensitive to correctness. We hypothesize that (1) the geometry of this candidate set — number of competitors and the margin between the top competitor and the correct answer — is linearly readable at intermediate layers and predicts *which failure mode* occurs (interference-driven wrong answer vs. genuine ignorance), and (2) knowledge that is stored but not expressed typically loses this competition to a better-primed distractor, such that reweighting the competition (suppressing the winning distractor's direction) recovers the correct answer more selectively than amplifying the correct fact.
Related Work: A large literature shows internal states carry a knowledge/recall-strength signal (KEEN, 2024; SAPLMA, 2023; in-advance correctness probes, 2025; hallucination-risk probes, 2024; SCIURus shows uncertainty and factuality share circuits, 2025). Critically, 'LLMs Do NOT Really Know What They Don't Know' (2025) shows associated hallucinations and true facts share the same recall geometry, implying internal signals track *retrieval activity* not *truth*. Inside-Out (2025) documents a 40% internal-vs-external hidden-knowledge gap. Knowledge-editing work (ROME, MEMIT) localizes facts to MLPs. None of these characterize retrieval as a *competition among multiple co-activated candidates* whose resolution — not storage — determines the answer, nor do they use the competitor-set geometry to predict failure *type* or to recover hidden knowledge by distractor suppression. My prior proposals concern single-fact routing gates and multiple format-bound copies of the *same* fact; this proposal is orthogonal: it concerns interference between *different* candidate facts.
Abstract: Large language models often store a fact yet answer with a different, confidently wrong one. We propose that this is a symptom of retrieval as competition: a factual query co-activates a set of candidate answers in the residual stream, and the model resolves this set in a winner-take-all manner that is largely blind to correctness. Under this view, a stored fact fails to surface not because it is absent or ungated, but because it loses to a better-primed distractor (e.g., a more frequent entity, a lexically closer neighbor, or a co-occurring associate). We develop a method to read out the competitor set from intermediate layers by projecting the residual stream through the unembedding and identifying entity-typed candidates, then measuring competition geometry: the number of viable competitors and the logit margin between the top distractor and the correct answer. We test three claims: (1) competition geometry is linearly decodable and predicts whether a given failure is interference-driven (a specific distractor dominates) or genuine ignorance (the correct answer has near-zero internal support), distinguishing failure types that current confidence probes conflate; (2) hidden-knowledge failures (correct answer present internally but not generated) are disproportionately interference-driven; and (3) a targeted intervention that subtracts the winning distractor's direction recovers correct answers with higher specificity and less collateral damage than amplifying the correct-answer direction or ROME editing. Experiments span GPT-J-6B, Llama-3-8B, and Qwen2.5-7B on PopQA, T-REx, and EntityQuestions, evaluating failure-type classification AUROC, recovery rate, specificity, and fluency. Confirming these claims reframes knowledge failures as resolution failures and yields a cheap, non-destructive way to surface out-competed knowledge.
Experiments: Experiment 1 (H1 - a readable competitor set exists): Tests that factual queries co-activate a readable set of answer-type-consistent candidates with measurable competition geometry. Data: PopQA (14,282 questions, 16 relations), T-REx/LAMA (~34k, 41 relations), EntityQuestions (24 relations, ~176k); sample 10,000 single-token-first-entity facts stratified by relation and popularity, fewer than the pool because we restrict to single-token-first entities for clean vocabulary readout and cache per-layer projections. Model: Llama-3-8B (8B, decoder-only), frozen; project the last-token residual at each layer through a tuned-lens (trained once, then frozen) restricted to a precomputed answer-type entity vocabulary per relation; seed 0. Systems compared: tuned-lens vs. raw logit-lens readout; the top-k competitor set vs. a shuffled-vocabulary null. Decisive metric: coverage = fraction of queries whose gold or a plausible distractor appears in the top-k answer-type set above a support threshold (first); supporting: number of viable competitors, top1-to-gold logit margin, candidate-distribution entropy, and the overtake layer. Convincing: >=70% coverage with the tuned-lens and geometry features that are non-degenerate (median >=2 competitors). Undecidable band: coverage 50-70% means readout is noisy - restrict later analyses to covered facts and report the restriction. Negative: <50% coverage, or no better than the shuffled-vocabulary null, means the competitor-set construct is not readable, blocking H2/H3.

Experiment 2 (H2 - competition geometry predicts which failure mode): Tests that geometry features separate interference-driven wrong answers from genuine ignorance. Data: failures from Experiment 1, hand-verifiable-labeled by rule into (a) interference (a specific wrong entity has high internal support and the gold answer is also internally present) vs (b) ignorance (gold has near-zero support at all layers); target 4,000 labeled failures. Model: Llama-3-8B, frozen; a trainable linear probe on the competition-geometry features predicts failure type, seeds 0/1/2, label-shuffle control. Systems compared: geometry probe vs. a KEEN-style single-scalar confidence/correctness probe vs. chance. Decisive metric: AUROC of the geometry probe distinguishing interference from ignorance (first); supporting: the confidence-probe AUROC it must beat, and calibration. Convincing: geometry-probe AUROC >=0.75 and >=0.07 above the confidence probe - geometry carries failure-mode information a scalar confidence signal conflates. Undecidable band: AUROC 0.60-0.75 or within 0.07 of the confidence baseline means geometry helps but does not cleanly separate the modes - report a graded taxonomy. Negative: AUROC <=0.60 or no gain over the confidence probe falsifies the predictiveness half of H2.

Experiment 3 (H3 - hidden knowledge loses to a better-primed distractor): Tests that stored-but-unexpressed facts are disproportionately interference-driven. Data: hidden-knowledge failures identified with an internal-vs-external gap protocol (gold internally supported but not generated) from Experiment 1's pool; target 2,500 hidden failures plus a matched baseline-failure set. Model: Llama-3-8B, frozen; classify each hidden failure as interference vs. ignorance using Experiment 2 labels; regress distractor properties (frequency, lexical similarity, subject co-occurrence) on winning. Systems compared: hidden failures vs. matched non-hidden failures (chi-square on interference rate); distractor-property regression vs. intercept-only. Decisive metric: difference in interference-driven proportion between hidden and baseline failures (first); supporting: regression coefficients on distractor frequency/similarity/co-occurrence. Convincing: hidden failures are interference-driven at a rate >=15 percentage points above baseline (chi-square p<0.001) and winning distractors are reliably higher-frequency/more-primed. Undecidable band: a 5-15 point gap is a real but modest association - report hidden knowledge as often, not usually, interference-driven, softening H3. Negative: <5 point gap means hidden failures are not distinctively competition-driven, falsifying the H3 mechanism.

Experiment 4 (H3 - suppressing the distractor beats amplifying the fact): Tests that reweighting the competition recovers hidden facts more selectively than boosting the correct direction or editing. Data: interference-driven hidden facts from Experiment 3, held out, target 800. Model: Llama-3-8B, frozen except the ROME comparator; at the competition layers, project out the winning distractor's unembedding-aligned direction, vs. (a) adding the gold-answer direction, (b) a ROME edit, (c) a random-direction control; scale swept, seeds 0/1/2. Systems compared: distractor-suppression vs. correct-amplification vs. ROME vs. random. Decisive metric: recovered-facts-per-unit-collateral = recovery rate / accuracy drop on 200 unrelated facts (first); supporting: raw recovery, held-out perplexity change. Convincing: distractor-suppression recovers >=40% with <5% unrelated-accuracy drop and beats correct-amplification on recovered-per-collateral by >=1.5x. Undecidable band: a 1.0-1.5x advantage over amplification means suppression is comparable, not clearly more selective - report parity. Negative: suppression recovered-per-collateral <=amplification, or recovery <20%, falsifies the selective-reweighting half of H3.

Experiment 5 (H1/H2 - competition geometry is causal, not correlational): Tests that manipulating distractor support changes outcomes as the geometry predicts. Data: 1,000 correctly-answered facts (to induce errors) and 1,000 interference failures (to fix), from Experiment 1. Model: Llama-3-8B, frozen; activation-patch the distractor's supporting subject/context signal into correct runs to induce interference errors on demand, and remove distractor support from failing runs; random-direction control. Systems compared: induced-error rate under distractor injection vs. random injection; fix rate under distractor removal vs. random removal. Decisive metric: induced-error rate from injecting distractor support (first); supporting: fix rate from removing it. Convincing: distractor injection induces errors in >=30% of correct cases (vs <=5% random) and removal fixes >=30% of failures - competition geometry is causally tied to the outcome. Undecidable band: 10-30% induced-error rate is weak causal control - report competition as contributory but not decisive. Negative: <10%, near the random control, means geometry is only correlational, undercutting H1/H2's causal reading.

Experiment 6 (H2 - geometry improves selective prediction): Tests that geometry features let the model abstain on ignorance while attempting recovery on interference. Data: the mixed failure set from Experiments 2-3 (target 6,000 failures) plus correct answers, held-out split. Model: Llama-3-8B, frozen; a selective-prediction policy over geometry features vs. a confidence-probe policy, seeds 0/1/2. Systems compared: geometry-based abstention+recovery vs. confidence-threshold abstention. Decisive metric: area under the risk-coverage curve (first, lower risk at equal coverage is better); supporting: recovery-attempt precision on interference cases. Convincing: geometry policy lowers risk at matched coverage by >=15% relative to the confidence baseline. Undecidable band: 5-15% improvement is a modest gain - report as incremental. Negative: <5% improvement means geometry adds no selective-prediction value beyond confidence.

Experiment 7 (H1-H3 generality - architecture-general competition): Tests that competitor sets, failure-mode prediction, and the hidden-knowledge link hold beyond one model. Data: reuse the Experiment 1 sampling (10,000 facts) per model. Model: repeat Experiments 1-4 on GPT-J-6B and Qwen2.5-7B, frozen, identical seeds/hyperparameters. Systems compared: Llama-3-8B vs. GPT-J-6B vs. Qwen2.5-7B on each decisive metric. Decisive metric: sign-consistency of the Experiment 2 AUROC gain, Experiment 3 interference-gap, and Experiment 4 suppression advantage across models (first); supporting: per-model coverage. Convincing: all three show geometry-probe AUROC >=0.70, a positive interference-gap, and a suppression advantage >=1.2x. Undecidable band: the pattern in 2 of 3 models is partial generality - scope accordingly. Negative: reversal in the majority means competition dynamics are model-specific.
Risk Factors and Limitations: Vocabulary projection of the residual stream is noisy and can produce spurious 'candidates'; mitigated by tuned-lens, answer-type filtering, and causal patching validation rather than relying on logit-lens alone.
The interference-vs-ignorance dichotomy may be a continuum; a graded result would weaken the clean taxonomy but remain informative, and we report continuous competition metrics.

Distractor suppression could introduce new errors or degrade fluency if the subtracted direction overlaps with useful representations; strict specificity and perplexity controls are included and the intervention may prove impractical even if the analysis holds.
Correct answers may share directions with distractors (entity superposition), making clean subtraction impossible for some facts, limiting recovery coverage.
Multi-token entity answers complicate single-token logit-lens readout; we restrict primary analysis to single-token-first entities and report coverage.
Findings on 6-8B models may not transfer to frontier-scale models beyond an academic budget.

novelty.reasoning: Core technical claims: (1) factual queries co-activate multiple candidate answers in the residual stream; (2) the geometry of that candidate set (count of viable competitors, correct-vs-top-distractor margin) is linearly readable at intermediate layers; (3) that geometry predicts failure type, especially interference-driven wrong answers vs genuine ignorance; (4) hidden-knowledge failures are disproportionately interference-driven; (5) subtracting the winning distractor direction recovers the correct answer more selectively than amplifying the gold answer or doing weight editing. The novelty lives mainly in the mechanism/finding plus a mild new classification setting. This is not a wholly new broad idea: competitor suppression, additive logit contributions, and recall interference already have direct precedents (especially Forbidden Facts, Summing Up The Facts, and interference/working-memory papers). The non-trivial delta is the explicit readout of competitor-set geometry as a predictor of failure TYPE and using distractor subtraction as a targeted recovery intervention. That is a reasonable extension rather than an obvious baseline, but it is still close to known logit-lens / steering / suppression analyses. The closest prior family is retrieval-interference and competitor-suppression interpretability work; the actual delta is moving from 'there is competition' to 'we can quantify candidate-set geometry, classify failure mode, and causally intervene by subtracting the distractor.'

impact.reasoning: Phenomenon under study: why an LLM with latent knowledge outputs the wrong answer, and whether that failure is due to competition among internal candidates versus true lack of knowledge. Who cares: interpretability researchers, hallucination/reliability folks, and knowledge-editing / model-debugging practitioners. Strongest one-line case: if hidden knowledge is often blocked by a few competing activations rather than absent, we can diagnose failures more precisely and intervene more selectively. So what? If true, this changes how people think about hallucinations and hidden knowledge: not as a single confidence/ignorance axis, but as a retrieval-competition problem with actionable internal geometry. That is useful and could influence probes, selective prediction, and editing. However, the real-world reach is moderate: the evaluation is likely on curated factual QA and internal diagnostics, so the downstream impact is mostly on model analysis tooling rather than direct user-facing product behavior. Uptake/citation potential is decent because it connects several active threads, but it is not obviously direction-shifting unless the classifier and subtraction intervention are robust across models and datasets. Phenomenon value is solid because it targets an important explanatory gap, but the practical consequence is narrower than a broadly deployable reliability method.

review.reasoning: Main logical gaps: the proposal assumes a clean separation between interference-driven failure and genuine ignorance, but the cited literature already suggests shared recall geometry for truth and hallucination, which may confound the taxonomy. The 'competitor set' reconstructed from unembedding may be noisy and may reflect the model's output distribution rather than an internal set of co-activated candidates; that distinction needs validation. The distractor-subtraction idea risks collapsing into known logit steering / contrastive decoding / logit-difference interventions unless the causal specificity is demonstrated. The hypothesis is testable but needs sharper falsifiability: define exactly how 'viable competitor,' 'interference-driven,' and 'genuine ignorance' are labeled, and pre-register thresholds. Related work is fairly specific, but it underplays closest analogs like contrastive decoding, logit lens, and steering-based interventions. Experiments are mostly feasible and controlled, but some are underspecified: the coverage criterion for competitor readout, the rule-labeled failure taxonomy, the matched baseline for hidden-knowledge gaps, and the causal intervention controls. Missing controls include random-direction subtraction matched for norm, top-distractor vs second-distractor subtraction, gold-direction amplification with equal logit change, and causal mediation/patching to verify the proposed geometry actually mediates the error. If executed well, this could be a solid interpretability/reliability venue paper, but as written it is not yet submission-ready for a serious ML venue because the central claims are a bit too broad and the taxonomy/intervention need stronger operational definitions. Minimum viable edits: narrow the claims to one dataset family and one clear failure taxonomy; add causal validation of the competitor geometry; add strong ablations against logit steering baselines; and specify a reproducible labeling protocol for interference vs ignorance.

Name: strategy_arbitration
Title: Retrieve or Assemble? How LLMs Arbitrate Between Memorized Shortcuts and Compositional Computation, and Why Choosing Wrong Hides Known Knowledge
Short Hypothesis: For many derivable facts an LLM has two internal pathways to the answer: a memorized 'shortcut' that recalls the answer atomically, and a 'compositional' pathway that assembles it from intermediate sub-facts. We hypothesize an internal, query-conditioned arbiter selects which pathway drives the output; a distinct and common failure mode is misarbitration — the model commits to whichever pathway is weaker for that query even though the other pathway holds the correct answer. We predict (1) which pathway is selected is linearly decodable at intermediate layers before the answer is written, (2) misarbitration accounts for a substantial fraction of failures on facts the model can otherwise produce via the alternate pathway, and (3) a lightweight steering intervention that biases the arbiter toward the stronger pathway recovers these hidden answers more selectively than weight editing.
Related Work: Prior work shows LLMs solve two-hop tasks either compositionally (with detectable intermediate variables) or 'directly'/idiomatically, and that mechanism choice is only weakly correlated with accuracy and tracks embedding-space linearity (How Do LLMs Compose Functions?, 2025); probabilistic recall-and-extract and distributional parallel-reasoning accounts describe internal multi-hop dynamics (Layer-Order Inversion, 2026; Distributional Reasoning, 2024); co-occurrence shortcuts are distinguished from true factual associations by layer (Co-occurrence is not Factual Association, 2024); grokking integrates memorized facts into reasoning circuits (Grokked Transformers, 2024). All of these characterize that two mechanisms exist or describe multi-hop dynamics, but none ask whether the model actively *arbitrates* between an atomic-shortcut pathway and a compositional pathway on a per-query basis, whether that arbitration is predictable/steerable before the answer, or whether *misarbitration* is a recoverable failure mode. My prior proposals concern single-fact routing gates, format-bound duplicate copies, and interference among competing candidate facts; this proposal is orthogonal: it concerns selection between two *procedurally distinct* routes to the same answer.
Abstract: Large language models can reach the same fact by different internal routes: recalling it as a memorized association, or assembling it from constituent sub-facts. We hypothesize that the model arbitrates between these routes on a per-query basis, and that a common, overlooked failure mode is misarbitration — committing to whichever route is weaker for the current query even though the alternate route encodes the correct answer. We study this on derivable facts (e.g., 'the capital of the country where X was born') for which both a memorized shortcut and a two-hop compositional path can in principle yield the answer. We first build, per fact, evidence for which routes are viable: probing whether the compositional intermediate (bridge entity) is decodable in the residual stream, and whether the atomic shortcut fires (via co-occurrence-based and single-hop-recall diagnostics). We then test three claims: (1) which route drives the output is linearly decodable from intermediate activations before the answer token is written; (2) using activation patching to isolate the pathways, misarbitration failures — where the model outputs the wrong answer despite the alternate route being internally viable — form a substantial and identifiable fraction of errors; and (3) a low-rank steering vector that biases the arbiter toward the viable route recovers correct answers with higher specificity and lower collateral damage than ROME/MEMIT editing. Experiments span GPT-J-6B, Llama-3-8B, and Qwen2.5-7B on SOCRATES, PopQA, and T-REx-derived two-hop sets, evaluating route-prediction AUROC, misarbitration prevalence, recovery rate, specificity, and fluency. Confirming these claims reframes many knowledge failures as strategy-selection errors and yields a cheap, non-destructive way to surface answers the model could compute but does not.
Experiments: Experiment 1 (H2 - dual-route facts with measured route availability): Builds two-hop facts g(f(x)) with a compositional route and a possible atomic shortcut, and measures per-model route competence - the substrate for the misarbitration-prevalence test. Data: two-hop items from SOCRATES (a two-hop latent-recall benchmark), plus compositions assembled from PopQA and T-REx/LAMA single-hop relations; we build 6,000 g(f(x)) facts (e.g. capital-of-birth-country) where both single hops f(x) and g(z) are individually answerable by the model, fewer than all possible compositions because each needs single-hop verification on every model. Model: Llama-3-8B (8B, decoder-only), frozen; measure single-hop accuracy on f(x) and g(z), direct-composition accuracy on g(f(x)), and shortcut viability via co-occurrence diagnostics (does x co-appear with the answer); seed 0. Systems compared: single-hop vs. composed accuracy per fact. Decisive metric: coverage = fraction of facts where at least one route is viable (both single hops answerable, or shortcut co-occurrence present) (first); supporting: per-relation route-availability breakdown. Convincing: >=60% of facts have >=1 viable route and >=25% have both, giving a usable arbitration substrate. Undecidable band: 40-60% coverage is a thin substrate - proceed but flag power. Negative: <40% coverage means too few facts admit an alternate route, so misarbitration cannot be studied at scale here.

Experiment 2 (H1 - per-fact route viability labeling): Labels, per fact, whether the compositional route (bridge f(x) decodable) and the shortcut route (answer decodable without a bridge signature) are internally available. Data: the 6,000 dual-route facts from Experiment 1. Model: Llama-3-8B, frozen; a tuned-lens (trained once, frozen) reads the bridge entity f(x) from intermediate-layer residuals at the last-subject position, and reads the answer directly for shortcut viability; label-shuffle control. Systems compared: tuned-lens vs. raw logit-lens bridge decoding. Decisive metric: bridge-decoding accuracy at the best intermediate layer (first); supporting: fraction of facts with each route labeled viable. Convincing: bridge decoding reaches >=0.7 accuracy on facts the model composes correctly (validating the lens signal) and yields clear per-fact route labels for >=70% of facts. Undecidable band: bridge decoding 0.5-0.7 makes route labels noisy - restrict downstream analysis to high-confidence labels and report coverage. Negative: <0.5 bridge decoding, near shuffle, means route viability cannot be read, blocking the decoding and prevalence tests.

Experiment 3 (H1 - route choice is linearly decodable before the answer): Tests that which route drives the output is decodable from intermediate residuals before the answer token, using patching-derived ground truth. Data: facts with a patching-established route label from Experiment 4; target 3,000 with clean labels. Model: Llama-3-8B, frozen; a trainable linear probe on pre-answer intermediate-layer residuals predicts compositional-vs-shortcut route, seeds 0/1/2, label-shuffle control. Systems compared: route probe vs. shuffled-label control; probe AUROC across layers. Decisive metric: cross-validated AUROC of route prediction (first); supporting: earliest layer at which AUROC exceeds 0.7. Convincing: AUROC >=0.75 at a layer preceding answer commitment - route choice is decodable in advance. Undecidable band: AUROC 0.60-0.75 means route choice is partially anticipable - report weak decodability. Negative: AUROC <=0.60 or no better than shuffle means route selection is not linearly pre-decodable, falsifying H1.

Experiment 4 (H1/H2 - causal pathway isolation and ground truth): Causally separates the two routes and defines the route-usage ground truth used by Experiment 3. Data: 2,000 correctly-answered dual-route facts. Model: Llama-3-8B, frozen; (a) patch/ablate the bridge-entity representation at the last-subject position to knock out composition and see if output survives via shortcut; (b) suppress the early atomic-shortcut signal and see if output survives via composition; random-direction control. Systems compared: bridge-ablation vs. shortcut-suppression vs. random control. Decisive metric: fraction of facts where exactly one manipulation changes the output, giving a clean route label (first); supporting: per-route causal contribution. Convincing: >=50% of facts yield a single-route causal label (one manipulation flips, the other does not) vs <=10% for the random control. Undecidable band: 25-50% clean-label rate means routes are partly entangled - report coverage limits and treat ambiguous facts separately. Negative: <25%, near control, means the two routes are not causally separable, undermining the arbiter framing.

Experiment 5 (H2 - misarbitration is a substantial share of failures): Tests that many errors occur despite a viable alternate route. Data: all errors on dual-route facts across the datasets and the three models; target 5,000 errors on Llama-3-8B for the primary count. Model: Llama-3-8B, frozen; classify each error as misarbitration (alternate route viable per Experiments 2/4) vs. genuine ignorance (neither route viable). Systems compared: misarbitration rate vs. a frequency/similarity-matched null estimating chance co-viability. Decisive metric: fraction of errors that are misarbitration, above the matched null (first); supporting: per-relation breakdown. Convincing: >=25% of errors are misarbitration, >=10 points above the matched null - a common, distinct failure mode. Undecidable band: 10-25% above null of <10 points means misarbitration is real but minor - report as a secondary failure mode, narrowing H2. Negative: <10% misarbitration or indistinguishable from the null means errors are dominated by genuine ignorance, falsifying H2.

Experiment 6 (H3 - arbiter steering recovers hidden answers more selectively than editing): Tests that biasing the arbiter toward the viable route recovers misarbitration failures. Data: held-out misarbitration failures from Experiment 5, target 800. Model: Llama-3-8B, frozen except the ROME/MEMIT comparators; a rank<=8 steering vector = mean activation difference between correct compositional runs and matched misarbitrated failures (and a symmetric shortcut-biasing vector), added at the Experiment 3 route-decodable layer, alpha swept; random-direction control; seeds 0/1/2. Systems compared: arbiter steering vs. ROME vs. MEMIT vs. random. Decisive metric: recovered-facts-per-unit-collateral = recovery / accuracy drop on 200 unrelated facts (first); supporting: raw recovery, held-out perplexity change. Convincing: >=40% recovery with <5% unrelated-accuracy drop, beating ROME/MEMIT on recovered-per-collateral by >=1.5x. Undecidable band: a 1.0-1.5x advantage over editing is parity - report as comparable. Negative: recovery <20% or no advantage over editing falsifies the selectivity half of H3.

Experiment 7 (H3 - one arbiter vector generalizes across relations): Tests whether a single steering vector transfers rather than being fact-specific. Data: train the vector on one relation subset (target 20 relations), apply to held-out relations (target 10), on their misarbitration failures. Model: Llama-3-8B, frozen; single trained vector applied unchanged, seeds 0/1/2. Systems compared: cross-relation transfer vs. within-relation (oracle) steering. Decisive metric: cross-relation recovery rate (first); supporting: gap to the within-relation oracle. Convincing: cross-relation recovery >=25% and within 0.5x of the oracle - a general arbitration signal. Undecidable band: recovery 10-25% or below 0.3x of oracle means the signal is largely relation-specific - report limited transfer. Negative: <10% cross-relation recovery means no general arbiter vector exists, limiting H3's generality.

Experiment 8 (H1-H3 generality - architecture-general arbitration): Tests that route decodability, misarbitration prevalence, and steering hold beyond one model. Data: reuse the Experiment 1 dual-route set (6,000 facts) per model. Model: repeat Experiments 2-6 on GPT-J-6B and Qwen2.5-7B, frozen, identical seeds/hyperparameters. Systems compared: Llama-3-8B vs. GPT-J-6B vs. Qwen2.5-7B on each decisive metric. Decisive metric: sign-consistency of route-probe AUROC, misarbitration-vs-null gap, and steering advantage across models (first); supporting: per-model coverage. Convincing: all three show route AUROC >=0.70, positive misarbitration gap, and steering advantage >=1.2x. Undecidable band: the pattern in 2 of 3 models is partial generality - scope accordingly. Negative: reversal in the majority means arbitration is model-specific.
Risk Factors and Limitations: Shortcut vs compositional 'routes' may not be cleanly separable when representations are entangled (superposition); patching-based dissociation may leave ambiguous cases, which we report as coverage limits rather than force into the dichotomy.
Logit-lens/tuned-lens decoding of the bridge entity is noisy; we mitigate with tuned-lens, answer-type filtering, and causal patching as the decisive test rather than lens readouts alone.

Route choice may be graded/mixed (both pathways contribute) rather than a discrete arbiter; a graded result would weaken the clean arbitration framing but remains informative, and we report continuous route-contribution measures.

Steering toward a 'viable' route could induce confident hallucination on facts where the route only appears viable; strict specificity and perplexity controls are essential and may cap practical utility.
A single transferable arbiter vector may not exist if arbitration is fact-specific, limiting the intervention's generality though still scientifically informative.
Distinguishing misarbitration from subtle storage weakness is hard; matched-pair design and route-availability controls reduce but may not fully eliminate confounds.
Findings on 6-8B models may not transfer to frontier-scale models beyond an academic budget.

novelty.reasoning: Core claims to judge: (1) there is an explicit per-query internal arbiter that chooses between memorized shortcut and compositional route; (2) the chosen route is linearly decodable before the answer token; (3) many failures are misarbitration cases where the weaker route is selected despite the alternate route containing the correct answer; (4) a low-rank steering vector can bias the arbiter and recover these hidden answers more selectively than weight editing. The existence of two routes, decodable bridge entities, and route-biasing/patching are already well covered by prior work in the multi-hop reasoning literature. The potentially novel part is the specific arbitration/misarbitration framing plus pre-answer route-decodability and steering as a recovery mechanism. However, this is closest to a re-interpretation of known route-choice phenomena unless the paper isolates a distinct causal arbiter signal, not just correlation with bridge presence. So: not a new task/problem definition, but a possibly new explanation/mechanistic framing in an existing setting. The actual delta over prior work is from 'there are two routes and we can patch the bridge' to 'there is a query-conditioned, decodable arbiter whose failure causes recoverable errors, and steering the arbiter is a better intervention than editing.'

Who cares: mechanistic interpretability, reasoning/compositionality, knowledge editing, and reliability/safety researchers; also anyone trying to make models answer hard factual queries more faithfully.
