Name: familiarity_before_retrieval
Title: Feeling of Knowing Before Knowing: A Dissociable Metacognitive Familiarity Estimate That Gates Retrieval Effort in LLMs
Short Hypothesis: LLMs compute a fast, early metacognitive 'familiarity' (feeling-of-knowing) estimate about a query that is largely driven by surface cues (entity/relation popularity, lexical familiarity) and is computed *before and independently of* actual content retrieval. This estimate gates how much retrieval effort is expended, so miscalibration of familiarity — not content storage — causes two symmetric failures: false-high familiarity yields confident confabulation with no retrieved content, and false-low familiarity suppresses retrieval of a fact that is actually stored (a 'give-up' failure appearing as abstention/hedging). We predict the familiarity estimate and the retrieved-content signal are linearly separable and causally dissociable, and that recalibrating familiarity alone (without touching stored facts) selectively fixes both failure modes.
Related Work: Prior knowledge-boundary work shows answerability/confidence is linearly readable in middle layers and can be steered (Slobodkin et al. 2023; (Un)answerability directions 2025; C3 2025; cross-lingual boundary 2025), that popularity predicts boundary perception (Knowledge Popularity 2025), that probabilistic 'belief' during generation diverges from parametric knowledge and causally drives retraction (When Do LLMs Admit Mistakes 2025), and that entropy/token-frequency neurons regulate confidence (Confidence Regulation Neurons 2024). All treat the boundary as a single confidence/answerability signal correlated with correctness. None decompose it into two dissociable computations — a *pre-retrieval familiarity/coverage estimate* versus the *actual retrieved content* — nor test whether familiarity is computed before content and causally *gates retrieval effort*, nor show that recalibrating familiarity alone (leaving stored facts untouched) fixes both over- and under-retrieval failures. This is also orthogonal to my prior proposals on expression gating, format-bound copies, candidate competition, and route arbitration: here the object of study is the model's *estimate of its own coverage* and its causal effect on whether retrieval is even attempted.
Abstract: Large language models sometimes confabulate confidently about things they do not know, and other times fail to produce facts they demonstrably store. We propose that both stem from a single overlooked mechanism: a fast metacognitive familiarity estimate — a 'feeling of knowing' about the query — that LLMs compute early, largely from surface cues, before and separately from actually retrieving content, and that this estimate gates how much retrieval effort is spent. When familiarity is falsely high, the model commits to answering with little retrieved content, producing fluent confabulation; when falsely low, it suppresses retrieval of a stored fact and abstains or hedges. We test three claims. (1) Dissociability: separate linear probes recover a familiarity signal (predictive of surface popularity and verbalized confidence) and a content signal (predictive of the specific correct answer), and these become decodable at different layers, with familiarity emerging earlier. (2) Miscalibration causes failures: by constructing mismatched items — high-familiarity/low-content (obscure facts phrased around popular entities) and low-familiarity/high-content (stored facts about rare entities) — we show confabulation concentrates in the former and give-up failures in the latter, at rates far above a single-confidence baseline. (3) Causal gating and recalibration: activation patching of the early familiarity direction changes downstream retrieval effort and answer attempts, and a low-rank recalibration steering vector that adjusts familiarity alone reduces confabulation and unlocks give-up failures with higher specificity than confidence-threshold abstention or ROME editing. Experiments span GPT-J-6B, Llama-3-8B, and Qwen2.5-7B on PopQA, T-REx, and EntityQuestions, evaluating probe separability, layer-onset ordering, failure-mode prevalence, recovery/abstention accuracy, specificity, and fluency.
Experiments: Experiment 1 (H1/H3 - familiarity is decodable early and separable from content): Tests that a familiarity signal becomes decodable at earlier layers than retrieved content and that the two are separable. Data: PopQA (14,282), T-REx/LAMA (~34k), EntityQuestions (~176k); sample 10,000 single-token-first-entity facts stratified by relation and popularity, fewer than the pool for per-layer probe training and clean content readout. Model: Llama-3-8B (8B, decoder-only), frozen; two trainable per-layer linear probes on the last-token residual - a familiarity probe (target: will the model attempt a confident answer; regressed on entity/relation popularity and verbalized confidence) and a content probe (target: the gold answer via tuned-lens); seeds 0/1/2, label-shuffle controls. Systems compared: familiarity vs. content probe onset layers, with bootstrap CIs. Decisive metric: onset-layer difference (first-layer at AUROC>=0.7) between familiarity and content (first, familiarity should precede content); supporting: per-layer AUROC/accuracy of each. Convincing: familiarity onset precedes content onset by >=3 layers with non-overlapping bootstrap CIs, both probes above shuffle. Undecidable band: an onset gap of 1-3 layers, or overlapping CIs, cannot establish temporal precedence over probe-difficulty artifacts - defer the precedence claim to the causal test (Experiment 5). Negative: content onset at or before familiarity, or familiarity at shuffle level, falsifies the early-familiarity half of H1.

Experiment 2 (H3 - familiarity and content carry non-redundant information): Tests that the two directions are not collinear. Data: the residual activations from Experiment 1 (10,000 facts). Model: Llama-3-8B, frozen; measure cosine similarity and cross-linear-predictability of the familiarity and content directions, then residualize each on the other, seeds 0/1/2. Systems compared: familiarity predicting popularity/verbalized-confidence before vs. after removing content-predictive variance. Decisive metric: retained familiarity->popularity/confidence predictive AUROC after residualizing out content (first); supporting: direction cosine similarity. Convincing: familiarity still predicts popularity/confidence at AUROC >=0.70 after residualization and direction cosine <=0.5 - non-redundant signals. Undecidable band: post-residualization AUROC 0.55-0.70 or cosine 0.5-0.75 indicates partial entanglement - report a graded separability. Negative: post-residual AUROC <=0.55 or cosine >0.75 means the signals are effectively one direction, falsifying the separability half of H3.

Experiment 3 (H2 - familiarity x content mismatch dataset): Builds items that cross familiarity with content so the two failure modes can be isolated. Data: four cells - HF-LC (obscure attributes of popular entities the model does not store), LF-HC (stored facts about rare entities recoverable under strong prompting), plus HF-HC and LF-LC controls; target 1,500 items/cell (6,000), constructed by filtering the Experiment 1 pool with popularity statistics and content-probe/strong-prompt recovery, fewer per cell because each needs storage and familiarity validation. Model: Llama-3-8B, frozen; content availability validated by strong retrieval prompts + content probe, familiarity by verbalized confidence + popularity. Systems compared: the four cells. Decisive metric: cell purity = fraction of items meeting both their familiarity and content criteria (first); supporting: per-cell popularity and content-probe distributions. Convincing: >=70% purity in all four cells - a clean 2x2. Undecidable band: 50-70% purity means noisy cells - report with wider CIs. Negative: <50% purity in LF-HC (the hardest cell) means stored-but-rare facts cannot be reliably assembled, weakening the give-up-failure test.

Experiment 4 (H2 - the two symmetric failure modes localize to the predicted cells): Tests that confabulation concentrates in HF-LC and give-up failures in LF-HC. Data: the 6,000-item 2x2 from Experiment 3. Model: Llama-3-8B, frozen; per cell, rate of (a) confident confabulation (high-probability wrong attempt) and (b) give-up (abstain/hedge despite internally available content). Systems compared: cell-conditioned failure rates vs. a KEEN/answerability single-scalar-confidence baseline; chi-square and calibration curves. Decisive metric: difference in confabulation rate (HF-LC minus others) and give-up rate (LF-HC minus others), each above the confidence-probe baseline (first); supporting: calibration curves. Convincing: confabulation is >=20 points higher in HF-LC and give-up >=20 points higher in LF-HC, both beyond what the scalar confidence probe predicts (chi-square p<0.001). Undecidable band: 8-20 point concentrations, or gaps the scalar probe also captures, mean the two-factor account adds little over confidence - report as partial. Negative: <8 point concentration means failures do not localize by familiarity x content, falsifying H2.

Experiment 5 (H1/H2 - familiarity causally precedes and gates retrieval): Tests that patching the early familiarity direction changes whether an answer is attempted and downstream content strength. Data: matched HF/LF paraphrase pairs of the same fact, target 1,500. Model: Llama-3-8B, frozen; patch the early familiarity direction from a high- into a low-familiarity run (and vice versa) at the Experiment 1 onset layer, query held fixed via matched paraphrases; random-direction control. Systems compared: familiarity patch vs. random-direction patch. Decisive metric: change in answer-attempt rate induced by the familiarity patch (first); supporting: change in later-layer content-probe strength and final-answer change. Convincing: raising familiarity increases attempt rate by >=25 points (and lowering it decreases attempts), vs <=5 points for random - familiarity causally gates retrieval effort. Undecidable band: a 10-25 point effect is weak causal control - report familiarity as contributory. Negative: <10 point effect, near control, means familiarity does not causally gate retrieval, falsifying the gating half of H1/H2.

Experiment 6 (H4 - recalibrating familiarity alone fixes both failure modes): Tests that a familiarity-only steering vector converts HF-LC confabulation to abstention and LF-HC give-ups to correct answers. Data: held-out HF-LC and LF-HC items, target 800 each. Model: Llama-3-8B, frozen except the ROME comparator; a rank<=8 vector moving familiarity toward its calibrated target (down for HF-LC, up for LF-HC), from mean differences of calibrated vs. miscalibrated matched states, alpha swept; seeds 0/1/2. Systems compared: familiarity recalibration vs. confidence-threshold abstention vs. an (un)answerability steering direction vs. ROME. Decisive metric: net-correct-behavior-per-unit-collateral = (confabulation->abstention rate on HF-LC + give-up->correct rate on LF-HC) / accuracy drop on 200 well-calibrated facts (first); supporting: per-cell conversion rates, held-out perplexity. Convincing: >=40% appropriate conversion in each cell with <5% collateral, beating the baselines on net-per-collateral by >=1.5x. Undecidable band: 20-40% conversion or a 1.0-1.5x advantage means recalibration works but not clearly better than baselines - report parity. Negative: <20% conversion or no advantage falsifies H4.

Experiment 7 (H4 generality - one recalibration vector transfers across relations, directions, and models): Tests transfer of the recalibration and architecture-generality of the core results. Data: train one recalibration vector on a relation subset, apply to held-out relations and both failure directions; reuse the Experiment 1 pool per model. Model: single trained vector applied unchanged on Llama-3-8B; repeat Experiments 1, 4, 6 on GPT-J-6B and Qwen2.5-7B, frozen, identical seeds. Systems compared: cross-relation/both-direction transfer vs. within-relation oracle; three models per decisive metric. Decisive metric: cross-relation conversion rate and cross-model sign-consistency of the Experiment 4 concentration and Experiment 6 advantage (first); supporting: per-model onset gaps. Convincing: cross-relation conversion >=25% in both directions and all three models show the failure-localization and a recalibration advantage >=1.2x. Undecidable band: transfer 10-25%, or the pattern in 2 of 3 models, is partial generality - scope accordingly. Negative: <10% transfer or majority model reversal means the mechanism is fact/model-specific.

Experiment 8 (H1 - familiarity is surface-driven): Tests that the familiarity estimate is mostly explained by surface cues rather than retrieved content. Data: the Experiment 1 familiarity-probe outputs over 10,000 facts. Model: Llama-3-8B, frozen; regress familiarity-probe output on entity popularity, relation co-occurrence frequency, and query lexical familiarity, with the content-probe strength as a competing regressor. Systems compared: surface-cue regressors vs. content-probe regressor. Decisive metric: share of familiarity variance explained by surface cues (partial R^2), reported first; supporting: content-probe partial R^2. Convincing: surface cues explain >=50% of familiarity variance and >=3x the content-probe share - familiarity is largely surface-driven. Undecidable band: surface share 30-50% or <2x content means familiarity is mixed - soften the 'surface-cue' claim to partial. Negative: surface cues explain <30% or less than content means familiarity is content-grounded, falsifying the surface-driven half of H1.
Risk Factors and Limitations: The familiarity and content signals may be entangled rather than cleanly separable; residualization and independent predictive targets mitigate this, but a graded/overlapping result would weaken the strong dissociation claim while remaining informative.

Layer-onset ordering (familiarity earlier than content) could be an artifact of probe difficulty rather than genuine computational timing; we use tuned-lens, matched probe capacities, and causal patching (Exp 5) as the decisive test rather than probe onset alone.

'Give-up' failures require confidently establishing that a fact is actually stored; strong-prompt recovery and content-probe evidence can overestimate storage, so we report coverage limits and use conservative thresholds.
Recalibration steering could induce new confabulation when raising familiarity, or over-abstain when lowering it; strict specificity and fluency controls are essential and may cap practical utility.
A single transferable recalibration vector may not exist if familiarity miscalibration is fact-specific, limiting generality though still scientifically informative.
Multi-token answers complicate content-probe readout; primary analysis restricts to single-token-first entities with reported coverage.
Findings on 6-8B models may not transfer to frontier-scale models beyond an academic budget.

novelty.reasoning: Core claims that must be novel: (1) LLMs compute a fast pre-retrieval familiarity/FOK signal from surface cues, earlier than content retrieval; (2) this signal is dissociable from actual retrieved-content representations; (3) miscalibrated familiarity explains two symmetric failures-false-high confabulation and false-low give-up abstention; (4) manipulating familiarity alone causally gates retrieval effort and can fix both failure modes; (5) the novelty lives mainly in the mechanism + ordering claim, not the setting. Relative to the search summary, the component ideas are crowded: FOK/answerability/confidence steering/popularity effects all exist. The actual delta is the explicit familiarity-vs-content decomposition, layer-onset ordering, and symmetric failure account with familiarity-only recalibration. That is non-trivial if it survives controls. Closest prior family: knowledge-boundary/confidence probes, solvability-vs-verbalization, and confidence-steering work. Actual delta: they model one boundary signal; this proposal claims two separable computations and that one is upstream and causally controlling retrieval effort. It is not fully genuinely new in pieces, but the combined claim is plausibly novel in this exact framing and test.

Who cares: anyone working on calibration, abstention, retrieval gating, safety/reliability, and interpretability. Downstream change if true: a more surgical way to fix answer behavior by adjusting metacognitive familiarity rather than editing knowledge, which could improve selective answering and reduce hallucinations with less collateral damage. If this holds, it suggests a new control knob for hallucination/abstention beyond thresholds and knowledge editing. Importance is real, but not obviously direction-shifting unless the causal dissociation is robust and general; uptake would likely be good in interpretability/reliability circles, moderate broader citation potential, and some real-world reach in RAG/assistant systems. review.reasoning: Logical gaps: the proposal assumes the early familiarity signal is distinct from early content evidence and from generic confidence/correctness, but that separation is exactly what needs hard causal proof. The 'before and independently of content' claim is vulnerable to probe artifact and confounding. The hypothesis is scoped and falsifiable, which is good. Related work is reasonably specific, especially given the summary, but it should more directly contrast with confidence/answerability, solvability/verbalization, and popularity-driven boundary perception. Experiments are mostly feasible and targeted, but some are under-specified: how familiarity/content labels are constructed, how 'retrieval effort' is measured, what counts as stored fact vs not, and how causal patching is matched for layer and magnitude. Strong enough for a serious ML venue if executed well? Yes, if the causal dissociation and symmetric-failure fix are demonstrated with careful controls; otherwise it risks being a probe study with incremental interpretation. Minimum viable edits: sharpen the claim to one sentence, add a tight causal test plan, pre-register the success criteria for each experiment, and include a table mapping each experiment to the specific alternative hypothesis it rules out.

Name: property_collapse
Title: Property Collapse: When Shared Relational Subspaces Cause LLMs to Retrieve the Right Property but the Wrong Attribute
Short Hypothesis: LLMs organize relational knowledge around coarse-grained shared 'properties' (e.g., a country-of-X subspace serving country-of-capital, country-of-food, country-of-birthplace). We hypothesize a distinct, previously uncharacterized failure mode—property collapse—in which the model correctly retrieves the shared property value but fails to preserve the fine-grained relation-specific distinction, producing a confidently wrong attribute drawn from a sibling relation that shares the property. We predict (1) errors concentrate on relations that share a property with a competing relation, (2) the shared-property subspace is causally responsible (patching it transfers answers across sibling relations while patching the residual relation-specific component does not), and (3) a targeted 'relation-disambiguation' steering vector that sharpens the relation-specific component recovers correct attributes more selectively than weight editing.
Related Work: Hernandez et al. (2023) show relation decoding is often linear (LRE); Chen et al. (2025, 'Structure of Relation Decoding Linear Operators') show these decoders are property-centric—shared across semantically-close relations rather than relation-specific—explaining limited relation-wise generalization. 'On Relation-Specific Neurons' (2025) reports neuron versatility and interference (deactivating one relation's neurons changes another's recall). 'Does Knowledge Localization Hold True?' (2024) shows entity and relation knowledge are stored separately. Non-linear relational composition (2025) shows generalization scales with entity semantic similarity. All of these characterize that relational structure is shared/property-based, but none identify property collapse as a concrete, predictable failure mode of factual answering, none causally decompose retrieval into a shared-property component and a relation-specific component to localize the failure, and none propose sharpening the relation-specific component as a non-destructive fix. This is orthogonal to my prior proposals (expression gating, format-bound copies, candidate competition, route arbitration, pre-retrieval familiarity): here the object is the shared geometry of relation decoders and the relation-confusion errors it produces.
Abstract: Recent interpretability work shows large language models decode relational facts using linear operators that are not relation-specific but property-centric: a single 'country-of-X' subspace, for example, is reused across country-of-capital, country-of-food, and country-of-birthplace. We ask whether this shared organization creates a predictable failure mode. We propose property collapse: when answering a query, the model reliably retrieves the shared coarse property (the right country) but fails to preserve the fine-grained relation-specific distinction, yielding a confident attribute belonging to a sibling relation that shares the property. Under this account, some knowledge failures are not storage or gating failures but binding failures within a collapsed shared subspace. We test three claims. (1) Prevalence: factual errors concentrate on relations that share a property with a competing relation, and the wrong answers are disproportionately valid attributes of a sibling relation for the same subject, above frequency- and similarity-matched baselines. (2) Causal decomposition: using linear relational embeddings we split each relation's decoder into a shared-property component (common across sibling relations) and a relation-specific residual; activation patching shows the shared component transfers answers across siblings while the residual carries the disambiguating signal, and property-collapse errors correspond to a weak relation-specific residual. (3) Intervention: a low-rank relation-disambiguation steering vector that amplifies the residual component recovers correct attributes with higher specificity and less collateral damage than ROME editing. Experiments span GPT-J-6B, Llama-3-8B, and Qwen2.5-7B on LRE relation sets and T-REx/PopQA, evaluating error-type prevalence, causal transfer, recovery rate, specificity, and fluency.
Experiments: Experiment 1 (H1 - sibling-relation groups with per-subject ground truth): Builds relation groups sharing a coarse property and subjects participating in multiple siblings, so sibling attributes are known ground truth. Data: the LRE relation set (~47 relations) plus T-REx/LAMA and PopQA; group relations by shared property (e.g. country-of-capital, country-of-food, country-of-birthplace share country-of-X) following a property-centric taxonomy; build subject sets in >=1 sibling group, target 8 sibling groups covering 4,000 subjects with all sibling attributes labeled from Wikidata, fewer because we require multi-relation participation and single-token-first attributes. Model: Llama-3-8B (8B, decoder-only), frozen; per-subject sibling attributes recorded; seed 0. Systems compared: within-group relations. Decisive metric: coverage = subjects with >=2 sibling attributes both single-token and Wikidata-verified (first); supporting: per-group sibling overlap. Convincing: >=8 groups and >=3,000 usable subjects, enough for per-group statistics. Undecidable band: 1,500-3,000 usable subjects is thin - report reduced power. Negative: <1,500 usable subjects means the sibling structure is too sparse to test property collapse here.

Experiment 2 (H1 - property-collapse errors over-represent on high-sibling-overlap relations): Tests that errors concentrate where a sibling relation competes. Data: model errors on the sibling-group queries from Experiment 1. Model: Llama-3-8B, frozen; classify each error as (a) property-collapse (answer is a valid sibling attribute of the same subject - right property, wrong relation), (b) property error (wrong property value), (c) generic. Systems compared: property-collapse rate on high- vs. low-sibling-overlap relations, against a null matched on answer frequency and entity/relation lexical similarity (logistic regression / chi-square). Decisive metric: odds ratio of property-collapse errors with sibling overlap, above the matched null (first); supporting: per-group collapse rates. Convincing: sibling overlap raises property-collapse odds by >=2x over the matched null (p<0.001). Undecidable band: odds ratio 1.3-2x means a real but modest concentration - report property collapse as a minor, localized mode. Negative: odds ratio <=1.3x or null-indistinguishable means collapse is not driven by sibling competition, falsifying H1.

Experiment 3 (H2 - decoder decomposes into shared-property and relation-specific components): Estimates per-relation linear relational embeddings (LREs) and splits each into a shared-property subspace and a relation-specific residual. Data: few-shot prompts to estimate an LRE per relation in the 8 groups. Model: Llama-3-8B, frozen; align/average sibling LRE operators to get the shared low-rank subspace, subtract to get the relation-specific residual; restrict to linearly-decodable relations. Systems compared: full LRE vs. shared-only vs. residual-only decoding. Decisive metric: decoding accuracy retained by each component alone (first); supporting: rank of the shared subspace. Convincing: the shared component alone retains >=60% of sibling-common decoding while the residual carries the relation-specific distinction (residual-only distinguishes siblings at >=0.6 accuracy) - a meaningful decomposition. Undecidable band: shared component retaining 40-60% indicates entangled components - defer to the causal test (Experiment 4) rather than relying on the decomposition. Negative: neither component isolates its role (both near full or near chance) means the decomposition is not meaningful, weakening H2's operationalization.

Experiment 4 (H2 - the shared-property subspace is causally responsible): Tests that patching the shared component transfers answers across siblings while patching the residual does not. Data: matched subjects appearing in relation A and sibling B, target 1,500 pairs. Model: Llama-3-8B, frozen; (a) patch the shared-property component of A into a run of B (should collapse B toward A), (b) patch only the relation-specific residual (should flip to the correct relation-specific attribute); random-component control. Systems compared: shared-component patch vs. residual patch vs. random. Decisive metric: fraction of cases where the shared-component patch flips B toward A's answer minus the fraction where the residual patch does (first, the causal signature of property collapse); supporting: residual-patch disambiguation rate. Convincing: shared-component patches flip >=40% of cases while residual patches flip <=10% toward A (and residual patches instead restore the correct attribute >=30%) - the shared subspace carries the collapse. Undecidable band: a shared-minus-residual flip gap of 10-25 points means partial localization - report weak causal support. Negative: no gap, or residual patches transferring as much as shared, means the shared subspace is not the locus, falsifying H2.

Experiment 5 (H1/H2 - weak relation-specific residual predicts collapse): Tests that collapse errors have a systematically weaker relation-specific residual than correct answers. Data: property-collapse errors vs. correct answers on the same relations, target 3,000 each. Model: Llama-3-8B, frozen; measure the magnitude/alignment of the relation-specific residual in the subject representation via LRE projection; label-shuffle control. Systems compared: residual-strength features for collapse vs. correct, real vs. shuffled labels. Decisive metric: AUROC of residual-strength predicting collapse (first); supporting: effect size of the residual-magnitude difference. Convincing: AUROC >=0.70 with collapse cases showing reliably weaker residual signal. Undecidable band: AUROC 0.58-0.70 is a weak association - report as suggestive. Negative: AUROC <=0.58 or shuffle-level means residual strength does not predict collapse, weakening H1/H2's account.

Experiment 6 (H3 - relation-disambiguation steering recovers attributes more selectively than editing): Tests that sharpening the relation-specific residual recovers correct attributes without breaking siblings. Data: held-out collapse errors, target 800. Model: Llama-3-8B, frozen except the ROME/MEMIT comparators; a rank<=8 per-group vector amplifying the queried relation's residual (from calibrated-vs-collapsed matched-state differences), alpha swept; random-direction control; seeds 0/1/2. Systems compared: disambiguation steering vs. ROME vs. MEMIT vs. random. Decisive metric: recovered-per-unit-collateral = recovery / accuracy drop on 200 unrelated facts and on sibling relations (first, sibling accuracy guards against over-sharpening); supporting: raw recovery, held-out perplexity. Convincing: >=40% recovery with <5% drop on unrelated and sibling facts, beating ROME/MEMIT on recovered-per-collateral by >=1.5x. Undecidable band: a 1.0-1.5x advantage, or 5-10% sibling degradation, is parity/marginal - report as comparable with a sibling-cost caveat. Negative: recovery <20%, or sibling accuracy dropping >10%, falsifies the selective-recovery half of H3.

Experiment 7 (H3 - one disambiguation vector generalizes within a property group): Tests transfer rather than relation-pair-specific fixes. Data: train the vector on one relation pair per group, apply to held-out sibling pairs. Model: Llama-3-8B, frozen; single vector per group applied unchanged, seeds 0/1/2. Systems compared: cross-pair transfer vs. within-pair oracle. Decisive metric: cross-pair recovery rate (first); supporting: gap to oracle. Convincing: cross-pair recovery >=25% and within 0.5x of oracle. Undecidable band: 10-25% recovery or below 0.3x oracle means largely pair-specific - report limited transfer. Negative: <10% cross-pair recovery means no general shared-subspace-sharpening signal, limiting H3.

Experiment 8 (H1-H3 generality - architecture-general property collapse): Tests that concentration, causal locus, and steering hold beyond one model. Data: reuse the Experiment 1 sibling-group set (4,000 subjects) per model. Model: repeat Experiments 2-6 on GPT-J-6B and Qwen2.5-7B, frozen, identical seeds/hyperparameters. Systems compared: Llama-3-8B vs. GPT-J-6B vs. Qwen2.5-7B on each decisive metric. Decisive metric: sign-consistency of the Experiment 2 odds ratio, Experiment 4 shared-minus-residual gap, and Experiment 6 steering advantage (first); supporting: per-model coverage. Convincing: all three show collapse odds >=1.5x, a positive shared-minus-residual gap, and steering advantage >=1.2x. Undecidable band: the pattern in 2 of 3 models is partial generality - scope accordingly. Negative: reversal in the majority means property collapse is model-specific.
Risk Factors and Limitations: Property collapse may be rare relative to generic errors, making the effect small; the frequency/similarity-matched baseline is essential and a modest but significant effect would still be informative.
LRE decoders are only linear for ~half of relations (Hernandez et al.); analysis is restricted to linearly-decodable relation groups, limiting coverage, which we report explicitly.

The shared/residual decomposition is a modeling choice; if the shared and residual components are entangled, the causal patching test (Exp 4) rather than the decomposition itself is the decisive evidence.

Wrong answers matching a sibling attribute could arise from generic co-occurrence rather than true property collapse; per-subject ground-truth sibling attributes and residual-strength causal tests mitigate but may not fully eliminate this confound.

Disambiguation steering could corrupt sibling-relation recall (over-sharpening); we explicitly measure sibling accuracy pre/post as a specificity control, and utility may be capped even if the analysis holds.
A single transferable disambiguation vector may not exist if collapse is relation-pair-specific, limiting practical generality though still scientifically informative.
Multi-token attributes complicate LRE readout; primary analysis restricts to single-token-first attributes with reported coverage.
Findings on 6–8B models may not transfer to frontier-scale models beyond an academic budget.

novelty.reasoning: Core claims: (1) a named failure mode where LLMs retrieve the correct coarse property but the wrong sibling attribute; (2) this error should concentrate on relation pairs sharing a property, above matched baselines; (3) a linear-relation-decoder decomposition into shared-property + relation-specific residual causally explains the error; (4) a low-rank steering vector can selectively recover the correct attribute better than editing; (5) the novelty lives mostly in the failure-mode framing and causal/residual intervention, not in the shared-property geometry itself. Existing work already establishes property-centric LREs and sibling interference, so the underlying mechanism is not new. The proposal is non-trivial if it really shows a predictable, quantifiable error concentration and a causal shared-vs-residual split. Closest prior family: Chen et al. 2025 property-centric LREs, Hernandez et al. 2023 LREs, and relation-specific neuron interference work. Actual delta: turning a structural observation into a concrete failure taxonomy plus a causal patching/steering story. Genuine novelty is moderate, but somewhat incremental relative to the cited 2025 findings.
revision_notes: State explicitly what is new beyond Chen et al. 2025: the falsifiable failure distribution and causal decomposition, not the existence of property-centric subspaces.
Add a sharper distinction between 'property collapse' and previously observed sibling confusion/interference at the neuron level.
Specify whether the steering vector is derived from the residual alone, and why this is not just another edit method.
Clarify the exact setting where novelty lives: LRE-amenable sibling relations on T-REx/PopQA, not general factual retrieval.

impact.reasoning: Problem: factual reliability in relational knowledge retrieval, especially when semantically related relations compete. Who cares: interpretability, knowledge editing, factual robustness, and possibly model debugging/safety researchers. If true, the downstream change is a new diagnostic for when models are likely to give plausible-but-wrong sibling attributes, plus a less destructive intervention than weight editing. Strongest one-line case: LLMs may know the right property family but confuse sibling attributes, and we can diagnose and selectively fix that without blunt edits. Importance is moderate because this is a specific failure mode inside factual recall, not a broad capability leap. Uptake/citation potential is decent if the effect is robust and the intervention works, since both interpretability and editing communities like concrete mechanisms and interventions. Direction-shifting is limited unless the phenomenon is large-scale and general. Real-world reach is narrower than the title suggests, but valuable for model reliability and knowledge editing pipelines. So the impact is real but specialized.
revision_notes: Broaden the 'so what' beyond interpretability jargon: explain why sibling-attribute confusion matters for user-visible factual errors or editing safety.
Quantify how often this failure would affect practical QA or editing benchmarks, not just crafted sibling sets.
Emphasize whether the diagnostic predicts when editing will fail or cause collateral damage; that is the most actionable downstream value.
Avoid overstating real-world reach unless experiments show the effect persists beyond small linearizable relation subsets.

review.reasoning: The proposal is coherent and testable, but it leans heavily on a very recent prior result and risks rebranding an already-known sibling-interference phenomenon. The hypothesis is mostly precise and falsifiable, but some terms need operational definitions: what exactly counts as 'property collapse,' how shared-property groups are constructed, and how matched baselines are chosen. The experiments are reasonably concrete and mostly feasible, especially the concentration test and causal patching; however, several thresholds look arbitrary and the decomposition could become post-hoc unless the causal patching is decisive. Missing controls include strong frequency/co-occurrence baselines, random-but-equally-linearizable relation groups, non-sibling close relations, and ablations against alternative decompositions. Related work should be more specific about what Chen et al. already showed versus what this paper adds. If executed well, it could fit an interpretability or knowledge-editing venue, but not at top-tier strength unless the failure mode is broad, robust across models, and the steering fix clearly outperforms editing with low collateral damage.

Name: premature_lexicalization
Title: Right Concept, Wrong Word: Premature Lexical Commitment as a Distinct Knowledge-Retrieval Failure in LLMs
Short Hypothesis: When answering factual queries, LLMs internally select the correct target entity as an abstract, token-agnostic concept representation, but the final answer is produced through a separate, later lexicalization step that maps concept to first output token. We hypothesize a distinct failure mode—premature lexicalization—in which the model commits to a high-prior or low-perplexity first token before the concept representation is fully resolved, causing it to emit a lexically-adjacent wrong entity (one sharing the committed first token/subword) even though the correct concept was internally selected. We predict (1) the concept selection and lexical commitment are dissociable and decodable at different layers, (2) a substantial fraction of factual errors are 'right-concept-wrong-word' cases where the correct entity is decodable as a concept but is out-competed at the lexicalization stage by a first-token-sharing distractor, and (3) delaying/re-weighting the lexical commitment (suppressing the prematurely-committed first token direction) recovers the correct entity more selectively than weight editing.
Related Work: A large body of work studies layer-wise commitment: 'Guess-then-Refine' (2025) shows early layers propose high-frequency tokens later refined; Iterative Inference / commitment-depth studies (2024–2026) track when models lock in answers; 'How LLMs Use Their Depth' (2025) shows first tokens of multi-token facts need more depth. Geva et al. (2023) describe attribute extraction via attention over an enriched subject. Concept-vs-language separation has been studied for multilingual models (language-agnostic concept spaces) but not for the concept-vs-lexeme distinction within a single language for factual recall. Confidence Regulation / entropy neurons (2024) and token-frequency effects on recall are documented. None of these identify premature lexicalization—a specific dissociation between token-agnostic concept selection and first-token lexical commitment—as a concrete, predictable factual-error mode, nor propose suppressing a prematurely-committed first-token direction as a non-destructive fix. This is orthogonal to my prior proposals (expression gating, format-bound copies, candidate competition among entities, route arbitration, pre-retrieval familiarity, property collapse): here the failure is not choosing the wrong entity but choosing the wrong *word* for a correctly-chosen entity, driven by first-token statistics.
Abstract: Large language models sometimes produce a factual answer that is close to but not the correct entity—e.g., a name that shares a first syllable or subword with the right one. We propose that some of these errors reflect a distinct, overlooked mechanism: premature lexicalization. Under this view, factual recall proceeds in two stages—selecting the target entity as a token-agnostic concept, then lexicalizing that concept into output tokens—and errors arise when the model commits to a high-prior first token before the concept is fully resolved, emitting a lexically-adjacent wrong entity while the correct concept was internally selected. We test three claims. (1) Dissociability: a concept probe (predicting the correct entity in a token-agnostic representation, e.g., via aliases/paraphrastic descriptions) and a lexical probe (predicting the committed first output token) are separable and become decodable at different layers, with concept selection preceding or coexisting with a later lexical-commitment surge. (2) Prevalence: 'right-concept-wrong-word' errors—where the correct entity is decodable as a concept yet the output is a first-token-sharing distractor—form an identifiable fraction of factual errors, concentrated where the correct entity's first token is high-perplexity/rare and a distractor shares a common first token, above frequency-matched baselines. (3) Intervention: suppressing the prematurely-committed distractor first-token direction (or re-scoring the first token conditioned on the concept representation) recovers correct entities with higher specificity and less collateral damage than ROME editing. Experiments span GPT-J-6B, Llama-3-8B, and Qwen2.5-7B on PopQA, T-REx, and EntityQuestions, evaluating probe separability, layer-onset ordering, error-type prevalence, recovery rate, specificity, and fluency.
Experiments: Experiment 1 (H1 - concept and lexical signals are decodable at different layers): Tests that a token-agnostic concept representation becomes decodable before the first-token lexical commitment. Data: PopQA (14,282), T-REx/LAMA (~34k), EntityQuestions (~176k); sample 9,000 facts whose answer entity has >=2 attested aliases/paraphrastic descriptions, fewer than the pool because alias sets are needed for the concept probe. Model: Llama-3-8B (8B, decoder-only), frozen; two trainable per-layer probes on the last-token residual - a concept probe (target: a shared concept ID invariant across aliases, trained on one surface form and tested on held-out aliases) and a lexical probe (target: the emitted first token); seeds 0/1/2, label-shuffle and alias-shuffle controls. Systems compared: concept vs. lexical onset layers, bootstrap CIs. Decisive metric: onset-layer difference (first-layer at AUROC>=0.7) between concept and the lexical-commitment surge (first, concept should precede); supporting: per-layer accuracy/AUROC. Convincing: concept onset precedes lexical commitment by >=3 layers with non-overlapping CIs, both above shuffle. Undecidable band: a 1-3 layer gap or overlapping CIs cannot separate timing from probe difficulty - defer precedence to the causal test (Experiment 4). Negative: lexical onset at/before concept, or concept at alias-shuffle level, falsifies H1.

Experiment 2 (H1 - concept and lexical directions carry non-redundant information): Tests they are not collinear. Data: the residual activations from Experiment 1. Model: Llama-3-8B, frozen; cross-linear-predictability and residualization of the two directions, seeds 0/1/2. Systems compared: concept predicting the correct entity before vs. after removing first-token-predictive variance. Decisive metric: retained concept->entity accuracy after residualizing out lexical variance (first); supporting: direction cosine similarity. Convincing: concept still predicts the correct entity at >=0.7 relative accuracy after residualization and cosine <=0.5. Undecidable band: retained accuracy 0.5-0.7 or cosine 0.5-0.75 indicates partial entanglement - report graded separability. Negative: retained accuracy <=0.5 or cosine >0.75 means the two collapse to one signal, falsifying the two-stage claim.

Experiment 3 (H2 - right-concept-wrong-word errors are a substantial, statistically distinct share): Tests that many errors are concept-correct but lexically out-competed by a first-token-sharing distractor. Data: model errors on Experiment 1 facts. Model: Llama-3-8B, frozen; classify errors into (a) premature-lexicalization (concept probe recovers the correct entity but the emitted answer shares the early committed first token/subword with a distractor), (b) genuine wrong-concept, (c) other. Systems compared: type-(a) rate when the correct entity's first token is rare and a competitor shares a common first token, against a null controlling for entity frequency and overall lexical similarity (logistic regression / chi-square). Decisive metric: fraction of errors that are premature-lexicalization, above the matched null (first); supporting: odds ratio with the rare-correct-token / shared-distractor-token condition. Convincing: >=20% of errors are premature-lexicalization, >=10 points above the null, with the predicted first-token-statistics dependence. Undecidable band: 8-20% above a null gap <10 points means the mode is real but minor - narrow H2 to a secondary mode. Negative: <8% or null-indistinguishable means the failure is not distinct from wrong-concept errors, falsifying H2.

Experiment 4 (H1/H2 - the failure lives in lexicalization, not concept selection): Causally dissociates the two stages. Data: premature-lexicalization failures (target 1,200) plus wrong-concept failures (target 1,200) from Experiment 3. Model: Llama-3-8B, frozen; (a) patch the concept representation from a correct run into a premature-lexicalization failure (should NOT fix it if the failure is lexical), (b) suppress the distractor's first-token direction at the commitment layers (should fix it), (c) amplify the concept direction alone; random-direction control. Systems compared: concept-patch vs. first-token-suppression vs. concept-amplification vs. random, on the two failure types. Decisive metric: fix-rate gap = first-token-suppression fix rate minus concept-patch fix rate on premature-lexicalization failures (first, the causal signature); supporting: the reverse pattern on wrong-concept failures. Convincing: on premature-lexicalization failures, first-token suppression fixes >=35% while concept patching fixes <=10% (gap >=25 points), and the pattern reverses for wrong-concept failures. Undecidable band: a 10-25 point gap means partial localization - report weak causal support. Negative: no gap, or concept patching fixing as much as suppression, means the failure is not lexicalization-stage, falsifying the H1/H2 mechanism.

Experiment 5 (H1 - lexical commitment can precede concept resolution): Tests that for these errors the committed first token overtakes early and before the concept is resolved. Data: the premature-lexicalization vs. correct-answer cases from Experiments 3-4. Model: Llama-3-8B, frozen; tuned-lens locates the layer where the eventual first token overtakes competitors and where the concept probe first recovers the correct entity. Systems compared: concept-correct layer vs. lexical-commitment layer, and committed-token early prior for error vs. correct cases. Decisive metric: fraction of premature-lexicalization errors with concept-correct-layer <= lexical-commitment-layer AND an anomalously early/high first-token prior (first); supporting: distribution of the layer gap. Convincing: >=60% of these errors satisfy both conditions vs a correct-answer base rate <=30%. Undecidable band: 40-60% means the timing signature is inconsistent - report as partial. Negative: <40%, near the correct-case base rate, means premature commitment is not the signature, falsifying H1's timing prediction.

Experiment 6 (H3 - re-weighting lexical commitment recovers the entity more selectively than editing): Tests suppression / concept-conditioned re-ranking against weight editing. Data: held-out premature-lexicalization failures, target 800. Model: Llama-3-8B, frozen except the ROME/MEMIT comparators; (a) suppress the committed distractor first-token direction at commitment layers, (b) re-score the first token by projecting the concept representation to constrain candidates; random-direction control; alpha swept; seeds 0/1/2. Systems compared: suppression / re-ranking vs. ROME vs. MEMIT vs. random. Decisive metric: recovered-per-unit-collateral = recovery / accuracy drop on 200 unrelated facts (first); supporting: raw recovery, held-out perplexity. Convincing: >=40% recovery with <5% collateral, beating ROME/MEMIT on recovered-per-collateral by >=1.5x. Undecidable band: a 1.0-1.5x advantage is parity - report as comparable. Negative: recovery <20% or no advantage falsifies the selectivity half of H3.

Experiment 7 (H3 generality - one recipe transfers across relations and models): Tests transfer and architecture-generality. Data: train the suppression/re-ranking identification on one relation subset, apply to held-out relations; reuse the Experiment 1 pool per model. Model: single recipe on Llama-3-8B; repeat Experiments 1, 3, 4, 6 on GPT-J-6B and Qwen2.5-7B, frozen, identical seeds. Systems compared: cross-relation transfer vs. within-relation oracle; three models per decisive metric. Decisive metric: cross-relation recovery rate and cross-model sign-consistency of the Experiment 3 concentration and Experiment 6 advantage (first); supporting: per-model onset gaps. Convincing: cross-relation recovery >=25% and all three models show the concentration and a recovery advantage >=1.2x. Undecidable band: transfer 10-25% or the pattern in 2 of 3 models is partial generality - scope accordingly. Negative: <10% transfer or majority model reversal means the mechanism is fact/model-specific.

Experiment 8 (H2 - the failure is driven by first-token statistics): Tests that premature-lexicalization rate rises with adverse first-token statistics. Data: per-fact premature-lexicalization outcomes over the 9,000 facts. Model: Llama-3-8B, frozen; regress error rate on correct-answer first-token frequency, first-token overlap with high-frequency distractors, and answer token length. Systems compared: first-token-statistics regressors vs. an entity-frequency-only baseline. Decisive metric: partial R^2 of the first-token features beyond entity frequency (first); supporting: sign and magnitude of each coefficient. Convincing: first-token features add partial R^2 >=0.10 with the predicted signs (rare correct first token, common shared distractor token, longer answers all raise the rate). Undecidable band: partial R^2 0.03-0.10 is a weak trend - report as suggestive. Negative: partial R^2 <0.03 means first-token statistics do not drive the failure, falsifying the core mechanistic claim of H2.
Risk Factors and Limitations: Defining a truly token-agnostic 'concept' probe is hard; alias-based invariance is imperfect and may leak surface information. We use held-out aliases and paraphrastic descriptions and report coverage; the causal patching test (Exp 4) is the decisive evidence rather than probe onset alone.

Premature-lexicalization errors may be rare relative to genuine wrong-concept errors, yielding a small effect; the frequency/similarity-matched baseline is essential and a modest significant effect remains informative.

Concept and lexical stages may be entangled (not cleanly two-stage), weakening the strong dissociation claim; graded results would still be scientifically informative and we report continuous measures.

Suppressing a first-token direction could degrade fluency or introduce new errors when the direction overlaps useful features; strict specificity and perplexity controls are included and utility may be capped even if the analysis holds.
Analysis focuses on entities where first-token distinctions are meaningful; single-token answers and heavily subword-fragmented names complicate readout, and we report coverage restrictions.
A single transferable intervention recipe may not exist if the failure is fact-specific, limiting practical generality though still scientifically informative.
Findings on 6–8B models may not transfer to frontier-scale models beyond an academic budget.

novelty.reasoning: Core claims that need to be novel: (1) a distinct factual error mode where the model has the right entity-concept but commits to the wrong lexically-adjacent first token; (2) a measurable dissociation between concept decoding and first-token lexical commitment at different layers; (3) a causal fix via suppressing the committed first-token direction / concept-conditioned rescoring; (4) a frequency/perplexity signature where rare correct first tokens plus shared distractor prefixes concentrate errors. The underlying two-stage concept-to-lexeme geometry is not new: guess-then-refine, depth/commitment analyses, inner-lexicon/token-erasure, and multilingual concept/language separation already establish much of the mechanism. The proposal's novelty is mainly in naming and operationalizing this as a within-language factual failure mode and showing a specific intervention. That is plausible but not a clean conceptual leap. The setting is different enough from prior work (factual recall errors rather than multilingual representation) that the result could still be novel if the error class is frequent and separable. Relative to its own related work, the core claim is non-trivial because it requires showing actual right-concept/wrong-word cases, not just generic early-token bias. Closest prior family: guess-then-refine / depth-based lexical commitment / concept-vs-lexeme separation; actual delta is the failure-mode characterization plus first-token-suppression recovery.
revision_notes: State explicitly what is new vs established: the two-stage mechanism is prior art; the novelty is the error class and causal intervention.
Add an ablation that rules out trivial tokenizer/prefix artifacts and ordinary wrong-entity mistakes.
Define a strict criterion for 'right concept' that is independent of lexical overlap.
Clarify whether the intervention is fundamentally different from existing contrastive decoding / reranking / logit suppression methods.

impact.reasoning: Problem: factual recall reliability-models giving a near-miss entity with the wrong word/prefix. Who cares: interpretability, factual QA, decoding/reliability, and knowledge editing. If true, it changes how we diagnose some hallucination-like errors and suggests a cheaper inference-time fix than weight editing. Strongest one-line case: 'Some factual errors are not wrong knowledge but premature lexical commitment, and fixing the first token can recover the right answer without editing the model.' Importance is moderate: it matters if the failure mode is common enough, measurable, and general across models/tasks. Uptake/citation potential is decent in interpretability/knowledge-editing circles, but not obviously broad unless the phenomenon is shown to be widespread. Direction-shifting value is modest-to-moderate: it reframes a subclass of errors and could influence decoding diagnostics, but it is not obviously a new general paradigm. Real-world reach depends on prevalence in deployed QA systems; if rare, impact drops sharply. Phenomenon value is the strongest aspect: even if the fix is narrow, characterizing a concrete internal failure mode is useful.

Explain whether the method is inference-time, cheap, and compatible with production decoding.

review.reasoning: The hypothesis is testable, but several parts are underspecified and at risk of circularity. Another gap is causal direction: a decodable first-token direction does not by itself show it causes the error rather than merely correlates with it. Experiments are directionally good but need tighter controls: matched difficulty, matched answer frequency, tokenizer segmentation controls, nulls for alias leakage, and comparisons against simpler decoding baselines (reranking, logit biasing, constrained generation). The intervention should be evaluated on held-out relations and with fluency/collateral damage metrics. Venue strength is good if the causal story holds, but the current narrative risks sounding like a rebranding of known lexicalization/commitment phenomena unless the error-mode signature is very clean. Minimum viable edits: sharpen the falsifiable hypothesis, tighten the operational definition of concept, add stronger causal controls, and benchmark against simpler decoding baselines.

Name: schema_overregularization
Title: Overregularization in LLMs: When a Stored Exception Loses to a Generalizable Rule It Contradicts
Short Hypothesis: LLMs store both broad generalizable rules/schemata (e.g., 'the plural of X is X+s', 'a country's capital is its largest city', 'company founders are CEOs') and specific exception facts that violate those rules. We hypothesize a distinct, predictable failure mode—overregularization—in which the model retrieves and produces the rule-consistent answer even when it internally stores the correct exception, because the rule pathway and the exception pathway compete and the rule wins on ambiguous or low-frequency exceptions. We predict (1) rule application and exception recall are causally dissociable pathways decodable at different depths, (2) overregularization errors concentrate on low-frequency exceptions where the rule is strong, above matched baselines, and (3) suppressing the rule pathway (not amplifying the fact) selectively recovers the stored exception with high specificity, whereas ROME-style fact editing does not address the root cause.
Related Work: Prior work shows reasoning/generalization and memorization occupy separable-but-interacting circuits and layers (Disentangling Recall and Reasoning, 2025; Decoupling Knowledge and Reasoning, 2025; Demystifying LLM Layers, 2025), that memorization builds on and coexists with generalization mechanisms with intermediate reasoning outputs computed even when a memorized label is emitted (Reason to Rote, 2025), and that a single linear direction mediates a reasoning-vs-memorization switch (LiReFs, 2025). Declarative statements causally shape generalization (Tell, don't show, 2023). All of these characterize that rule/generalization and fact/memorization mechanisms co-exist, but none identify overregularization—the rule pathway overriding a correctly-stored exception—as a concrete, predictable factual-answering failure, none causally localize the failure to rule-vs-exception competition, and none propose rule-pathway suppression as a non-destructive fix. This is also orthogonal to my prior proposals (expression gating, format-bound copies, entity-candidate competition, retrieve-vs-assemble route arbitration, pre-retrieval familiarity, property collapse, premature lexicalization): here the competition is between a productive rule and a fact that violates it, mirroring the classic human overregularization phenomenon (e.g., 'goed' for 'went').
Abstract: Large language models generalize from productive rules and schemata—regular plurals, default relational patterns, statistical regularities—while also storing specific facts that violate those rules. We propose that this dual organization creates a distinct, overlooked failure mode we call overregularization: when a query targets an exception, the model produces the rule-consistent answer even though it internally stores the correct exception, because a rule-application pathway competes with and overrides an exception-recall pathway. Under this account, some knowledge failures are neither storage nor gating failures but rule-vs-exception arbitration failures, directly paralleling human overregularization ('goed' for 'went'). We build controlled rule/exception item sets across three domains—morphology (irregular inflection), factual relations with statistical defaults (e.g., capital≠largest-city, founder≠CEO), and numeric/temporal regularities—and identify exceptions that the model stores (recoverable under strong prompting or by a linear content probe) yet answers with the rule-consistent value. We test three claims. (1) Dissociability: a rule-strength probe (predicting the rule-consistent output) and an exception-content probe (predicting the correct stored exception) are separable and decodable at different layers, with rule signals emerging early. (2) Prevalence: overregularization errors concentrate on low-frequency exceptions with high rule support, above frequency- and similarity-matched baselines, and the wrong answers are disproportionately the exact rule-predicted value. (3) Intervention: suppressing the rule pathway (via a learned low-rank rule direction) recovers the stored exception with higher specificity and less collateral damage than amplifying the fact or ROME editing, and preserves correct rule application on true regulars. Experiments span GPT-J-6B, Llama-3-8B, and Qwen2.5-7B, evaluating probe separability, layer-onset ordering, error-type prevalence, causal transfer, recovery rate, specificity, and fluency.
Experiments: Experiment 1 (H2 - rule/exception items with rule-predicted and true values): Builds controlled items where a productive rule and a stored exception diverge. Data: constructed from three domains - (a) morphology: regular vs. irregular inflections (plurals, past tense) from a standard English inflection list (~2,000 irregulars available; use 1,500); (b) factual defaults with documented exceptions - capital-vs-largest-city, founder-vs-CEO, author-vs-most-famous-work - built from Wikidata (target 3,000 exception items where rule-predicted != correct); (c) numeric/temporal regularities (e.g. month-length exceptions). Per item we record the rule-predicted answer, the correct answer, and an exception flag; fewer than all candidates because each needs verified rule-vs-exception divergence. Model: Llama-3-8B (8B, decoder-only), frozen; seed 0. Systems compared: rule-predicted vs. true value per item. Decisive metric: coverage = verified exception items with single-token-first answers across the three domains (first); supporting: per-domain counts. Convincing: >=3,500 verified exception items spanning all three domains. Undecidable band: 1,500-3,500 items is thin - report reduced power. Negative: <1,500 usable exceptions means the phenomenon cannot be tested at scale here.

Experiment 2 (H1/H2 - exceptions are actually stored): Confirms the model stores each exception, so overregularization is a retrieval-not-storage failure. Data: the exception items from Experiment 1. Model: Llama-3-8B, frozen; storage confirmed by (i) strong retrieval prompts / few-shot demonstrations and (ii) a trainable linear content probe decoding the correct answer from the residual stream, seeds 0/1/2, conservative thresholds. Systems compared: strong-prompt recovery and content-probe recovery vs. a label-shuffle control. Decisive metric: fraction of exceptions with positive storage evidence by both criteria (first, defines the stored-exception set); supporting: content-probe AUROC. Convincing: >=50% of exceptions pass both criteria, giving a solid stored-exception set. Undecidable band: 30-50% pass means the stored set is modest and strong-prompt leakage is a risk - report conservative coverage. Negative: <30% pass, or content probe at shuffle level, means few exceptions are genuinely stored, so overregularization cannot be distinguished from ignorance.

Experiment 3 (H1 - rule and exception signals decodable at different depths): Tests that the rule signal is decodable earlier than the exception content. Data: the stored-exception set from Experiment 2. Model: Llama-3-8B, frozen; two trainable per-layer probes - a rule-strength probe (target: the rule-predicted token / a scalar rule-applicability score) and an exception-content probe (target: the correct answer); onset-layer test with bootstrap CIs, residualization orthogonality check, seeds 0/1/2, label-shuffle controls. Systems compared: rule vs. exception onset layers. Decisive metric: onset-layer difference (first-layer at AUROC>=0.7), rule expected earlier (first); supporting: post-residualization retained predictiveness of each. Convincing: rule onset precedes exception onset by >=3 layers with non-overlapping CIs, and each retains predictiveness after residualizing out the other (retained AUROC >=0.70). Undecidable band: a 1-3 layer gap or overlapping CIs cannot establish depth separation - defer to the causal test (Experiment 5). Negative: exception onset at/before rule, or the two collapsing under residualization, falsifies H1.

Experiment 4 (H2 - overregularization concentrates on low-frequency exceptions with strong rules): Tests the prevalence pattern. Data: errors on the stored-exception set. Model: Llama-3-8B, frozen; classify errors into (a) overregularization (emitted answer equals the exact rule-predicted value while the exception is stored), (b) other, (c) correct. Systems compared: overregularization rate vs. exception frequency and rule support, against a null controlling for exception-answer frequency and lexical similarity to the rule-predicted answer (logistic regression / chi-square). Decisive metric: odds ratio linking low exception frequency + high rule support to overregularization, above the matched null (first); supporting: per-domain rates. Convincing: odds ratio >=2x over the null (p<0.001) - overregularization concentrates as predicted. Undecidable band: odds ratio 1.3-2x is a modest but real concentration - report as a localized minor mode. Negative: <=1.3x or null-indistinguishable falsifies H2's concentration claim.

Experiment 5 (H1/H3 - rule suppression, not fact amplification, is the effective lever): Causally dissociates weak exception recall from an overriding rule pathway. Data: overregularization failures (target 1,500) plus true regulars (target 1,000 as a positive control). Model: Llama-3-8B, frozen; (a) patch the exception-content representation from a correct run into a failure, (b) suppress the rule direction (from Experiment 3) at rule-onset layers, (c) amplify the exception-content direction alone; positive control: rule suppression on true regulars must degrade their correct rule-based answers; random-direction control. Systems compared: content-patch vs. rule-suppression vs. content-amplification vs. random, plus the regulars control. Decisive metric: exception recovery under rule-suppression minus recovery under content-amplification (first, the causal signature that the rule pathway is the lever); supporting: degradation of true regulars under rule suppression (must be substantial). Convincing: rule suppression recovers >=35% of exceptions while content amplification recovers <=15% (gap >=20 points), AND rule suppression degrades true regulars by >=30% (confirming the rule pathway was manipulated). Undecidable band: a 10-20 point recovery gap, or <15% regulars degradation, means the rule pathway is only partly the lever - report weak causal support. Negative: no gap (amplification works as well), or no regulars degradation, means we did not isolate an overriding rule pathway, falsifying H1/H3's mechanism.

Experiment 6 (H3 - rule-suppression steering recovers exceptions selectively; editing does not address the cause): Tests a training-free rule-suppression vector against fact editing. Data: held-out overregularization failures, target 800. Model: Llama-3-8B, frozen except the ROME/MEMIT comparators; a rank<=8 rule vector (mean difference of rule-dominant vs. exception-dominant matched states) subtracted, alpha swept; random-direction control; seeds 0/1/2. Systems compared: rule-suppression vs. exception-direction amplification vs. ROME/MEMIT editing of the exception vs. random. Decisive metric: recovered-exceptions-per-unit-collateral = recovery / accuracy drop on (i) 200 unrelated facts and (ii) held-out true regulars (first, regulars must stay correct); supporting: raw recovery, held-out perplexity. Convincing: >=40% recovery with <5% drop on unrelated facts and true regulars, beating ROME/MEMIT on recovered-per-collateral by >=1.5x. Undecidable band: a 1.0-1.5x advantage, or 5-10% regulars degradation, is parity/marginal - report with a caveat. Negative: recovery <20%, or regulars degrading >10%, falsifies the selective-recovery half of H3.

Experiment 7 (H3 generality - one rule-suppression vector transfers across families and models): Tests transfer and architecture-generality. Data: train on one domain/rule family, apply to held-out ones; reuse the Experiment 1 items per model. Model: single vector on Llama-3-8B; repeat Experiments 2-6 on GPT-J-6B and Qwen2.5-7B, frozen, identical seeds. Systems compared: cross-family transfer vs. within-family oracle; three models per decisive metric. Decisive metric: cross-family recovery rate and cross-model sign-consistency of the Experiment 4 concentration and Experiment 6 advantage (first); supporting: per-model onset gaps. Convincing: cross-family recovery >=25% and all three models show concentration and a recovery advantage >=1.2x. Undecidable band: transfer 10-25% or the pattern in 2 of 3 models is partial generality - scope accordingly. Negative: <10% transfer or majority model reversal means the mechanism is family/model-specific.

Experiment 8 (H2 - the failure is driven by rule strength versus exception weakness): Tests the source of overregularization. Data: per-item overregularization outcomes across domains. Model: Llama-3-8B, frozen; regress overregularization rate on exception-answer frequency, rule productivity (fraction of the family following the rule), and the frequency ratio between rule-predicted and true answers. Systems compared: rule-strength regressors vs. an exception-frequency-only baseline. Decisive metric: partial R^2 of rule productivity + frequency ratio beyond exception frequency (first); supporting: coefficient signs. Convincing: rule-strength features add partial R^2 >=0.10 with the predicted signs (higher productivity and higher rule:exception frequency ratio raise the rate). Undecidable band: partial R^2 0.03-0.10 is a weak trend - report as suggestive. Negative: partial R^2 <0.03 means rule strength does not drive the failure, falsifying the core mechanistic claim of H2.
Risk Factors and Limitations: Cleanly separating 'rule' from 'exception' representations may be hard when they are entangled (superposition); the causal patching and rule-suppression tests (Exp 5–6), rather than probe onset alone, are the decisive evidence, and graded results would still be informative.
Overregularization errors may be rare relative to generic errors; the frequency/similarity-matched baseline is essential and a modest but significant, well-localized effect remains publishable.
Establishing that an exception is truly 'stored' risks overestimation from strong-prompt leakage; we use conservative content-probe thresholds and held-out verification and report coverage limits.

Rule suppression could break correct rule application on genuine regulars or degrade fluency; the true-regulars specificity control (Exp 5c/6) is central and utility may be capped even if the analysis holds.
A single transferable rule-suppression vector may not exist if rules are family-specific, limiting practical generality though still scientifically informative.
Multi-token answers complicate probe/logit-lens readout; primary analysis restricts to single-token-first answers with reported coverage.
Findings on 6–8B models may not transfer to frontier-scale models beyond an academic budget.

novelty.reasoning: Core claims: (1) LLMs exhibit a distinct overregularization failure mode where a stored exception loses to a rule-consistent answer; (2) this is driven by competing rule vs exception pathways that are causally separable/decodable; (3) errors should concentrate on low-frequency exceptions with strong rule support and often produce the exact rule-predicted value; (4) suppressing the rule pathway should recover exceptions better than fact-editing methods like ROME; (5) this should generalize across morphology and factual/statistical-default domains. The main issue is that the mechanism and even a single switch direction are already close to prior work (especially LiReFs, Reason to Rote, disentangling recall/reasoning). The proposal's novelty is mostly in relabeling and re-framing an established mechanism as a concrete cross-domain factual failure mode, plus the rule-suppression intervention. That is a real delta, but not a deep one. The cross-domain taxonomy and the storage-vs-retrieval diagnostic may still be publishable if executed cleanly, but the core causal story is likely incremental relative to the cited family.

Who cares: interpretability, knowledge editing, factual QA, and cognitively motivated NLP audiences. If true, it gives a useful failure taxonomy and a different repair principle: suppress the generic rule rather than patch the fact. Downstream change: better diagnostics for exception failures and potentially safer targeted interventions. Strongest one-line case: LMs don't just hallucinate randomly; they can overapply a learned rule and thereby hide a stored exception. Impact is moderate because the phenomenon is conceptually interesting but likely niche unless shown robustly at scale and across real benchmarks. Citation potential is decent in interpretability/knowledge-editing, less likely to shift mainstream modeling unless the effect is broad and practically actionable.

Quantify prevalence at scale so the phenomenon reads as a general reliability issue, not a curiosity.
