Name: temporal_anchor_override
Title: Anchored in the Past: How a Default-Time Prior Overrides Query-Specified Time and Hides Time-Correct Knowledge in LLMs
Short Hypothesis: LLMs carry an implicit, query-independent 'default-time anchor' (a residual-stream time direction skewed toward the pretraining-dominant era, e.g., ~2019 for LLaMA2) that competes with the time specified in a query. Many temporal-recall failures are anchor-override failures: the model stores the correct fact for the queried year but produces the default-time answer because the default anchor out-weights the query's temporal signal. We predict (1) the default anchor and the query-time signal are separately decodable directions, (2) override failures concentrate where the query time is far from the anchor and the correct answer is low-frequency, and (3) suppressing the default-anchor direction (not amplifying the fact) selectively recovers the time-correct answer with higher specificity than weight editing.
Related Work: Prior work shows LLMs encode linear space/time directions (Gurnee & Tegmark 2023), have Temporal Heads that recall time-specific facts (Temporal Heads 2025), linearly encode training-order recency (Fresh in Memory 2025), and default to a stale internal 'current year' (~2019) despite later cutoffs, with temporal alignment via finetuning/prompting improving accuracy up to 62% (Set the Clock 2024). MuLan (2024) and DynamicQA (2024) show mutable facts have distinct representations and intra-memory conflict. TARDIS (2025) and Time Vectors (2023) steer temporal misalignment but at the distributional/domain level, not to recover specific stored-but-suppressed facts. Crucially, none of these frame temporal-recall failure as a *causal competition between a query-independent default-time anchor and the query-specified time*, none show the two are separable directions whose imbalance predicts which specific facts fail, and none demonstrate that *suppressing the anchor* (rather than editing the fact or globally realigning the model) selectively unlocks time-correct knowledge the model already stores. This is orthogonal to my prior (time-agnostic) proposals on gating, format-copies, entity competition, route arbitration, familiarity, property collapse, lexicalization, and overregularization.
Abstract: Large language models store facts that change over time, yet often answer time-scoped questions with an outdated value even when they demonstrably store the correct one for the queried year. Prior work shows LLMs carry an internal 'default sense of time' skewed toward a pretraining-dominant era. We propose a mechanistic account of the resulting failures: a query-independent default-time anchor in the residual stream competes with the temporal signal specified by the query, and anchor-override failures occur when the anchor out-weights the query time, so the model emits the default-era answer despite storing the time-correct fact. We test three claims on time-mutable relations (office-holders, team rosters, champions, spouses). (1) Dissociability: a linear 'anchor' probe (predicting a fixed default year, correlated with training-era frequency) and a 'query-time' probe (predicting the year named in the prompt) are separable, non-redundant directions decodable at different layers. (2) Prevalence and geometry: override failures concentrate when the query year is far from the anchor and the correct answer is low-frequency, and the wrong answer is disproportionately the default-era value; the imbalance between anchor and query-time signal magnitudes predicts override on held-out facts. (3) Causal intervention: subtracting the default-anchor direction (or scaling up the query-time direction) at the identified layers recovers time-correct answers with higher specificity and less collateral damage than ROME/MEMIT editing or global temporal realignment. We verify storage via strong prompting and content probing, use activation patching to establish causality, and replicate across GPT-J-6B, Llama-3-8B, and Qwen2.5-7B, evaluating probe separability, override prevalence, recovery rate, specificity, and fluency.
Experiments: Experiment 1 (H2 - time-mutable dataset with per-year ground truth): Builds year-scoped queries over relations whose answer changes yearly, the substrate for the override-prevalence test. Data: constructed from Wikidata for relations head-of-state, sports champions, team rosters, spouses, CEOs across 2000-2023, with per-(subject, year) ground truth; target 6,000 (subject, year) items rendered as explicit time-scoped queries ('In {year}, who was ...'), fewer than all Wikidata timelines because we require single-token-first answers and reliable per-year truth. Per-answer training-era frequency proxies come from Wikidata edit dates / entity popularity. Model: Llama-3-8B (8B, decoder-only), frozen; seed 0. Systems compared: per-year answers within a subject. Decisive metric: coverage = items with single-token-first, per-year-verified answers and a frequency proxy (first); supporting: distribution of query years relative to the model era. Convincing: >=5,000 usable items spanning the full year range. Undecidable band: 2,500-5,000 usable items is thin - report reduced power. Negative: <2,500 means too few clean time-mutable facts to test override here.

Experiment 2 (H2/H3 - year-scoped facts are actually stored): Confirms the model stores the correct year-specific fact, so override is retrieval-not-storage. Data: items the model answers wrong from Experiment 1. Model: Llama-3-8B, frozen; storage confirmed by (i) strong few-shot/chain-of-thought retrieval prompts and (ii) a trainable linear content probe decoding the correct answer, conservative thresholds, seeds 0/1/2. Systems compared: strong-prompt and content-probe recovery vs. label-shuffle control. Decisive metric: fraction of wrong items with positive storage evidence by both criteria (first, defines the override-candidate set); supporting: content-probe AUROC. Convincing: >=50% of wrong items pass both criteria. Undecidable band: 30-50% pass means a modest set with strong-prompt-leakage risk - report conservative coverage. Negative: <30% pass means the year-specific facts are mostly not stored, so override cannot be distinguished from ignorance.

Experiment 3 (H1 - default anchor and query-time signal are separate directions): Tests that a model-specific default-time anchor and the query-named year are separately decodable. Data: the override-candidate set plus time-unspecified queries. Model: Llama-3-8B, frozen; two trainable per-layer probes - an anchor probe (target: the model-specific default year, estimated as the year the model prefers when time is unspecified; regressed on training-era frequency) and a query-time probe (target: the year named in the prompt); onset-layer test, residualization, label-shuffle controls, seeds 0/1/2. Systems compared: anchor vs. query-time directions. Decisive metric: post-residualization retained predictiveness of each direction for its own target after removing the other (first); supporting: per-layer AUROC and onset difference. Convincing: each direction retains AUROC >=0.70 for its target after residualizing out the other, and both are above shuffle - two non-redundant directions. Undecidable band: retained AUROC 0.55-0.70 indicates partial entanglement with each other or with entity/frequency features - report graded separability. Negative: retained AUROC <=0.55 means anchor and query-time are not separable directions, falsifying H1.

Experiment 4 (H2 - override concentrates when query time is far from the anchor and the answer is low-frequency): Tests the prevalence pattern. Data: errors on the override-candidate set. Model: Llama-3-8B, frozen; classify into (a) anchor-override (emitted answer equals the default-era value while the correct year-answer is stored), (b) other, (c) correct. Systems compared: override rate vs. |query_year - anchor_year| and correct-answer frequency, against a null controlling for answer frequency and lexical similarity (logistic regression / chi-square); also test whether the query-time:anchor signal-magnitude ratio predicts override on held-out facts. Decisive metric: odds ratio linking large |query_year - anchor_year| + low answer frequency to override, above the null (first); supporting: AUROC of the signal-ratio predictor. Convincing: odds ratio >=2x over the null (p<0.001) and signal-ratio AUROC >=0.70. Undecidable band: odds ratio 1.3-2x or AUROC 0.58-0.70 is a modest effect - report as a localized minor mode. Negative: <=1.3x and AUROC <=0.58 falsifies H2's concentration claim.

Experiment 5 (H1/H3 - anchor suppression, not query-time amplification, is the lever): Causally dissociates weak query-time encoding from an overriding anchor. Data: override failures (target 1,500) plus time-unspecified queries (target 1,000 as a positive control). Model: Llama-3-8B, frozen; (a) patch the query-time representation from a correct run into a failure, (b) suppress the anchor direction (from Experiment 3) at anchor-onset layers, (c) amplify the query-time direction alone; positive control: suppressing the anchor on time-unspecified queries must shift default answers; random-direction control. Systems compared: query-time-patch vs. anchor-suppression vs. query-time-amplification vs. random, plus the time-unspecified control. Decisive metric: recovery under anchor-suppression minus recovery under query-time-amplification (first, the causal signature); supporting: shift in default answers on time-unspecified queries under anchor suppression (must be substantial). Convincing: anchor suppression recovers >=35% while query-time amplification recovers <=15% (gap >=20 points), AND anchor suppression shifts >=30% of time-unspecified default answers. Undecidable band: a 10-20 point gap, or <15% default shift, means the anchor is only partly the lever - report weak causal support. Negative: no gap, or no default shift, means no overriding anchor was isolated, falsifying H1/H3's mechanism.

Experiment 6 (H3 - anchor-suppression steering recovers time-correct answers more selectively than editing): Tests a training-free anchor vector against editing and global realignment. Data: held-out override failures, target 800. Model: Llama-3-8B, frozen except the ROME/MEMIT comparators; a rank<=8 default-anchor vector (mean difference of default-era-dominant vs. query-time-dominant matched states) subtracted, alpha swept; random-direction control; seeds 0/1/2. Systems compared: anchor-suppression vs. query-time amplification vs. ROME/MEMIT edit vs. a Set-the-Clock-style global temporal realignment (prompt/finetune) vs. random. Decisive metric: recovered-per-unit-collateral = recovery / accuracy drop on (i) 200 unrelated time-invariant facts and (ii) correctly-answered time-scoped facts (first); supporting: raw recovery, held-out perplexity. Convincing: >=40% recovery with <5% collateral on both control sets, beating ROME/MEMIT and global realignment on recovered-per-collateral by >=1.5x. Undecidable band: a 1.0-1.5x advantage is parity - report as comparable. Negative: recovery <20% or no advantage falsifies the selective-recovery half of H3.

Experiment 7 (H3 generality - one anchor vector transfers across relations/years and models): Tests transfer and architecture-generality. Data: train the anchor vector on one relation/year subset, apply to held-out ones; reuse the Experiment 1 items per model. Model: single vector on Llama-3-8B; repeat Experiments 2-6 on GPT-J-6B and Qwen2.5-7B, frozen, identical seeds. Systems compared: cross-relation/year transfer vs. within-subset oracle; three models per decisive metric. Decisive metric: cross-subset recovery rate and cross-model sign-consistency of the Experiment 4 concentration and Experiment 6 advantage (first); supporting: per-model anchor-year estimates. Convincing: cross-subset recovery >=25% and all three models show concentration and a recovery advantage >=1.2x. Undecidable band: transfer 10-25% or the pattern in 2 of 3 models is partial generality - scope accordingly. Negative: <10% transfer or majority model reversal means the anchor is relation/model-specific.

Experiment 8 (H2 - override is driven by the anchor's pull toward high-frequency default-era answers): Tests the source of override. Data: per-item override outcomes over the override-candidate set. Model: Llama-3-8B, frozen; regress override rate on |query_year - anchor_year|, correct-answer training-era frequency, and default-era answer frequency; where feasible, cross-check the frequency link on Pythia (open training data). Systems compared: anchor-pull regressors vs. a distance-only baseline. Decisive metric: partial R^2 of default-era answer frequency + correct-answer frequency beyond year-distance (first); supporting: coefficient signs and the Pythia cross-check. Convincing: frequency features add partial R^2 >=0.10 with the predicted signs (high default-era frequency and low correct-answer frequency raise override). Undecidable band: partial R^2 0.03-0.10 is a weak trend - report as suggestive, noting frequency-proxy limits for closed models. Negative: partial R^2 <0.03 means the frequency-pull account does not hold, falsifying the core mechanistic claim of H2.
Risk Factors and Limitations: The 'default anchor' may be a distributed/graded prior rather than a clean single direction; the causal patching and suppression tests (Exp 5-6), not probe onset alone, are the decisive evidence, and graded results remain informative.
Anchor-override may be rare relative to genuine ignorance of the year-specific fact; frequency/distance-matched baselines are essential and a modest, well-localized effect is still publishable.

Verifying that a year-scoped fact is truly stored risks overestimation from strong-prompt leakage; conservative content-probe thresholds and held-out verification with reported coverage mitigate this.

Anchor and query-time directions may be entangled or share representation with entity/frequency features, weakening the strong dissociation claim; residualization and continuous reporting address this.

Suppressing the anchor could corrupt correctly-answered facts or degrade fluency; specificity controls on time-invariant and correctly-answered time-scoped facts are central and utility may be capped even if the analysis holds.
Frequency proxies for pretraining-era prevalence are imperfect for closed models; we report proxy limitations and, where feasible, use an open-data small model (Pythia) to check the frequency link.
Multi-token answers complicate probe/logit-lens readout; primary analysis restricts to single-token-first answers with reported coverage.
Findings on 6-8B models may not transfer to frontier-scale models beyond an academic budget.

Name: consistency_seams
Title: Consistency Seams: Predicting Ripple Failures from the Pre-Existing Geometry of an LLM's Knowledge, Before Any Edit
Short Hypothesis: Whether editing a fact ripples correctly to its logical consequences is largely predetermined by how the model *already* stores the related facts: logically-entailed fact pairs occupy shared, aligned representational subspaces when the model is internally consistent, and disconnected 'consistency seams' when it is not. We hypothesize that a purely observational, edit-free measure of representational coupling between two facts (shared-subspace alignment of their subject/relation representations) predicts ripple success at edit time better than gradient-based predictors, and that facts across a seam are causally the ones that fail to ripple.
Related Work: Ripple-effect work (RippleEdits 2023, MQuAKE 2023, ReCoE 2024, RippleBench 2025) benchmarks propagation failures of editing methods; ChainEdit/PropMEND/distillation propose fixes; GradSim (2024) explains failures via cosine similarity of the *gradients* of the original fact and its related knowledge, requiring an edit to be specified. All of these treat ripple as a property of the edit + method. Our proposal is distinct in three ways: (1) it is *observational and edit-free* — we ask whether the model's native, unedited representations of two logically-linked facts are coupled, independent of any editing method or target; (2) it introduces a static representational-geometry predictor (subspace alignment / coupling) rather than a gradient-based one that presupposes an edit direction; (3) it makes a causal claim that ripple failures concentrate at 'consistency seams' — pairs stored in misaligned subspaces — and tests this with subspace-targeted editing. Our seam measure requires no backprop through an edit, no target answer, and predicts across editing methods, which GradSim cannot.
Abstract: Editing a single fact in a large language model should ripple to its logical consequences (edit 'X's employer to Google' and 'X's boss' should follow), but existing methods propagate updates inconsistently. Prior explanations tie ripple failure to the edit itself — e.g., gradient similarity between the edited fact and its consequence. We propose that ripple success is largely determined *before any edit* by the geometry of how the model already stores the two facts. When the model is internally consistent about a logically-linked pair, their subject/relation representations occupy a shared, aligned subspace so an update to one is naturally read out by the other; when they are stored in misaligned, disconnected subspaces — a 'consistency seam' — updates cannot propagate. We introduce a static, edit-free coupling measure: for a fact pair (A, B) where B is entailed by A, we quantify the alignment between the subspaces that carry A's and B's answer-relevant information (via linear relational embeddings and CCA/subspace-angle between the residual-stream directions that read out each answer). We test three claims. (1) Predictiveness: pre-edit coupling predicts per-pair ripple success at edit time (ROME/MEMIT/in-context) with higher AUROC than GradSim, and does so without computing any edit. (2) Causality: ripple failures concentrate on low-coupling 'seam' pairs above frequency- and hop-matched baselines; injecting the missing coupling (aligning the subspaces) improves ripple. (3) Native inconsistency: even unedited, seam pairs already exhibit belief inconsistency (the model affirms A and B's rule but denies the entailed answer) more than coupled pairs. Experiments span GPT-J-6B, Llama-3-8B, and Qwen2.5-7B on RippleEdits and MQuAKE, evaluating AUROC of ripple prediction, seam prevalence, causal recovery, and specificity.
Experiments: Experiment 1 (H1 - edit-free coupling score between entailed fact pairs): Constructs logically-linked fact pairs and an observational coupling measure computed with no reference to any edit. Data: fact pairs (A, B) where B is a logical/compositional consequence of A (two-hop, sibling, inverse), extracted from RippleEdits (~5k edit instances with entailed-fact tests) and MQuAKE (multi-hop chains); target 4,000 pairs with single-token-first answers, fewer than the full benchmarks because both facts must admit a reliable readout direction. Model: Llama-3-8B (8B, decoder-only), frozen; estimate each fact's answer-readout subspace via linear relational embeddings (LREs) and tuned-lens answer-token probes at subject and last positions; the pre-edit coupling score = principal-subspace angle / CCA correlation between A's and B's readout subspaces, computed with no edit and no target answer; seed 0. Systems compared: coupling for pairs later observed to ripple vs. not. Decisive metric: coverage = pairs with a reliable coupling score for both facts (first); supporting: coupling-score distribution. Convincing: >=2,500 pairs admit a reliable coupling score, spanning coupled and low-alignment cases. Undecidable band: 1,200-2,500 usable pairs is thin - report reduced power and restricted relations. Negative: <1,200 usable pairs means readout directions are too unreliable to build the coupling measure here.

Experiment 2 (H1 - edit-free coupling predicts ripple better than a gradient predictor): Tests the central claim that observational coupling forecasts ripple success without any edit. Data: the coupled pairs from Experiment 1. Model: Llama-3-8B, frozen except during the edits being evaluated; apply ROME, MEMIT, and in-context editing to A and measure per-pair ripple success on B; seeds 0/1/2. Systems compared: pre-edit coupling score vs. GradSim (which requires the edit) vs. controls (entity/answer frequency, hop count, lexical overlap). Decisive metric: AUROC of coupling predicting ripple success, pooled and per-method (first); supporting: AUROC of GradSim and the controls it must match/beat. Convincing: coupling reaches AUROC >=0.70 and comes within 0.03 of, or beats, GradSim while using no edit-specific gradient - an edit-free predictor as good as the gradient one. Undecidable band: coupling AUROC 0.60-0.70, or trailing GradSim by 0.03-0.10, means coupling predicts but does not match the gradient predictor - report as a cheaper, weaker signal. Negative: AUROC <=0.60 or no better than the frequency/hop controls falsifies H1.

Experiment 3 (H1/H2 - ripple failures concentrate on seams): Tests that low-alignment 'seam' pairs fail to ripple above matched baselines and characterizes seams. Data: the pairs from Experiment 2, split into coupled vs. seam by a cross-validated coupling threshold. Model: Llama-3-8B, frozen (edits as in Experiment 2). Systems compared: ripple-failure rate on seam vs. coupled pairs against a frequency-/hop-matched null (logistic regression / chi-square); seam predictors = relation type, entity-popularity asymmetry, co-occurrence proxy (on Pythia where feasible). Decisive metric: ripple-failure-rate difference between seam and coupled pairs, above the matched null (first); supporting: which features predict seams. Convincing: seam pairs fail to ripple at a rate >=20 points above coupled pairs beyond the matched null (p<0.001). Undecidable band: a 8-20 point gap is a real but modest concentration - report seams as a contributing, not dominant, factor. Negative: <8 points or null-indistinguishable means seams do not track ripple failure, falsifying the seam account of H2.

Experiment 4 (H2 - seams reflect pre-existing inconsistency, not edit artifacts): Tests that the model already holds inconsistent beliefs on seam pairs before any edit. Data: seam and coupled pairs from Experiment 3. Model: Llama-3-8B, frozen, no editing; probe whether the model correctly answers A, affirms the connecting rule, yet fails/denies the entailed B; multiple rule phrasings for robustness. Systems compared: native-inconsistency rate on seam vs. coupled pairs. Decisive metric: difference in native (edit-free) inconsistency rate between seam and coupled groups (first); supporting: robustness across rule phrasings. Convincing: seam pairs show native inconsistency >=20 points above coupled pairs, stable across phrasings - seams are pre-existing organizational fractures. Undecidable band: an 8-20 point difference is a modest signal - report as partial support. Negative: <8 points, or a phrasing-dependent effect, means seams do not reflect pre-existing inconsistency, weakening H2's 'before any edit' framing.

Experiment 5 (H2 - restoring coupling causally enables ripple): Tests that aligning a seam pair's subspaces makes the edit propagate. Data: seam pairs from Experiment 3, target 800. Model: Llama-3-8B, frozen except the evaluated edit; learn a low-rank alignment map that rotates B's readout subspace toward A's (estimated from coupled pairs of the same relation family), inject it, then edit A and re-measure ripple to B; controls: no alignment, a ChainEdit-style logical-chain in-context prompt, and a random-rotation control; seeds 0/1/2. Systems compared: subspace-alignment vs. no-alignment vs. chain-prompt vs. random-rotation. Decisive metric: ripple-recovery rate on seam pairs under alignment, minus the no-alignment and random-rotation baselines (first); supporting: specificity (unrelated-fact accuracy and unrelated-pair ripple pre/post), held-out perplexity. Convincing: alignment recovers ripple on >=35% of seam pairs, >=20 points above no-alignment and random-rotation, with <5% collateral - restoring coupling causally enables propagation. Undecidable band: a 8-20 point recovery gain means partial causal support - report coupling as contributory. Negative: <8 point gain over controls, or collateral wiping out gains, means aligning subspaces does not enable ripple, falsifying the causal half of H2.

Experiment 6 (H1/H2 generality - coupling transfers across families and models): Tests cross-family predictive transfer and architecture-generality, including whether larger models have fewer seams. Data: compute coupling on one relation family, predict ripple on held-out families; reuse the Experiment 1 pipeline per model. Model: Llama-3-8B; repeat Experiments 1-4 on GPT-J-6B and Qwen2.5-7B, frozen, identical seeds/hyperparameters. Systems compared: cross-family coupling-AUROC vs. within-family; three models on seam prevalence and prediction. Decisive metric: cross-family AUROC of coupling predicting ripple (first); supporting: per-model seam fraction and whether it falls with model size. Convincing: cross-family AUROC >=0.65 and all three models show coupling predicting ripple above controls, with seam fraction not increasing with size. Undecidable band: cross-family AUROC 0.55-0.65 or the pattern in 2 of 3 models is partial generality - scope accordingly. Negative: cross-family AUROC <=0.55 or majority model reversal means coupling is family/model-specific, limiting H1's reach.
Risk Factors and Limitations: The coupling/subspace-alignment measure is a modeling choice; LREs are linear for only ~half of relations, limiting coverage — we report which relations admit reliable readout directions and restrict primary analysis accordingly.

Coupling may correlate with simple confounds (co-occurrence, popularity, hop count); matched baselines and multivariate regression are essential, and the edit-free predictor's value rests on beating GradSim after controls.

Predicting ripple 'before any edit' could still leak information if the readout subspaces implicitly encode edit-relevant structure; we mitigate by computing coupling with no target answer and validating on held-out relation families.

The causal subspace-alignment intervention may fail if coupling is not a single low-rank map or if aligning subspaces damages unrelated readouts; strict specificity/fluency controls are included and the causal claim may hold only partially even if prediction succeeds.
Native-inconsistency measurement depends on eliciting the model's 'belief' about the rule, which is prompt-sensitive; we use multiple phrasings and report robustness.
Multi-token answers complicate readout-direction estimation; primary analysis restricts to single-token-first answers with reported coverage.
Co-occurrence origin analysis is only feasible on small open-data models (Pythia) and may not transfer to the 6–8B evaluation models.
Findings on 6–8B models may not transfer to frontier-scale models beyond an academic budget.

novelty.reasoning: Core claims needing novelty: (1) ripple success is pre-determined by pre-edit representational geometry of linked facts, not by the edit/method; (2) an observational, edit-free coupling score over entailed pairs (subspace alignment via LRE+CCA/subspace angle) predicts ripple success across methods; (3) this static measure outperforms GradSim, the closest prior edit-conditioned baseline; (4) 'consistency seams' are the failure locus and can be causally probed by subspace-targeted intervention. Compared to RippleEdits/MQuAKE/ReCoE/ChainEdit/PropMEND, the delta is real and clean: they benchmark/fix propagation, while this predicts and explains propagation from unedited geometry. Compared to GradSim, the novelty is in removing the need for an edit/target and using representational rather than gradient similarity. This is new enough to be interesting, though the underlying idea is adjacent to existing geometry/consistency analyses and may be partly a reframing unless the predictive lift/generalization is strong.

Name: inheritance_failure
Title: Does a Canary Have Skin? Property-Inheritance Failures Reveal How LLMs Store Conceptual Taxonomies
Short Hypothesis: LLMs store conceptual knowledge as a taxonomic hierarchy with properties attached at superordinate category nodes, and answering whether a subordinate instance has an inherited property requires an internal inheritance-composition step that can fail even when both the category-membership fact and the property-at-category fact are individually stored. We predict a graded inheritance-failure signature - accuracy on inherited-property queries decreases with taxonomic distance between the instance and the property-owning category - mirroring the classic Collins-Quillian sentence-verification latency effect in humans, and that this failure is causally an inheritance-binding failure (the category-node representation is present but not composed into the instance representation), recoverable by injecting the category-binding rather than by editing either atomic fact.
Related Work: A large literature dissociates recall from reasoning by layer/head/direction (Disentangling Recall and Reasoning 2025; Decoupling Knowledge and Reasoning 2025; LiReFs 2025; Demystifying LLM Layers 2025) and shows conceptual complexity is encoded at increasing depth (Concept Depth 2024; Hierarchical Deconstruction / DepthQA 2024). The clinical dissociation work (Knowledge-Reasoning Dissociation in Clinical NLI 2025) shows models possess facts but cannot compose them. None of these study property inheritance in conceptual taxonomies as a specific, gradable behavioral phenomenon, nor connect it to the classic Collins-Quillian (1969) semantic-network verification effect, nor causally localize the failure to a missing category-membership binding. This differs from my prior proposals: consistency_seams concerns edit-time ripple across logically-linked facts; strategy_arbitration concerns retrieve-vs-assemble routing for factual two-hop chains; property_collapse concerns confusing sibling relations sharing a subspace. Here the object is native (unedited) taxonomic inheritance of conceptual properties and the human-derived graded-distance signature.
Abstract: Since Collins and Quillian (1969), cognitive science has held that conceptual knowledge is organized hierarchically with properties stored economically at their most general applicable category and inherited by subordinate instances - predicting that verifying 'a canary has skin' takes longer than 'a canary can fly' because 'has skin' is stored several taxonomic levels up. We ask whether large language models exhibit an analogous inheritance structure, and whether property-inheritance failures constitute a distinct, gradable class of conceptual-knowledge failure. We construct a controlled probe set from WordNet/ConceptNet taxonomies: for each (instance, property) pair we record the taxonomic distance to the category that owns the property, verify that the model independently stores both the membership fact (instance is-a category) and the property fact (category has property), and then test the inherited-property query directly. We predict three things. (1) Behavioral signature: direct-query accuracy on inherited properties decreases monotonically with taxonomic distance even when both atomic facts are stored, and confidence/latency-analogues (token probability, answer-onset depth) track distance, mirroring the human effect. (2) Mechanism: the failure is an inheritance-binding failure - the property-owning category is decodable in the residual stream but is not composed into the instance representation on failing queries; activation patching of the category-binding from a same-instance run that names the category restores the inherited property. (3) Intervention: injecting the missing category-binding recovers inherited properties more selectively than editing either atomic fact via ROME. Experiments span GPT-J-6B, Llama-3-8B, and Qwen2.5-7B, evaluating distance-accuracy curves, storage-controlled failure prevalence, causal recovery, and specificity.
Experiments: Experiment 1 (H1 — taxonomic-probe construction and atomic-fact eligibility): Test the precondition that both atomic facts an inheritance query depends on — category membership and property-at-category — are individually stored, so that later failures cannot be dismissed as missing knowledge. Data: constructed from WordNet 3.0 hypernym paths (via NLTK) crossed with ConceptNet 5.7 property assertions (HasA/CapableOf/HasProperty); we enumerate ~5,000 (instance, property, owning-category, distance) tuples where the property is canonically attached at a superordinate node and instances sit 1-4 is-a hops below, filter to a high-agreement subset by requiring the property assertion to appear on the owning category and none of the intervening nodes, yielding ~1,200 tuples; distance = number of is-a hops. Model: Llama-3-8B, fully frozen; queries in a fixed template ('Does a {instance} have {property}? Answer yes or no.') plus 3 paraphrases. Systems compared: for each tuple, direct membership query, direct property-at-category query, and a logistic-regression content probe (seeds {0,1,2}, L2, 5-fold) reading the yes/no fact from the last-token residual stream. Decisive metric: fraction of tuples where BOTH atomic facts are answered correctly AND probe-decodable (the 'inheritance-eligible' set), reported first with per-distance coverage. Convincing: eligible set >= 400 tuples spread across all four distances (>=60 per distance). Indecision band: eligible coverage 250-400 tuples — usable but under-powered; below 250 we cannot separate inheritance failure from missing knowledge and H1 is not testable on this model. Negative result (eligibility collapses at large distance) would itself indicate atomic knowledge, not composition, degrades with distance and would reframe H2.

Experiment 2 (H2 — graded taxonomic-distance failure signature): Test that inheritance-query accuracy falls with taxonomic distance even when both atomic facts are stored. Data: the inheritance-eligible set from Experiment 1. Model: Llama-3-8B frozen; measure per-tuple direct-query accuracy, yes-token probability, and answer-onset layer (first layer at which logit-lens top token is the correct yes/no). Systems compared: inherited-property queries vs a matched control of non-inherited-but-true properties attached directly at the instance level (distance 0), balanced on property and instance unigram frequency and query token length. Decisive metric (first): OLS slope of per-tuple accuracy on distance with instance-frequency, property-frequency, and length as covariates, plus cluster-robust SEs by owning-category; secondary, slope of onset-layer on distance and Spearman correlation with the Collins-Quillian human latency ordering. Convincing: accuracy slope <= -0.05 per hop (95% CI excludes 0) for inherited properties while the control slope's CI includes 0. Indecision band: accuracy slope in (-0.05, -0.02) per hop — a weak trend that neither confirms nor refutes a graded signature; H2 then rests on the onset-layer slope. Negative (slope CI includes 0, or control shows the same slope) means no distance-specific composition cost and undercuts the inheritance-step account.

Experiment 3 (H3 — owning category present but uncomposed on failures): Test that on inheritance failures the property-owning category is still internally represented (present) rather than absent, distinguishing a binding failure from missing knowledge. Data: inheritance-eligible set, split into model-correct ('success') and model-incorrect ('failure') inheritance queries. Model: Llama-3-8B frozen; train a logistic-regression probe (seeds {0,1,2}, 5-fold, label-shuffle null) to decode the owning-category identity from the instance-token and last-token residual streams at each layer, trained on success cases only, tested on held-out success and on failure cases. Systems compared: category-decoding AUROC on failures vs successes vs shuffle null, layer by layer. Decisive metric: peak-layer category-decoding AUROC on failure cases. Convincing: failure AUROC >= 0.75 and within 0.05 of success AUROC (category present despite wrong answer). Indecision band: failure AUROC 0.60-0.75 — partial presence, consistent with a graded rather than binary binding; report as weak support. Negative (failure AUROC <= 0.60, near success-minus-0.15) means the category is genuinely absent on failures and the 'present-but-uncomposed' claim in H3 is wrong.

Experiment 4 (H4 — causal inheritance-binding via activation patching): Test that supplying the category-binding causally restores the inherited answer, and removing it induces failure. Data: matched same-instance pairs from the eligible set — a 'category-primed' run (prompt prepends 'A {instance} is a {category}.') and a 'bare-query' run. Model: Llama-3-8B frozen; activation patching (TransformerLens) copying the residual stream at instance/last-token positions from primed into failing bare runs, swept over all layers; reverse direction ablates (mean-patches) the binding in success runs. Systems compared: restore-patch vs random-position patch vs random-source patch; ablate-patch vs random-ablation. Decisive metric (first): recovery rate = fraction of failures flipped to correct by the binding patch, minus the random-patch flip rate. Convincing: net recovery >= 25 percentage points at the best layer, AND reverse ablation lowers success accuracy by >= 25 points, with random controls < 5 points. Indecision band: net recovery 10-25 points — the binding contributes but is not sufficient alone; H4's 'recoverable by injecting the binding' holds only partially. Negative (< 10 points, or indistinguishable from random) means the failure is not a missing binding and refutes H4's causal core.

Experiment 5 (H4 — recovery by category-binding steering vs editing atomic facts): Test that a reusable low-rank binding direction restores inheritance and does so more cleanly than editing either atomic fact. Data: eligible set, instance-disjoint train/test split; steering vector = mean residual difference (category-primed minus bare) over training instances, seeds {0,1,2}. Model: Llama-3-8B frozen except the injected direction (rank<=4). Systems compared: (a) binding-steering injection on held-out failures, (b) ROME edit of the membership fact, (c) ROME edit of the property-at-category fact, (d) random-direction control. Decisive metric (first): recovered-per-unit-collateral = recovery rate divided by accuracy drop on 200 unrelated held-out facts; secondary, specificity (accuracy change on non-inherited direct properties), fluency (held-out perplexity delta). Convincing: steering recovery >= 30% with < 3-point drop on the 200 unrelated facts, and a strictly better recovered-per-collateral ratio than both ROME edits. Indecision band: steering recovery 15-30% or collateral drop 3-6 points — competitive but not decisively better than atomic edits; report as parity. Negative (steering no better than random, or worse collateral than ROME) means the binding is not a clean reusable direction, bounding H4's editing claim.

Experiment 6 (H4 — transfer and generality of the binding direction): Test that the category-binding is a general composition operation, not a per-category memorized patch. Data: eligible tuples partitioned by WordNet subtree; steering vector estimated on one subtree, applied to held-out subtrees and held-out taxonomic domains. Model: Llama-3-8B frozen. Systems compared: within-subtree steering (upper bound), cross-subtree steering, random-direction control. Decisive metric: cross-subtree recovery rate relative to within-subtree recovery. Convincing: cross-subtree recovery >= 60% of within-subtree recovery and clearly above random. Indecision band: 35-60% of within-subtree — partial generality, consistent with a mix of shared and category-specific structure. Negative (< 35% or at random) means binding is category-specific and H4's single-mechanism reading is too strong.

Experiment 7 (H2 — architecture-generality replication): Test that the graded signature and its binding basis are not idiosyncratic to one model. Data: the same eligible-set construction (Experiment 1) recomputed per model. Models: GPT-J-6B, Qwen2.5-7B, Pythia-6.9B, all frozen; re-run Experiments 2-4 (distance slope, category decodability, patching recovery), seeds {0,1,2}. Decisive metric (first): sign and magnitude of the accuracy-vs-distance slope, replicated per model. Convincing: negative distance slope (CI excludes 0) in >= 2 of 3 models with matching present-but-uncomposed decodability. Indecision band: replication in exactly 1 of 3 — model-dependent, report scope limits. Negative (no replication) confines H1-H4 to Llama-3-8B.

Experiment 8 (H1 — composition vs surface co-occurrence, and scale): Test whether inheritance reflects genuine hierarchical composition rather than direct instance-property co-occurrence, and whether scale flattens the distance curve. Data: eligible set on Pythia (open pretraining corpus) enabling instance-property co-occurrence counts from the Pile; Pythia sizes 1.4B, 2.8B, 6.9B, frozen. Decisive metric (first): partial regression coefficient of inheritance-failure rate on taxonomic distance after controlling for log instance-property co-occurrence and property abstractness. Convincing: distance coefficient remains significant (CI excludes 0) with co-occurrence partialled out, and the distance slope's magnitude decreases monotonically across the three scales. Indecision band: distance coefficient CI half-width overlapping 0 by < 0.02 — co-occurrence and composition are statistically entangled at this sample size; report as inconclusive on mechanism source. Negative (co-occurrence fully absorbs the distance effect) means the signature is surface statistics, not composition, directly refuting H1's hierarchical-storage claim.
Risk Factors and Limitations: WordNet/ConceptNet taxonomies are noisy and some 'inherited' properties may not be cleanly owned by a single category; we curate a high-agreement subset and report coverage.

Inheritance failures could reflect surface co-occurrence (instances rarely co-occur with abstract properties) rather than a genuine composition step; the co-occurrence regression (Exp 8) and the causal category-binding patching (Exp 4) are the decisive controls.

The category-binding may be distributed/graded rather than a clean injectable direction; patching (Exp 4) rather than the steering vector alone is the decisive causal evidence, and graded results remain informative.
Verifying atomic-fact storage risks overestimation from prompt leakage; conservative content-probe thresholds and held-out verification mitigate this.

Answer-onset-layer as a latency analogue is only loosely comparable to human reaction time; we treat the human parallel as motivation, not identity, and report the behavioral distance curve on its own terms.
Binding injection could induce over-attribution (yes to non-inherited false properties); the non-inherited-property specificity control (Exp 5) is central and utility may be capped.
Multi-token properties/instances complicate readout; primary analysis restricts to single-token-first items with reported coverage.
Findings on 6-8B models may not transfer to frontier-scale models beyond an academic budget.

novelty.reasoning: Core novelty is a mechanistic/causal reinterpretation of property inheritance failures: a graded taxonomic-distance effect plus a binding/composition failure localizable by patching, rather than just a behavioral inheritance test. The closest prior family is COMPS and similarity-vs-taxonomy work; the actual delta is from behavioral description to causal mechanism. This is non-trivial, but the behavioral distance effect itself is adjacent to the Collins-Quillian / taxonomy literature, so the novelty hinges heavily on the binding claim and causal intervention.

impact.reasoning: The problem is meaningful to mechanistic interpretability, knowledge editing, and cognitive-science-inspired LM work, but it is still a fairly specialized question about conceptual-taxonomy behavior. If true, it would affect how researchers think about compositional storage and inheritance in LMs and could guide intervention methods. However, the practical downstream reach is modest unless the binding story generalizes broadly beyond this probe family. So what: serious researchers would care, but likely only within a niche.

review.reasoning: The proposal is testable and fairly well-controlled, but it is overstuffed and some central claims are not yet fully defensible. The biggest risks are construct validity (WordNet/ConceptNet ownership is noisy), leakage/surface-cooccurrence confounds, and whether the proposed probe/patching really isolates a binding operation rather than generic context effects. The hypothesis is broadly falsifiable, but some experiments mix levels of analysis and there is a lot of dependence on one model and one curated dataset. With tighter scope and cleaner causal controls, this could be submission-ready.

Name: articulation_use_dissociation
Title: Say vs. Use: A Causal Double Dissociation Between the Knowledge LLMs Articulate and the Knowledge They Act On
Short Hypothesis: The knowledge an LLM can verbally articulate and the knowledge it actually uses to make an implicit downstream decision are carried by partially distinct internal representations, producing a causal double dissociation: (A) facts the model states correctly but does not use ('inert articulation'), and (B) facts the model uses correctly in a downstream computation but cannot state ('tacit knowledge'). We hypothesize these two failure directions have distinct, separable internal loci, such that steering the 'articulation' locus changes what the model says without changing what it uses, and steering the 'use' locus does the reverse.
Related Work: Prior work establishes an acquisition-vs-utilization gap (Kandpal/Chen 2023; Physics of LMs 3.2, 2023), a 'know but don't tell' disconnect in long context (2024), missing-vs-unused knowledge in patents (2025), knowledge-reasoning dissociation in clinical NLI (2025), and comprehension-without-competence 'split-brain' framing (2025). Self-explanation-faithfulness work (NeuroFaith 2025) checks whether stated reasoning matches internal computation. All of these (i) treat the gap as unidirectional (model has knowledge but fails to apply/reason), (ii) are largely behavioral or measure a single direction, and (iii) do not test whether articulation and use are *causally separable representations*. Our contribution is distinct: we posit and test a *bidirectional* dissociation including the under-studied 'tacit knowledge' direction (used-but-unsayable), and we make it a *causal* claim — that separate internal loci carry the say-pathway and the use-pathway — validated by targeted, direction-specific interventions. This is orthogonal to my prior proposals, which all concern retrieval-to-output for direct factual queries; here the object is the mismatch between verbal articulation and implicit use of the same underlying fact.
Abstract: Large language models are known to 'possess' knowledge they fail to 'use', but the relationship between what a model can say and what it actually acts on remains unclear. We propose that articulation and use draw on partially distinct internal representations, and that this predicts a causal double dissociation. For a fixed fact f about a subject, we build two probes: an articulation query that asks the model to state f directly, and a use query that requires f only implicitly to succeed at a downstream task (e.g., choosing between two options where f is a hidden discriminator, or completing a task whose correct answer depends on f but never names it). We first document the behavioral double dissociation: inert-articulation facts (stated correctly, not used) and tacit-knowledge facts (used correctly, cannot be stated), quantifying their prevalence above matched baselines. We then test the mechanistic claim that a 'say' locus and a 'use' locus are separable: using linear probing we identify residual-stream directions predicting articulation success and use success, and with activation patching and steering we test direction-specificity — amplifying the say-locus improves articulation without changing use, and amplifying the use-locus improves task success without changing what the model states. We further test whether tacit-knowledge facts can be surfaced by patching from the use-pathway into the articulation-pathway. Experiments span GPT-J-6B, Llama-3-8B, and Qwen2.5-7B on PopQA, T-REx, and comparison/classification tasks derived from Physics-of-LMs manipulation setups, evaluating dissociation prevalence, probe separability, and direction-specific causal effects with strict specificity controls. Confirming the hypothesis reframes the utilization gap as a representational split between saying and doing, with implications for interpretability-based oversight (a model may use knowledge it never verbalizes).
Experiments: Experiment 1 (H0 — paired say/use task construction and validity): Build the measurement instrument and verify the use-query truly requires the fact, so downstream dissociation cannot be an artifact of an unsolvable or fact-independent task. Data: adapted from PopQA (14,282 QA pairs, 16 relations) and T-REx; for each fact f = (subject, relation, object) we build an articulation query ('What is X's {relation}?') and a use query where f is only an implicit discriminator (a comparison 'Which of A or B is larger in {attribute}?' or a classification 'Is X's {attribute} before 2000?'). Target ~2,000 facts spanning >=8 relations after filtering to single-token-first objects. Model: Llama-3-8B, frozen. Decisive metric (first): use-query correctness when f is made indeterminate (matched query about an unknown subject) — must drop to chance (within +-5 points of the format's guessing rate). Convincing: >= 1,500 facts pass this validity gate. Indecision band: 1,000-1,500 facts pass — proceed with reduced power and report it; below 1,000 the use-query is contaminated by non-f cues and H1-H3 are not testable. Negative (use-queries solvable without f) means the format leaks and must be rebuilt before any dissociation claim.

Experiment 2 (H1 — behavioral double dissociation exists): Test that both off-diagonal cells (say-correct/use-wrong = inert articulation; use-correct/say-wrong = tacit knowledge) occur beyond what a single shared knowledge signal predicts. Data: validated facts from Experiment 1. Model: Llama-3-8B frozen; cross-tabulate per-fact articulation-success x use-success (2x2). Systems compared: observed off-diagonal mass vs a single-signal null — a per-fact logistic model with a shared latent difficulty plus per-task bias, from which we test the residual say x use interaction (permutation null, 1,000 permutations). Decisive metric (first): residual say-use interaction coefficient (log-odds) with 95% CI, plus prevalence of each off-diagonal cell. Convincing: interaction CI excludes 0 AND each off-diagonal cell holds >= 8% of facts. Indecision band: interaction CI excludes 0 but one off-diagonal cell is 3-8% — a one-sided dissociation, weaker than the claimed double dissociation. Negative (interaction CI includes 0, off-diagonals explained by shared difficulty) refutes H1: say and use behave as one signal.

Experiment 3 (H1 — off-diagonal cells are genuine, not shortcuts): Test that tacit-knowledge cases genuinely use f and inert-articulation cases genuinely state f. Data: the two off-diagonal cells from Experiment 2. Model: Llama-3-8B frozen. Systems compared: for tacit facts, (i) counterfactually flip f in an in-context statement and check the use-answer flips, (ii) confirm the use-query fails when f is indeterminate; for inert facts, check articulation consistency across 4 paraphrases. Decisive metric (first): fraction of tacit facts whose use-answer flips with the counterfactual (genuine-use rate) and fraction of inert facts consistent across paraphrases (genuine-articulation rate). Convincing: both rates >= 70%. Indecision band: 50-70% — a substantial minority are shortcuts/guesses; retain only the passing subset and report shrinkage. Negative (< 50%) means the off-diagonal cells are largely artifacts and H1's interpretation fails.

Experiment 4 (H2 — separable internal loci by probing): Test that say-success and use-success are carried by partially distinct residual-stream information. Data: validated facts with say/use outcomes. Model: Llama-3-8B frozen; train a say-probe and a use-probe (logistic regression, seeds {0,1,2}, 5-fold, label-shuffle null) on subject-token and last-token residuals at each layer. Systems compared: each probe's own-task AUROC, and — after residualizing each probe's features against the other task's label — the unique per-task AUROC that survives. Decisive metric (first): unique (residualized) use-probe AUROC and say-probe AUROC at their best layers. Convincing: each retains AUROC >= 0.65 after residualization (task-specific information exists beyond shared signal). Indecision band: unique AUROC 0.55-0.65 — weak separability; the representations are mostly shared. Negative (unique AUROC <= 0.55, at shuffle level) means say and use share one representation and H2 is unsupported.

Experiment 5 (H3 — direction-specific causal double dissociation): Test that steering the say-locus changes what the model states without changing what it uses, and steering the use-locus does the reverse. Data: matched say-correct/say-wrong and use-correct/use-wrong states; say-direction and use-direction = mean residual differences, seeds {0,1,2}. Model: Llama-3-8B frozen except the injected direction. Systems compared: amplify say-direction, amplify use-direction, opposite-direction control, random-direction control, on both articulation and use readouts. Decisive metric (first): specificity index = on-target task change minus off-target task change (percentage points), for each direction. Convincing: say-direction specificity >= 20 points and use-direction specificity >= 20 points, with random/opposite controls < 5 points — a genuine causal double dissociation. Indecision band: specificity 8-20 points for one direction — partial, single-sided dissociation. Negative (both specificity indices < 8 points or match random) refutes H3: the two functions cannot be steered independently.

Experiment 6 (H3 — surfacing tacit knowledge by cross-pathway patching): Test the strong form of the use-locus claim — that information used but not stated can be routed into articulation. Data: tacit-knowledge facts (Experiment 3, genuine-use subset). Model: Llama-3-8B frozen; patch the use-pathway residual (from the run where f is demonstrably used) into the articulation run at the probe-identified layers/positions. Systems compared: cross-pathway patch vs say-direction amplification vs ROME edit vs random-patch. Decisive metric (first): articulation-recovery rate (tacit facts now stated correctly) net of random-patch rate; secondary, specificity (accuracy on 200 unrelated held-out facts) and fluency (held-out perplexity delta). Convincing: net recovery >= 20 points with < 3-point unrelated-fact drop, beating say-direction amplification. Indecision band: net recovery 8-20 points or 3-6-point collateral — tacit content is partially routable; report as suggestive. Negative (< 8 points or ROME/say-direction do as well) means use-pathway content is not separately routable into articulation.

Experiment 7 (H2/H3 — transfer and architecture generality): Test that say/use directions are a general split, not relation- or model-specific. Data: facts partitioned by relation; directions estimated on a subset of relations, applied to held-out relations. Models: GPT-J-6B, Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, frozen; re-run Experiments 2, 4, 5, seeds {0,1,2}. Decisive metric (first): cross-relation steering specificity index relative to within-relation, plus replication of the behavioral interaction (Experiment 2) per model. Convincing: cross-relation specificity >= 50% of within-relation AND behavioral dissociation replicates in >= 2 of 3 models. Indecision band: replication in exactly 1 model or cross-relation specificity 30-50% — model/relation-dependent. Negative (no cross-relation transfer, no replication) confines H2-H3 to specific relations on one model. Also report whether the dissociation shrinks with model size.

Experiment 8 (H1 — task-format robustness): Test that the dissociation tracks say-vs-use rather than a particular use-query format or its difficulty. Data: each validated fact rendered in three use formats (comparison, classification, implicit completion), difficulty-matched by per-format chance rate. Model: Llama-3-8B frozen. Decisive metric (first): correlation of per-fact use-success across the three formats, and whether the say x use interaction (Experiment 2) survives within each format after controlling per-format difficulty. Convincing: interaction CI excludes 0 in >= 2 of 3 formats and per-fact use-success correlates r >= 0.5 across formats. Indecision band: interaction survives in exactly 1 format — format-specific, weakening generality. Negative (interaction vanishes once format/difficulty controlled) means the dissociation is a task-demand artifact, not a say/use representational split.
Risk Factors and Limitations: The dissociation could be an artifact of use-query difficulty (extra task demands) rather than a representational say/use split; the single-signal null baseline (Exp 2), format-robustness check (Exp 8), and counterfactual controls (Exp 3) are essential and a residual interaction after controls is the decisive behavioral evidence.

Say and use representations may be entangled rather than cleanly separable; the direction-specific steering test (Exp 5), not probe onset alone, is decisive, and a graded/partial dissociation would weaken the strong claim but remain informative.

Establishing that tacit-knowledge facts are genuinely 'used' (not solved by a shortcut) is hard; counterfactual flipping and indeterminacy controls mitigate but may not fully eliminate confounds, and coverage will be limited.
Cross-pathway patching to surface tacit knowledge may induce confident confabulation on facts not actually held; strict specificity and fluency controls are required and utility may be capped.
A single transferable say/use direction may not exist if the split is fact-specific, limiting generality though still scientifically informative.
Multi-token answers complicate probe/logit-lens readout; primary analysis restricts to single-token-first answers with reported coverage.
Findings on 6-8B models may not transfer to frontier-scale models beyond an academic budget.

novelty.reasoning: Core claims: (1) a bidirectional say-vs-use dissociation, including the understudied used-but-unsayable case; (2) a causal representational split with separable residual-stream loci; (3) direction-specific steering/patching that selectively changes say vs use; (4) surface tacit knowledge by cross-pathway patching. Relative to prior acquisition-vs-utilization and faithfulness work, the main novelty is not the existence of a gap but the bidirectional framing plus causal intervention claim. That is non-trivial, but the setting is still an extension of known dissociation work rather than a wholly new task or theory. Closest prior family is utilization-gap / know-but-don't-tell / self-explanation faithfulness; the delta is moving from behavioral one-way mismatch to causal double dissociation with interventions.

impact.reasoning: The phenomenon under study is whether models can act on knowledge they cannot verbalize, and whether saying vs using knowledge are dissociable. That matters to interpretability, oversight, and knowledge-editing: if true, auditing via direct questioning is incomplete. This has a strong one-line case: a model may use hidden knowledge even when it cannot state it, so behavioral transparency is insufficient. Serious researchers in safety/interpretability would likely care, and positive results would likely be cited. The main caveat is that practical reach depends on whether the 'use' construct is genuinely validated rather than a task-shortcut proxy.

Name: late_polarity_binding
Title: Content First, Polarity Last: Why LLMs Retrieve the Fact but Ignore Whether the Query Denied It
Short Hypothesis: When answering factual queries, LLMs retrieve the subject-attribute content association early and largely polarity-blind, then apply the query's polarity (affirmation vs. negation) in a separate, later, weaker step. Because content is bound before polarity, a stored true negation is frequently overridden by the positively-retrieved content, producing confident affirmation of a fact the model 'knows' is false. We predict content-recall and polarity-application are decodable at different layers, that negation-override errors concentrate where positive content is strongly primed, and that amplifying/binding the late polarity signal (not editing the fact) selectively fixes these errors while preserving affirmative recall.
Related Work: Behavioral work shows a 'belief conflict': LLMs answer polar negative questions correctly but generate positively-biased text about negative commonsense (Say What You Mean, 2023), attributing this to reporting bias and statistical shortcuts, and negated-LAMA studies (Understanding by Understanding Not, 2021; Kassner & Schutze) show models complete negated cloze the same as affirmative. Strong-hallucinations-from-negation (2024) treats negation theoretically as a latent operation and proposes a fix, but does not localize a mechanism. INLP work (2020) shows negation leaves a linear imprint. Entity-recognition (Do I Know This Entity, 2024) and answerability directions (2023) concern coverage/self-knowledge, not the polarity of a specific factual query. None of these localize a *content-before-polarity* two-stage retrieval mechanism, test polarity-application timing causally, or show that a targeted intervention on a late polarity signal recovers stored true-negation knowledge. This is orthogonal to all my prior proposals (gating, format copies, entity competition, route arbitration, familiarity, property collapse, lexicalization, overregularization, temporal anchors, consistency seams, inheritance, say-vs-use): here the object is the *polarity* of the query and its late binding to polarity-blind content.
Abstract: Large language models often affirm a fact even when the query negates it, and generate positively-biased statements about things they can correctly deny when asked yes/no questions—the 'belief conflict.' Prior work documents this behaviorally and blames pretraining reporting bias, but offers no mechanistic account. We propose that factual retrieval is two-stage and polarity-blind at its core: the model retrieves the subject-attribute content association early, then applies the query's polarity (affirm vs. negate) in a separate, later, and comparatively weak step. Because content is bound before polarity is resolved, strongly-primed positive content overrides a stored true negation, yielding confident wrong-polarity answers. We test three claims. (1) Timing/dissociability: a content probe (predicting the retrieved subject-attribute association, polarity-invariant) and a polarity probe (predicting the query's affirmative/negative frame) are separable residual-stream directions decodable at different layers, with content emerging before polarity is applied to the answer. (2) Prevalence/geometry: negation-override errors—correct polar-QA answer but wrong-polarity generation, or affirmation of a negated cloze—concentrate where positive content is strongly primed (high subject-attribute association), above frequency-matched baselines, and the strength imbalance between content and polarity signals predicts override on held-out items. (3) Causal intervention: amplifying the late polarity direction (or patching it from a correct-polarity run) recovers correct-polarity answers with higher specificity and less collateral damage than fact editing, while preserving affirmative recall. Experiments span GPT-J-6B, Llama-3-8B, and Qwen2.5-7B on negated-LAMA, T-REx, and negative-commonsense sets (CSK-PN), evaluating probe separability, layer-onset ordering, override prevalence, causal recovery, and specificity.
Experiments: Experiment 1 (H0 — polarity-paired dataset and true-polarity baseline): Build minimally-contrasting affirmative/negative pairs and establish, per fact, the model's 'true' polarity knowledge so override can later be separated from ignorance. Data: adapted from LAMA/T-REx and PopQA (factual) plus CSK-PN negative-commonsense assertions; for each fact build an affirmative cloze/question, its negation, and a matched polar-QA form ('True or false: ...'). Restrict to single-token-first answers; target ~2,500 pairs across >=8 relations/domains after filtering; report coverage. Model: Llama-3-8B, frozen. Decisive metric (first): fraction of facts where the polar-QA form is answered correctly for BOTH the affirmative and the negated statement (the 'polarity-aware' eligible set). Convincing: >= 1,500 eligible pairs. Indecision band: 1,000-1,500 eligible — reduced power, reported; below 1,000 the model lacks the polarity knowledge whose late application H1-H3 concern, so those hypotheses are untestable here. Negative (polar-QA at chance) means the model does not store the negations and the study cannot proceed on this model.

Experiment 2 (H1 — content decodable before polarity across layers): Test that the polarity-invariant subject-attribute content is decodable earlier than the query's polarity. Data: eligible pairs from Experiment 1. Model: Llama-3-8B frozen; train a content probe (predict the fact's object, trained across both polarities) and a polarity probe (predict affirmative vs negative) via logistic regression on subject-token and last-token residuals at every layer (seeds {0,1,2}, 5-fold, label-shuffle null, tuned-lens matched-capacity control). Decisive metric (first): onset-layer difference = (layer at which polarity probe first exceeds 0.7 AUROC) minus (layer at which content probe first exceeds 0.7 AUROC), with bootstrap 95% CI; secondary, residualized unique AUROC of each probe. Convincing: onset difference >= 4 layers (polarity later), CI excludes 0, both probes non-redundant after residualization. Indecision band: onset difference 1-4 layers — a weak ordering; timing rests on the causal test (Experiment 4). Negative (difference CI includes 0 or reversed) refutes the content-before-polarity ordering in H1.

Experiment 3 (H2 — negation-override concentrates where positive content is primed): Classify and predict override errors. Data: negated/negative queries from the eligible set. Model: Llama-3-8B frozen; classify each response as (a) negation-override (affirmative-content answer given, but polar-QA shows the true polarity is known), (b) genuine ignorance (polar-QA also wrong), (c) correct. Systems compared: override rate as a function of positive-content priming (affirmative-form answer confidence and subject-attribute association strength) vs a null logistic model controlling answer frequency and lexical similarity. Decisive metric (first): partial coefficient of content-priming on override probability (log-odds, CI), and out-of-sample AUROC of the Experiment-2 content-vs-polarity signal imbalance predicting override on held-out items. Convincing: priming coefficient CI excludes 0 and held-out AUROC >= 0.70. Indecision band: AUROC 0.60-0.70 — priming predicts override only weakly. Negative (coefficient CI includes 0, AUROC ~0.5) means override is not driven by positive-content dominance, refuting H2.

Experiment 4 (H1 — causal two-stage timing via patching): Test causally that the failure is late/weak polarity application, not missing content. Data: matched correct-polarity and override runs. Model: Llama-3-8B frozen; (a) patch the polarity representation from a correct-polarity run into an override run at the polarity-onset layers and check the answer flips to correct polarity with content unchanged; (b) ablate the polarity signal in a correct affirmative run (reverse control) and check it induces spurious negation; (c) patch content alone and confirm polarity is not fixed. Systems compared: polarity-patch vs content-patch vs random-position patch. Decisive metric (first): net polarity-correction rate = fraction of overrides flipped to correct polarity by the polarity patch minus the random-patch rate. Convincing: net correction >= 25 points, reverse ablation drops affirmative accuracy >= 25 points, content-patch and random < 5 points. Indecision band: net correction 10-25 points — polarity contributes but is not solely decisive. Negative (< 10 points or content-patch fixes it) refutes the late-polarity causal account.

Experiment 5 (H3 — polarity amplification recovery without editing the fact): Test that boosting the late polarity signal fixes override while preserving affirmative recall. Data: eligible set, instance-disjoint train/test; polarity steering vector = mean residual difference (correct-polarity minus override), seeds {0,1,2}, rank<=4. Model: Llama-3-8B frozen except the injected direction. Systems compared: polarity-steering, content-direction manipulation, ROME/MEMIT fact edit, and a random-direction control. Decisive metric (first): recovered-per-unit-collateral = override-recovery rate divided by accuracy drop on a held-out set of correctly-answered affirmative queries (the critical over-negation control); secondary, accuracy on 200 unrelated affirmative facts, fluency (held-out perplexity delta). Convincing: recovery >= 30% with < 3-point drop on correct affirmatives and on the 200 facts, beating all comparators on recovered-per-collateral. Indecision band: recovery 15-30% or collateral 3-6 points — over-negation risk caps utility; report parity with fact-editing. Negative (no better than random, or affirmative accuracy collapses) refutes the steering claim in H3.

Experiment 6 (H1/H3 — transfer and architecture generality): Test that late polarity binding and its fix are general, not relation- or model-specific. Data: pairs partitioned by relation and by factual-vs-commonsense domain; polarity vector trained on a subset, applied to held-out relations/domains. Models: GPT-J-6B, Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, frozen; re-run Experiments 2-5, seeds {0,1,2}. Decisive metric (first): cross-relation override-recovery relative to within-relation, plus replication of the content-before-polarity onset ordering per model. Convincing: cross-relation recovery >= 50% of within-relation AND onset ordering replicates in >= 2 of 3 models. Indecision band: replication in 1 model or cross-relation 30-50% — model/relation-dependent. Negative (no transfer/replication) confines H1-H3 to one model. Also report whether larger models bind polarity earlier (lower override rate).

Experiment 7 (H2 — source of late binding): Quantify how much override is driven by positive-content dominance versus negation reporting bias. Data: eligible set; Pythia sizes 1.4B/2.8B/6.9B (open Pile corpus) for co-occurrence counts, plus entity-popularity proxies. Model: frozen. Decisive metric (first): partial regression coefficients of override rate on (subject-attribute association strength, affirmative-vs-negative pretraining-frequency asymmetry, syntactic distance of the negation cue to the answer), with CIs. Convincing: association-strength and frequency-asymmetry coefficients CI-exclude 0 and jointly explain a majority of override variance, with override decreasing across Pythia scale. Indecision band: coefficients CI half-width overlapping 0 by < 0.02 — sources statistically entangled at this sample size; report as inconclusive on relative contribution. Negative (neither predictor significant) means override has another source than positive-content dominance, qualifying H2's mechanistic reading.
Risk Factors and Limitations: The content and polarity signals may be entangled rather than cleanly separable; the causal patching test (Exp 4), not probe onset alone, is decisive, and a graded/partial dissociation would weaken the strong two-stage claim while remaining informative.

Negation-override may be conflated with genuine ignorance; the polar-QA control (establishing the model 'knows' the true polarity) is essential, and strong-prompt leakage could overestimate knowledge—we use conservative thresholds and report coverage.

Polarity amplification could over-negate—making the model deny true affirmative facts; the correctly-answered-affirmative specificity control (Exp 5) is central and utility may be capped even if the analysis holds.
Timing (content before polarity) could be a probe-difficulty artifact; tuned-lens, matched-capacity probes, and causal patching mitigate this.
A single transferable polarity vector may not exist if polarity handling is relation-specific, limiting practical generality though still scientifically informative.
Cloze-form negation ('is not ___') is under-determined (many valid completions); we prioritize verification/polar and single-answer negation formats and report format-specific results.
Multi-token answers and multi-cue negation complicate readout; primary analysis restricts to single-token-first answers and single negation cues, with reported coverage.
Findings on 6–8B models may not transfer to frontier-scale models beyond an academic budget.

novelty.reasoning: The core mechanism overlaps substantially with recent mechanistic work on negation processing, which already argues that negation failure comes from later overshadowing rather than absent negation ability. The proposal's real novelty is narrower: a precise timing claim (content before polarity), causal activation patching of polarity, and a low-rank steering fix with less collateral than fact editing. Those are nontrivial, but mostly an incremental refinement of an already-emerging mechanism rather than a wholly new theory.
