Name: recite_vs_execute
Title: It Can State the Rule but Runs a Different One: The Recitation-Execution Gap in LLM Procedural Knowledge
Short Hypothesis: LLMs store a procedure's declarative description (which they can recite) and the executable pathway that actually runs during forward-pass computation as partially distinct representations, so a model frequently executes a simpler heuristic that contradicts the very rule it just stated correctly. We hypothesize this recitation-execution gap is a distinct, gradable failure mode, that the recited-rule representation is only weakly causally coupled to the execution circuit, and that steering the execution pathway toward the stated rule's representation makes the model actually follow it without changing what it recites.
Related Work: Prior work shows arithmetic is a 'bag of heuristics' rather than an algorithm (Arithmetic Without Algorithms, 2024) and undergoes 'algorithmic phase transitions' across subtasks (2024); procedural pretraining installs modular reusable circuits, mostly in attention (Procedural Pretraining, 2026; Modular Structures, 2025); Programming by Backprop (2025) finds execution-from-instruction is far less reliable than in-context instructions; procedures generalize poorly across code/graph/NL representations (Generalize Procedures Across Representations, 2026). Circuit-reuse work (2023) shows shared algorithmic building blocks. All of these characterize the enacted procedure or its reusability, but none isolate the *dissociation between the rule a model can recite and the rule it actually executes* as a behavioral phenomenon, nor test whether the recited-rule representation is causally connected to the execution circuit, nor show that binding recitation to execution fixes execution. This also differs from my prior say-vs-use proposal, which concerns implicit *use of a fact* rather than *execution of a procedure that contradicts a correctly-stated rule*.
Abstract: Large language models can often correctly state how to perform a procedure—the rule for pluralization, a sorting comparator, a modular-arithmetic step, a game rule—yet, when they actually carry it out, they execute a different, usually simpler procedure that contradicts the rule they just recited. We call this the recitation-execution gap and propose that it arises because a procedure's declarative description and the executable pathway that runs in the forward pass are carried by partially distinct internal representations that are only weakly causally coupled. We first document the phenomenon behaviorally across procedure families (string/morphology rules, list operations, modular and base-conversion arithmetic, rule-following games): for each item we elicit the model's stated rule, verify it is correct, and separately measure whether its execution obeys that rule, quantifying the gap and its dependence on procedure complexity and input difficulty. We then test the mechanistic claim with Location + Causal Intervention: linear probes identify a residual-stream representation of the recited rule and the components of the execution circuit (following bag-of-heuristics and circuit-reuse methods); activation patching tests whether the recited-rule representation is present-but-uncoupled during execution (patching a correct-execution rule representation into a gap case should not fix execution if the pathways are decoupled), and a steering intervention that injects the recited-rule representation into the execution circuit tests whether we can bind recitation to execution—making the model follow its own stated rule—without changing what it recites. Experiments span GPT-J-6B, Llama-3-8B, and Qwen2.5-7B, evaluating gap prevalence, probe separability, causal coupling, execution recovery, and specificity.
Experiments: Experiment 1 (H0 — procedure dataset construction): Build controlled items where a rule can be both stated and executed and where a contradicting heuristic output is well-defined, so the gap is measurable. Data: constructed programmatically across four families — (a) string/morphology transforms (reverse, remove-vowels, regular vs irregular inflection), (b) list operations (sort-by-key, filter, dedup), (c) explicit-algorithm arithmetic (modular addition, base conversion, carrying), (d) stated-move rule games — 400 items per family, 1,600 total, each with a canonical rule-consistent output and a plausible heuristic-consistent output. Model: Llama-3-8B, frozen; greedy decoding, temperature 0, 3 prompt seeds. Decisive metric (first): fraction of items for which the rule-consistent and heuristic-consistent outputs are distinct AND a matched-difficulty control confirms the heuristic is a real attractor (a model prompted only with examples produces the heuristic output > 50% of the time). Convincing: >= 1,200 items pass, >=250 per family. Indecision band: 800-1,200 pass — reduced per-family power, reported; below 800 the heuristic is not a genuine competitor and the gap is ill-defined. Negative (heuristic never competes) means there is no shortcut to contradict recitation and the phenomenon cannot be studied on these families.

Experiment 2 (H0 — recitation elicitation and verification): Establish, per item, that the model can state the correct rule, so execution failures are not mere ignorance. Data: passing items from Experiment 1. Model: Llama-3-8B frozen; elicit the stated rule in natural language/pseudocode. Systems compared: canonical-string match plus an LLM judge (GPT-4o) with human spot-checks on a 100-item calibration sample. Decisive metric (first): fraction of items whose recited rule is verified correct (the 'analysis set'); report judge-vs-human agreement (Cohen's kappa) on the calibration sample. Convincing: analysis set >= 800 items with judge-human kappa >= 0.8. Indecision band: kappa 0.6-0.8 — judge noisy; fall back to string-match-only labels and report shrinkage. Negative (analysis set < 400 or kappa < 0.6) means recitation cannot be reliably verified and downstream gap claims are unfounded.

Experiment 3 (H1 — recitation-execution gap is a distinct, gradable failure mode): Test that models recite a correct rule yet execute the contradicting heuristic, at a rate exceeding a shared-competence null. Data: analysis set. Model: Llama-3-8B frozen; classify each item as (a) recite-execute gap, (b) both correct, (c) both wrong. Systems compared: observed gap-cell mass vs a null where recitation and execution share one latent competence with independent per-task noise (logistic model; permutation test, 1,000 permutations); gap rate regressed on rule length/step count and input difficulty. Decisive metric (first): residual recite-execute interaction (log-odds, CI) and gap prevalence per family. Convincing: interaction CI excludes 0 and gap cell >= 10% in >= 3 of 4 families, rising with complexity. Indecision band: gap cell 4-10% or interaction CI just excluding 0 in <3 families — weak/partial gap. Negative (interaction CI includes 0) means recitation and execution reflect one competence, refuting H1.

Experiment 4 (H1 — separable recited-rule and execution-state representations): Test that the recited rule carries information distinct from the enacted execution state during the forward pass. Data: analysis set with per-item gap labels. Model: Llama-3-8B frozen; train a rule-representation probe (decode recited-rule identity, trained on the recitation forward pass) and an execution-state probe (decode which branch/heuristic is being applied) via logistic regression at each layer (seeds {0,1,2}, 5-fold, label-shuffle null). Decisive metric (first): residualized unique AUROC of the recited-rule direction during the EXECUTION pass, after partialling out the execution-state signal. Convincing: unique rule AUROC >= 0.65 and execution-state probe >= 0.75 at its best layer. Indecision band: unique rule AUROC 0.55-0.65 — mostly shared representation. Negative (<= 0.55, at shuffle) means recited rule and execution share one representation, weakening H1's 'distinct representations'.

Experiment 5 (H2 — recited rule is weakly causally coupled to execution): Test the coupling strength causally. Data: gap items and matched both-correct runs of the same procedure. Model: Llama-3-8B frozen; patch the recited-rule representation from a both-correct run into a failing execution run at the identified layers/positions; reverse control ablates the recited-rule representation in both-correct runs; also patch execution-circuit components to confirm they carry the enacted procedure. Systems compared: rule-patch vs execution-component-patch vs random-position patch. Decisive metric (first): execution-flip rate = fraction of gap items whose output becomes rule-consistent under the rule-patch, minus random-patch rate. Convincing (supports 'weak but usable coupling'): flip rate 10-40 points; very strong coupling would be > 40 points; 'present-but-uncoupled' would be < 10 points — the experiment distinguishes these three regimes and reports which. Indecision band: 8-12 points straddles the uncoupled/weak boundary; report as boundary and defer to Experiment 6. Negative direction for the intervention program: if flip rate < 8 points, H3's steering is unlikely to work and we say so up front.

Experiment 6 (H3 — binding the recited rule into execution fixes behavior without changing recitation): Test the steering claim. Data: analysis set, item-disjoint train/test; steering vector = mean residual difference (rule-consistent-execution minus heuristic-execution matched states), seeds {0,1,2}, rank<=4. Model: Llama-3-8B frozen except the injected direction. Systems compared: rule-binding steering, execution-state-direction amplification, fine-tuning on rule-consistent examples, random-direction control. Decisive metric (first): execution-recovery rate (gap items now rule-consistent) net of random; secondary specificity — recited rule unchanged (recitation accuracy delta), both-correct items still correct, accuracy on unrelated procedures, fluency (perplexity delta). Convincing: net recovery >= 25% with recitation and both-correct accuracy dropping < 3 points, beating execution-amplification. Indecision band: recovery 12-25% or both-correct drop 3-6 points — partial fix; report. Negative (no better than random, or recitation changes too) refutes H3.

Experiment 7 (H1/H3 — transfer and architecture generality): Test that the gap and its fix generalize across items/families and models. Data: items partitioned by family; steering vector trained on one family, applied to held-out families. Models: GPT-J-6B, Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, frozen; re-run Experiments 3-6, seeds {0,1,2}. Decisive metric (first): cross-family execution-recovery relative to within-family, plus replication of the gap prevalence (Experiment 3) per model. Convincing: cross-family recovery >= 40% of within-family AND gap replicates in >= 2 of 3 models. Indecision band: replication in 1 model or cross-family 25-40% — model/procedure-specific. Negative (no transfer/replication) confines findings to one model. Report whether larger models show a smaller gap.

Experiment 8 (H1 — source of the gap): Quantify how much the gap is execution defaulting to a well-primed heuristic. Data: analysis set. Model: Llama-3-8B frozen (plus Pythia 1.4B/2.8B/6.9B for scale). Decisive metric (first): partial regression coefficients of gap prevalence on (procedure complexity, heuristic-shortcut availability = how strongly the contradicting procedure fits the surface pattern, input-distribution familiarity), with CIs. Convincing: heuristic-availability coefficient CI-excludes 0 and dominates the others, gap decreasing across Pythia scale. Indecision band: coefficient CI half-width overlapping 0 by < 0.02 — sources entangled; report inconclusive. Negative (heuristic-availability not significant) means the gap has another driver, qualifying the mechanistic claim.

Name: context_priming_contamination
Title: Primed to Err: How Irrelevant Contextual Mentions Contaminate an LLM's Factual Recall
Short Hypothesis: Factual recall in LLMs is not a pure function of the query but is biased by entities/attributes recently activated in the context: merely mentioning a related but irrelevant entity earlier in the prompt causes the model to bleed that entity's attributes into the answer for an unrelated target. We hypothesize this context-priming contamination (1) is a gradable behavioral phenomenon that scales with the semantic similarity and recency of the primed distractor, (2) is carried by a residual-stream 'primed-entity' signal that attention over the distractor mention injects into the target's answer readout, and (3) can be causally suppressed by ablating the distractor-token attention or subtracting the primed-entity direction, restoring correct recall without editing the fact.
Related Work: Prior work on retrieval competition studies distractors co-activated by the query itself (my retrieval_competition proposal) or by logically-linked context (in-context knowledge conflict; Fakepedia 2023; DynamicQA 2024), where the injected context explicitly contradicts or grounds the fact. Distraction/irrelevant-context work (Shi et al. 2023, 'LLMs Easily Distracted by Irrelevant Context') shows accuracy drops on math with irrelevant sentences, but does not isolate a *factual-attribute-bleed* mechanism, does not require the distractor to be a semantically related entity, and offers no mechanistic locus or targeted fix. Induction-head / copy-mechanism work explains verbatim copying from context but not attribute contamination of parametric recall. My other proposals concern query-internal gating, format copies, arbitration, polarity, and procedures. None characterize *priming contamination*: that an incidental, non-contradictory mention of a neighbor entity systematically corrupts recall of an unrelated target, nor localize it to distractor-token attention, nor show a non-destructive suppression fix. We transfer the classic human semantic-priming / source-monitoring error into parametric factual recall and give it a causal account.
Abstract: Human memory retrieval is famously contaminated by recently activated but irrelevant material—semantic priming and source-monitoring errors. We ask whether large language models exhibit an analogous phenomenon in parametric factual recall: does merely mentioning a related but irrelevant entity earlier in the prompt corrupt the model's answer about an unrelated target? We call this context-priming contamination. We first document the behavior: for a target fact (e.g., the capital of country A), we prepend a neutral, non-contradictory sentence mentioning a semantically related distractor entity (e.g., neighboring country B) and measure how often the model answers with the distractor's attribute (B's capital) instead of A's. We predict contamination is gradable—rising with the semantic similarity between distractor and target and with the recency/salience of the mention—and concentrated on low-frequency targets, above frequency-matched neutral-prime baselines. We then test the mechanism with a Location + Causal Intervention strategy: a linear probe should recover a 'primed-entity' signal in the residual stream at the target's answer position that is absent under neutral primes; activation patching and attention-head analysis should show that attention over the distractor-mention tokens injects this signal; and ablating that attention or subtracting the primed-entity direction should restore correct recall with high specificity (unrelated facts and un-primed recall unchanged), whereas simply editing the fact does not address the cause. Experiments span GPT-J-6B, Llama-3-8B, and Qwen2.5-7B on PopQA, T-REx, and EntityQuestions, evaluating contamination rate, similarity/recency dose-response, probe recovery, causal recovery, and specificity.
Experiments: Experiment 1 (H0 — priming dataset construction and copying control): Build primed prompts where any contaminated answer must come from parametric recall, not surface copying, so H2 cannot be explained by induction. Data: adapted from PopQA, T-REx, and EntityQuestions; for each target fact (subject A, relation r, answer a) select a same-type distractor B with a different attribute value b != a, and record A-B semantic similarity (entity-embedding cosine, taxonomic/geographic distance). Build a related-prime prompt ('I was reading about {B} yesterday. What is the {relation} of {A}?'), a matched-length neutral-prime (dissimilar unrelated entity), and a no-prime control; crucially b never appears in the prompt. Target ~2,500 targets across >=8 relations after filtering to single-token-first answers; report coverage. Model: Llama-3-8B, frozen. Decisive metric (first): fraction of items where the model answers the no-prime query correctly (the eligible set — contamination is only meaningful where baseline recall works) AND b is absent from the prompt. Convincing: >= 1,500 eligible. Indecision band: 1,000-1,500 — reduced power; below 1,000 baseline recall is too weak to detect contamination. Negative (baseline recall at chance) means the model cannot recall these facts and priming cannot be studied.

Experiment 2 (H1 — context-priming contamination exists): Test that merely mentioning B raises the rate of answering b. Data: eligible set. Model: Llama-3-8B frozen. Systems compared: related-prime vs matched-length neutral-prime vs no-prime. Decisive metric (first): contamination-rate lift = P(answer = b | related-prime) minus P(answer = b | neutral-prime), tested against a null controlling answer frequency and lexical overlap (logistic regression; permutation CI). Convincing: lift >= 8 percentage points with 95% CI excluding 0, and neutral-prime not above no-prime by more than 2 points (ruling out generic distraction). Indecision band: lift 3-8 points — a weak effect that may be generic load rather than semantic priming; report as suggestive. Negative (lift CI includes 0, or neutral-prime equally raises b) refutes H1: mentioning B does not specifically contaminate recall.

Experiment 3 (H1 — dose-response on similarity and recency): Test that contamination scales with distractor-target similarity and mention recency/salience. Data: eligible set, crossed over similarity bins and recency (token distance to query, number of mentions, syntactic prominence). Model: Llama-3-8B frozen. Decisive metric (first): regression coefficients of contamination rate on similarity and on recency, with CIs; secondary, similarity x target-popularity interaction. Convincing: both similarity and recency coefficients CI-exclude 0 with monotone per-bin curves, and low-popularity targets more contaminated. Indecision band: exactly one of the two coefficients CI-excludes 0 — partial dose-response; report which factor drives it. Negative (neither coefficient significant) means contamination does not scale as claimed, refuting H1's gradable-scaling clause.

Experiment 4 (H2 — primed-entity signal in the residual stream): Test that a decodable primed-entity signal is present at the answer position and aligned with b's readout. Data: eligible set across related/neutral/no-prime runs. Model: Llama-3-8B frozen; train a logistic-regression probe (seeds {0,1,2}, 5-fold, label-shuffle null) to decode presence/identity of distractor B from the answer-position residual stream at each layer. Decisive metric (first): peak-layer AUROC for detecting the primed signal in related-prime vs neutral-prime, and cosine alignment of the primed-entity direction with b's unembedding vector. Convincing: AUROC >= 0.75 and alignment significantly above a random-direction null. Indecision band: AUROC 0.60-0.75 — a weak/partial signal; the causal test (Experiment 5) is then decisive. Negative (AUROC <= 0.60 or no unembedding alignment) means no primed-entity signal, undercutting H2.

Experiment 5 (H2/H3 — attention injects the contaminating signal, causally): Test that distractor-token attention is the injection route. Data: contaminated related-prime items. Model: Llama-3-8B frozen; (a) identify query/answer-position heads attending to distractor-mention tokens and ablate that attention; (b) activation-patch the answer-position residual from a no-prime run into a contaminated run and measure recovery of a; (c) reverse control — inject the primed-entity signal into a no-prime run to induce contamination on demand. Systems compared: distractor-attention ablation vs random-head attention ablation vs no-prime patch vs random-position patch. Decisive metric (first): contamination-reduction from distractor-attention ablation, net of random-head ablation. Convincing: distractor-attention ablation cuts contamination by >= 50% relative, no-prime patch recovers a in >= 25 points net, and reverse injection induces contamination >= 25 points; random controls < 5 points. Indecision band: attention-ablation reduction 20-50% relative — attention is one of several routes. Negative (ablation ~ random) means attention over the mention is not the causal route, refuting H2's mechanism.

Experiment 6 (H3 — suppression restores recall without editing the fact): Test that subtracting the primed-entity direction fixes contamination cleanly. Data: eligible set, item-disjoint train/test; steering vector = mean residual difference (contaminated minus neutral-prime matched states), seeds {0,1,2}, rank<=4, subtracted at the identified layers. Model: Llama-3-8B frozen except the subtracted direction. Systems compared: primed-entity subtraction, distractor-attention ablation (Experiment 5a), ROME edit of the target fact (expected not to help), random-direction control. Decisive metric (first): recovered-per-unit-collateral = contamination-recovery rate divided by accuracy drop on correctly-answered primed facts (over-correction control); secondary, accuracy on 200 unrelated un-primed facts, fluency (perplexity delta). Convincing: recovery >= 30% with < 3-point drop on correctly-answered primed facts and on the 200 facts, beating ROME. Indecision band: recovery 15-30% or collateral 3-6 points — partial; report parity. Negative (no better than random, or harms correct cases) refutes H3.

Experiment 7 (H1/H3 — transfer and architecture generality): Test generality across relations, distractor types, and models. Data: eligible items partitioned by relation; suppression vector trained on a subset, applied to held-out relations. Models: GPT-J-6B, Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, frozen; re-run Experiments 2-6, seeds {0,1,2}. Decisive metric (first): cross-relation contamination-recovery relative to within-relation, plus replication of the contamination lift (Experiment 2) per model. Convincing: cross-relation recovery >= 50% of within-relation AND lift replicates (CI excludes 0) in >= 2 of 3 models. Indecision band: replication in 1 model or cross-relation 30-50% — model/relation-specific. Negative (no transfer/replication) confines H1-H3 to one model. Report whether larger models contaminate less.

Experiment 8 (H1 — safety-domain transfer): Test that context-priming contamination produces higher-stakes errors. Data: constructed from a curated safe subset of medical facts (drug-indication or symptom-disease), with a benign related-drug/disease mention as the distractor; ~400 items, held to publicly documented, non-actionable facts. Model: Llama-3-8B frozen; replicate Experiments 2-3. Decisive metric (first): contamination-rate lift in the medical setting versus the general-knowledge lift. Convincing: medical lift CI excludes 0 and is at least as large as the general lift. Indecision band: medical lift 3-8 points — present but modest; report the elevated-stakes framing cautiously. Negative (no lift in medical domain) means the phenomenon does not transfer to this higher-stakes setting, bounding the practical claim.
Risk Factors and Limitations: The neutral prime may not be truly neutral (any prepended sentence adds tokens/attention load); matched-length neutral-prime and unrelated-entity controls are essential to attribute the effect to semantic priming rather than generic distraction.

Contamination could be driven by verbatim copying (induction) rather than parametric-recall corruption; we require the distractor's attribute b to NOT appear in the prompt, so any b in the answer must come from parametric recall, and the attention analysis distinguishes copying from attribute injection.
The primed-entity signal and target recall may be entangled; the causal patching/ablation tests (Exp 5), not probe AUROC alone, are decisive, and graded results remain informative.

Suppression could over-correct (harm cases where contextual mention is legitimately relevant) or degrade fluency; the correctly-answered-primed and unrelated-fact specificity controls are central and utility may be capped.
A single transferable suppression vector may not exist if contamination is relation- or distractor-specific, limiting practical generality though still scientifically informative.
Multi-token answers complicate readout; primary analysis restricts to single-token-first answers with reported coverage.
Findings on 6–8B models may not transfer to frontier-scale models beyond an academic budget.

That said, the behavioral phenomenon is close to existing irrelevant-context degradation and contextual token boosting, so novelty hinges on whether the effect survives controls and is not just generic semantic priming or entrainment.

Name: presupposition_writeback
Title: Presupposition Writeback: How a False Aside About an Entity Silently Corrupts an Unrelated Fact the Model Knows
Short Hypothesis: When a query embeds a false presupposition about one attribute of a subject as an incidental aside (not the thing being asked), LLMs 'write back' that counterfactual attribute into the subject's early representation, and this corruption then bleeds into recall of a *different, unrelated* attribute the model otherwise answers correctly. We hypothesize this presupposition-writeback (1) is a gradable behavioral phenomenon whose error rate scales with the plausibility of the false presupposition and its semantic relatedness to the queried attribute, (2) is carried by a subject-position residual-stream 'writeback' signal injected early via attention over the presupposed-attribute tokens, and (3) can be causally suppressed by ablating that attention or subtracting the writeback direction, restoring correct recall of the unrelated attribute without editing any fact.
Related Work: False-premise work studies models answering the false-premise question itself: FAITH (2024) localizes 'false premise heads' that disturb knowledge extraction for the presupposed object; answerability-probe work (2023) and Ambiguity-Encoding Neurons (2025) study abstention; DecoPrompt (2024) reduces hallucination via prompt decoding; FalseQA/CREPE (2022-2023) benchmark rebuttal ability; 'LLMs Struggle to Reject False Presuppositions when Stakes are High' (2025) is behavioral-only. All of these concern whether the model detects/rejects the false premise or hallucinates an answer *to the premise's own attribute*. None study the *cross-attribute spillover*: that a false aside about attribute A silently corrupts recall of an *unrelated* attribute B of the same subject that the model would otherwise get right. This also differs from my context_priming_contamination proposal, which primes a *different distractor entity* (attribute bleed across entities); here the false content is about the *same* subject but a *different* attribute, and the query never asks about the false content. The writeback-into-subject mechanism and the cross-attribute suppression fix are new.
Abstract: Large language models are known to be misled when a question's premise is false and the question asks about that very premise. We study a subtler and more insidious phenomenon: a false presupposition slipped in as an incidental aside about one attribute of a subject silently corrupts the model's recall of a *different, unrelated* attribute it otherwise knows. For example, asking 'Given that Marie Curie was born in Germany, what field did she win her Nobel Prize in?' can degrade the correct 'Physics/Chemistry' answer even though nationality is irrelevant to the prize field. We call this presupposition writeback: the false attribute is written into the subject's early representation and then bleeds into orthogonal attribute recall. We first document the behavior across relation pairs, measuring how error on the queried (unrelated) attribute rises when a plausible false presupposition about a second attribute is present, versus a true-presupposition control and a no-presupposition control. We predict the effect is gradable, scaling with the presupposition's plausibility and its semantic relatedness to the queried attribute, and concentrating on low-frequency subjects. We then test the mechanism with a Location + Causal Intervention strategy: a linear probe should recover a 'writeback' signal at the subject position that carries the false attribute even though it was never queried; activation patching and attention analysis should show early attention over the presupposed-attribute tokens injects it into the subject representation; and ablating that attention or subtracting the writeback direction should restore correct recall of the unrelated attribute with high specificity. Experiments span GPT-J-6B, Llama-3-8B, and Qwen2.5-7B on PopQA/T-REx, evaluating writeback error rate, plausibility/relatedness dose-response, probe recovery, causal recovery, and specificity.
Experiments: Experiment 1 (H0 — cross-attribute presupposition dataset and eligibility): Build items where a false aside about attribute A can corrupt recall of an unrelated attribute B the model otherwise answers, with a true-presupposition baseline so the effect is attributable to falseness, not to adding a clause. Data: adapted from PopQA/T-REx, selecting subjects with >=2 known attributes under distinct relations; per subject a queried attribute B (relation r_B, correct b) and a presupposed attribute A (relation r_A, true a_true, plausible false a_false). Three conditions per item: no-presupposition, true-presupposition, false-presupposition; the query always asks only about B. Match a_false and a_true on token length; restrict to single-token-first B; target ~2,000 subjects across >=6 relation pairs; report coverage. Model: Llama-3-8B, frozen. Decisive metric (first): fraction of items answered correctly on B under BOTH no-presupposition and true-presupposition (the eligible set — writeback is only defined where recall is otherwise robust). Convincing: >= 1,200 eligible. Indecision band: 800-1,200 — reduced power; below 800 baseline B recall is too weak to detect corruption. Negative (B recall collapses under the true aside) means adding any clause breaks recall, so falseness cannot be isolated.

Experiment 2 (H1 — presupposition writeback corrupts an unrelated attribute): Test that a false aside lowers B accuracy beyond a true aside. Data: eligible set. Model: Llama-3-8B frozen; writeback error = B correct under no- and true-presupposition but wrong under false-presupposition. Systems compared: false- vs true-presupposition (the key paired baseline) vs no-presupposition. Decisive metric (first): writeback error-rate lift = P(B wrong | false) minus P(B wrong | true), paired McNemar test, controlling prompt length and b frequency. Convincing: lift >= 6 percentage points, CI excludes 0, with true-presupposition not worse than no-presupposition by more than 2 points. Indecision band: lift 2-6 points — a weak effect possibly from residual length/rarity mismatch; report as suggestive. Negative (lift CI includes 0) refutes H1: a false aside does not corrupt the unrelated attribute.

Experiment 3 (H1 — dose-response on plausibility and relatedness): Test that writeback error scales with a_false plausibility and r_A-r_B relatedness. Data: eligible set crossed over a_false plausibility bins (prior likelihood / type-match) and r_A-r_B relatedness (relation-embedding similarity, same- vs cross-domain). Model: Llama-3-8B frozen. Decisive metric (first): regression coefficients of writeback error on plausibility and on relatedness, with CIs; secondary, interaction with subject popularity. Convincing: both coefficients CI-exclude 0 with monotone per-bin curves, larger error for low-popularity subjects. Indecision band: exactly one coefficient CI-excludes 0 — partial dose-response; report which factor drives it and note the relatedness result specifically distinguishes targeted writeback from generic distraction. Negative (neither significant) refutes the gradable-scaling clause of H1.

Experiment 4 (H2 — the false attribute is written into the subject representation): Test that a_false becomes decodable in the subject-token residual stream even though A was never queried, and that correct b weakens. Data: eligible set across the three conditions. Model: Llama-3-8B frozen; train a logistic-regression probe (seeds {0,1,2}, 5-fold, label-shuffle null) to decode a_false from the subject-token residual at each layer, comparing false- vs true- vs no-presupposition. Decisive metric (first): peak-layer AUROC for detecting a_false in the subject representation under false-presupposition, and its cosine alignment with a_false's unembedding; secondary, drop in a decodable-b signal at the query position. Convincing: a_false AUROC >= 0.75 (above the true-presupposition run) with unembedding alignment above a random-direction null, and a measurable b-signal drop. Indecision band: AUROC 0.60-0.75 — weak/partial writeback signal; the causal test is then decisive. Negative (AUROC <= 0.60, no b-signal drop) means no subject-position writeback, undercutting H2.

Experiment 5 (H2/H3 — early attention writes back the false attribute, causally): Test that early subject-position attention over the a_false tokens is the injection route. Data: writeback-error items. Model: Llama-3-8B frozen; (a) identify early subject-position heads attending to the presupposed-attribute tokens and ablate that attention; (b) activation-patch the subject-token residual from a no-presupposition run into a false-presupposition run and measure recovery of b; (c) reverse control — inject the a_false direction into a no-presupposition run to induce B errors on demand. Systems compared: presupposition-attention ablation vs random-head ablation vs no-presupposition patch vs random-position patch. Decisive metric (first): writeback-error reduction from presupposition-attention ablation, net of random-head ablation. Convincing: ablation cuts writeback error >= 50% relative, no-presupposition patch recovers b >= 25 points net, reverse injection induces errors >= 25 points; random controls < 5 points. Indecision band: ablation reduction 20-50% relative — attention is one route among several. Negative (ablation ~ random) refutes H2's early-attention mechanism.

Experiment 6 (H3 — suppression restores unrelated-attribute recall without editing any fact): Test that subtracting the writeback direction fixes B cleanly. Data: eligible set, item-disjoint train/test; steering vector = mean subject-token difference (false-presupposition writeback-error minus matched true-presupposition states), seeds {0,1,2}, rank<=4, subtracted at the identified layers. Model: Llama-3-8B frozen except the subtracted direction. Systems compared: writeback subtraction, presupposition-attention ablation (Experiment 5a), ROME edit (expected not to help — no fact is wrong), FAITH false-premise-head constraint, random-direction control. Decisive metric (first): recovered-per-unit-collateral = B-recovery rate divided by accuracy drop on true-presupposition items (over-correction control); secondary, accuracy on 200 unrelated no-presupposition facts, fluency (perplexity delta). Convincing: recovery >= 30% with < 3-point drop on true-presupposition items and on the 200 facts, beating ROME and FAITH. Indecision band: recovery 15-30% or collateral 3-6 points — partial; report parity. Negative (no better than random, or harms true-presupposition cases) refutes H3.

Experiment 7 (H1/H3 — transfer and architecture generality): Test generality across relation pairs, subject types, and models. Data: eligible items partitioned by relation pair; suppression vector trained on a subset, applied to held-out relation pairs. Models: GPT-J-6B, Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, frozen; re-run Experiments 2-6, seeds {0,1,2}. Decisive metric (first): cross-relation-pair B-recovery relative to within-pair, plus replication of the writeback lift (Experiment 2) per model. Convincing: cross-pair recovery >= 50% of within-pair AND lift replicates (CI excludes 0) in >= 2 of 3 models. Indecision band: replication in 1 model or cross-pair 30-50% — model/relation-specific. Negative (no transfer/replication) confines H1-H3 to one model. Report whether larger models show lower writeback error.

Experiment 8 (H1 — safety-domain transfer): Test whether presupposition writeback produces higher-stakes cross-attribute errors. Data: constructed from a curated safe subset of clinical facts — a false aside about a drug's route-of-administration while asking its correct indication; ~400 items, restricted to publicly documented, non-actionable facts. Model: Llama-3-8B frozen; replicate Experiments 2-3. Decisive metric (first): writeback error-rate lift in the clinical setting versus the general-knowledge lift. Convincing: clinical lift CI excludes 0 and is at least as large as the general lift. Indecision band: clinical lift 2-6 points — present but modest; frame the elevated-stakes claim cautiously. Negative (no clinical lift) bounds the practical safety claim.
Risk Factors and Limitations: The true-presupposition control may not fully match the false one (a_false could be longer/rarer than a_true); we match token length and control for a_false frequency, and use the true-presupposition condition (not just no-presupposition) as the key baseline so any extra error must come from the falseness, not from adding a clause.

The effect could be generic distraction rather than attribute-specific writeback; the dose-response on r_A-r_B relatedness (Exp 3) and the subject-position decoding of a_false (Exp 4) distinguish targeted writeback from nonspecific interference.
The writeback signal and correct-b recall may be entangled; the causal patching/ablation tests (Exp 5), not probe AUROC alone, are decisive, and graded results remain informative.

Suppression could over-correct on cases where the presupposition is legitimately relevant, or degrade fluency; the true-presupposition and unrelated-fact specificity controls are central and utility may be capped.
Writeback errors may be rare relative to genuine ignorance; the paired within-subject design (same subject across conditions) maximizes power and a modest but significant lift is still informative.
A single transferable suppression vector may not exist if writeback is relation-pair-specific, limiting practical generality though still scientifically informative.
Multi-token B answers complicate readout; primary analysis restricts to single-token-first answers with reported coverage.
Findings on 6-8B models may not transfer to frontier-scale models beyond an academic budget.

Name: enumeration_closure_gate
Title: Knowing More Than It Lists: A Closure Signal That Terminates LLM Enumeration Before Its Knowledge Is Exhausted
Short Hypothesis: When an LLM enumerates the members of a set (e.g., 'list the countries bordering France'), it stops not because it has exhausted its stored members but because a distinct, query-independent 'closure' signal in the residual stream crosses a threshold. We hypothesize (1) at the moment the model emits a stop, additional valid members remain internally recoverable (a completeness gap), (2) a linear 'closure' direction predicts termination and is largely driven by count/list-length priors rather than by actual member-set exhaustion, and (3) suppressing this closure direction extends enumeration to recover more true members with high specificity, whereas it is not fixed by simply prompting 'list more'.
Related Work: Prior work explains the promote-then-suppress mechanism for generating *distinct* one-to-many answers (Promote-Suppress-Iterate 2025) and how counting is computed layerwise (CountScope 2025; When Can Transformers Count to n 2024). Benchmarks show LLMs cannot enumerate completely (Can LMs Store/Retrieve 1-to-N 2023; Do LLMs Know How Much They Know 2024; Olympic Rankings 2024), are brittle on set membership (Brittleness of Set Membership 2025), and cannot detect omissions (AbsenceBench 2025). Aggregation/completeness is studied at the systems level (AGGBench 2026; GraphRAG). Crucially, all of these describe how distinct answers are produced, how counting works, or that enumeration is incomplete behaviorally; none isolate the *termination decision* as a mechanism, none test whether stored members remain internally recoverable at the stop point, and none show a closure signal that gates completeness independent of exhaustion. This is orthogonal to my prior proposals (all single-answer recall/gating): here the object is the decision to *stop enumerating* and the completeness gap it causes.
Abstract: Large language models routinely stop listing set members before exhausting what they know: asked to list authors of an author, films of a director, or countries bordering a nation, they produce a plausible-length answer and stop, omitting members they can produce when prompted individually. Prior work explains how models generate distinct successive answers and how they count, but not why they decide to stop. We propose that enumeration termination is governed by a distinct, query-independent closure signal in the residual stream that crosses a threshold and halts listing—often before the model's stored member set is exhausted, producing a completeness gap. We test three claims on one-to-many factual queries. (1) Completeness gap: at the position where the model emits its stop token, additional valid members are still internally recoverable (via linear probing / logit-lens over member-typed candidates and via single-item verification prompts), showing the stop is premature relative to stored knowledge. (2) Closure locus and drivers: a linear closure direction, decodable at intermediate layers before the stop token, predicts termination, and regression shows it tracks generic list-length/count priors (position in list, typical set-size for the relation) more than actual set exhaustion. (3) Causal intervention: suppressing the closure direction (or ablating the attention that reads it) extends enumeration and recovers additional true members, with specificity controls ensuring the model does not fabricate members or degrade on sets it correctly completes, and outperforming a 'keep listing' re-prompt baseline. Experiments span GPT-J-6B, Llama-3-8B, and Qwen2.5-7B on curated one-to-many relations, evaluating completeness-gap prevalence, closure-prediction AUROC, recovered-member yield, precision, and fluency.
Experiments: Experiment 1 (H0 — one-to-many dataset with complete ground truth): Build set-valued queries with authoritative complete membership so a completeness gap can be measured. Data: constructed from Wikidata for five set-valued relations (countries bordering X; films directed by X; children of X; member states of an organization; elements in a chemical group), sampled to cover small (3-8) and large (15-40) true set sizes; target ~600 queries (>=100 per relation, balanced across size bins). For each, record the model's free enumeration and the ground-truth member set; restrict to single-token-first members where readout requires it; report coverage. Model: Llama-3-8B, frozen; temperature 0, 3 prompt seeds. Decisive metric (first): fraction of queries with complete, verifiable Wikidata ground truth and a well-defined stop token in the model's output (the eligible set). Convincing: >= 400 eligible across both size bins. Indecision band: 250-400 eligible — reduced power, reported; below 250 the ground-truth coverage is too thin to estimate gaps. Negative (few relations have clean complete membership) means the phenomenon cannot be measured with authoritative labels and the relation set must be revised.

Experiment 2 (H1 — completeness gap at the stop): Test that at the stop, additional true members remain internally recoverable. Data: eligible set. Model: Llama-3-8B frozen; at the list-ending token, (a) apply tuned-lens over member-typed candidate tokens (restricted to the relation's answer type, excluding already-listed members) and (b) run single-item verification prompts ('Is Y a member of {set}?') for the top unlisted candidates. Systems compared: observed recoverability vs a null where stopping coincides with exhaustion. Decisive metric (first): completeness-gap rate = fraction of stops with >= 1 unlisted true member that is BOTH lens-recoverable AND verification-confirmed. Convincing: gap rate >= 30%, concentrated on large sets. Indecision band: gap rate 15-30% — a real but modest gap; report and rely on the causal test for interpretation. Negative (gap rate < 15%, stops coincide with exhaustion) refutes H1: the model stops because it is out of members.

Experiment 3 (H2 — a decodable closure direction separable from exhaustion): Test that termination is predicted by a closure signal distinct from a remaining-members signal. Data: pre-stop steps from eligible enumerations. Model: Llama-3-8B frozen; train a stop-prediction probe (will the next step be a stop?) and a remaining-members probe (does the residual still encode unlisted members?) via logistic regression at each layer (seeds {0,1,2}, 5-fold, label-shuffle null). Decisive metric (first): stop-prediction peak-layer AUROC, and the residualized unique AUROC of each probe after partialling out the other. Convincing: stop AUROC >= 0.75 and each probe retains unique AUROC >= 0.65 after residualization (closure and exhaustion are separable). Indecision band: unique AUROC 0.55-0.65 — the two signals are largely entangled; H2's 'distinct direction' is weak. Negative (stop AUROC <= 0.6, or no unique closure signal) refutes the closure-direction claim.

Experiment 4 (H2 — closure is driven by length priors, not exhaustion): Test that the closure signal is dominated by generic count/list-length priors over true member-set exhaustion. Data: pre-stop steps. Model: Llama-3-8B frozen. Decisive metric (first): partial regression coefficients of the closure-probe output on (a) length priors (items already emitted, typical set-size for the relation from other subjects), (b) exhaustion signals (true members remaining, recoverability from Experiment 2), (c) surface cues (self-attention/repetition), with CIs and relative variance explained. Convincing: length-prior block explains a strictly larger share of closure variance than the exhaustion block, both CI-excluding 0. Indecision band: the two blocks' variance shares within 5 percentage points of each other — closure reflects both roughly equally; report as mixed. Negative (exhaustion dominates) refutes H2's 'driven by priors' clause: closure tracks real exhaustion.

Experiment 5 (H3 — closure suppression causally extends valid enumeration): Test that removing the closure signal continues true enumeration and that injecting it forces premature stops. Data: eligible queries with a completeness gap. Model: Llama-3-8B frozen; (a) subtract the learned low-rank closure vector at the identified layers when a stop is imminent; (b) ablate attention heads reading the closure signal; (c) reverse control — inject the closure direction early to force premature stopping. Systems compared: closure suppression vs random-direction suppression vs head-ablation vs random-head ablation. Decisive metric (first): additional true members recovered per query (net of random suppression), with precision of newly emitted tokens (fraction that are ground-truth members, not repeats/fabrications). Convincing: >= 1.0 additional true member per large-set query at precision >= 0.7, and reverse injection shortens lists >= 25%. Indecision band: 0.3-1.0 additional true members or precision 0.5-0.7 — extends lists but with rising fabrication; report the completeness-precision trade. Negative (no net gain, or precision at chance) refutes H3's causal core.

Experiment 6 (H3 — closure-suppression recovery beats re-prompting, with specificity): Test that suppression recovers members more cleanly than simply asking for more. Data: eligible set, query-disjoint train/test; dose-controlled suppression. Model: Llama-3-8B frozen except the subtracted direction. Systems compared: closure suppression vs 'are there more? continue listing' re-prompt vs temperature increase vs beam widening. Decisive metric (first): recovered-true-member yield at matched false-member rate; secondary specificity — on small sets the model already completes, the false-member rate must not rise (measured pre/post), and fluency (perplexity delta). Convincing: suppression recovers >= 50% more true members than the best re-prompt baseline at equal or lower false-member rate, with < 3-point false-member increase on already-complete small sets. Indecision band: 20-50% more, or a 3-6-point false-member increase — partial advantage; report parity with re-prompting. Negative (no advantage over 'list more', or fabrication explodes) refutes H3's specificity claim and its distinction from prompting.

Experiment 7 (H1/H3 — transfer and architecture generality): Test that the closure signal and its suppression generalize across relations/sizes and models. Data: eligible queries partitioned by relation; closure vector trained on a subset, applied to held-out relations. Models: GPT-J-6B, Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, frozen; re-run Experiments 2-6, seeds {0,1,2}. Decisive metric (first): cross-relation recovered-member yield relative to within-relation, plus replication of the completeness gap (Experiment 2) per model. Convincing: cross-relation yield >= 50% of within-relation AND completeness gap replicates in >= 2 of 3 models. Indecision band: replication in 1 model or cross-relation 30-50% — relation/model-specific. Negative (no transfer/replication) confines findings to one model. Report whether larger models have smaller completeness gaps.

Experiment 8 (H1/H2 — source of premature closure): Quantify whether premature closure is driven by generic length priors and tail-member obscurity rather than storage. Data: eligible set. Model: Llama-3-8B frozen (plus Pythia 1.4B/2.8B/6.9B for scale). Decisive metric (first): partial regression coefficients of completeness-gap rate on (true set size, member-popularity distribution / tail obscurity, relation frequency), with CIs. Convincing: set-size and tail-obscurity coefficients CI-exclude 0 and dominate, gap increasing with size and tail obscurity, decreasing across Pythia scale. Indecision band: coefficient CI half-width overlapping 0 by < 0.02 — sources entangled; report inconclusive. Negative (gap unrelated to size/obscurity) means closure is not a length-prior effect, qualifying H2's mechanistic reading.
Risk Factors and Limitations: The completeness gap could reflect that unlisted members are not truly stored (probe/logit-lens false positives); the single-item verification control (Exp 2b) with conservative thresholds is essential and coverage is reported.

Closure and exhaustion signals may be entangled rather than separable directions; the causal suppression/injection tests (Exp 5), not probe AUROC alone, are decisive, and graded results remain informative.

Closure suppression could induce fabrication or repetition (the model keeps listing false members); precision and false-member specificity controls (Exp 6) are central and utility may be capped if suppression trades completeness for hallucination.
Ground-truth set completeness is hard for open-ended relations; we restrict to relations with authoritative complete membership (Wikidata-verifiable) and report coverage limits.
A single transferable closure vector may not exist if termination is relation-specific, limiting practical generality though still scientifically informative.
Multi-token members and stop-token detection vary across tokenizers; primary analysis restricts to single-token-first members and canonical stop conditions with reported coverage.
Findings on 6-8B models may not transfer to frontier-scale models beyond an academic budget.

However, the premise that models stop early is already known, so novelty depends on successfully isolating a distinct termination mechanism rather than just re-describing incomplete enumeration.

Name: granularity_overcommitment
Title: Too Precise to Be Right: A Query-Independent Precision Prior That Makes LLMs Overcommit to a Granularity and Hide Coarser Correct Knowledge
Short Hypothesis: When answering a factual query that admits answers at multiple granularities (e.g., 'August 4, 1961' vs '1961' vs 'the 1960s' for a birth date), LLMs select the *specificity level* of the answer via a distinct, largely query-independent 'precision prior' computed before the specific content is fully resolved. Overcommitment to a too-fine granularity is a common failure mode: the model emits a confident, wrong specific value even though it reliably stores the coarser, correct value. We hypothesize (1) the chosen granularity is linearly decodable from intermediate activations before the answer, and is driven by generic format/precision priors more than by how confidently the fine-grained value is stored; (2) overcommitment errors concentrate on long-tail entities where the fine value is uncertain but a coarse value is stored; and (3) suppressing the precision-prior direction (not editing any fact) shifts the model to the correct coarser answer with high specificity, unlike a 'be less specific' re-prompt.
Related Work: GRANOLA QA (Yona et al. 2024) behaviorally shows LLMs default to overly specific answers that are often wrong, and that evaluating against multi-granularity answers reveals ~20 points of hidden knowledge (larger for rare entities); their fix, DRAG, is a decoding heuristic tied to output uncertainty, with no mechanistic account. Inside-Out (2025) and 'Empty Shelves or Lost Keys?' (2026) show a large recall/access gap between encoded and expressed knowledge but do not treat *answer granularity* as the axis of failure. Concept Depth (2024) and layer-wise knowledge-encoding studies characterize where concepts of varying complexity emerge but not a granularity-selection decision. Knowledge-editing granularity work (DiKE 2025, FiNE 2025) concerns editing precision at the fact level, not the model's own choice of answer specificity. Crucially, no prior work (i) isolates granularity/precision selection as a distinct internal decision separable from content retrieval, (ii) tests that it is driven by a query-independent precision prior rather than fine-value confidence, or (iii) causally recovers coarser correct knowledge by intervening on that decision. This is orthogonal to my prior proposals, which all concern single-granularity retrieval, competition, arbitration, or enumeration closure; here the object is the *specificity level* of the answer.
Abstract: Large language models often answer factual questions with a confidently wrong, overly specific value even when they reliably know a coarser, correct one—stating an exact but wrong date when they know the correct decade. Prior work documents this behaviorally and patches it at decoding time, but why models commit to a granularity is unknown. We propose that answer specificity is set by a distinct, largely query-independent precision prior computed in intermediate layers before the specific content is resolved, and that granularity overcommitment—emitting a too-fine, wrong value while the coarser correct value is internally available—is a systematic, mechanistically localizable failure. We test three claims on multi-granularity factual queries (dates, locations, quantities, taxonomic categories). (1) Dissociability and locus: a linear 'granularity' probe predicts the specificity level of the forthcoming answer before it is written, is separable (via residualization) from a content probe that predicts the specific value, and—by regression—tracks generic format/precision cues (relation type, prompt phrasing, entity popularity) more than the internal confidence in the fine-grained value. (2) Overcommitment geometry: overcommitment errors concentrate on long-tail entities where the fine value is uncertain but a coarser value is verifiably stored (via coarse-level probing and direct coarse-question verification), above frequency-matched baselines. (3) Causal recovery: suppressing the precision-prior direction, or patching it from a coarse-answer run, shifts the model to the correct coarser answer with high specificity—preserving cases where the fine answer is correct—and outperforms a 'be less specific' re-prompt and fact editing. Experiments span GPT-J-6B, Llama-3-8B, and Qwen2.5-7B on GRANOLA-EQ and multi-granularity T-REx/PopQA, evaluating probe separability, driver regression, overcommitment prevalence, causal recovery, and specificity.
Experiments: Experiment 1 (H0 — multi-granularity dataset): Build items with an ordered set of correct answers at increasing coarseness so granularity choice and correctness can be scored independently. Data: GRANOLA-EQ (multi-granularity EntityQuestions) as-is, augmented with items built from T-REx/PopQA for four answer types — dates (day/month/year/decade), locations (city/region/country), quantities (exact/rounded/order-of-magnitude), taxonomic categories (species/genus/family). Target ~2,500 items across the four types; for each record the ordered correct answers, the model's free-form answer, and its granularity level; restrict readout to single-token-first coarse answers where needed; report coverage. Model: Llama-3-8B, frozen; temperature 0. Decisive metric (first): fraction of items with a well-formed granularity ladder (>= 2 distinct correct coarseness levels) and a parseable model granularity level. Convincing: >= 1,500 usable items, >= 300 per answer type. Indecision band: 1,000-1,500 — reduced per-type power, reported; below 1,000 the ladders are too sparse to estimate granularity effects. Negative (few items admit multiple granularities) means the phenomenon is not well-posed for these types and the type set must be revised.

Experiment 2 (H0 — coarse-value storage verification): Establish, per wrong-fine item, that the coarser correct value is stored, so overcommitment is separable from ignorance. Data: usable items whose fine answer is wrong. Model: Llama-3-8B frozen; verify the coarse value via (a) a direct coarse-question prompt ('In what decade was X born?') and (b) a logistic-regression content probe decoding the coarse value from the residual stream (seeds {0,1,2}, 5-fold, label-shuffle null). Decisive metric (first): fraction of wrong-fine items where the coarse value is BOTH answered correctly directly AND probe-decodable (the 'overcommitment-candidate' set). Convincing: >= 600 candidates. Indecision band: 350-600 — reduced power, reported; below 350 overcommitment cannot be reliably separated from missing knowledge. Negative (coarse value rarely stored on wrong-fine items) means fine errors are genuine ignorance, not overcommitment, refuting the premise.

Experiment 3 (H1 — granularity decodable before content): Test that the answer's specificity level is decodable from intermediate activations before the fine value resolves. Data: usable items. Model: Llama-3-8B frozen; train a granularity probe (ordinal fine/mid/coarse) and a content probe (fine value) at every layer via logistic/ordinal regression (seeds {0,1,2}, 5-fold, label-shuffle null, tuned-lens capacity control). Decisive metric (first): onset-layer difference = (layer where content probe first resolves the fine value at >= 0.7) minus (layer where granularity probe first reaches >= 0.7), bootstrap CI; secondary, residualized unique granularity AUROC after partialling out content. Convincing: onset difference >= 3 layers (granularity earlier), CI excludes 0, unique granularity AUROC >= 0.65. Indecision band: onset difference 1-3 layers — weak ordering; H1's 'before content' rests on the causal test. Negative (difference CI includes 0 or granularity not uniquely decodable) refutes the pre-content precision-prior claim.

Experiment 4 (H1 — precision prior driven by format cues, not fine-value confidence): Test that granularity is dominated by generic precision priors over how confidently the fine value is stored. Data: usable items with granularity-probe output. Model: Llama-3-8B frozen. Decisive metric (first): partial variance in the granularity-probe output explained by the format block (relation type, prompt phrasing open/'be brief'/'be precise', fixed per-relation default granularity) versus the fine-confidence block (content-probe strength, top-fine logit margin), with CIs. Convincing: the format block explains a strictly larger variance share than the fine-confidence block, both CI-excluding 0. Indecision band: the two blocks' shares within 5 points of each other — granularity reflects both; report as mixed. Negative (fine-confidence dominates) refutes H1's 'query-independent prior' clause.

Experiment 5 (H2 — overcommitment concentrates on long-tail entities): Test that overcommitment errors concentrate where the entity is rare (fine value uncertain) but a coarse value is stored. Data: overcommitment-candidate set (fine wrong, coarse stored). Model: Llama-3-8B frozen. Systems compared: overcommitment rate as a function of entity popularity and per-relation default precision vs a null controlling answer frequency and lexical similarity (logistic regression; permutation CI). Decisive metric (first): partial coefficient of (low) entity popularity on overcommitment probability, and of default precision, with CIs. Convincing: both coefficients CI-exclude 0, with monotone concentration on long-tail entities and high-precision relations. Indecision band: exactly one coefficient CI-excludes 0 — partial concentration; report which factor drives it. Negative (neither significant) refutes H2.

Experiment 6 (H1/H3 — causal test of the precision-prior direction): Test that granularity is causally set by a separable direction, not by content. Data: overcommitment-candidate items and matched coarse-answer runs (elicited by a 'be approximate' prompt). Model: Llama-3-8B frozen; (a) subtract the learned low-rank granularity vector (mean coarse-answer minus fine-answer residual difference) at the identified layers and test a shift to the correct coarse answer; (b) patch the granularity representation from a coarse run into an overcommitment run; (c) reverse control — inject the fine-precision direction to force overcommitment; (d) content control — patch only the content direction and confirm granularity is unchanged. Systems compared: granularity suppression/patch vs content-only patch vs random-direction. Decisive metric (first): coarse-correct recovery rate = fraction of overcommitment items shifted to the correct coarse value (not a new wrong fine value), net of random. Convincing: net recovery >= 25 points, content-only patch < 5 points, reverse injection induces overcommitment >= 25 points. Indecision band: net recovery 10-25 points — granularity partly separable; report. Negative (< 10 points or content-patch equally shifts granularity) refutes the separable-precision-prior mechanism.

Experiment 7 (H3 — recovery beats re-prompting, with specificity): Test that suppressing the precision prior recovers the coarse-correct answer more cleanly than asking for less specificity. Data: candidate set, item-disjoint train/test; dose-controlled suppression. Model: Llama-3-8B frozen except the subtracted direction. Systems compared: granularity suppression vs 'be less specific / give the decade' re-prompt vs DRAG-style uncertainty decoding vs ROME edit (expected not to help) vs random-direction. Decisive metric (first): recovered-per-unit-collateral = coarse-correct recovery rate divided by the coarsening rate on 200 items the model answers correctly at fine granularity (the over-coarsening control); secondary, accuracy on 200 unrelated facts, fluency (perplexity delta). Convincing: recovery >= 30% with < 3-point coarsening of correct-fine items, beating the re-prompt baseline on recovered-per-collateral. Indecision band: recovery 15-30% or coarsening 3-6 points — partial; report parity with re-prompting. Negative (no advantage over 're-prompt', or correct-fine answers get coarsened) refutes H3.

Experiment 8 (H2/H3 — transfer, generality, and source): Test generality across relations/types and models, and quantify the precision-prior source. Data: candidate items partitioned by relation/answer type; suppression vector trained on a subset, applied to held-out. Models: GPT-J-6B, Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, frozen (plus Pythia 1.4B/2.8B/6.9B for scale); re-run Experiments 2-7, seeds {0,1,2}. Decisive metric (first): cross-relation coarse-correct recovery relative to within-relation, replication of overcommitment concentration (Experiment 5) per model, and partial regression coefficients of overcommitment rate on (entity popularity, per-relation default granularity, fine-value uncertainty). Convincing: cross-relation recovery >= 50% of within-relation, concentration replicates in >= 2 of 3 models, and the popularity/uncertainty coefficients CI-exclude 0 with overcommitment falling across Pythia scale. Indecision band: replication in 1 model, cross-relation 30-50%, or source coefficients CI half-width overlapping 0 by < 0.02 — model-specific or entangled sources; report inconclusive. Negative (no transfer, no source signal) confines H1-H3 to one model and one relation family.
Risk Factors and Limitations: Granularity and content signals may be entangled rather than cleanly separable; the causal patching/steering tests (Exp 6), not probe onset alone, are decisive, and a graded result would weaken the strong dissociation while remaining informative.
Verifying the coarse value is 'stored' risks overestimation from prompt leakage; conservative content-probe thresholds and direct coarse-question verification with reported coverage mitigate this.
Granularity is naturally ordinal/graded, not discrete; we model it ordinally and report continuous granularity scores rather than forcing clean levels.

Granularity suppression could over-coarsen—making the model vague even when it knows the precise answer; the correctly-answered-fine specificity control (Exp 7) is central and utility may be capped even if the analysis holds.

The precision prior may be partly query-dependent (some phrasings legitimately demand specificity); the driver regression separates format cues from fine-value confidence rather than claiming full query-independence.
A single transferable suppression vector may not exist if granularity control is relation-specific, limiting practical generality though still scientifically informative.
Multi-token coarse answers (e.g., month names, region names) complicate readout; primary analysis restricts to single-token-first answers with reported coverage.
Findings on 6–8B models may not transfer to frontier-scale models beyond an academic budget.

novelty.reasoning: The core novelty is not the behavioral phenomenon itself (GRANOLA already shows over-specific wrong answers), but a mechanistic account: a separable, largely query-independent precision prior that sets answer granularity before content resolution, plus causal steering of that axis. That is a meaningful delta over DRAG and nearby hidden-knowledge/access-gap work. The main risk is entanglement with content confidence and partial query dependence, which could reduce the strength of the claim if separability is weak.

impact.reasoning: The underlying problem is real: LLMs often overcommit to overly specific answers and hide coarser correct knowledge. That matters for factual QA, calibration, hallucination, and evaluation communities, and could change how people think about expressing uncertainty and answer granularity. The so-what test is positive because either outcome informs evaluation and intervention design. Still, the topic is somewhat specialized and the likely uptake is strongest in interpretability and knowledge-evaluation subfields rather than broad ML practice.
