Name: spontaneous_vs_provoked_confabulation
Title: Two Types of Confabulation: Why LLMs Refuse When Asked but Fabricate When They Speak Freely
Short Hypothesis: Borrowing the classic clinical double dissociation between provoked and spontaneous confabulation, we hypothesize LLMs have two distinct confabulation regimes with different internal mechanisms: (1) provoked confabulation, when directly queried about an unknown entity, is gated by the model's entity-recognition/knowledge-awareness signal (so it can refuse); (2) spontaneous confabulation, when the model freely generates extended text and fabricated facts appear unbidden, bypasses that same self-knowledge gate because generation-continuation pressure causally overrides it. The prediction: the model's own 'I don't know this' signal is present but causally disconnected during free generation, so an entity it would refuse to answer about when asked is confidently fabricated about when it produces the mention itself.
Related Work: The clinical literature (Kopelman 1987; Schnider et al. 1996) establishes a double dissociation between provoked confabulation (a normal gap-filling response to a faulty memory when questioned) and spontaneous confabulation (unbidden fabrication reflecting reality/temporal-monitoring failure). In LLMs, 'Do I Know This Entity?' (2024) finds causal entity-recognition directions that gate knowledge refusal under direct queries; 'LLMs Do NOT Really Know What They Don't Know' (2025) shows internal states track recall process not truth; answerability directions (2023) and factual self-awareness features (2025) are all measured under direct-query conditions. Crucially, every prior work studies the knowledge-awareness/refusal signal in the *provoked* setting (a question is posed). None test whether the same signal is *engaged versus bypassed* when the model spontaneously introduces an entity during free generation, nor establish a provoked-vs-spontaneous behavioral dissociation, nor localize why the self-knowledge gate fails to fire during generation momentum. This differs from all my prior proposals, which concern direct-query retrieval/expression; here the object is the generation *mode* (queried vs free) and its effect on whether self-knowledge causally gates output.
Abstract: Human neuropsychology distinguishes two confabulations: provoked (fabrication in response to a question, a normal reaction to faulty memory) and spontaneous (unbidden fabrication reflecting a failure to monitor reality). We ask whether large language models exhibit an analogous dissociation and whether the two arise from different mechanisms. LLMs are known to carry an internal entity-recognition signal that gates refusal when they are asked about an unknown entity. We hypothesize this gate is engaged when the model is provoked by a direct query but bypassed when the model spontaneously introduces an unknown entity mid-generation under coherence/continuation pressure, so a model that correctly refuses 'Who is <obscure name>?' will nonetheless fabricate a detailed biography for the same name when free-generating a passage that happens to mention it. We first document the behavioral dissociation: for matched unknown entities, compare fabrication rate and confidence across a provoked condition (direct query) and a spontaneous condition (free continuation where the entity is planted or self-introduced). We predict spontaneous fabrication far exceeds provoked fabrication for the same entities, above matched baselines. We then test the mechanism with a Location + Causal Intervention strategy: a linear/SAE entity-recognition probe should still fire ('unknown') during spontaneous fabrication, showing the self-knowledge signal is present but causally decoupled; activation patching and attention analysis should show that in the spontaneous regime the recognition direction fails to disrupt downstream attribute-extraction heads (unlike the provoked regime); and amplifying the recognition signal (or the attention path it acts through) at the entity position during free generation should re-engage the gate and convert spontaneous fabrication into appropriate hedging/refusal, with specificity controls preserving generation about known entities. Experiments span Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, and Gemma-2-9B, evaluating dissociation prevalence, probe firing under each regime, causal re-gating, and specificity.
Experiments: Experiment 1 (H0 — matched unknown/known entity dataset): Build entities the model demonstrably cannot recall (so any specific attribute is a fabrication) plus a matched known set. Data: constructed — ~250 clearly-unknown entities (nonexistent/fictional names generated to be plausible but absent from any corpus, plus ultra-long-tail real entities) and ~250 popularity-matched known entities; unknown status validated by direct probing and an entity-recognition probe; restrict the unknown set to entities the model refuses/hedges on under a direct query. Model: Llama-3-8B, frozen. Decisive metric (first): fraction of candidate unknowns that (a) are refused/hedged under a direct query and (b) read as 'unknown' by the recognition probe (the eligible unknown set), and the matched known set answered assertively. Convincing: >= 200 eligible unknowns and >= 200 knowns. Indecision band: 120-200 eligible unknowns — reduced power, reported; below 120 the dissociation test is under-powered. Negative (model does not reliably refuse any unknowns under direct query) means there is no provoked-refusal baseline and H1/H2 cannot be posed on this model.

Experiment 2 (H0 — provoked vs spontaneous elicitation and scoring): Create matched provoked and spontaneous conditions per entity and a fabrication scorer. Data: eligible entities. Model: Llama-3-8B frozen; (a) provoked prompt ('Who is X? What did X do?'); (b) spontaneous prompt embedding X in a free-generation task with continuation pressure ('Write a short encyclopedia paragraph:' with X as topic, or a narrative introducing X). Scoring: per-entity fabrication rate (asserts specific false attributes vs hedges/refuses) and asserted-attribute token probabilities, judged by GPT-4o plus attribute-level ground truth for fictional entities (any specific attribute = fabrication); human spot-check on 100 items for judge calibration (report kappa). Decisive metric (first): judge-human kappa on the calibration sample. Convincing: kappa >= 0.8, giving a usable fabrication label. Indecision band: kappa 0.6-0.8 — noisy scorer; restrict to fictional entities where fabrication is unambiguous and report shrinkage. Negative (kappa < 0.6) means fabrication cannot be scored reliably and the design must change.

Experiment 3 (H1 — provoked/spontaneous dissociation exists): Test that the same unknown entity is fabricated about more in the spontaneous than the provoked mode. Data: eligible unknowns, both modes. Model: Llama-3-8B frozen. Systems compared: spontaneous vs provoked fabrication rate (paired, same entity), vs a single-signal null treating fabrication as one entity-difficulty signal independent of mode (logistic regression with mode x entity; paired McNemar); matched-known control (should assert in both modes). Decisive metric (first): fabrication-rate lift = P(fabricate | spontaneous) minus P(fabricate | provoked), paired, CI. Convincing: lift >= 15 percentage points, CI excludes 0, while knowns assert in both modes. Indecision band: lift 5-15 points — a weak mode effect possibly from format; report as suggestive and lean on Experiment 4. Negative (lift CI includes 0) refutes H1: fabrication is mode-independent.

Experiment 4 (H2 — recognition signal is present in both regimes): Test that the 'unknown' self-knowledge signal fires equally under provoked and spontaneous modes, so spontaneous fabrication is a gate-bypass not a recognition failure. Data: eligible unknowns, both modes. Model: Llama-3-8B frozen; recover the entity-recognition direction via a linear probe on the entity-token residual stream (and SAE features where available), seeds {0,1,2}, label-shuffle null. Decisive metric (first): peak-layer unknown-vs-known probe AUROC at the entity position in the spontaneous mode, and the difference from the provoked mode. Convincing: spontaneous AUROC >= 0.75 and within 0.05 of provoked (signal present and mode-invariant). Indecision band: spontaneous AUROC 0.60-0.75 or 0.05-0.15 below provoked — the signal is partly weakened, a mix of bypass and recognition degradation; report as mixed. Negative (spontaneous AUROC << provoked, e.g., gap > 0.15) means the signal fails to fire in free generation — a recognition failure, not a bypass — refuting H2's core.

Experiment 5 (H2 — the gate is causally disconnected in free generation): Test that the recognition signal ceases to disrupt attribute-extraction in the spontaneous mode. Data: eligible unknowns, both modes. Model: Llama-3-8B frozen; (a) measure attention of attribute-extraction heads to the entity token in each mode; (b) activation-patch the entity-token recognition representation from a provoked (refusing) run into a spontaneous (fabricating) run and test whether fabrication is suppressed; (c) reverse control — patch spontaneous into provoked. Systems compared: recognition-patch vs random-position patch. Decisive metric (first): fabrication-suppression rate from the provoked->spontaneous recognition patch, net of random. Convincing: net suppression >= 25 points AND attribute-head attention to the entity is measurably higher in the spontaneous mode despite equal recognition firing (Experiment 4). Indecision band: net suppression 10-25 points — the gate is partly connected in free generation. Negative (< 10 points or no attention difference) means the gate is not specifically disconnected, refuting H2's causal-disconnection claim.

Experiment 6 (H2 — re-gating restores refusal in free generation): Test that restoring the recognition signal's effect converts spontaneous fabrication into hedging. Data: eligible unknowns, entity-disjoint train/test; amplify the 'unknown' direction (or restore its attention effect on attribute-extraction heads) at the entity position during free generation, seeds {0,1,2}, dose-controlled. Model: Llama-3-8B frozen except the injected effect. Systems compared: re-gating vs 'only state what you are sure of' system-prompt vs refusal fine-tuning vs random-direction. Decisive metric (first): recovered-per-unit-collateral = spontaneous-fabrication-to-hedge conversion rate divided by over-refusal rate on 200 known entities (which must stay assertive); secondary, accuracy on the 200 knowns, fluency (perplexity delta). Convincing: conversion >= 30% with < 5-point over-refusal on knowns, beating the system-prompt baseline on recovered-per-collateral. Indecision band: conversion 15-30% or over-refusal 5-10 points — partial; report parity with prompting. Negative (no better than system-prompt, or knowns get refused) refutes the re-gating claim.

Experiment 7 (H1 — continuation-pressure dose-response): Test that spontaneous fabrication scales with continuation pressure while the recognition signal stays constant (momentum overrides the gate). Data: eligible unknowns rendered at varied continuation pressure (entity position in the passage, how committed the prior text is to elaboration, sampling temperature 0.0-1.0). Model: Llama-3-8B frozen. Decisive metric (first): regression coefficient of fabrication rate on continuation-pressure index, with the entity-position recognition-probe AUROC measured at each level. Convincing: fabrication-rate coefficient CI excludes 0 (rises with pressure) while recognition AUROC stays within 0.05 across levels. Indecision band: coefficient CI excludes 0 but recognition AUROC also drifts > 0.05 — pressure both raises fabrication and erodes recognition, confounding the override story; report as mixed. Negative (fabrication flat in pressure) refutes the continuation-pressure override account in H1.

Experiment 8 (H1/H2 — transfer and architecture generality): Test that the dissociation and re-gating generalize across entity types and models. Data: eligible entities partitioned by type (fictional vs long-tail real); re-gating vector trained on one type, applied to the other. Models: Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, frozen; re-run Experiments 3-6, seeds {0,1,2}. Decisive metric (first): cross-type re-gating conversion relative to within-type, plus replication of the provoked/spontaneous lift (Experiment 3) per model. Convincing: cross-type conversion >= 50% of within-type AND the lift replicates (CI excludes 0) in >= 2 of 3 models. Indecision band: replication in 1 model or cross-type 30-50% — model/type-specific. Negative (no transfer/replication) confines H1-H2 to one model. Report whether larger models close the provoked-vs-spontaneous gap.
Risk Factors and Limitations: The provoked and spontaneous conditions differ in prompt format, so the dissociation could be a format artifact rather than a genuine mode effect; matched-known-entity controls, the single-signal null (Exp 3), and the constant-recognition-signal finding (Exp 4) are essential to attribute the effect to generation mode.

The recognition signal might in fact fire less in the spontaneous regime (a recognition failure, not a gate bypass); Exp 4 directly tests this and either outcome is informative, but it could weaken the specific bypass claim.

The recognition direction and its attention effect may be entangled/distributed; the causal patching and attention tests (Exp 5), not probe firing alone, are decisive, and graded results remain informative.
Re-gating could cause over-refusal on known entities or degrade fluency; the known-entity specificity control and over-refusal metric are central and utility may be capped.

Scoring 'fabrication' during free generation is noisy for real long-tail entities (some asserted facts may be true); using fictional/nonexistent entities where any specific attribute is a fabrication mitigates this, with reported coverage.
A single transferable re-gating vector may not exist if the bypass is entity-type-specific, limiting practical generality though still scientifically informative.
Findings on 7-9B models may not transfer to frontier-scale models beyond an academic budget.

novelty.reasoning: Core novelty is the proposed provoked-vs-spontaneous confabulation dissociation in LLMs, plus the claim that an entity-recognition/self-knowledge signal remains present but becomes causally disconnected during free generation. Relative to prior direct-query work, this is a non-trivial mode shift rather than a simple re-run. The closest prior family is entity-recognition/refusal direction work; the actual delta is testing the same gate under spontaneous generation pressure and attempting causal re-gating mid-generation. The main novelty risk is that it may reduce to a prompt-format/formatting effect or a weaker version of known self-knowledge findings.

impact.reasoning: The underlying phenomenon—models fabricating more when they speak freely than when directly asked—is practically important for hallucination, safety, and interpretability. If true, it could change how people evaluate honesty and how they intervene on generation-time failures. The strongest case is that it reveals a concrete safety-relevant failure mode and suggests a causal fix. Serious researchers and practitioners would likely care because it speaks to when self-knowledge signals do and do not protect against fabrication. The 'so what?' test is positive: if the result holds, people would likely adjust evals and mitigation strategies; if it fails, that still informs where safety interventions are brittle.

review.reasoning: The proposal is testable and has a clear causal story, but several claims are stronger than the current design can cleanly support. The biggest gaps are confounds between provoked and spontaneous prompts, noisy fabrication labeling, and the possibility that the signal simply weakens rather than stays constant and becomes disconnected. The mechanism is plausible but underspecified: probe presence, attention pathways, and causal gating need tighter separation. The experiments are ambitious and mostly feasible, but the proposal needs cleaner controls, a sharper falsifiable hypothesis, and a simpler primary experiment set. With execution, it could be venue-worthy, but only after tightening the story and reducing overclaim.

Name: self_commitment_lock_in
Title: Believing Its Own Words: How an LLM's Earlier Self-Generated Answer Overrides Correct Knowledge It Still Holds
Short Hypothesis: Within a multi-turn interaction, an LLM treats its own previously generated answer as high-credibility evidence and lets it override subsequent factual recall: once the model has committed to a (possibly wrong) claim earlier in the conversation, it will re-produce that claim on a later, independent query even when it stores the correct answer and would have produced it in a fresh context. We hypothesize this self-commitment lock-in is (1) a gradable behavioral phenomenon distinct from ordinary in-context copying, driven specifically by the answer being self-generated rather than merely present in context; (2) carried by an attention pathway that binds a 'self-authored commitment' signal at the prior-answer tokens into the current-query answer readout; and (3) causally suppressible by ablating that pathway or subtracting a learned self-commitment direction, restoring the correct answer without editing any fact.
Related Work: Contextual Entrainment (Llama See, Llama Do, 2025) shows LMs upweight any token present in context via 'entrainment heads', but treats all context tokens alike and does not isolate self-generated commitments or their credibility. Conversation-dynamics work (Linear representations change over a conversation, 2026) shows concept directions like factuality flip over dialogue but studies representational drift of high-level concepts, not corruption of specific factual recall by the model's own prior answer. When-Do-LLMs-Admit-Mistakes (2025) studies retraction of a stated belief, the reverse direction. Fakepedia/knowledge-conflict work injects *external* counterfactual context. Crucially, none isolate the *self-authored* nature of the committed answer as the causal driver, nor test whether correct-but-hidden knowledge is recoverable by intervening on a self-commitment pathway. This transfers the human phenomenon of self-generated-commitment bias and socially/self-shared retrieval-induced forgetting into LLM multi-turn factual recall, and is orthogonal to all my prior single-turn proposals (gating, format copies, competition, arbitration, familiarity, polarity, procedures, priming). The key novel control is authorship: same textual content, but attributed to the model itself versus to the user or a third party.
Abstract: Large language models increasingly operate over multi-turn conversations, where their own earlier outputs become part of the context for later queries. We ask whether a model treats its own prior answer as privileged evidence that overrides its stored knowledge. We propose self-commitment lock-in: once an LLM has produced a (possibly incorrect) factual claim earlier in a conversation, it re-produces that claim on a later, logically independent query even when it stores the correct answer and would give it in a fresh context. We first document the phenomenon behaviorally. For facts the model answers correctly in isolation, we engineer conversations in which the model is first led to commit to a wrong value for the fact (via a leading sub-question), then later asked the fact directly, and measure how often it now returns its own earlier wrong value. The decisive control is authorship: we compare identical wrong content attributed to (a) the model's own prior turn, (b) the user, and (c) a neutral third party, holding the text constant. We predict lock-in is strongest when the content is self-authored, scales with the committed answer's assertiveness and recency, and concentrates on low-frequency facts, above matched baselines. We then test the mechanism with a Location plus Causal Intervention strategy: a linear probe should recover a 'self-commitment' signal at the prior-answer tokens; attention analysis and activation patching should show a pathway that binds this signal into the current-query answer readout and that is stronger for self-authored than externally-authored content; and ablating that pathway or subtracting a learned self-commitment direction should recover the correct answer with high specificity. Experiments span Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, and Gemma-2-9B, evaluating lock-in prevalence, authorship dose-response, probe recovery, causal recovery, and specificity.
Experiments: Experiment 1 (H0 — fact and two-stage conversation construction): Build conversations where the model first commits to a wrong value and is later re-queried, over facts it answers correctly fresh. Data: adapted from PopQA/T-REx/EntityQuestions; select facts (subject, relation, correct a) the model answers correctly single-turn, then build a Stage-1 leading exchange that induces the model to assert a specific wrong a_false (verified it was actually produced) and a Stage-2 direct query. Restrict to single-token-first answers; target ~2,500 facts across >=8 relations; report coverage. Model: Llama-3-8B, frozen. Decisive metric (first): fraction of facts that are BOTH answered correctly fresh AND successfully induced to a_false in Stage 1 (the eligible set — lock-in requires both a correct baseline and a committed error). Convincing: >= 1,500 eligible. Indecision band: 1,000-1,500 — reduced power, reported; below 1,000 the design is under-powered. Negative (few facts can be induced to a_false, or fresh accuracy is low) means the premise cannot be set up and H1-H3 are untestable here.

Experiment 2 (H0 — authorship-controlled conditions): Create matched conditions that hold the wrong content a_false constant while varying its author, isolating authorship from mere presence in context. Data: eligible facts. Model: Llama-3-8B frozen; conditions: (a) self-authored (model produced a_false in Stage 1), (b) user-authored (user asserted a_false), (c) third-party-authored (a quoted neutral source asserts a_false), (d) no-commitment control (Stage 1 present, a_false never stated). The a_false string and its position are held identical across (a)-(c). Decisive metric (first): verification that all four conditions are well-formed and that a_false text/position is matched across (a)-(c) (manual audit of a 100-item sample). Convincing: >= 95% of the sample correctly matched. Indecision band: 85-95% matched — minor leakage between conditions; fix templates and re-audit. Negative (< 85% matched) means the authorship manipulation is confounded with content/position and must be rebuilt before any lock-in claim.

Experiment 3 (H1 — self-commitment lock-in exceeds generic entrainment): Test that Stage-2 reproduction of a_false is driven specifically by self-authorship, above any in-context mention. Data: eligible facts across the four conditions. Model: Llama-3-8B frozen. Systems compared: self-authored vs user-authored vs third-party vs no-commitment, paired per fact, against a null treating all in-context mentions of a_false identically (logistic regression author x fact; paired McNemar). Decisive metric (first): self-authorship lift = P(Stage-2 = a_false | self-authored) minus P(Stage-2 = a_false | user-authored), paired, CI; secondary, dose-response on Stage-1 assertiveness (hedged vs confident), recency (turns), and target popularity. Convincing: lift >= 8 percentage points, CI excludes 0, with a monotone assertiveness dose-response. Indecision band: lift 3-8 points — a weak self-authorship effect atop generic entrainment; report as suggestive. Negative (lift CI includes 0) refutes H1: lock-in is ordinary in-context copying, not self-commitment.

Experiment 4 (H0 — storage verification: knowledge hidden, not lost): Confirm that in lock-in cases the correct answer a is still stored, separating lock-in from genuine belief change. Data: self-authored lock-in cases from Experiment 3. Model: Llama-3-8B frozen; verify a via (i) a fresh single-turn query and (ii) a logistic-regression content probe decoding a from the Stage-2 residual stream (seeds {0,1,2}, 5-fold, label-shuffle null). Decisive metric (first): fraction of lock-in cases where a is BOTH answered correctly fresh AND probe-decodable during Stage 2 (verified-stored, true lock-in). Convincing: >= 60% of lock-in cases are verified-stored. Indecision band: 40-60% — a substantial minority reflect belief change rather than hidden knowledge; restrict downstream analysis to the verified subset and report shrinkage. Negative (< 40% verified-stored) means most 'lock-in' is genuine belief updating, undercutting the hidden-knowledge premise.

Experiment 5 (H2 — a self-authored commitment signal is decodable): Test that a signal distinguishing self- from externally-authored identical content exists and feeds the query readout. Data: verified-stored lock-in cases and matched externally-authored cases. Model: Llama-3-8B frozen; train a logistic-regression probe (seeds {0,1,2}, label-shuffle null) at the prior-answer (a_false) token positions and the Stage-2 answer position to distinguish self- from externally-authored content. Decisive metric (first): peak-layer AUROC distinguishing self- from externally-authored identical content, and cosine alignment of the query-position signal with a_false's unembedding. Convincing: AUROC >= 0.75 with unembedding alignment above a random-direction null. Indecision band: AUROC 0.60-0.75 — a weak/partial authorship signal; the causal test is then decisive. Negative (AUROC <= 0.60) means self-authorship is not separately encoded, undercutting H2.

Experiment 6 (H2/H3 — causal self-commitment pathway via attention and patching): Test that specific attention heads bind the self-authored commitment into the Stage-2 answer. Data: verified-stored lock-in cases. Model: Llama-3-8B frozen; (a) identify Stage-2 answer-position heads attending to the prior-answer tokens and compare their attention weight for self- vs externally-authored content; (b) ablate their attention to the prior-answer tokens; (c) activation-patch the Stage-2 answer-position residual from a no-commitment run into a lock-in run and measure recovery of a; (d) reverse control — inject the self-commitment signal into a no-commitment run to induce lock-in. Systems compared: candidate-head ablation vs random-head ablation vs no-commitment patch vs random-position patch. Decisive metric (first): lock-in reduction from ablating the candidate heads' attention to prior-answer tokens, net of random-head ablation. Convincing: net reduction >= 50% relative, no-commitment patch recovers a >= 25 points net, reverse injection induces lock-in >= 25 points, and candidate heads attend more to self- than externally-authored content; random controls < 5 points. Indecision band: net reduction 20-50% relative — attention is one of several routes. Negative (ablation ~ random) refutes H2's attention-pathway mechanism.

Experiment 7 (H3 — suppression restores the correct answer without editing any fact): Test that subtracting the self-commitment direction fixes lock-in cleanly. Data: verified-stored cases, fact-disjoint train/test; steering vector = mean residual difference (lock-in minus no-commitment matched states), seeds {0,1,2}, rank<=4, subtracted at the identified layers. Model: Llama-3-8B frozen except the subtracted direction. Systems compared: self-commitment subtraction, entrainment-head ablation (Experiment 6b), 'reconsider independently' re-prompt, ROME edit (expected not to help — no fact is wrong), random-direction control. Decisive metric (first): recovered-per-unit-collateral = correct-answer recovery rate divided by the accuracy drop on cases where the prior commitment was correct (over-correction control); secondary, accuracy on 200 unrelated facts, fluency (perplexity delta). Convincing: recovery >= 30% with < 3-point drop on correct-prior-commitment cases and on the 200 facts, beating the re-prompt baseline on recovered-per-collateral. Indecision band: recovery 15-30% or collateral 3-6 points — partial; report parity with re-prompting. Negative (no better than random/re-prompt, or harms correct-prior cases) refutes H3.

Experiment 8 (H1/H3 — transfer, generality, and safety): Test generality across relations and models and whether lock-in produces higher-stakes errors. Data: eligible facts partitioned by relation; suppression vector trained on a subset, applied to held-out relations. Models: Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, frozen; re-run Experiments 3-7, seeds {0,1,2}. Safety transfer: replicate Experiments 2-3 on a curated safe subset of clinical facts (~400 items, publicly documented and non-actionable), where a benign early wrong commitment about a drug indication corrupts a later independent answer. Decisive metric (first): cross-relation recovery relative to within-relation, replication of the self-authorship lift (Experiment 3) per model, and the self-authorship lift in the clinical setting. Convincing: cross-relation recovery >= 50% of within-relation, lift replicates (CI excludes 0) in >= 2 of 3 models, and the clinical lift CI excludes 0. Indecision band: replication in 1 model, cross-relation 30-50%, or clinical lift 3-8 points — model/relation/domain-specific; report scope. Negative (no transfer/replication, no clinical lift) confines H1-H3 to one model and general-knowledge prompts. Also report whether larger models lock in more.
Risk Factors and Limitations: The self-vs-external authorship conditions differ in surface framing, so the effect could be a framing artifact rather than genuine self-commitment; matched-content controls, the generic-entrainment null (Exp 3), and the constant-text authorship manipulation are essential, and a residual self-authorship effect after controls is the decisive behavioral evidence.

Lock-in could reflect genuine belief updating rather than hidden knowledge; the storage-verification step (Exp 4) with conservative content-probe thresholds separates the two, though strong-prompt leakage may overestimate storage.
The self-commitment signal and correct-answer recall may be entangled; the causal patching/ablation tests (Exp 6), not probe AUROC alone, are decisive, and graded results remain informative.

Suppression could over-correct (make the model discard legitimately-relevant prior context) or degrade fluency; the correct-prior-commitment and unrelated-fact specificity controls are central and utility may be capped.
Lock-in may overlap with contextual entrainment; the authorship contrast is designed to separate them, but partial overlap would weaken the 'distinct mechanism' claim while remaining informative.
A single transferable suppression vector may not exist if lock-in is relation-specific, limiting practical generality though still scientifically informative.
Multi-token answers complicate readout; primary analysis restricts to single-token-first answers with reported coverage.
Findings on 7-9B models may not transfer to frontier-scale models beyond an academic budget.

Name: scalar_incoherence
Title: Ordered but Incoherent: When LLMs Answer Comparisons Pairwise Instead of From a Shared Scalar, Breaking Transitivity
Short Hypothesis: LLMs can store a coherent scalar for an entity attribute in a linear subspace, yet many comparative-recall queries are answered not by reading that scalar but by an ad-hoc pairwise 'who-is-bigger' shortcut. Transitivity violations (A>B, B>C, yet C>=A) concentrate precisely on triples the model resolves via the pairwise shortcut rather than the scalar subspace, because pairwise decisions need not cohere into a global order. We hypothesize (1) whether a comparison is decided by the scalar subspace vs. the pairwise shortcut is decodable and gradable, (2) transitivity violations concentrate on shortcut-decided comparisons with small true scalar margins, and (3) forcing the answer to be read from the shared scalar subspace (steering/patching) restores transitivity without editing any stored attribute value.
Related Work: The Geometry of Numerical Reasoning (2024) shows LLMs extract numeric attributes into linear subspaces and that causal intervention in those subspaces alters comparison answers; Interpreting Multi-Attribute Confounding (2025) shows attributes share overlapping subspaces and are perturbed by irrelevant context. BERT IS-A transitivity (2022) and NLI/veridicality transitivity work show behavioral transitivity failure but offer no mechanism. Relational-reasoning-and-inductive-bias (2025) studies transitive inference via in-weights vs in-context circuits on synthetic ordinals, not stored real-world attributes. Rationality/transitivity-axiom benchmarks (2025) are purely behavioral. Crucially, all prior mechanistic work assumes comparisons are read from a single scalar subspace and does NOT ask whether the model instead uses a competing pairwise shortcut, does not test that transitivity violations are the signature of that shortcut, and does not show that forcing scalar-based reading restores global coherence. This reframes comparative-recall failure as a scalar-vs-pairwise arbitration problem, orthogonal to all my prior single-fact and set-level proposals.
Abstract: Large language models can answer 'Was Einstein born before Curie?' and encode entity attributes like birth year in linear subspaces, yet they violate transitivity: told nothing false, they will affirm A>B and B>C but deny A>C. Prior mechanistic work assumes comparisons are read from a single shared scalar subspace, which would guarantee transitivity, so it cannot explain why violations occur. We propose that comparative recall is not always scalar-based: for many pairs the model uses an ad-hoc pairwise 'who-is-bigger' shortcut driven by local lexical/frequency cues, and because pairwise decisions need not cohere, this shortcut is the source of transitivity violations. We test three claims on comparative queries over ordered attributes (birth/death year, latitude, elevation, population, physical size). (1) Dissociability: a probe over the attribute's scalar subspace predicts the correct comparison, while a separable 'pairwise-shortcut' signal predicts the model's answer independently of the scalar; whether a given comparison is scalar- or shortcut-decided is gradable via the alignment between the answer and the scalar-subspace projection. (2) Violation geometry: transitivity-violating triples concentrate on shortcut-decided comparisons with small true scalar margins, above frequency- and margin-matched baselines, and the scalar-margin/shortcut-strength imbalance predicts violations on held-out triples. (3) Causal repair: patching the answer to be read from the shared scalar subspace, or suppressing the pairwise-shortcut direction, restores transitivity and improves comparison accuracy with high specificity, whereas editing individual attribute values does not. Experiments span Llama-3-8B, Mistral-7B, and Qwen2.5-7B, evaluating probe separability, violation prevalence, causal recovery, and specificity.
Experiments: Experiment 1 (H2 — Ordered-attribute dataset and transitivity-violation prevalence): Tests the premise behind H2, that transitivity violations exist above what a single stored scalar with noise would produce. Data: constructed from Wikidata (existing knowledge base, >1M entities carry the target scalars) plus the existing THINGS/size-norm set for commonsense physical size. Across five attributes (birth year, death year, latitude, elevation, city population) we sample 2,000 entities each (10,000) spread evenly over each attribute's magnitude range, and form 3,000 known-order triples per attribute (15,000 triples = 45,000 pairwise yes/no queries); this many gives >=200 triples per margin bin for stable estimates and is capped there by inference cost. Each query uses one fixed template plus 3 paraphrases. Model: Llama-3-8B, Mistral-7B, Qwen2.5-7B, weights frozen (bf16, single 80GB GPU), greedy decoding, no trainable parameters. Systems compared: observed cyclic-violation rate per triple vs a fitted single-scalar null (each pairwise answer sampled from one per-entity latent scalar with per-pair logistic noise fit to the data). Decisive metric (stated before data): excess cyclic-violation rate over the null, per attribute, with 95% bootstrap CI. Convincing = >=5 percentage-point (pp) excess with CI excluding 0 in >=3 of 5 attributes. Negative (<=1pp excess) = violations are explained by scalar-storage noise and H2's premise fails. Indecision band 1-5pp: report as inconclusive for that attribute and do NOT advance the shortcut interpretation there.

Experiment 2 (H1 — Scalar-subspace vs pairwise-shortcut probes): Tests H1's claim that whether a comparison is scalar- or shortcut-decided is decodable via two separable signals. Data: the 45,000 pairwise queries from Exp 1, split 80/20 by entity (no entity in both train and test). Model: same three frozen models; two trainable linear probes on the last-token residual stream at each layer -- (a) a PLS/linear scalar-subspace probe fit to each entity's ground-truth scalar, giving a scalar-difference prediction, and (b) a logistic 'answer probe' predicting the model's actual yes/no. L2-regularized, trained with seeds {0,1,2}, layer chosen by 5-fold CV on train only. Systems compared: scalar-difference sign vs true order; answer-probe vs model answer; and, by residualizing the answer probe on the scalar projection, the residual predictivity of the model's answer. Decisive metric (before data): residual AUROC of the answer probe after removing the scalar projection, best layer, test set. Convincing = residual AUROC >=0.70 (a competing shortcut carries answer information beyond the scalar). Negative = <=0.55 (answer fully explained by the scalar; no separable shortcut, H1 fails). Indecision band 0.55-0.70: report a graded, weak shortcut and do not claim clean dissociability. Label-shuffle control must sit at 0.50.

Experiment 3 (H2 — Violation geometry: concentration on shortcut-decided, small-margin triples): Tests H2's specific geometry claim. Data: the Exp 1 triples, each pairwise comparison tagged with (a) scalar margin = |difference of scalar projections| from Exp 2 and (b) answer-vs-scalar alignment; shortcut-decided = answer diverges from scalar prediction or margin near zero with a confident answer. Model: same frozen three; the Exp 2 probes reused (no new training). Systems compared: violation rate on shortcut-decided small-margin triples vs frequency- and margin-matched scalar-decided triples; a mixed-effects logistic regression predicts held-out violations from margin, shortcut-flag, entity co-occurrence frequency, and lexical similarity. Decisive metric (before data): odds ratio for the shortcut-flag predicting violations, controlling for frequency and margin, on held-out triples. Convincing = OR >=2.0 with CI excluding 1 and held-out AUROC >=0.65. Negative = OR CI includes 1 (violations not tied to shortcut decisions; H2 fails). Indecision band OR 1.3-2.0: report weak concentration, insufficient to attribute violations to the shortcut.

Experiment 4 (H3 — Causal repair by forcing scalar reading): Tests H3's core causal claim that forcing the answer to be read from the shared scalar subspace restores transitivity without editing any stored value. Data: 1,000 held-out shortcut-decided violating triples (from Exp 3), never used in probe training. Model: same frozen three; interventions are activation edits, no weight training. Systems compared, all at matched edit norm: (a) patch the comparison-answer position with the injected scalar projections of both entities computed in isolation; (b) suppress the learned pairwise-shortcut direction (low-rank difference of shortcut- vs scalar-decided matched states); (c) reverse control -- amplify the shortcut direction to induce violations; plus random-direction and no-op controls. Dose alpha swept over {0,0.5,1,2,4}x the direction norm. Decisive metric (before data): per-triple transitivity-restoration rate (fraction of violating triples made consistent) for (a)/(b) vs random-direction control. Convincing = >=30pp absolute gain over random control at a dose that keeps held-out perplexity within 5%. Negative = <=5pp gain (forcing scalar reading does not restore coherence; H3 fails). Indecision band 5-30pp: report partial causal support. Reverse control must raise violations by >=10pp to confirm directionality.

Experiment 5 (H3 — Repair specificity and collateral cost): Tests that H3's repair is specific -- it restores coherence without editing stored values or harming unrelated behavior. Data: the Exp 4 held-out triples, plus 1,000 scalar-decided comparisons the model already answers correctly, plus 200 unrelated non-comparison facts sampled from PopQA (existing, ~14k questions). Model: same frozen three, best intervention and dose from Exp 4. Systems compared: our scalar-reading/shortcut-suppression vs a 'recall each value first, then compare' re-prompt, ROME editing of individual attribute values (existing method, expected null since values are not wrong), and random-direction control. Decisive metric (before data), reported first: net transitivity-violation reduction MINUS accuracy drop on already-correct scalar-decided comparisons (recovered-per-unit-collateral). Convincing = violation reduction >=20pp while scalar-decided accuracy drops <=3pp and unrelated-fact accuracy drops <=2pp and perplexity rises <=5%. Negative = collateral drop >=10pp or no net gain. Indecision band: scalar-decided drop 3-10pp -> utility is capped; report the trade-off curve rather than a clean repair. ROME expected to give <=5pp violation reduction, confirming the failure is not per-value.

Experiment 6 (H1/H3 — Cross-attribute and cross-model transfer): Tests whether the H1 signals and H3 repair generalize rather than being attribute- or model-specific. Data: probes/directions fit on birth-year comparisons (from Exp 2/4) applied unchanged to elevation and city-population held-out triples (1,000 each). Model: repeat on all three frozen models. Systems compared: transferred direction vs an attribute-matched direction refit in-domain vs random-direction. Decisive metric (before data): transitivity-restoration rate of the transferred direction as a fraction of the in-domain-refit rate. Convincing = transferred achieves >=60% of in-domain rate on >=2 attributes and >=2 models. Negative = <=20% (repair is attribute-specific; practical generality fails, though the per-attribute science stands). Indecision band 20-60%: report partial transfer. Also report whether larger models show fewer violations (Spearman rho between parameter count and violation rate across the three models), with rho <=-0.3 taken as suggestive only given N=3.

Experiment 7 (H2 — Source analysis: lexical/frequency drivers of the shortcut): Tests the mechanistic source behind H2 -- that shortcut reliance is driven by local lexical/frequency 'who-is-bigger' cues rather than scalar retrieval. Data: all Exp 1 comparisons with per-pair features: scalar margin, entity-pair co-occurrence frequency (from an open web-corpus n-gram count), attribute type, lexical similarity. Model: frozen three, reusing Exp 2 shortcut-flags; no new training. Systems compared: nested regressions predicting shortcut reliance and violation rate with vs without the frequency/lexical features. Decisive metric (before data): incremental variance explained (Delta R^2) by frequency/lexical cues over margin-and-attribute-only, on held-out comparisons. Convincing = Delta R^2 >=0.10 with the frequency coefficient sign positive (more co-occurrence -> more shortcut) across >=2 models. Negative = Delta R^2 <=0.02 (shortcut not lexically driven; the source claim is unsupported though the behavioral/causal claims may stand). Indecision band 0.02-0.10: report frequency as a partial driver.
Risk Factors and Limitations: The scalar subspace and the model's answer may be so tightly coupled that a separable 'shortcut' signal is not identifiable; the residualization (Exp 3) and the causal induction of violations (Exp 5c) are the decisive tests, and a graded result remains informative.

Transitivity violations could reflect genuine scalar-storage noise rather than a distinct shortcut; the margin-matched null (Exp 2) and shortcut-vs-scalar arbitration measure (Exp 4) are designed to separate these, but the distinction may be partly a continuum.
Forcing scalar-based reading could degrade cases where the pairwise answer was actually correct, or hurt fluency; the scalar-decided specificity control (Exp 6) is central and utility may be capped.

Fitting a reliable scalar subspace requires enough entities per attribute and is noisiest for physical-size/commonsense attributes; we report which attributes admit reliable subspaces and restrict primary analysis accordingly.
A single transferable repair recipe may not exist if the shortcut is attribute-specific, limiting practical generality though still scientifically informative.
Comparison answers depend on template phrasing (larger vs smaller framing); we use paraphrases and report robustness, since framing itself may modulate shortcut reliance.
Findings on 7-8B models may not transfer to frontier-scale models beyond an academic budget.

Name: acquisition_language_anchor
Title: Anchored to Where It Was Learned: A Per-Fact Acquisition-Language Anchor That Hides Cross-Lingual Knowledge
Short Hypothesis: Each fact carries a per-fact 'acquisition-language anchor' — the language in which the model predominantly encountered it — and cross-lingual recall is routed through that anchor's representation regardless of the query language. Many cross-lingual failures are anchor-override failures: when the query language differs from the fact's anchor, the model fails even though the fact is stored, and the failure direction is predicted by the anchor rather than by a fixed English hub. We hypothesize (1) the anchor is decodable from intermediate activations, (2) which query directions fail is predicted by anchor-vs-query mismatch above a fixed-English-hub baseline, and (3) suppressing anchor-language routing (or steering toward the query language earlier) recovers the fact without editing it.
Related Work: Prior mechanistic work shows multilingual LLMs recall facts through an English-centric pipeline then translate to the target language (Paths Not Taken 2025; Lost in Multilinguality 2025), and that cross-lingual inconsistency has a middle/final-layer bottleneck (Are Knowledge and Reference Cross-Lingually Consistent 2025). Beyond the Rosetta Stone (2025) shows unified-vs-separate representations form early in training and drive transfer. Language Models' Factuality Depends on the Language of Inquiry (2025) and ECLeKTic (2025) benchmark the phenomenon that a fact known in one language fails in another. Crucially, all mechanistic accounts privilege a fixed English hub and treat failure as insufficient engagement of the English mechanism or bad translation. None posit a per-fact, data-driven acquisition-language anchor that can be non-English, none show that the *direction* of failure (which query language fails) is predicted by anchor-vs-query mismatch better than a fixed-English-hub model, and none demonstrate recovery by suppressing anchor-language routing. This is orthogonal to all my prior (monolingual) proposals; it transfers my temporal_anchor_override logic from time to language: a query-independent default (the acquisition language) overrides the query-specified frame.
Abstract: Multilingual LLMs often 'know' a fact in one language yet fail to produce it in another. The prevailing mechanistic account routes all recall through an English-centric hub and blames failure on weak English engagement or faulty back-translation. We propose a different, per-fact account: each fact has an acquisition-language anchor — the language in which the model predominantly encountered it during training — and cross-lingual recall is routed through that anchor's representation regardless of query language. Under this view, whether a given query language succeeds is governed by anchor-vs-query mismatch, and failures are anchor-override failures: the fact is stored (recoverable in the anchor language) but the query language cannot access it. We test three claims across a controlled multilingual fact set (country-anchored entities, culturally-anchored facts, and Wikipedia-article-presence-derived items following ECLeKTic) with anchors that are frequently non-English. (1) Localization: a linear probe recovers a per-fact anchor-language signal from intermediate activations, distinct from the query-language signal. (2) Predictiveness: anchor-vs-query mismatch predicts which query directions fail, with higher AUROC than a fixed-English-hub baseline, and non-English-anchored facts show reverse-direction failures (fail in English, succeed in the anchor). (3) Causal recovery: suppressing anchor-language routing, or steering the language-transition earlier toward the query language, recovers stored facts with higher specificity and less collateral damage than fact editing or generic English-pivot prompting. Experiments span Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, and Gemma-2-9B, evaluating probe separability, mismatch-predicted failure geometry, causal recovery, and specificity.
Experiments: Experiment 1 (H2 — Anchor-labeled dataset and reverse-direction prevalence): Tests the premise of H2, that non-English-anchored facts fail in the reverse direction (recalled in the anchor, failed in English), which a fixed-English-hub account forbids. Data: constructed. Source (a) country/culture-anchored entities (people, places, dishes) whose Wikipedia coverage is dominant in a specific non-English language, using per-language article length/presence as anchor proxy following ECLeKTic (existing, ~2.5k items); source (b) Language-Specific-Knowledge items (existing). We assemble 3,000 facts, each with semantically-equivalent queries in 6 languages (spanning Latin/Cyrillic/CJK/Arabic scripts) plus verified translations, restricted to single-token-first answers (report coverage; expect ~60% retained). 3,000 x 6 = 18,000 queries is enough for >=300 facts per anchor language and fits an academic inference budget. Model: Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, frozen (bf16), greedy. Systems compared: observed best-recall language per fact vs the fixed-English-hub null (English strongest for all). Decisive metric (before data): fraction of non-English-anchored facts whose best-recall language is non-English AND English fails. Convincing = >=25% of non-English-anchored facts show this reverse pattern, CI excluding a 5% chance rate. Negative = <=5% (English hub holds; the anchor premise fails). Indecision band 5-25%: report weak anchoring, insufficient to displace the English-hub account.

Experiment 2 (H2 — Anchor-vs-query mismatch predicts which query directions fail): Tests H2's predictiveness claim against the fixed-English-hub baseline. Data: all (fact, query-language) pairs from Exp 1 (~18,000), split 80/20 by fact. Model: same three frozen models; a logistic regression over pair features, trained seeds {0,1,2}. Systems compared: predictor A = per-fact anchor-vs-query mismatch; baseline B = fixed-English-hub (mismatch := query != English); baseline C = per-language fact-frequency only; all controlling for answer frequency and script similarity. Decisive metric (before data), first: held-out AUROC of A minus AUROC of B for predicting recall failure. Convincing = A beats B by >=0.05 AUROC with paired bootstrap CI excluding 0, and A's absolute AUROC >=0.70. Negative = A <= B (per-fact anchor adds nothing over an English hub; H2 fails). Indecision band 0.00-0.05 AUROC gain: report the anchor as a marginal refinement of the English-hub model, not a replacement.

Experiment 3 (H1 — Anchor-signal localization): Tests H1, that a per-fact anchor language is decodable from intermediate activations, distinct from the query-language signal. Data: activations for the Exp 1 queries; probe train/test split 80/20 by fact. Model: same three frozen models; two linear probes per layer on the subject-token and last-token residual stream -- one decoding the per-fact anchor label, one decoding the query language -- L2-regularized, seeds {0,1,2}, layer by CV. Systems compared: anchor probe vs query-language probe vs label-shuffle control (chance); anchor probe residualized on the query-language signal to test non-redundancy. Decisive metric (before data): residual per-fact anchor AUROC after removing query-language information, best layer, held-out. Convincing = residual AUROC >=0.70 and the resolution layer overlaps the known language-transition band. Negative = <=0.55 (anchor not separable from query language; H1 fails). Indecision band 0.55-0.70: report an entangled, graded anchor signal. Shuffle control must sit at ~0.50.

Experiment 4 (H3 — Storage verification and causal recovery of hidden facts): Tests H3, that suppressing anchor-language routing (or steering the transition earlier toward the query language) recovers a stored fact without editing it. Data: anchor-override failures = (fact, query-language) pairs that fail in the query language but succeed in the anchor language AND whose answer is decodable by a content probe during the failing run (verified-stored; report coverage; exclude facts with answer tokens shared across languages). Target 1,200 verified-override pairs. Model: same three frozen models; interventions are activation edits at the identified transition layers (from Exp 3), no weight training; dose alpha in {0,0.5,1,2,4}. Systems compared, matched norm: (a) patch anchor-language routing from a successful anchor run; (b) suppress the anchor-language direction; (c) steer the transition earlier toward the query language; (d) reverse control injecting the anchor direction; plus random-direction control. Decisive metric (before data): per-pair recovery rate (correct answer now emitted IN the query language) over random control. Convincing = >=30pp gain over random at a dose keeping per-language perplexity within 5%. Negative = <=5pp (routing suppression does not recover; H3 fails). Indecision band 5-30pp: partial causal support; reverse control must raise override by >=10pp.

Experiment 5 (H3 — Recovery specificity and collateral cost): Tests that H3's recovery is specific. Data: Exp 4 held-out override pairs; 1,000 (fact, query-language) pairs already recalled correctly in the query language; 200 unrelated facts. Model: same three frozen, best intervention/dose from Exp 4. Systems compared: our intervention vs the Paths-Not-Taken translation/recall vectors (existing), English-pivot prompting ('answer in English then translate'), ROME editing (existing, expected null since the fact is stored), and random-direction control. Decisive metric (before data), first: recovery rate MINUS accuracy drop on already-correct query-language pairs (recovered-per-unit-collateral). Convincing = recovery >=25pp while already-correct accuracy drops <=3pp, unrelated-fact accuracy drops <=2pp, per-language perplexity rises <=5%. Negative = collateral drop >=10pp or no net recovery. Indecision band 3-10pp already-correct drop: utility capped; report the trade-off. ROME expected <=5pp recovery, confirming the fact is hidden, not absent.

Experiment 6 (H3 — Cross-relation and cross-language-pair transfer): Tests whether a single anchor-suppression/early-transition vector generalizes rather than being pair-specific. Data: vector fit on a subset of relations/language pairs (from Exp 4) applied unchanged to held-out relations and held-out language pairs (800 override pairs). Model: all three frozen models. Systems compared: transferred vector vs in-domain-refit vector vs random-direction. Decisive metric (before data): transferred recovery rate as a fraction of in-domain-refit recovery. Convincing = >=60% of in-domain on >=2 models. Negative = <=20% (anchoring is pair-specific; practical generality fails). Indecision band 20-60%: partial transfer. Also report Spearman rho between model scale and override rate across the three models (rho <=-0.3 = suggestive that larger models anchor less, N=3 caveat).

Experiment 7 (H1 — Anchor-proxy validation and source analysis on an open-data model): Tests that the Wikipedia-coverage anchor proxy used throughout tracks true training-corpus language and thereby underpins the H1 anchor construct. Data: OLMo-7B (existing open-data model whose training-corpus language distribution is inspectable); for 1,000 facts compute the true per-fact dominant training language from corpus counts and the Wikipedia-coverage proxy. Model: OLMo-7B frozen; reuse the Exp 1-3 pipeline. Systems compared: proxy-derived anchor vs corpus-derived anchor. Decisive metric (before data): agreement (Cohen's kappa) between proxy anchor and corpus anchor, and whether corpus-derived mismatch predicts failure at least as well as proxy-derived mismatch (AUROC). Convincing = kappa >=0.5 and corpus-mismatch AUROC within 0.03 of proxy-mismatch AUROC. Negative = kappa <=0.2 (proxy invalid; all anchor labels suspect, weakening H1/H2 interpretation). Indecision band kappa 0.2-0.5: treat the anchor as approximate and flag proxy limits, as the Risk section already notes.
Risk Factors and Limitations: The acquisition-language anchor is estimated via a Wikipedia-coverage proxy, which may be inaccurate for closed models; we validate the proxy on an open-data model (OLMo) and report proxy limitations, treating the anchor as approximate.

The anchor account may collapse to the fixed-English-hub account if most facts are in fact English-anchored; the deliberate inclusion of strongly non-English-anchored facts (Exp 1-2) and the AUROC comparison (Exp 3) are the decisive tests, and a partial improvement over the English-hub baseline is still informative.
Anchor-language and query-language signals may be entangled; the causal patching/steering tests (Exp 6), not probe AUROC alone, are decisive, and graded results remain informative.

Verifying a fact is 'stored' via anchor-language recall risks overestimation from surface entity-token leakage (shared names); we exclude facts with shared answer tokens across languages and use conservative content-probe thresholds, reporting coverage.

Interventions could degrade fluency in the query language or over-recover (force English-derived answers awkwardly); per-language specificity and perplexity controls are central and utility may be capped.
A single transferable intervention vector may not exist if anchoring is language-pair-specific, limiting practical generality though still scientifically informative.
Multi-token answers and cross-script tokenization complicate readout; primary analysis restricts to single-token-first answers with reported coverage.
Findings on 7-9B models may not transfer to frontier-scale models beyond an academic budget.

Relative to prior work, the delta is not just a new benchmark but a new mechanistic account that directly challenges the English-centric hub story. Name: magnitude_prior_regression
Title: Regressing Toward the Typical: How a Compressed Magnitude Prior Distorts LLMs' Recall of Numeric Facts
Short Hypothesis: LLMs store numeric factual quantities (populations, distances, dates, masses, prices) but read them out through a query-independent compressed magnitude prior that pulls the answer toward the scale-typical value for that quantity type. Many numeric-recall errors are not missing facts but prior-regression distortions: the correct magnitude is internally decodable, yet the emitted number is systematically shrunk toward the category's typical order of magnitude. We hypothesize (1) this compression/regression is a gradable behavioral phenomenon whose distortion increases with the fact's distance from the category-typical magnitude, (2) the internally decodable magnitude is more accurate than the verbalized answer, and (3) suppressing the compression prior (or steering toward the decoded internal magnitude) recovers accurate values without editing any fact.
Related Work: Numeracy-probing work shows LLMs linearly encode log-magnitudes yet verbalize poorly ('LLMs Know More About Numbers than They Can Say', 2026), that number representations are sublinearly/logarithmically compressed like the human mental number line (Number Representations as Human Perception 2025; ALBERT numeracy 2024; Representational Geometry of Number 2026), and that digit-frequency (Benford) biases cause numerical hallucination (Benford's Curse 2025). Cognitive science documents systematic magnitude underestimation and log-to-linear shifts (Adults Underestimate Decimals 2022; Straightening Up 2011). Crucially, all prior work studies magnitude encoding/verbalization of *presented* numbers or digit-generation bias; none isolate a *prior-regression distortion of recalled factual quantities* — that the model shrinks a stored fact's magnitude toward its category-typical value — nor test that the correct value is internally hidden and recoverable by suppressing the compression prior. This is orthogonal to my prior proposals (all about entity/attribute fact retrieval, gating, competition), transferring the human production-estimation regression bias into LLM numeric factual recall with a causal mechanism and non-destructive fix.
Abstract: Large language models often produce a confidently wrong number when recalling a factual quantity — stating a city's population, a mountain's height, or a country's GDP with a magnitude that is off in a systematic direction. Prior interpretability work shows LLMs encode numeric magnitude on a compressed, logarithmic-like internal scale and know more about numbers than they verbalize, but does not connect this to errors in recalling real numeric facts. We propose magnitude-prior regression: when recalling a numeric fact, the model reads the stored magnitude out through a query-independent compressed prior that pulls the answer toward the typical order of magnitude for that quantity type, so atypically large or small facts are systematically distorted even when the correct value is internally available. We test three claims. (1) Behavioral signature: recalled-number error is directional and grows with the fact's log-distance from the category-typical magnitude — large values are underestimated, small values overestimated — mirroring human production-estimation regression, above frequency- and popularity-matched baselines. (2) Internal-vs-verbalized gap: a linear magnitude probe on intermediate activations recovers the fact's true magnitude more accurately than the model's verbalized answer, and the verbalized answer aligns with a shrunk-toward-prior version of the internal estimate. (3) Causal recovery: suppressing the compression-prior direction, or steering the readout toward the decoded internal magnitude, reduces regression distortion and recovers accurate values with high specificity, unlike a 'be precise' re-prompt or fact editing. Experiments span Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, and Mistral-7B on curated numeric-fact sets across quantity types, evaluating directional-distortion dose-response, probe-vs-verbalized accuracy, causal recovery, and specificity.
Experiments: Experiment 1 (H1 — Numeric-fact dataset and directional-distortion dose-response): Tests H1, that recalled-number error is directional and grows with the fact's log-distance from the category-typical magnitude. Data: constructed from Wikidata (existing). Seven quantity types (city population, country population, mountain elevation, river length, country GDP, country area, celestial-body distance) with authoritative ground truth and wide within-category range; sample 1,500 facts per type (10,500) balanced across log-magnitude, each with 1 direct query plus 3 paraphrases; compute per-category typical magnitude (median log-value) and each fact's log-distance. This size gives >=150 facts per log-distance decile for stable slope estimates. Model: Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Mistral-7B, frozen (bf16), greedy; record the verbalized number. Systems compared: observed signed error (log emitted - log true) vs an unbiased-noise null (zero-slope). Decisive metric (before data): per-category regression slope of signed error on log-distance-from-typical, controlling for entity popularity, answer digit-length, query length. Convincing = negative slope (large underestimated, small overestimated) with CI excluding 0 in >=5 of 7 categories. Negative = slope CI includes 0 in a majority (no regression-to-typical; H1 fails). Indecision band |slope| < 0.05 (log-units per log-distance-unit) with CI crossing 0: report as no reliable directional distortion for that category.

Experiment 2 (H2 — Internal magnitude probe vs verbalized answer): Tests H2, that the internally decodable magnitude is more accurate than the verbalized answer, which equals a shrunk-toward-prior transform of it. Data: Exp 1 facts, 80/20 split by entity. Model: same three frozen models; a linear log-magnitude probe on the subject-token/last-token residual stream at each layer, L2-regularized, seeds {0,1,2}, layer by CV; restrict to facts where the probe generalizes to held-out entities (report coverage). Systems compared: probe-decoded log-magnitude vs the model's verbalized log-magnitude, both against ground truth; and a fitted shrinkage model verbalized = k*internal + (1-k)*prior. Decisive metric (before data), first: mean absolute log-error of probe MINUS that of verbalized answer on held-out facts. Convincing = probe error lower by >=0.15 log-units (CI excluding 0) AND fitted shrinkage k<1 with CI excluding 1. Negative = probe no better than verbalized (difference CI includes 0), refuting the hidden-accurate-magnitude claim; H2 fails. Indecision band 0.00-0.15 log-units advantage: report a weak internal-vs-verbalized gap. Label-shuffle probe must be at chance.

Experiment 3 (H1 — Compression-prior localization): Tests the internal correlate behind H1's regression -- a separable category-typical prior direction. Data: Exp 1 activations, atypical vs typical facts contrasted within each category. Model: same three frozen; contrastive mean-difference direction plus logit-lens/tuned-lens over number tokens across layers; no weight training. Systems compared: a 'prior' probe (predicts category-typical value) residualized on the fact-magnitude probe (Exp 2) to test separability. Decisive metric (before data): residual AUROC/ R^2 of the prior signal after removing the fact-specific magnitude, best layer. Convincing = residual R^2 >=0.15 for the prior AND logit-lens shows monotone shrinkage of the number-token estimate toward the prior across the last third of layers. Negative = residual R^2 <=0.03 (no separable prior; the regression has no distinct locus). Indecision band 0.03-0.15: report an entangled prior, weakening the mechanistic localization but not the behavioral H1.

Experiment 4 (H3 — Causal suppression/steering of the prior): Tests H3's causal claim that suppressing the compression prior or steering toward the decoded internal magnitude recovers accurate values without editing the fact. Data: 1,000 held-out atypical facts (top/bottom log-distance quartiles) not used in probe fitting. Model: same three frozen; activation edits at the Exp 3 layers, dose alpha in {0,0.5,1,2,4}; no weight training. Systems compared, matched norm: (a) suppress the compression-prior direction; (b) steer toward the probe-decoded internal magnitude; (c) reverse control amplifying the prior; plus random-direction and content control (non-numeric answers unchanged). Decisive metric (before data): reduction in signed distortion (|log emitted - log true|) on atypical facts vs random control. Convincing = >=0.20 log-unit reduction over random at a dose keeping perplexity within 5%. Negative = <=0.03 log-unit change (no causal role; H3 fails). Indecision band 0.03-0.20 log-units: partial causal support. Reverse control must increase distortion by >=0.10 log-units to confirm directionality.

Experiment 5 (H3 — Recovery specificity and collateral cost): Tests that H3's recovery is specific to atypical facts and does not corrupt typical facts or unrelated behavior. Data: Exp 4 held-out atypical facts; 1,000 typical facts (near category median, already near-correct); 200 unrelated non-numeric facts (PopQA). Model: same three frozen, best intervention/dose. Systems compared: our intervention vs a 'give the precise value / think carefully' re-prompt, auxiliary-probe finetuning per the numeracy literature (existing), ROME editing (existing, expected null since regression is systematic not per-fact), and random-direction control. Decisive metric (before data), first: atypical-fact log-error reduction MINUS typical-fact log-error increase. Convincing = atypical reduction >=0.15 log-units while typical error rises <=0.03 log-units, unrelated-fact accuracy drops <=2pp, perplexity <=5%. Negative = typical error rises >=0.10 log-units or no net gain (over-correction). Indecision band typical increase 0.03-0.10 log-units: utility capped; report the trade-off curve.

Experiment 6 (H3 — Cross-category and cross-model transfer): Tests whether a single prior-suppression/magnitude-steering recipe generalizes. Data: direction fit on population facts (Exp 4) applied unchanged to elevation and GDP held-out atypical facts (800 each). Model: all three frozen. Systems compared: transferred vs in-domain-refit vs random-direction. Decisive metric (before data): transferred distortion-reduction as a fraction of in-domain-refit reduction. Convincing = >=60% of in-domain on >=2 categories and >=2 models. Negative = <=20% (category-specific prior; generality fails). Indecision band 20-60%: partial transfer. Report Spearman rho between model scale and regression-slope magnitude across the three models (rho <=-0.3 suggestive that larger models compress less; N=3 caveat).

Experiment 7 (H1 — Source analysis on an open-data model): Tests H1's mechanistic source -- that distortion is driven by the compressed prior, not tail-value obscurity. Data: OLMo-7B (existing open-data model); for 1,000 facts across categories compute the frequency distribution of each fact's magnitude in comparable corpus text and each fact's log-distance-from-typical. Model: OLMo-7B frozen; reuse Exp 1-2 pipeline. Systems compared: nested regression predicting distortion from log-distance-from-typical vs from raw corpus frequency of the true value. Decisive metric (before data): incremental variance (Delta R^2) explained by log-distance-from-typical over frequency-only. Convincing = Delta R^2 >=0.10 with the distance coefficient sign consistent with regression-to-typical. Negative = Delta R^2 <=0.02 (distortion is just tail obscurity, not a prior; the source claim fails). Indecision band 0.02-0.10: report the prior as a partial driver alongside obscurity.
Risk Factors and Limitations: Numeric-recall errors could reflect genuinely missing facts (tail obscurity) rather than prior regression; the internal-probe recovery (Exp 3) and log-distance dose-response controlling for popularity (Exp 2) are the decisive separators, and coverage is reported for facts where the probe generalizes.
The compression-prior and fact-magnitude signals may be entangled; the causal suppression/steering tests (Exp 5), not probe accuracy alone, are decisive, and graded results remain informative.

Prior suppression could over-correct — introducing wild large values or degrading typical-fact accuracy; the typical-fact specificity control (Exp 6) is central and utility may be capped even if the analysis holds.

Multi-token number readout (large numbers span many tokens) complicates logit-lens and steering; primary analysis uses log-magnitude probes and order-of-magnitude accuracy metrics rather than exact-digit recovery, with reported coverage.

Directional distortion may be small relative to noise for some categories; per-category dose-response and the paired within-category design maximize power, and a modest but significant regression slope is still informative.
A single transferable intervention recipe may not exist if the prior is category-specific, limiting practical generality though still scientifically informative.
Frequency proxies for magnitude distribution are only inspectable on open-data models; we validate the source claim on OLMo and treat closed-model proxies as approximate.
Findings on 7-8B models may not transfer to frontier-scale models beyond an academic budget.
