Name: persona_knowledge_suppression
Title: In Character, Out of Knowledge: How a Low-Competence Persona Suppresses Facts the Model Still Stores
Short Hypothesis: When an LLM adopts a low-competence or non-expert persona (e.g., 'answer as a young child', 'as a medieval peasant', 'as someone who failed science'), it fails factual queries it answers correctly in the default assistant voice, not because the fact is lost but because a persona-competence signal computed early in the network causally gates expression of the stored fact. We hypothesize (1) the correct answer remains linearly decodable from intermediate activations during persona failures (hidden, not erased), (2) a persona-competence direction predicts and causally drives suppression, and (3) suppressing this direction (not editing the fact) reopens the hidden knowledge while leaving the persona's stylistic behavior intact.
Related Work: Prior behavioral work shows low-knowledge personas (child, toddler, layperson) reduce factual accuracy (Prompting Science Report 4, 2025; LLMs downplay cognitive abilities, 2024), that persona assignment triggers abstentions and stereotype-driven errors (Bias Runs Deep, 2023), and that inquiry personas alter QA accuracy and cause hallucinated limitations/refusals (Who's Asking?, 2025). Mechanistic work localizes persona information to early MLP layers and identity-token positions (Dissecting Persona-Driven Reasoning, 2025; Localizing Persona Representations, 2025) and builds role/steering vectors that improve reasoning (Role Vectors, 2025; SRPS, 2025). Split Personality Training (2026) uses a second persona to read latent knowledge for auditing. Entity-cell work (Friends and Grandmothers in Silico, 2026) localizes and causally toggles stored facts. None of these test the specific claim that a competence-signaling persona causally *gates expression of a fact that is still stored*, that the correct answer stays decodable during persona failures, or that a targeted competence-direction suppression non-destructively reopens hidden knowledge while preserving persona style. This is orthogonal to all my prior single-turn retrieval/gating proposals: here the gating variable is the persona's implied competence, and the object is knowledge suppressed by role-play.
Abstract: Large language models will happily role-play as a young child, a medieval peasant, or someone who failed high-school science—and when asked a factual question in such a low-competence persona, they often get it wrong even though the same model answers correctly as the default assistant. Prior work documents that low-knowledge personas degrade accuracy but treats this as a capability change. We propose instead that it is a knowledge-suppression failure: the fact remains stored and internally recoverable, but a persona-competence signal computed early in the network causally gates its expression. We test three claims on factual queries wrapped in personas of varying implied competence (expert, default, layperson, child, incompetent-character). (1) Hidden knowledge: on persona-induced failures, a linear probe on intermediate activations recovers the correct answer at rates far above the model's verbalized accuracy, showing the fact is present but unexpressed, above matched baselines. (2) Localization and drivers: a persona-competence direction, decodable early and separable (via residualization) from the fact-content signal, predicts suppression, and its strength scales with the persona's implied incompetence rather than with genuine fact difficulty. (3) Causal, style-preserving recovery: suppressing the persona-competence direction (or patching it from a default-voice run) reopens hidden facts with high specificity—the persona's stylistic behavior is retained—outperforming a 'be accurate' reminder and fact editing. Experiments span Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, and Gemma-2-9B on PopQA, T-REx, and a medical-fact subset, evaluating hidden-knowledge recovery, competence-direction prediction, causal recovery, style preservation, and specificity.
Experiments: Experiment 1 (H2 — Persona-graded dataset and suppression scaling with implied competence): Tests the behavioral premise of H2, that a persona-competence signal (not mere style) drives suppression that scales with implied incompetence. Data: constructed from PopQA (~14k), T-REx (LAMA subset ~34k), EntityQuestions (~176k); select 2,500 facts the model answers correctly in the default voice, wrapped in a fixed template under five competence conditions (matched expert, default, layperson, young child, in-character incompetent) plus two competence-neutral style controls (cheerful, formal). Single-token-first answers only; report coverage. 2,500 x 7 = 17,500 prompts fits budget and gives tight per-condition estimates. Model: Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, frozen (bf16), greedy. Systems compared: accuracy across competence conditions vs the style-only controls; ordinal (mixed-effects logistic) regression of accuracy on implied competence. Decisive metric (before data), first: accuracy drop from default to the incompetent persona, and the monotonic ordinal slope across competence, vs a null where persona only adds output-format noise (style-control accuracy). Convincing = incompetent-persona drop >=15pp AND monotonic ordinal slope CI excluding 0 AND style controls drop <=3pp (tracks competence, not style). Negative = drop <=3pp or style controls drop as much (no competence-specific suppression; premise fails). Indecision band 3-15pp drop: report weak suppression.

Experiment 2 (H1 — Hidden-knowledge probe): Tests H1, that the correct answer stays linearly decodable during persona failures. Data: persona-suppression cases from Exp 1 (correct under default, wrong under a low-competence persona); 80/20 split by fact; label-shuffle control. Model: same three frozen; a linear answer probe on the subject-token/last-token residual stream, L2-regularized, seeds {0,1,2}, layer by CV on held-out facts. Systems compared: probe recovery accuracy under the low-competence persona vs the model's verbalized accuracy there vs the default-voice probe (upper bound). Decisive metric (before data), first: probe recovery accuracy minus verbalized accuracy on suppression cases. Convincing = probe recovers the correct answer at >=40pp above verbalized accuracy and within 10pp of the default-voice probe (fact hidden, not erased). Negative = probe within 10pp of verbalized accuracy (fact truly gone; H1 fails). Indecision band 10-40pp above verbalized: partial hidden knowledge; report as graded. Shuffle probe must be at chance.

Experiment 3 (H2 — Persona-competence direction: localization and driver): Tests H2's localization and that the direction tracks implied competence, not fact difficulty. Data: Exp 1 activations across competence conditions. Model: same three frozen; contrastive mean-difference persona-competence direction per layer; a fact-content probe for residualization; no weight training. Systems compared: the competence direction's activation regressed on implied competence vs on true fact difficulty (baseline default-voice confidence); competence direction residualized on the fact-content signal. Decisive metric (before data): standardized regression coefficient on implied competence minus that on fact difficulty, plus residual decodability of competence after removing content. Convincing = competence coefficient >=2x the difficulty coefficient AND residual competence AUROC >=0.70, at an early MLP/identity-token layer as prior persona-localization predicts. Negative = difficulty coefficient >= competence coefficient, or residual AUROC <=0.55 (no separable competence signal; H2 localization fails). Indecision band residual AUROC 0.55-0.70: report an entangled, graded competence signal.

Experiment 4 (H2 — Causal drive of suppression): Tests H2's causal claim that the competence direction drives suppression. Data: 1,000 held-out suppression cases (Exp 1). Model: same three frozen; activation edits at Exp 3 layers, dose alpha in {0,0.5,1,2,4}; no weight training. Systems compared, matched norm: (a) suppress the competence direction; (b) patch the competence representation from a default-voice run; (c) reverse control injecting the low-competence direction into a default run; (d) content control (fact-content signal unchanged); plus random-direction control. Decisive metric (before data): per-fact recovery rate (correct answer, matching the default-voice answer) over random control. Convincing = >=30pp over random at a dose with perplexity within 5%, AND reverse control induces >=15pp suppression in default runs. Negative = <=5pp recovery (direction not causal; H2 fails). Indecision band 5-30pp: partial causal support.

Experiment 5 (H3 — Style-preserving recovery and specificity): Tests H3, that suppressing the direction reopens knowledge while leaving persona style intact and unrelated behavior unharmed. Data: Exp 4 held-out suppression cases; 1,000 facts the persona already answers correctly; 200 unrelated facts. Model: same three frozen, best intervention/dose. Systems compared: our suppression vs a 'be accurate regardless of persona' reminder, dropping the persona entirely (which trivially recovers knowledge but destroys style), ROME editing (existing, expected null), random-direction control. Decisive metric (before data), first: recovery rate AT constant persona-style retention -- style retention judged by a persona classifier / GPT-4o rating that the output is still in character. Convincing = recovery >=25pp while style-retention drops <=5pp vs the persona baseline, already-correct accuracy drops <=3pp, unrelated accuracy drops <=2pp, perplexity <=5%. Negative = recovery forces style-retention drop >=20pp (knowledge and style inseparable) or no recovery. Indecision band style-drop 5-20pp: dissociation is partial; report the recovery-vs-style trade-off.

Experiment 6 (H3 — Cross-persona and cross-model transfer): Tests whether a single competence-suppression vector generalizes. Data: vector fit on a subset of personas/relations (Exp 4) applied unchanged to held-out personas and relations (800 cases). Model: all three frozen. Systems compared: transferred vs in-domain-refit vs random-direction. Decisive metric (before data): transferred recovery as a fraction of in-domain-refit. Convincing = >=60% of in-domain on >=2 personas and >=2 models. Negative = <=20% (persona-specific; generality fails). Indecision band 20-60%: partial transfer. Report Spearman rho between model scale and suppression magnitude across the three models (rho <=-0.3 suggestive that larger models suppress less; N=3 caveat).

Experiment 7 (H1/H2 — Safety-domain transfer): Tests whether H1 hidden-knowledge and H2 competence-driven suppression appear in a higher-stakes domain. Data: a curated medical/clinical factual-recall subset (drug indications, symptom-disease facts) drawn from an existing medical QA set (e.g. MedQA/DrugBank-derived), 800 facts the model answers correctly in the default voice, wrapped in low-competence inquiry personas ('I'm just a worried parent with no medical background'). Model: same three frozen. Systems compared: replicate Exp 1 prevalence and Exp 2 hidden-knowledge probe and Exp 4 causal drive on this subset vs the general-knowledge result. Decisive metric (before data): suppression prevalence and hidden-knowledge gap in the medical subset. Convincing = suppression prevalence >=15pp and hidden-knowledge gap >=40pp, i.e. at least as large as general knowledge, demonstrating higher-stakes hidden failures. Negative = medical prevalence <=3pp (suppression does not transfer to this domain). Indecision band 3-15pp: report domain-attenuated suppression.
Risk Factors and Limitations: Persona-induced errors could reflect genuine strategy change (the model deliberately 'dumbs down') rather than knowledge suppression; the hidden-knowledge probe (Exp 3) and the causal, style-preserving recovery (Exp 6) are the decisive separators—if recovering the fact necessarily breaks the persona, the gating claim is weakened but still informative.
The persona-competence and fact-content signals may be entangled; the causal patching/steering tests (Exp 5), not probe accuracy alone, are decisive, and graded results remain informative.

Style preservation and knowledge recovery may trade off (suppressing the competence direction could also erase persona style); the persona-classifier metric (Exp 6) quantifies this and utility may be capped if the two cannot be dissociated.

Suppression prevalence may be modest for some persona/relation combinations; the ordinal competence gradient and paired within-fact design maximize power, and a significant monotonic effect is still informative.
A single transferable competence-suppression vector may not exist if suppression is persona-specific, limiting practical generality though still scientifically informative.
The style-vs-competence control persona may imperfectly isolate competence from other persona attributes; multiple control personas and regression on implied competence mitigate this.
Multi-token answers complicate readout; primary analysis restricts to single-token-first answers with reported coverage.
Findings on 7–9B models may not transfer to frontier-scale models beyond an academic budget.

Name: prefetch_slot_override
Title: Reserved but Wrong: How Early Plan-Slot Prefetching Overrides Fresh Retrieval of Facts Stated Later in an Answer
Short Hypothesis: When an LLM plans a multi-fact answer, it reserves 'slots' for facts it will state later and prefetches a coarse placeholder for each slot before the generation cursor reaches it. We hypothesize a distinct failure mode—prefetch-slot override—in which a prematurely committed placeholder (a plausible but wrong entity, often the more typical/frequent one) overrides fresh, correct retrieval when the model actually reaches the slot, so the model states a fact it does not hold for the subject even though it would retrieve the correct value if that fact were queried first or in isolation. We predict (1) the reserved-slot placeholder is decodable in the residual stream before the slot is generated, (2) override errors concentrate on later slots where the placeholder was mis-prefetched while the correct value remains internally recoverable, and (3) suppressing the stale placeholder (not editing the fact) restores fresh retrieval of the correct value with high specificity.
Related Work: A growing body shows LLMs encode future-output attributes in advance: Emergent Response Planning (2025) probes future structure/content/behavior attributes; ParaScopes (2025) decodes paragraph-scale plans from the residual stream; Future Lens (2023) recovers subsequent tokens from a single hidden state; look-ahead work in chess (Jenner et al. 2024) shows future targets are represented and moved 'backward in time.' All of these establish that planning/lookahead information is *encoded and decodable*, and treat it as a capability. None ask whether an *early reserved slot for a specific upcoming fact can be filled with the wrong value that then overrides correct retrieval at generation time*, none identify this as a concrete factual-recall failure mode distinct from single-query retrieval failure, and none show a targeted intervention that suppresses the stale placeholder to recover the fact. This is also orthogonal to my prior proposals, which all concern single-query recall/gating/competition; here the object is a *within-answer, position-dependent* corruption caused by premature slot commitment during multi-fact generation, connecting the planning literature to knowledge-retrieval failures.
Abstract: Large language models increasingly produce answers packed with multiple facts about a subject, and recent work shows they encode plans for their future output in advance. We ask whether this planning has a dark side for factual accuracy. We propose prefetch-slot override: when generating a multi-fact answer, the model reserves slots for facts it will state later and prefetches a coarse placeholder for each slot before the generation cursor arrives; when the placeholder is a plausible-but-wrong value (often the category-typical or more frequent entity), it overrides fresh, correct retrieval at the slot, so the model asserts a fact it does not actually hold for the subject—even though it would retrieve the correct value if that same fact were asked first or in isolation. We test three claims on templated multi-fact generation about entities. (1) Prefetch decodability: the reserved slot's placeholder value is linearly decodable from the residual stream several tokens before the slot is generated, at a position/layer distinct from where the earlier facts are being produced. (2) Override geometry: within-answer errors concentrate on later slots whose placeholder was mis-prefetched, while the correct value remains internally recoverable (via probing and via querying the fact first), above position- and frequency-matched baselines; the same fact is answered correctly in a first-slot or isolated position. (3) Causal repair: suppressing the stale placeholder direction, or patching the slot representation from an isolated-query run, restores the correct value with higher specificity and less collateral damage than fact editing or a 'double-check each fact' re-prompt. Experiments span Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, and Gemma-2-9B, evaluating prefetch-decoding AUROC, override prevalence and position dependence, causal recovery, and specificity.
Experiments: Experiment 1 (H2 — Multi-fact dataset and position-dependent override prevalence): Tests H2's behavioral core, that within-answer errors concentrate on later slots for the same fact that is answered correctly early or in isolation. Data: constructed from Wikidata (existing). Select 2,000 subjects each having >=4 single-token-first attributes under distinct relations (person: birth city, nationality, occupation, notable award; city: country, founding decade, mayor, region). For each subject build (i) a fixed-order K-slot multi-fact prompt, (ii) isolated single-fact queries, (iii) permuted-order versions placing each attribute early vs late. ~2,000 x (1 + 4 + 4) fits budget and yields >=1,500 paired early-vs-late items per attribute. Model: Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, frozen (bf16), greedy. Systems compared: accuracy of an attribute in an early slot vs a late slot vs isolation; a null where each fact is retrieved independently of position. Decisive metric (before data), first: increase in error rate from early/isolated to late slot for the SAME attribute (paired McNemar; mixed-effects logistic with slot-position x attribute), controlling for cumulative generation length. Convincing = late-slot error exceeds early/isolated by >=10pp with CI excluding 0 in >=3 relations, and late-slot wrong answers are disproportionately the category-typical/frequent entity. Negative = <=2pp position effect (no override; H2 fails). Indecision band 2-10pp: report weak position dependence.

Experiment 2 (H2 — Storage verification that the correct value is recoverable): Tests the 'hidden, not absent' half of H2. Data: override cases from Exp 1 (correct in isolation/early slot, wrong in a late slot). Model: same three frozen; a linear content probe on the residual stream at the pre-slot position, 80/20 split by fact, seeds {0,1,2}, label-shuffle control. Systems compared: (i) isolated/first-slot recall of the same fact, (ii) content-probe decoding of the correct value during the failing multi-fact run. Only cases passing both count as override (report coverage). Decisive metric (before data), first: content-probe recovery accuracy of the correct value at the pre-slot position minus the model's late-slot verbalized accuracy. Convincing = probe recovers the correct value at >=40pp above late-slot verbalized accuracy. Negative = probe within 10pp of verbalized (the fact is genuinely not retrieved; override reframed as ignorance). Indecision band 10-40pp: partial hidden storage; restrict downstream causal tests to high-confidence cases.

Experiment 3 (H1 — Ahead-of-time prefetch-placeholder decoding): Tests H1, that the reserved slot's placeholder is decodable several tokens before the slot is generated, at a position distinct from where earlier facts are produced. Data: Exp 1 multi-fact runs; probe train/test 80/20 by subject. Model: same three frozen; a linear probe decoding the value the model will emit at slot k, evaluated at offsets of 2/4/8 tokens before slot k while earlier facts are still being produced; seeds {0,1,2}, offset and layer by CV; label-shuffle and offset controls. Systems compared: override cases (does an early-decodable placeholder differ from the isolated-query answer?) vs correct cases; decoding at the pre-slot position vs at the earlier-fact positions. Decisive metric (before data), first: per-offset AUROC for decoding the emitted slot value ahead of time, and the fraction of override cases where a WRONG placeholder is decodable >=4 tokens early. Convincing = ahead-of-time AUROC >=0.70 at offset 4 AND >=50% of override cases show an early wrong placeholder that matches the later error. Negative = AUROC <=0.55 (no reserved placeholder; H1 fails). Indecision band 0.55-0.70: report weak prefetching.

Experiment 4 (H3 — Causal repair by suppressing the stale placeholder): Tests H3, that suppressing the stale placeholder (or patching from an isolated-query run) restores fresh retrieval without editing the fact. Data: 1,000 held-out override cases (Exp 2). Model: same three frozen; activation edits at the pre-slot positions/layers from Exp 3, dose alpha in {0,0.5,1,2,4}; no weight training. Systems compared, matched norm: (a) suppress the stale-placeholder direction (low-rank override-vs-correct difference); (b) patch the slot representation from an isolated-query run; (c) reverse control injecting a placeholder into an early slot; (d) content control (earlier correct slots unchanged); plus random-direction control. Decisive metric (before data): per-slot recovery rate (emitted value flips to the isolated-query-correct value) over random control. Convincing = >=30pp over random at a dose with perplexity within 5%, AND reverse control induces >=15pp override in early slots. Negative = <=5pp recovery (placeholder not causal; H3 fails). Indecision band 5-30pp: partial causal support.

Experiment 5 (H3 — Repair specificity and collateral cost): Tests that H3's repair does not corrupt earlier correct slots or unrelated facts. Data: Exp 4 held-out override cases; the earlier correct slots in those same answers; 200 unrelated facts (PopQA). Model: same three frozen, best intervention/dose. Systems compared: our suppression/patch vs a 'double-check each fact independently' re-prompt, re-querying each fact in isolation (upper bound), ROME editing (existing, expected null), random-direction control. Decisive metric (before data), first: late-slot recovery rate MINUS accuracy drop on earlier correct slots (recovered-per-unit-collateral). Convincing = late-slot recovery >=25pp while earlier-slot accuracy drops <=3pp, unrelated accuracy drops <=2pp, perplexity <=5%. Negative = earlier-slot drop >=10pp or no net gain. Indecision band earlier-slot drop 3-10pp: utility capped; report trade-off.

Experiment 6 (H3 — Transfer, generality, and source): Tests whether a single suppression/patch recipe generalizes and whether override is driven by premature commitment to the category-typical value. Data: recipe fit on a subset of relations/positions (Exp 4) applied to held-out relations and positions (800 cases); plus a regression over all Exp 1 override rates on slot position, placeholder-vs-correct frequency gap, and inter-slot semantic relatedness. Model: all three frozen. Systems compared: transferred vs in-domain-refit vs random-direction; and the frequency-gap regressor vs position-only. Decisive metric (before data): (i) transferred recovery as a fraction of in-domain-refit; (ii) incremental Delta R^2 from the placeholder-vs-correct frequency gap over position-only. Convincing = transfer >=60% of in-domain on >=2 models AND frequency-gap Delta R^2 >=0.10 with positive sign (placeholder is the more frequent value). Negative = transfer <=20% OR frequency Delta R^2 <=0.02 (relation-specific and/or not frequency-driven). Indecision band: transfer 20-60% or Delta R^2 0.02-0.10 -> report partial generality/source. Report Spearman rho between model scale and override rate (N=3 caveat).
Risk Factors and Limitations: Position-dependent errors could arise from generic long-generation degradation or attention dilution rather than a specific stale-placeholder mechanism; the isolated-query control, permuted-order design (same fact early vs late), and the ahead-of-time placeholder decoding (Exp 4) are the decisive separators, and length controls are included.
The prefetched placeholder and the correct-value signal may be entangled; the causal patching/suppression tests (Exp 5), not probe AUROC alone, are decisive, and graded results remain informative.

Verifying a fact is 'stored' via isolated recall risks overestimation from format effects; conservative content-probe thresholds and first-slot recall as an additional check with reported coverage mitigate this.
Suppression could corrupt earlier correct slots or degrade fluency; the earlier-slot and unrelated-fact specificity controls (Exp 6) are central and utility may be capped even if the analysis holds.

Override may be rare relative to genuine ignorance for some attributes; the paired within-subject early-vs-late design maximizes power and a modest but significant position effect is still informative.
A single transferable intervention recipe may not exist if prefetching is relation-specific, limiting practical generality though still scientifically informative.
Ahead-of-time decoding is noisiest when slots are close together; primary analysis uses prompts with clear inter-slot separation and single-token-first answers, with reported coverage.
Findings on 7-9B models may not transfer to frontier-scale models beyond an academic budget.

novelty.reasoning: Core novel claims appear to be: (1) a distinct failure mode where an early reserved slot is prefetched with a plausible-but-wrong placeholder that later overrides fresh retrieval; (2) the wrong placeholder is decodable before the slot is generated and predicts the later error; (3) suppressing that stale placeholder causally repairs the answer; (4) the key setting is within-answer, late-slot factual generation with paired isolated-vs-late controls. Compared with planning/lookahead work, the delta is not a new planning capability but a new failure mechanism linking planning to factual errors. Compared with factual-recall degradation/long-context distraction, the proposal claims a more specific slot-level interference mechanism rather than generic degradation. That is non-trivial if borne out, but the novelty rests heavily on whether the effect is truly distinct from ordinary context dilution, recency/position bias, or ignorance. Closest prior family: future-token decoding / response planning + factual recall interference. Actual delta: a within-answer, position-dependent override phenomenon with causal repair, not just predictability of future tokens.

Pre-register what would falsify the mechanism vs support it (e.g., if wrong answers track retrieval failure equally in isolation, the claim collapses to generic ignorance).

impact.reasoning: The phenomenon matters if real because it targets a concrete reliability failure in multi-fact answering: models can answer a fact correctly alone but wrong when it appears later in the same response. Who cares: interpretability researchers, hallucination/factuality researchers, and anyone using LLMs for long-form synthesis, QA, or structured reporting. Strongest one-line case: if LLMs misfill later answer slots with stale, precommitted placeholders, then factual reliability depends on generation order, not just knowledge, which could change how we evaluate and mitigate hallucinations. The impact is moderate-to-high but not obviously field-shifting unless the effect is common, robust across scales/tasks, and leads to a broadly useful intervention. Real-world reach is plausible for long answers, but the proposal does not yet show broad prevalence or downstream benefits beyond the diagnostic setting.

Demonstrate a practical mitigation that preserves earlier slots and generalizes across models/tasks.

The main confound is ordinary position/length degradation, generic distraction, or true retrieval failure; isolated-query correctness alone does not prove that the late-slot error was caused by stale prefetching. Venue-wise this could be solid if the effect is robust and the causal story is nailed down; as written it is promising but not yet senior-reviewer-tight.

Name: retrieval_induced_suppression
Title: Retrieval-Induced Forgetting in LLMs: How Recalling Competing Facts Suppresses a Related Fact the Model Still Stores
Short Hypothesis: Borrowing the classic retrieval-induced forgetting (RIF) effect from human memory, we hypothesize that when an LLM recalls some members of a shared category earlier in its output, it actively *suppresses* subsequent access to related-but-non-recalled members it otherwise stores. The suppression is not passive competition at the query but a lingering inhibition imprinted by the earlier retrieval act: a related fact answered correctly in isolation becomes inaccessible after the model has retrieved its competitors, even when the competitors are no longer contextually favored. We predict (1) this is a gradable behavioral phenomenon distinct from ordinary in-context interference, scaling with the semantic overlap and retrieval-effort of the earlier recall; (2) the correct answer remains linearly decodable during suppressed recall (hidden, not erased); and (3) suppressing an inhibitory 'recently-retrieved-competitor' direction (not editing the fact) restores access with high specificity.
Related Work: Human cognitive science establishes retrieval-induced forgetting (Anderson et al. 1994) and belief-inhibition-impairs-memory effects (De Neys & Franssens 2007; retrieval-induced impairment of analogical reasoning, 2019): actively retrieving some category members inhibits recall of related non-retrieved members. In LLMs, prior work studies reasoning-vs-retrieval competition (Reasoning or Retrieval? 2025; Knowledge-Neuron factual-recall behaviors 2024), Toxic CoT where reasoning turns correct answers wrong via question-information loss in shallow layers (Focus on Your Question! 2024), and knowledge-conflict from *externally injected* context (Fakepedia). My own prior proposals cover query-internal candidate competition (retrieval_competition), context-priming by a distractor entity, and enumeration closure. Crucially, none transfer the RIF phenomenon: that the model's *own earlier retrieval act* leaves a lingering inhibitory trace that suppresses a related stored fact even after the competitors are no longer favored. Toxic CoT blames question-information loss, not inhibition of a specific competing associate; retrieval_competition and context-priming concern co-activation at the query, not a residual after-effect of prior retrieval. This is a new behavioral phenomenon (RIF-in-LLMs) with its own causal locus and non-destructive fix.
Abstract: Human memory exhibits retrieval-induced forgetting (RIF): recalling some members of a category actively inhibits later recall of related, non-recalled members. We ask whether large language models exhibit an analogous effect and, if so, what mechanism produces it. We propose retrieval-induced suppression: when an LLM recalls some facts from a shared category earlier in its output, the act of retrieval imprints a lingering inhibition that suppresses subsequent access to a related-but-non-recalled fact the model otherwise stores, even after the earlier competitors are no longer contextually favored. Using a controlled RIF paradigm adapted to factual recall, we (1) document the behavior: for facts a model answers correctly in isolation, we first have it recall some competitors from the same category, then query a related non-recalled fact, and measure the drop in accuracy relative to matched baselines (recalling *unrelated* facts, or an equal-length filler). We predict suppression scales with the semantic overlap between the recalled competitors and the target and with how much retrieval effort the earlier recall demanded. (2) We test the storage claim: a linear probe should recover the correct answer from intermediate activations during suppressed recall, showing the fact is hidden, not erased. (3) We test the mechanism with a Location + Causal Intervention strategy: a linear 'recently-retrieved-competitor' inhibition signal should be decodable and, via activation patching, causally drive suppression; subtracting this inhibition direction (not editing the fact) should restore access with high specificity, outperforming a 'consider each item independently' re-prompt and fact editing. Experiments span Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, and Gemma-2-9B on category-structured factual sets, evaluating suppression prevalence, overlap/effort dose-response, hidden-knowledge recovery, causal recovery, and specificity.
Experiments: Experiment 1 (H1 — RIF dataset and suppression prevalence with matched controls): Tests H1's core behavioral claim, that recalling category competitors suppresses a related non-recalled stored fact beyond ordinary interference. Data: constructed from Wikidata (existing). Build category-structured sets (films directed by X, countries in region Y, works by author Z, drugs treating condition C); for each category designate practiced competitors Rp+, related-unpracticed targets Rp-, and unrelated-baseline items Nrp. Use 300 categories, ~2,000 Rp- targets the model answers correctly in isolation, single-token-first answers; report coverage. Model: Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, frozen (bf16), greedy. Systems compared, output length matched: (a) suppression (recall Rp+ competitors, then query Rp-), (b) unrelated-recall control (recall Nrp, then query), (c) equal-length filler control. Decisive metric (before data), first: accuracy drop of Rp- targets in suppression vs the two controls (paired McNemar; mixed-effects logistic), the human RIF signature (Rp- < baseline, driven by category-related recall only). Convincing = suppression accuracy >=8pp below BOTH controls with CI excluding 0 in >=3 categories. Negative = suppression within 2pp of controls, or unrelated-recall drops equally (generic interference, not RIF; H1 fails). Indecision band 2-8pp: report weak RIF. A protective/opposite effect is recorded as an informative cross-species divergence.

Experiment 2 (H1 — Overlap and retrieval-effort dose-response): Tests H1's gradedness, that suppression rises with semantic overlap and competitive retrieval effort. Data: Exp 1 items, with (a) competitor-target overlap (entity-embedding similarity / taxonomic distance) and (b) retrieval effort (number of competitors recalled; easy high-frequency vs hard low-frequency competitors) varied. Model: same three frozen. Systems compared: suppression magnitude across overlap and effort levels; regression with overlap x effort. Decisive metric (before data): slope of suppression on overlap and on effort, plus the prediction that low-frequency targets suppress more. Convincing = both slopes positive with CI excluding 0, and effortful (low-frequency competitor) recall suppresses >=1.5x more than easy recall. Negative = both slopes' CI include 0 (suppression not graded by the RIF drivers; the RIF account weakens). Indecision band |standardized slope| < 0.1 with CI crossing 0: report as no reliable dose-response for that driver.

Experiment 3 (H2 — Hidden-knowledge probe): Tests H2, that the correct target stays linearly decodable during suppressed recall. Data: suppression cases from Exp 1; 80/20 split by fact; label-shuffle control. Model: same three frozen; linear answer probe on subject-token/last-token residual stream, seeds {0,1,2}, layer by CV. Systems compared: probe recovery in the suppression condition vs the model's verbalized accuracy there vs the isolation-condition probe (upper bound). Decisive metric (before data), first: probe recovery minus verbalized accuracy on suppression cases. Convincing = probe recovers at >=40pp above verbalized and within 10pp of the isolation probe (hidden, not erased). Negative = probe within 10pp of verbalized (target genuinely lost; H2 fails). Indecision band 10-40pp: partial hidden knowledge, report as graded.

Experiment 4 (H3 — Inhibition-signal localization): Tests the internal correlate underpinning H3 -- a separable 'recently-retrieved-competitor' inhibition direction. Data: Exp 1 activations at the target query, suppression vs unrelated-recall contrast. Model: same three frozen; contrastive mean-difference inhibition direction per layer; target-content probe for residualization; no weight training. Systems compared: inhibition direction residualized on target-content (it should track presence/overlap of recalled competitors, not the specific target). Decisive metric (before data): residual decodability (AUROC) of the inhibition signal after removing target-content, best layer, and whether its magnitude correlates with attention over the earlier-recalled tokens. Convincing = residual AUROC >=0.70 and positive correlation with competitor-attention. Negative = residual AUROC <=0.55 (no separable inhibition signal; H3's locus fails). Indecision band 0.55-0.70: report an entangled, graded inhibition signal.

Experiment 5 (H3 — Causal recovery): Tests H3's causal claim, that suppressing the inhibition direction restores access. Data: 1,000 held-out suppression cases. Model: same three frozen; activation edits at Exp 4 layers, dose alpha in {0,0.5,1,2,4}; no weight training. Systems compared, matched norm: (a) suppress the inhibition direction; (b) patch the target-query residual stream from an unrelated-recall run; (c) reverse control injecting the inhibition direction into an unrelated-recall run; (d) content control (unrelated facts unchanged); plus random-direction control. Decisive metric (before data): per-target recovery rate (matches the isolation-condition answer) over random control. Convincing = >=30pp over random at a dose with perplexity within 5%, AND reverse control induces >=15pp suppression. Negative = <=5pp recovery (inhibition not causal; H3 fails). Indecision band 5-30pp: partial causal support.

Experiment 6 (H3 — Recovery specificity and collateral cost): Tests that H3's recovery is specific. Data: Exp 5 held-out cases; the recalled Rp+ competitors; Rp- targets already correct under suppression; 200 unrelated facts. Model: same three frozen, best intervention/dose. Systems compared: our suppression vs a 'consider each item independently / ignore earlier answers' re-prompt, fresh-context re-query (upper bound), ROME editing (existing, expected null), random-direction control. Decisive metric (before data), first: target recovery rate MINUS accuracy drop on Rp+ competitors and already-correct Rp- (recovered-per-unit-collateral). Convincing = recovery >=25pp while Rp+/already-correct accuracy drops <=3pp, unrelated <=2pp, perplexity <=5%. Negative = collateral drop >=10pp or no net gain. Indecision band 3-10pp collateral: utility capped; report trade-off.

Experiment 7 (H3 — Transfer, generality, and safety): Tests whether a single inhibition-suppression vector generalizes and whether RIF causes higher-stakes omissions. Data: vector fit on a subset of categories (Exp 5) applied to held-out categories (800 cases); plus a clinical replication of Exp 1-2 on a curated safe medical subset (after recalling several common treatments, does the model suppress a correct less-common but critical treatment/contraindication?), 600 items from an existing medical QA source. Model: all three frozen. Systems compared: transferred vs in-domain-refit vs random-direction; clinical suppression vs general-knowledge suppression. Decisive metric (before data): (i) transferred recovery as a fraction of in-domain-refit; (ii) clinical suppression prevalence. Convincing = transfer >=60% of in-domain on >=2 models AND clinical suppression >=8pp (at least as large as general). Negative = transfer <=20% OR clinical suppression <=2pp. Indecision band: transfer 20-60% or clinical 2-8pp -> partial. Report Spearman rho between model scale and RIF magnitude (N=3 caveat).
Risk Factors and Limitations: The suppression could be ordinary in-context interference or generic long-output degradation rather than a genuine RIF after-effect; the matched unrelated-recall and equal-length filler controls (Exp 2), the overlap dose-response (Exp 3), and the RIF-specific prediction that only *category-related* non-recalled items are impaired are the decisive separators.

A key RIF prediction (impairment specific to related, competitively-retrieved items) may not hold in LLMs; a null or opposite result (recalling competitors *helps* via priming) would refute the transfer but is itself an informative finding about how LLM memory differs from human memory.
Verifying the target is 'stored' via isolation recall risks overestimation from format effects; conservative content-probe thresholds and fresh-context re-query with reported coverage mitigate this.
The inhibition and target-content signals may be entangled; the causal patching/steering tests (Exp 6), not probe accuracy alone, are decisive, and graded results remain informative.

The recovery intervention could re-corrupt the recalled competitors or degrade fluency; the Rp+/Rp-/unrelated specificity controls (Exp 7) are central and utility may be capped even if the analysis holds.
A single transferable inhibition-suppression vector may not exist if RIF is category-specific, limiting practical generality though still scientifically informative.
Multi-token answers complicate readout; primary analysis restricts to single-token-first answers with reported coverage.
Findings on 7-9B models may not transfer to frontier-scale models beyond an academic budget.

novelty.reasoning: Core novel claims: (1) a true retrieval-induced forgetting/RIF signature in LLMs, i.e. earlier retrieval of category competitors causes later suppression of a related non-recalled fact; (2) this is distinct from ordinary in-context interference/overwriting/recency effects because it has a residual after-effect with matched unrelated and filler controls; (3) the target fact is still stored/linearly decodable during impairment; (4) there is a decodable causal inhibition direction whose suppression restores access. Closest prior family is generic LLM interference/working-memory papers (proactive interference, in-context superposition, transformers remember first/forget last), but those study co-activation, overwriting, or ordering effects at query time, not the post-retrieval suppression signature. The actual delta is decent: importing a specific cognitive phenomenon into LLMs with controls that would distinguish it from generic interference. However, the idea is still a transfer of a known human effect and may collapse into standard interference/priming if the controls fail, so novelty is moderate-high rather than breakthrough.

That said, the downstream change is unclear unless the effect is robust, large, and practically exploitable; this is more a conceptual/diagnostic contribution than an immediate product or benchmark shift. Reach is moderate across memory, probing, and interpretability communities, but not obviously broad outside them.

Name: conditional_suppression_effect
Title: Suppressed by an Aside: Transferring the Human Conditional-Suppression Effect into LLMs and Locating the Premise-Gating Mechanism
Short Hypothesis: LLMs exhibit the classic human conditional-reasoning suppression effect: adding a logically-irrelevant *additional-condition* premise to a valid modus ponens / modus tollens argument suppresses the model's endorsement of the deductively valid conclusion, whereas adding an *alternative-condition* premise selectively suppresses the invalid inferences (denial-of-antecedent / affirmation-of-consequent) - exactly the double dissociation observed in humans. We hypothesize this is not a competence failure but a premise-gating failure: the model still 'derives' the valid conclusion internally (it is linearly decodable), but a distinct signal triggered by the extra premise gates its expression, and suppressing that signal restores the valid inference without editing the rule.
Related Work: Human cognitive science established the suppression effect (Byrne 1989; Bonnefon; Quelhas & Johnson-Laird 2016; 'Suppression of Inferences From Counterfactual Conditionals' 2020): a valid modus ponens is suppressed by an *additional* premise while invalid inferences are suppressed by an *alternative* premise - a precise double dissociation. In LLMs, mechanistic work on fact-vs-counterfactual competition (Ortu et al. 2024; Fakepedia 2023) and RULEBREAKERS (2024) shows models over-rigidly apply logic and mis-integrate world knowledge, and semantic-vs-symbolic reasoning work (2023) shows reliance on surface semantics. Crucially, none of these transfer the *conditional suppression effect* - the selective, premise-type-dependent suppression of a specific inference form by a logically-non-defeating additional premise - into LLMs, none test whether it reproduces the human additional-vs-alternative double dissociation, and none localize a premise-gating mechanism or show that the valid conclusion remains internally derivable but expression-gated. This is orthogonal to all my prior proposals, which concern factual/entity retrieval; here the object is defeasible conditional inference and how an incidental premise gates a correctly-computed logical conclusion.
Abstract: Since Byrne (1989), cognitive science has documented the suppression effect: people who correctly infer 'she got wet' from 'if she watered the plants she got wet' and 'she watered the plants' will stop endorsing that valid modus ponens conclusion once an additional premise ('if the sprinkler was on she got wet') is added - even though it does not logically defeat the inference - while an alternative premise instead suppresses the invalid inferences. We ask whether LLMs exhibit this human signature and, if so, what mechanism produces it. We first document the behavior: on controlled conditional-reasoning items (modus ponens, modus tollens, denial-of-antecedent, affirmation-of-consequent) we measure endorsement of each inference in a baseline two-premise form versus forms augmented with an additional-condition or an alternative-condition premise, testing whether LLMs reproduce the human additional-vs-alternative double dissociation and how it scales with premise plausibility and model size. We then test a mechanistic hypothesis with a Location + Causal Intervention strategy: the valid modus-ponens conclusion is still internally derived (linearly decodable from intermediate activations) even when the model behaviorally withholds it, and a distinct 'premise-gating' signal - triggered by the added premise and separable from the conclusion content - causally suppresses its expression. Activation patching from a baseline (no-extra-premise) run and subtraction of a learned premise-gating direction should restore the valid conclusion with high specificity, while the same direction should, when injected, induce suppression on demand. Experiments span Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, and Gemma-2-9B, evaluating suppression prevalence, the additional-vs-alternative dissociation, hidden-conclusion recovery, causal recovery, and specificity.
Experiments: Experiment 1 (H1 — Suppression dataset and additional-vs-alternative double dissociation): Tests H1's behavioral core, the human double dissociation (additional-condition premise suppresses valid inferences; alternative-condition premise suppresses invalid inferences). Data: constructed by adapting the classic Byrne/Quelhas conditional-reasoning paradigm (existing stimuli, tens of items) into 1,200 controlled items: each base 'if A then C' yields four inference probes (modus ponens, modus tollens valid; denial-of-antecedent, affirmation-of-consequent invalid) x three versions (baseline; +additional-condition; +alternative-condition), in both everyday-semantics and abstract/letter forms; endorsement via a fixed yes/no/uncertain template plus 3 paraphrases. 1,200 items x 4 x 3 x 2 forms fits budget and gives >=100 items per cell. Model: Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, frozen (bf16), greedy. Systems compared: endorsement across premise-type x inference-type vs a null where any added premise adds uniform noise. Decisive metric (before data), first: the premise-type x inference-type interaction (additional suppresses valid; alternative suppresses invalid) in a mixed-effects logistic regression, in the ABSTRACT form (isolating logic from world knowledge). Convincing = interaction CI excluding 0 in >=2 models AND additional-premise drop on valid inferences >=15pp. Negative = no interaction (uniform or no suppression; H1 fails as a human-signature). Indecision band interaction present only in everyday but not abstract form: report as semantics-driven, not a form-level suppression effect.

Experiment 2 (H1 — Plausibility and scale dose-response): Tests H1's gradedness, that suppression scales with the added premise's plausibility. Data: Exp 1 items with the added premise's plausibility/salience varied over 4 levels (rated by an existing plausibility norm / GPT-4o). Model: Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B (and, where an intra-family size series is affordable, two sizes of one family), frozen. Systems compared: suppression magnitude across plausibility levels; and across model scale. Decisive metric (before data): slope of suppression on premise plausibility. Convincing = positive slope with CI excluding 0 in >=2 models, mirroring the human graded effect. Negative = flat slope (suppression not plausibility-graded; the human-likeness claim weakens). Indecision band |standardized slope| < 0.1 with CI crossing 0: report as no reliable dose-response. Scale effect reported as Spearman rho between size and suppression (N small; suggestive only), distinguishing 'more human-like defeasibility' from 'over-rigid logic'.

Experiment 3 (H2 — Hidden-conclusion probe): Tests the first half of H2, that the valid conclusion is still internally derived when behaviorally withheld. Data: suppression cases from Exp 1 (valid inference endorsed at baseline, withheld under the additional premise); 80/20 split by item; label-shuffle control. Model: same three frozen; a linear probe on the conclusion-position/last-token residual stream decoding whether valid conclusion C is derived; seeds {0,1,2}, layer by CV. Systems compared: probe recovery under suppression vs verbalized endorsement vs the baseline run (upper bound). Decisive metric (before data), first: probe recovery of the valid conclusion minus verbalized endorsement on suppression cases. Convincing = probe recovers at >=40pp above verbalized and within 10pp of baseline (derived but expression-gated). Negative = probe within 10pp of verbalized (the model did not derive C; H2 fails). Indecision band 10-40pp: partial internal derivation, report as graded.

Experiment 4 (H2 — Premise-gating signal localization): Tests the second half of H2, a separable premise-gating direction that mirrors the behavioral dissociation. Data: Exp 1 activations, additional-premise (suppressing) vs baseline contrast. Model: same three frozen; contrastive mean-difference gating direction per layer; conclusion-content probe for residualization; no weight training. Systems compared: gating direction residualized on conclusion-content (should track added-premise presence/plausibility, not the specific conclusion); and whether the same direction is engaged by additional premises for valid inferences AND by alternative premises for invalid inferences (mechanistic counterpart of Exp 1). Decisive metric (before data): residual AUROC of the gating signal after removing conclusion-content, and its cross-engagement across the dissociation. Convincing = residual AUROC >=0.70 and the direction engaged in both dissociation arms. Negative = residual AUROC <=0.55 (no separable gating signal; H2 localization fails). Indecision band 0.55-0.70: report entangled gating.

Experiment 5 (H2/H3 — Causal intervention): Tests H2's causal drive and H3's restoration. Data: 1,000 held-out suppression cases. Model: same three frozen; activation edits at Exp 4 layers, dose alpha in {0,0.5,1,2,4}; no weight training. Systems compared, matched norm: (a) patch the conclusion-position residual stream from a baseline (no-extra-premise) run; (b) subtract the learned gating direction; (c) reverse control injecting the gating direction into a baseline run; (d) content control (unrelated inferences unchanged); plus random-direction control. Decisive metric (before data): per-item recovery of the valid conclusion (matches baseline endorsement) over random control. Convincing = >=30pp over random at a dose with perplexity within 5%, AND reverse control induces >=15pp suppression. Negative = <=5pp recovery (gating not causal; H2/H3 causal link fails). Indecision band 5-30pp: partial causal support.

Experiment 6 (H3 — Recovery specificity: preserving legitimate defeasibility): Tests H3's key specificity requirement, that reopening valid inferences does not indiscriminately restore inferences that SHOULD be suppressed. Data: Exp 5 held-out suppression cases; a genuinely-defeasible set where the added premise is a TRUE blocking condition that should reduce confidence (300 items); 200 unrelated reasoning/factual items. Model: same three frozen, best intervention/dose. Systems compared: our intervention vs a 'reason strictly from the premises' re-prompt, chain-of-thought, random-direction control. Decisive metric (before data), first: valid-inference recovery rate MINUS inappropriate restoration on genuinely-defeasible items (recovered-per-unit-over-restoration). Convincing = valid recovery >=25pp while genuinely-defeasible confidence is restored <=5pp, unrelated accuracy unchanged (<=2pp), perplexity <=5%. Negative = genuinely-defeasible items restored >=20pp (we broke legitimate defeasibility) or no valid recovery. Indecision band 5-20pp over-restoration: utility capped; report the selectivity trade-off.

Experiment 7 (H3 — Transfer, generality, and optional safety): Tests whether a single gating-suppression vector generalizes across inference forms and domains. Data: vector fit on a subset of forms/domains (Exp 5) applied to held-out forms and item domains (600 cases); optional safety replication of Exp 1-2 on curated clinical/procedural conditional rules ('if symptom X and no contraindication, give treatment T'), 400 safe items. Model: all three frozen. Systems compared: transferred vs in-domain-refit vs random-direction; clinical suppression vs general. Decisive metric (before data): transferred recovery as a fraction of in-domain-refit; plus clinical suppression prevalence. Convincing = transfer >=60% of in-domain on >=2 models (architecture-general mechanism). Negative = transfer <=20% (inference-form-specific; generality fails). Indecision band 20-60%: partial transfer. Clinical arm reported descriptively: suppression >=15pp there flags a higher-stakes error mode.
Risk Factors and Limitations: The behavioral suppression could be a genuine, appropriate defeasibility response rather than an unwanted gating of a valid inference; the abstract-form items (isolating logical form from world knowledge) and the additional-vs-alternative double-dissociation test (Exp 2) are the decisive separators - only the human-signature selectivity distinguishes suppression-effect from rational defeasance.

LLMs might not reproduce the human double dissociation at all (e.g. suppress uniformly or over-rigidly apply logic per RULEBREAKERS); a null or divergent pattern is itself an informative cross-species comparison, though it would weaken the 'human-like suppression' framing.
The premise-gating and conclusion-content signals may be entangled; the causal patching/injection tests (Exp 6), not probe decoding alone, are decisive, and graded results remain informative.

The recovery intervention could indiscriminately restore inferences that *should* be suppressed (breaking legitimate defeasibility) or degrade fluency; the genuine-defeasibility specificity control (Exp 7) is central and utility may be capped even if the analysis holds.
Endorsement is prompt-sensitive (yes/no/uncertain framing, phrasing); we use multiple paraphrases and report robustness, since framing itself may modulate suppression.
A single transferable gating vector may not exist if suppression is inference-form-specific, limiting practical generality though still scientifically informative.
Findings on 7-9B models may not transfer to frontier-scale models beyond an academic budget.

novelty.reasoning: Core novel claims: (1) LLMs reproduce the human conditional-suppression double dissociation; (2) the valid conclusion is still internally derived/linearly decodable when behaviorally withheld; (3) there is a separable premise-gating mechanism that causally suppresses expression and can be edited to restore only the valid inference; (4) the effect transfers across additional vs alternative premise forms with dose-response. From the proposal + search summary, the behavioral suppression effect itself is only partially novel: prior LLM work already shows conditional fallacies and at least some additional-vs-alternative distinction. The genuinely new part is the mechanistic story (internal derivation + causal gating localization). That said, the mechanistic delta is non-trivial but still somewhat speculative because it depends on the behavioral effect being reproducible in the first place. Closest prior family is conditional/modal reasoning and defeasible-reasoning in LLMs; the actual delta is moving from behavioral inconsistency to a mechanistic account of expression gating with causal interventions.
revision_notes: Sharpen the novelty claim to the mechanistic delta only; do not claim first behavioral transfer of suppression unless you can prove the exact human double dissociation in abstract forms.
State explicitly what prior LLM work does not do: no hidden-state probe for a decodable conclusion, no causal localization of a premise-gating direction, no specificity-preserving intervention.
If possible, define the exact operational criterion for 'suppression' vs generic fallacy/ambiguity to separate from existing conditional reasoning papers.

However, the practical reach is limited because the target phenomenon is a niche classic effect and the proposed benefit is mainly explanatory rather than broad product impact. Strongest one-line case: 'LLMs may know the valid conclusion but suppress it via a premise-gating circuit, revealing a tractable failure mode in reasoning expression.'

Name: fragmentary_recall
Title: On the Tip of the Model's Tongue: Structured Partial Knowledge of Unproducible Answers in LLMs
Short Hypothesis: When an LLM fails to produce a specific factual answer, it is not in a binary known/unknown state: like humans in a tip-of-the-tongue (TOT) state, it internally holds structured *partial knowledge* of the specific unproduced target - its semantic category, its first letter/subword, its length, and its lexical neighbors - and this partial knowledge is (a) graded and correct at above-chance rates that track the human accessibility signature, (b) linearly decodable from intermediate activations even though the full answer is not, and (c) carried by a representation distinct from the model's scalar correctness/self-knowledge signal, such that assembling the fragments (constrained decoding conditioned on the decoded partial attributes) recovers answers the model otherwise cannot produce.
Related Work: Cognitive science establishes that in a TOT state humans reliably access *correct fragments* of an unrecallable target - first letter, syllable count, semantic features - and that feeling-of-knowing tracks the amount of *correct* partial knowledge (Brown 1991/2011; Schwartz; the 2016 FoK-partial-knowledge study; 1975 decoding-failure account; 2008 multi-word-name study). In LLMs, prior interpretability work encodes only a *scalar* self-knowledge/correctness signal: in-advance correctness directions (No Answer Needed, 2025), factual self-awareness directions (2025), truthfulness in answer tokens (LLMs Know More Than They Show, 2024), answerability directions (2023), and entity-recognition known/unknown directions (Do I Know This Entity, 2024). All treat the failed-recall state as binary or one-dimensional and predict *whether* the model will be right, not *what structured fragments of the specific wrong-to-produce target* it still holds. This proposal is distinct from those and from my prior proposals (premature_lexicalization concerns committing to a wrong first token; familiarity_before_retrieval concerns a scalar coverage estimate): here the object is a *multi-attribute, graded, correct partial representation of the specific unproduced answer*, transferring the human TOT/partial-knowledge phenomenon into LLMs, testing its human accessibility signature, and using it to recover hidden answers.
Abstract: Humans who cannot recall a word are often not simply ignorant of it: in a tip-of-the-tongue (TOT) state they reliably retrieve correct fragments of the unrecallable target - its first letter, its length, its semantic category - and their feeling-of-knowing tracks how much correct partial knowledge they hold. We ask whether large language models exhibit an analogous structured partial-knowledge state when they fail to produce a factual answer. Existing interpretability work encodes only a scalar 'will I be right' signal and treats failed recall as binary. We hypothesize instead that on failed factual queries the model internally holds graded, correct fragments of the specific unproduced target - semantic category, first letter/subword, token length, and lexical neighbors - decodable from intermediate activations even though the full answer is not, and carried by a representation separable from the scalar correctness direction. We test three claims. (1) Fragmentary retrieval: for facts the model cannot generate, linear probes recover partial attributes of the correct answer at rates well above frequency- and category-matched chance, and the correctness of these fragments follows the human accessibility signature (fragment correctness predicts recognition/short-list success; correct partial knowledge is present without the full answer). (2) Structure not scalar: the partial-attribute directions are separable (via residualization) from the model's in-advance-correctness/self-knowledge direction, so partial knowledge is multi-dimensional, not a single confidence axis. (3) Assembly recovery: constrained decoding conditioned on the decoded fragments (first letter + length + category), or steering with the fragment directions, recovers correct answers the model otherwise fails to produce, with higher yield than free generation, temperature sampling, or a 'guess the first letter' re-prompt, and with high specificity. Experiments span Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, and Gemma-2-9B on PopQA, T-REx, and EntityQuestions.
Experiments: Experiment 1 (H2 — Failed-recall dataset and fragmentary-retrieval decoding): Tests H2, that partial attributes of the specific unproduced target are linearly decodable even though the full answer is not. Data: constructed from PopQA (~14k), T-REx (LAMA subset ~34k), EntityQuestions (~176k); for each model split into produced (correct free-generation) and failed (wrong/refused) sets matched by relation, answer frequency, and answer length; target 3,000 failed items with unambiguous partial attributes (semantic category, first letter/subword, length bucket, lexical neighbors); report coverage. Model: Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, frozen (bf16), greedy. Trainable: linear probes on subject-token/last-token residual stream per attribute, L2-regularized, seeds {0,1,2}, layer by CV, held-out entities, label-shuffle control. Systems compared: probe accuracy on the failed set vs frequency/category-matched chance vs a produced-set upper bound. Decisive metric (before data), first: per-attribute decoding accuracy above matched chance on the failed set, and the fraction of failed items with >=1 correct decodable fragment. Convincing = first-letter and category probes exceed matched chance by >=15pp (CI excluding 0) and >=50% of failed items carry >=1 correct fragment. Negative = probes within 3pp of chance (no partial knowledge; H2 fails). Indecision band 3-15pp above chance: report weak, graded partial knowledge.

Experiment 2 (H1 — Human accessibility-signature test): Tests H1, that fragments are CORRECT at rates tracking the human accessibility signature (correct partial knowledge predicts recognition/short-list success; incorrect fragments do not). Data: the Exp 1 failed items. Model: same three frozen. Systems compared: (a) recognition test -- present a short list (true answer + distractors) and measure recognition; correlate recognition success with the number of CORRECT decoded fragments vs the number of INCORRECT fragments; (b) verbalized-fragment test -- prompt the model to guess first letter/category/length of the answer it could not produce, correlate verbalized-fragment correctness with probe-decoded-fragment correctness. Decisive metric (before data), first: increase in recognition accuracy per additional correct decoded fragment (logistic slope), and the contrast that incorrect fragments confer no such benefit. Convincing = positive slope for correct fragments (CI excluding 0) AND near-zero slope for incorrect fragments, plus verbalized-vs-probe fragment agreement above chance (kappa >=0.2). Negative = correct and incorrect fragments confer equal recognition benefit (fragments not diagnostic; H1's accessibility signature fails). Indecision band correct-fragment slope CI including 0 but point estimate positive: report weak accessibility signature.

Experiment 3 (H3 — Structure-vs-scalar dissociation): Tests the first half of H3, that partial-attribute directions are separable from the scalar correctness/self-knowledge signal. Data: Exp 1 activations. Model: same three frozen; recover the scalar in-advance-correctness/self-knowledge direction following existing methods (No-Answer-Needed / factual-self-awareness / Do-I-Know-This-Entity); residualize each partial-attribute probe on this scalar signal. Systems compared: partial-attribute decodability before vs after removing the scalar signal. Decisive metric (before data), first: residual per-attribute AUROC after removing the scalar direction. Convincing = residual AUROC >=0.70 for >=2 attributes (partial knowledge is multi-dimensional, not one confidence axis). Negative = residual AUROC <=0.55 for all attributes (partial knowledge collapses to the scalar signal; H3's structure claim fails). Indecision band 0.55-0.70: report a partial (graded) dissociation, weakening the strong 'structured' claim.

Experiment 4 (H3 — Causal steering/ablation of fragment directions): Tests that the decoded fragments are causal handles, supporting H3's assembly claim. Data: failed items with >=1 correct decodable fragment (from Exp 1), 1,000 held-out. Model: same three frozen; activation edits at the probe layers, dose alpha in {0,0.5,1,2,4}; no weight training. Systems compared, matched norm: (a) amplify decoded fragment directions (first-letter, category) and measure the correct answer's probability; (b) reverse control ablating a fragment direction and confirming its decodability and recognition benefit drop; (c) content control (unrelated answers unchanged); random-direction control. Decisive metric (before data): change in correct-answer log-probability / rank under fragment amplification vs random control. Convincing = correct-answer log-prob rises by >=0.5 nats (or rank improves by >=5 positions) over random control at a dose with perplexity within 5%, and ablation drops fragment decodability by >=15pp. Negative = <=0.1 nat change (fragments not causal). Indecision band 0.1-0.5 nats: partial causal support.

Experiment 5 (H3 — Assembly-recovery intervention): Tests the second half of H3, that assembling decoded fragments recovers answers the model otherwise cannot produce. Data: 1,000 held-out failed items; plus 300 nonexistent-entity controls (to measure fabrication). Model: same three frozen; a constrained-decoding pipeline that decodes first letter/subword + length + category from the failed-recall activations and constrains generation to matching answers over the model's own candidate distribution. Systems compared: constrained-assembly vs free generation, temperature/beam sampling, a 'guess the first letter then answer' re-prompt, and a random-constraint control. Decisive metric (before data), first: recovery rate of correct answers on held-out failed items MINUS false-answer rate on nonexistent-entity controls (recovered-per-unit-fabrication). Convincing = assembly recovers >=15pp more correct answers than the best baseline while false-answer rate on nonexistent controls rises <=5pp. Negative = <=3pp recovery gain, or fabrication rises >=15pp (assembly just induces confident guessing). Indecision band 3-15pp recovery with fabrication 5-15pp: report a capped-utility recovery.

Experiment 6 (H2/H3 — Cross-relation and cross-model transfer): Tests whether probes and the assembly pipeline generalize rather than being relation-specific. Data: probes/directions fit on a subset of relations (Exp 1) applied unchanged to held-out relations (800 failed items). Model: all three frozen. Systems compared: transferred probes/pipeline vs in-relation-refit vs chance/random-constraint. Decisive metric (before data): transferred fragment-decoding accuracy above chance and transferred assembly-recovery as a fraction of in-relation-refit. Convincing = transferred fragment decoding >=10pp above chance AND assembly transfer >=60% of in-relation on >=2 models. Negative = transferred decoding <=3pp above chance (relation-specific encoding; the assembly pipeline does not generalize). Indecision band 3-10pp / 20-60%: partial transfer. Report Spearman rho between model scale and correct-fragments-per-failed-item (N=3 caveat).

Experiment 7 (H1 — Source and graded 'closeness-to-production' analysis): Tests H1's graded prediction, that failed items with more correct fragments are closer to production. Data: all Exp 1 failed items with per-item features (answer frequency, entity popularity, relation hops). Model: same three frozen. Systems compared: regression of per-item fragment correctness on frequency/popularity/hops; and a test that fragment count predicts 'closeness' (lower answer rank, higher recognition). Decisive metric (before data): correlation between number of correct fragments and closeness-to-production (answer rank / recognition), controlling for frequency. Convincing = correct-fragment count predicts lower answer rank and higher recognition with CI excluding 0, above frequency alone (Delta R^2 >=0.05). Negative = no residual predictive value (Delta R^2 <=0.01) (partial knowledge is not graded toward production; the weak-trace account fails). Indecision band 0.01-0.05: report a weak graded effect.
Risk Factors and Limitations: Above-chance fragment decoding could reflect probe exploitation of query-side correlations (e.g., relation type predicts category) rather than genuine partial knowledge of the specific target; frequency/category-matched chance baselines, held-out entities, subject-token vs query-token probe comparisons, and the correctness-specific accessibility signature (Exp 3, where only *correct* fragments confer recognition benefit) are the decisive controls.

Partial knowledge may collapse to the existing scalar self-knowledge signal; the residualization dissociation (Exp 4) is the key test, and a partial (graded) dissociation would weaken the strong 'structured' claim while remaining informative.

Assembly recovery could induce confident fabrication on genuinely-unknown items; nonexistent-entity controls and false-answer-rate specificity metrics (Exp 6) are essential and may cap practical utility.

First-letter/length fragments depend on tokenization and are noisiest for heavily subword-fragmented multi-token names; primary analysis restricts to answers with clean first-subword/length attributes and reports coverage.
The human accessibility parallel is motivational, not identity; recognition and verbalized-fragment tests are LLM-native operationalizations and are reported on their own terms.
Fragment directions may not transfer across relations if partial-knowledge encoding is relation-specific, limiting the generality of the assembly pipeline though still scientifically informative.
Findings on 7-9B models may not transfer to frontier-scale models beyond an academic budget.

novelty.reasoning: Core claims that must be novel: (1) failed recall contains structured, target-specific partial knowledge (category/first letter/length/lexical neighbors), not just a scalar know/don't-know signal; (2) this structure is decodable and follows a human TOT-style accessibility signature; (3) the structured fragment representation is separable from scalar correctness/self-knowledge; (4) constrained assembly of fragments can recover answers the model otherwise does not generate. Closest prior family: scalar self-knowledge / answerability directions and hidden-answer recoverability work (Inside-Out, LLMs Know More Than They Show, Do I Know This Entity, Empty Shelves or Lost Keys). Actual delta: from binary/scalar or full-answer latent recovery to multi-attribute, specific-to-unproduced-target partial knowledge plus assembly. That is a real and non-trivial reframing, and the human TOT analogy is a meaningful new setting. The main caveat is that some fragment signals (length, category, first letters) may be weakly implied by the query or tokenization rather than genuinely latent.
revision_notes: State explicitly which fragment attributes are genuinely target-specific versus query-predictable; include matched-chance baselines.
Clarify the exact novelty over Inside-Out: not full-answer hidden recoverability, but structured partial knowledge + accessibility signature + separability.
Pre-register which attributes count as success and which are considered leakage to avoid overclaiming.

impact.reasoning: Who cares: interpretability, hallucination/abstention, calibration, and knowledge-elicitation researchers, plus anyone trying to exploit latent knowledge without eliciting fabrication. Phenomenon value: whether a model can hold and expose TOT-like partial knowledge when it cannot directly answer. Downstream change: could improve abstention, probing, candidate generation, and safer answer recovery; it also sharpens the theory of what 'hidden knowledge' means. Strongest one-line case: models may fail to say the answer yet still encode recoverable, structured fragments of that exact answer, changing how we think about uncertainty and elicitation. However, the practical reach is moderate because the likely gains are specialized and the assembly step risks fabrication; this is more an interpretability/phenomenon paper than a broadly deployment-shifting method.
revision_notes: Emphasize the phenomenon first: what this reveals about latent knowledge states, not just probe performance.
Quantify downstream utility beyond recovery accuracy: abstention calibration, retrieval quality, or error reduction.
Show why fragmentary structure matters beyond existing full-answer recovery methods, or impact will read as incremental.

review.reasoning: The hypothesis is interesting but currently underspecified and vulnerable to confounds. Main logical gaps: fragment decoding may be driven by query/relation leakage rather than knowledge of the specific unproduced target; residualization against a scalar correctness direction may not prove a distinct representation, since linear orthogonalization is not causal separation; assembly recovery could simply turn weak priors into confident hallucinations. The proposal needs a sharper falsifiable claim: e.g., on held-out entities and matched-chance controls, correct target-specific fragments should predict human-style recognition better than incorrect fragments and better than query-only baselines. Related work is directionally cited but not specific enough on how this differs from prior full-answer hidden recoverability and scalar self-knowledge work. Experiments are feasible, but controls are missing: nonexistent-entity controls, tokenization controls for first-letter/length, relation-matched random fragment baselines, and ablations separating semantic category from surface form cues. Venue strength is decent if the controls are tight and the cognitive analogy is used carefully; otherwise it risks reading as a probe/assembly demo. Minimum viable edits: narrow the claims to 2-3 crisp hypotheses, add matched-chance/leakage baselines, define the fabrication metric for assembly, and specify the exact causal test for separability beyond residual AUROC.
