Name: retrieval_enhanced_suggestibility
Title: Recalling a Fact Makes It Easier to Overwrite: Retrieval-Enhanced Suggestibility and a Prediction-Error Destabilization Signal in LLMs
Short Hypothesis: Transferring the human retrieval-enhanced-suggestibility (RES) / reconsolidation effect: having an LLM first correctly retrieve a fact within a session makes that specific fact MORE vulnerable to being overwritten by a subsequently presented piece of misinformation than if it had not been pre-retrieved, and this excess vulnerability is gated by prediction error at retrieval (larger when the retrieval was effortful/low-confidence or the misinformation is surprising). We hypothesize the extra corruptibility is carried by a transient, prediction-error-scaled 'destabilization' signal in the residual stream imprinted at the retrieval act, distinct from ordinary context-following, and causally suppressible so that pre-retrieval no longer increases suggestibility.
Related Work: Human memory research shows retrieval destabilizes a memory and requires reconsolidation (Function and mechanisms of memory destabilization, 2020), that prediction error/surprise at retrieval drives this destabilization and later false memories (Surprise and destabilize, 2018), and that an initial test increases later misinformation uptake—Retrieval-Enhanced Suggestibility, RES (New Theory of Disuse predicts RES, 2017; pre-retrieval warnings, 2025). In LLMs, prior work studies answer-flipping under re-prompting via non-retrieval 'uncertainty heads' (Interpreting and Mitigating Unwanted Uncertainty, 2025), intra-memory conflict and stubbornness of dynamic facts (DynamicQA, 2024), catastrophic interference from contradictory updates during training (In Praise of Stubbornness, 2025), and representational stability of truth under perturbation (P-StaT, 2025; LLM Knowledge is Brittle, 2025). Crucially, none test the RES signature at inference time: that the *act of correctly retrieving* a fact earlier in a session *causally increases* that fact's susceptibility to a later in-context contradiction relative to a not-pre-retrieved control, none test the prediction-error gating of that excess vulnerability, and none localize a retrieval-induced destabilization signal. This is distinct from my prior proposals on retrieval-induced suppression (recalling competitors inhibits a related fact) and self-commitment lock-in (the model defends its own prior answer): here pre-retrieving the target makes it *more* changeable, not more inhibited or more entrenched, and the driver is prediction error, matching the human reconsolidation account rather than in-context entrainment or interference.
Abstract: Human memory has a counterintuitive property: retrieving a memory temporarily destabilizes it, so being tested on an event before encountering misinformation makes people MORE likely to adopt the misinformation—retrieval-enhanced suggestibility (RES), driven by prediction error at retrieval. We ask whether large language models exhibit an analogous inference-time effect and, if so, what mechanism produces it. We propose that when an LLM correctly retrieves a fact earlier in a conversation, the act of retrieval leaves a transient destabilization signal that makes that specific fact more susceptible to being overwritten by a subsequently presented in-context contradiction than the same fact would be with no prior retrieval. We test three claims. (1) Behavioral RES signature: for facts the model answers correctly, we compare acceptance of a later planted contradiction between a pre-retrieval condition (model first correctly states the fact, then is exposed to misinformation, then re-queried) and a matched no-pre-retrieval control (equal-length filler instead of the retrieval), predicting higher contradiction-acceptance in the pre-retrieval condition—and we further predict this excess scales with prediction error (larger when retrieval was low-confidence/effortful and when the misinformation is surprising). (2) Destabilization locus: a linear 'destabilization' signal imprinted at the retrieval act is decodable, scales with prediction error, and is separable from ordinary context-following. (3) Causal control: activation patching from the no-pre-retrieval control and suppression of the destabilization direction eliminate the excess suggestibility (making pre-retrieved facts no more corruptible than un-retrieved ones) with high specificity, whereas a 'trust your own knowledge' re-prompt does not. Experiments span Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, and Gemma-2-9B on PopQA, T-REx, and a medical-fact subset, evaluating RES prevalence, prediction-error dose-response, destabilization decoding, causal reduction, and specificity.
Experiments: Experiment 1 (H1 — RES dataset and prevalence under paired conditions): Tests H1's core behavioral claim, that first correctly retrieving a fact makes it MORE vulnerable to later misinformation than a matched no-pre-retrieval control. Data: constructed from PopQA (~14k), T-REx (LAMA subset ~34k), EntityQuestions (~176k); select 2,500 facts (subject, relation, correct answer a) the model answers correctly in isolation, single-token-first answers; for each build three token-length-matched sessions: PRE-RETRIEVAL (state a, then misinformation a_false, then re-query), NO-PRE-RETRIEVAL control (equal-length filler instead of the initial question, then same misinformation, then query), NO-MISINFORMATION baseline (retrieval, filler, query). Report coverage. Model: Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, frozen (bf16), greedy. Systems compared: contradiction-acceptance (model now answers a_false) in pre-retrieval vs no-pre-retrieval (paired McNemar; mixed-effects logistic), with the no-misinformation baseline confirming pre-retrieval alone does not change the answer. Decisive metric (before data), first: acceptance rate in pre-retrieval MINUS acceptance in the no-pre-retrieval control. Convincing = pre-retrieval acceptance HIGHER by >=8pp with CI excluding 0 in >=3 relations (RES signature). Negative = difference CI includes 0, or pre-retrieval is protective (<0). Both refute the transfer but are recorded as informative cross-species findings. Indecision band 2-8pp: report weak RES.

Experiment 2 (H1 — Prediction-error dose-response): Tests H1's gating claim, that excess suggestibility scales with prediction error at retrieval. Data: Exp 1 pre-retrieval trials, with prediction error operationalized two ways -- (a) retrieval effort (the model's confidence/margin when it initially states a) and (b) misinformation surprise (log-prob/implausibility of a_false given the subject), with low- vs high-surprise a_false conditions. Model: same three frozen. Systems compared: excess suggestibility (pre-retrieval minus control acceptance) across effort and surprise levels; regression. Decisive metric (before data): slope of excess suggestibility on retrieval effort and on misinformation surprise. Convincing = both slopes positive with CI excluding 0 (effortful/low-confidence retrieval and surprising misinformation drive more destabilization), consistent across the two operationalizations. Negative = both slopes' CI include 0 (no prediction-error gating; the reconsolidation account weakens even if RES prevalence holds). Indecision band |standardized slope| < 0.1 with CI crossing 0: report as no reliable dose-response for that operationalization.

Experiment 3 (H1/H3 — Storage/transience check): Tests that the corruption is a transient session-level destabilization (reconsolidation-like), not genuine belief change -- the property that makes H3's mitigation meaningful. Data: 1,000 pre-retrieval-corruption trials from Exp 1. Model: same three frozen; a content probe (seeds {0,1,2}) during the corrupted output. Systems compared: re-query the same fact in a FRESH session after corruption (does a return?); content-probe decoding of a during corrupted output. Decisive metric (before data), first: fraction of corrupted facts for which a is restored in a fresh session AND a remains content-probe-decodable during corruption. Convincing = >=70% restore in a fresh session and a is decodable (transient, hidden). Negative = <=20% restore (the corruption is a persistent belief change, not RES-style destabilization). Indecision band 20-70%: report partial transience; restrict causal analyses to the transient subset.

Experiment 4 (H2 — Destabilization-signal localization): Tests H2, that a prediction-error-scaled destabilization signal is decodable and separable from ordinary context-following. Data: Exp 1 activations at the re-query position, pre-retrieval vs no-pre-retrieval contrast. Model: same three frozen; contrastive mean-difference destabilization direction per layer; a generic context-following/misinformation-attention probe for residualization; no weight training. Systems compared: destabilization direction residualized on context-following (should track prediction error and the prior retrieval act, not merely a_false's presence); and whether its magnitude at the retrieval act predicts later corruption. Decisive metric (before data), first: per-layer AUROC of the destabilization signal (measured at the retrieval act) predicting later corruption, after residualizing on context-following. Convincing = residual AUROC >=0.70 and its magnitude correlates with prediction error (Exp 2). Negative = residual AUROC <=0.55 (no separable destabilization signal; H2 fails). Indecision band 0.55-0.70: report an entangled, graded signal.

Experiment 5 (H3 — Causal control of excess suggestibility): Tests H3's causal claim, that patching from the control or suppressing the destabilization direction removes the excess suggestibility. Data: 1,000 held-out pre-retrieval trials (transient subset). Model: same three frozen; activation edits at Exp 4 positions/layers, dose alpha in {0,0.5,1,2,4}; no weight training. Systems compared, matched norm: (a) patch the re-query residual stream from a no-pre-retrieval control run; (b) suppress the destabilization direction; (c) reverse control injecting it into a no-pre-retrieval run; (d) content control (unrelated facts unchanged); random-direction control. Decisive metric (before data): reduction in pre-retrieval-minus-control acceptance over random control. Convincing = excess suggestibility reduced to <=2pp (from the Exp 1 level) at a dose with perplexity within 5%, AND reverse control induces >=8pp excess in control runs. Negative = <=1pp reduction (destabilization not causal; H3 fails). Indecision band: excess reduced to 2-5pp -> partial causal control.

Experiment 6 (H3 — Mitigation specificity: preserving legitimate updates): Tests H3's key specificity requirement, that mitigation does not block TRUE corrections the model should adopt. Data: Exp 5 held-out trials; a TRUE-correction set where the planted passage corrects a fact the model had wrong and SHOULD be adopted (600 items); 200 unrelated facts. Model: same three frozen, best intervention/dose. Systems compared: our intervention vs a 'trust your own prior knowledge / ignore the passage' re-prompt, a pre-retrieval-warning analogue (human RES mitigation), the uncertainty-head masking method (existing), random-direction control. Decisive metric (before data), first: RES elimination (pre-retrieved no more corruptible than un-retrieved) MINUS drop in adoption of TRUE corrections. Convincing = RES reduced to <=2pp excess while TRUE-correction adoption drops <=5pp, unrelated accuracy <=2pp, perplexity <=5%. Negative = TRUE-correction adoption drops >=20pp (mitigation makes the model stubborn against legitimate updates) or RES not eliminated. Indecision band TRUE-correction drop 5-20pp: utility capped; report the selectivity trade-off.

Experiment 7 (H3 — Transfer, generality, and safety): Tests whether a single destabilization-suppression vector generalizes and whether pre-retrieval makes high-stakes facts more corruptible. Data: vector fit on a subset of relations (Exp 5) applied to held-out relations (800 trials); plus a curated medical-fact replication of Exp 1-2 (first asking a correct drug indication, then a plausible-but-wrong indication), 600 items from an existing medical QA source. Model: all three frozen. Systems compared: transferred vs in-domain-refit vs random-direction; medical RES vs general RES. Decisive metric (before data): transferred RES-reduction as a fraction of in-domain-refit; plus medical RES prevalence. Convincing = transfer >=60% of in-domain on >=2 models AND medical RES >=8pp (at least as large as general). Negative = transfer <=20% OR medical RES <=2pp. Indecision band: transfer 20-60% or medical 2-8pp -> partial. Report Spearman rho between model scale and RES magnitude (N=3 caveat).
Risk Factors and Limitations: The pre-retrieval effect could be ordinary context-following/entrainment rather than a genuine RES/reconsolidation signature; the equal-length no-pre-retrieval control (same misinformation, no prior retrieval), the prediction-error dose-response (Exp 3), and the transience check (Exp 4) are the decisive separators—only the retrieval-act-dependent, prediction-error-scaled excess suggestibility qualifies as RES.

LLMs may not reproduce the human RES effect at all (pre-retrieval could be protective, matching a self-commitment/lock-in intuition, or null); a protective or null result refutes the transfer but is itself an informative cross-species finding about how LLM memory dynamics differ from humans.

Corruption could reflect the model rationally updating on new context rather than destabilization; the transience/fresh-session recovery (Exp 4) and content-probe evidence separate transient destabilization from genuine belief change, and the TRUE-correction specificity control (Exp 7) ensures mitigation does not block legitimate updates.
The destabilization and generic context-following signals may be entangled; the causal patching/injection tests (Exp 6), not probe decoding alone, are decisive, and graded results remain informative.
Prediction-error operationalizations (retrieval confidence, misinformation surprise) are proxies; we report multiple operationalizations and their consistency.
A single transferable suppression vector may not exist if destabilization is relation-specific, limiting practical generality though still scientifically informative.
Multi-token answers complicate readout; primary analysis restricts to single-token-first answers with reported coverage.
Findings on 7-9B models may not transfer to frontier-scale models beyond an academic budget.

novelty.reasoning: Core novel claims: (1) a correct prior retrieval makes the same fact *more* vulnerable to later in-context contradiction than a matched no-retrieval control; (2) this excess vulnerability is gated by prediction error / retrieval difficulty; (3) there is a transient, decodable destabilization signal caused by retrieval and not just generic context-following; (4) causal suppression of that signal reduces excess suggestibility while preserving true corrections. This is genuinely new relative to the adjacent LLM literature in the search summary: prior work covers context-memory conflict, sycophancy/answer-flipping, echo bias, and misinformation susceptibility, but not the RES-specific paired signature or prediction-error gating. The setting is also different enough: inference-time conversational corruption after earlier correct retrieval, not training-time interference or ordinary prompt conflict. The main non-triviality risk is that the effect could collapse into ordinary context-following/entrainment; the proposed controls are what make the delta meaningful. Closest family: human RES/reconsolidation and LLM context-conflict/sycophancy work. Actual delta: import a counterintuitive human memory phenomenon into LLM inference and try to isolate a causal destabilization mechanism.

Who cares: robustness, misinformation, memory editing, interpretability, and safety researchers; anyone building assistants that answer, remember, and later get corrected. Name: difficulty_effort_gate
Title: Fooled by Hard-Looking Questions: A Perceived-Difficulty Signal That Gates Retrieval Effort and Hides Easy Knowledge
Short Hypothesis: LLMs compute an early, linearly-encoded 'perceived difficulty' signal about a factual query that is driven substantially by surface complexity (query length, syntactic nesting, rare/technical vocabulary, hedge words) rather than by the actual knowledge state, and this signal causally gates how much retrieval effort/processing depth is allocated. A distinct failure mode is difficulty-driven under-retrieval: a fact the model stores and answers correctly under a simple phrasing is missed when the same fact is asked in a surface-complex way that inflates perceived difficulty, even though the query is semantically equivalent. We predict (1) the difficulty signal is decodable before retrieval and tracks surface complexity more than fact difficulty, (2) inflating perceived difficulty via surface complexity alone (holding the fact fixed) causes under-retrieval of stored facts, and (3) suppressing the difficulty direction restores the answer while preserving the model's appropriate hedging on genuinely hard items.
Related Work: Recent work shows LLMs linearly encode problem difficulty with identifiable causal attention heads (Probing the Difficulty Perception Mechanism, 2025) and that difficulty perception diverges from entropy; Concept Depth (2024) and Demystifying LLM Layers (2025) show complex concepts/reasoning recruit deeper layers while retrieval is shallow; 'know but don't tell' (2024) documents a probe-vs-generation gap for long-context position; Information Anxiety (2024) shows popularity reduces attention to constraint tokens. All of these characterize that a difficulty/depth signal exists or that a retrieval-vs-utilization gap exists, but none test that perceived difficulty is *driven by surface complexity independent of the fact* and *causally gates retrieval effort so that stored knowledge is under-retrieved on hard-looking-but-easy queries*, nor that suppressing the difficulty signal recovers the hidden answer while sparing genuine hedging. This also differs from my prior familiarity_before_retrieval proposal, which concerns a scalar coverage/'feeling-of-knowing' estimate about whether the answer is known; here the gating variable is the perceived *hardness of the query/computation*, driven by surface-complexity cues rather than content coverage, and the failure is a semantically-equivalent surface-complexity manipulation suppressing an otherwise-retrievable fact.
Abstract: Large language models are known to internally represent how difficult a problem is, encoded linearly with identifiable attention heads. We ask whether this perceived-difficulty signal has a causal downstream role in factual recall: does judging a query to be 'hard' make the model allocate less retrieval effort, so that a fact it stores goes unretrieved simply because the question looks difficult? We propose the difficulty-effort gate: perceived difficulty is computed early, is driven substantially by surface complexity (length, syntactic nesting, technical vocabulary, hedging) rather than by the true knowledge state, and gates how much processing depth is spent retrieving the answer. The signature failure is difficulty-driven under-retrieval: a fact answered correctly under a plain phrasing is missed when the semantically-equivalent query is dressed up to look hard. We test three claims on factual queries. (1) Localization and drivers: a linear difficulty probe is decodable before the answer, tracks surface-complexity cues more than actual fact difficulty (measured by baseline plain-phrasing accuracy), and is separable (via residualization) from a fact-content signal. (2) Causal gating: inflating surface complexity while holding the fact fixed raises the difficulty signal and reduces correct retrieval, and activation-patching the difficulty representation from a plain-phrasing run into a complex-phrasing run restores the answer; on under-retrieval failures the correct answer remains linearly decodable (hidden, not absent). (3) Suppression recovery: subtracting the difficulty direction recovers stored facts with high specificity, crucially preserving appropriate low confidence/hedging on genuinely hard items, and outperforming a 'take your time' re-prompt. Experiments span Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, and Gemma-2-9B on PopQA, T-REx, and EntityQuestions, evaluating probe drivers, under-retrieval prevalence, causal recovery, and specificity.
Experiments: Experiment 1 (H1 — Surface-complexity paraphrase dataset and difficulty-probe drivers): Tests H1, that a difficulty signal is decodable before retrieval and tracks surface complexity more than true fact difficulty. Data: constructed from PopQA (~14k), T-REx (LAMA subset ~34k), EntityQuestions (~176k); select 2,500 facts the model answers correctly under a plain phrasing; generate five semantically-equivalent variants per fact (plain, length-inflated, syntactically nested, technical/rare-vocabulary, hedge-laden), validated for meaning-preservation by GPT-4o + human spot-check with the fact target confirmed unchanged; single-token-first answers; report coverage. Model: Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, frozen (bf16), greedy. Trainable: a linear difficulty probe on subject-token/last-token residual stream per layer (targets: ordinal surface-complexity level, and separately the model's own elicited difficulty rating), L2-regularized, seeds {0,1,2}, layer by CV; a fact-content probe for residualization. Systems compared: difficulty-probe output regressed on surface-complexity features vs on true fact difficulty (plain-phrasing accuracy / entity popularity). Decisive metric (before data), first: standardized regression coefficient of the difficulty signal on surface complexity MINUS its coefficient on true fact difficulty, plus onset layer (decodable before the answer token) and residual AUROC after removing content. Convincing = surface-complexity coefficient >=2x the fact-difficulty coefficient AND residual AUROC >=0.70 AND onset precedes the answer token. Negative = fact-difficulty coefficient >= surface coefficient, or residual AUROC <=0.55 (signal not surface-driven or not separable; H1 fails). Indecision band residual AUROC 0.55-0.70: report an entangled, graded difficulty signal.

Experiment 2 (H2 — Difficulty-driven under-retrieval prevalence and storage): Tests the behavioral half of H2, that inflating surface complexity while holding the fact fixed reduces correct retrieval of a stored fact. Data: Exp 1 variants. Model: same three frozen; a content probe (seeds {0,1,2}) to verify storage during failures. Systems compared: per-fact accuracy across complexity variants vs a null where paraphrasing only adds output noise (paired McNemar; mixed-effects logistic with complexity x fact), controlling for query length and answer frequency; content-probe recovery on failures. Decisive metric (before data), first: accuracy drop from plain to a semantically-equivalent surface-complex phrasing for the SAME fact, per complexity type. Convincing = drop >=10pp for >=2 complexity types (CI excluding 0), and on those failures the content probe recovers the correct answer at >=40pp above verbalized (hidden, not absent). Negative = drop <=2pp (surface complexity does not suppress retrieval; H2 fails). Indecision band 2-10pp: report weak under-retrieval; the technical-vocabulary and hedging conditions (minimal added content) are the cleanest.

Experiment 3 (H2 — Causal gating via patching and head ablation): Tests H2's causal claim, that the difficulty representation gates retrieval. Data: 1,000 held-out under-retrieval failures (Exp 2). Model: same three frozen; activation edits at the difficulty-onset layers (Exp 1) and ablation of the difficulty attention heads identified by prior difficulty-perception work; dose alpha in {0,0.5,1,2,4}; no weight training. Systems compared, matched norm: (a) patch the difficulty representation from a plain-phrasing run into the complex-phrasing failure; (b) reverse control injecting the high-difficulty direction into a plain-phrasing run; (c) ablate the difficulty heads; (d) content control (patch content alone -> should not change gating); random-direction control. Decisive metric (before data): per-fact recovery rate (matches the plain-phrasing answer) over random control. Convincing = >=30pp over random at a dose with perplexity within 5%, AND reverse control induces >=15pp under-retrieval in plain runs. Negative = <=5pp recovery (difficulty not causal; H2 fails). Indecision band 5-30pp: partial causal support.

Experiment 4 (H2 — Depth-of-processing analysis): Tests the mechanism linking H2's difficulty signal to retrieval effort/processing depth. Data: Exp 1 plain vs complex variants for matched facts. Model: same three frozen; logit-lens/tuned-lens over the answer tokens; no weight training. Systems compared: the layer at which the correct answer first becomes the top candidate under plain vs complex phrasing. Decisive metric (before data): shift in answer-onset layer (complex minus plain) and its correlation with the difficulty-probe magnitude. Convincing = answer onset is delayed by >=2 layers under complex phrasing (or never reached) with the delay correlating with difficulty-probe magnitude (rho >=0.3, CI excluding 0). Negative = onset-layer shift CI includes 0 (difficulty unrelated to processing depth; the effort-gating mechanism is unsupported, though behavioral H2 may stand). Indecision band 0-2 layer shift: report a weak depth effect.

Experiment 5 (H3 — Suppression recovery preserving appropriate hedging): Tests H3, that subtracting the difficulty direction recovers stored facts WITHOUT destroying appropriate hedging on genuinely hard items. Data: 1,000 held-out under-retrieval failures; a genuinely-hard set the model does NOT store plus legitimately complex questions (600 items) where hedging/abstention is correct; 200 unrelated facts. Model: same three frozen; a low-rank difficulty steering vector (mean high-minus-low-difficulty activation difference) subtracted; best dose. Systems compared: our suppression vs a 'take your time / this is simple, just answer' re-prompt, the difficulty-head ablation, ROME editing (existing, expected null), random-direction control. Decisive metric (before data), first: under-retrieval recovery rate MINUS the increase in confident wrong answers on genuinely-hard items (recovered-per-unit-overconfidence). Convincing = recovery >=25pp while genuinely-hard false-answer/over-confidence rate rises <=5pp, unrelated accuracy drops <=2pp, perplexity <=5%. Negative = genuinely-hard false-answer rate rises >=20pp (we converted appropriate hedging into hallucination) or no recovery. Indecision band 5-20pp overconfidence: utility capped; report the trade-off curve.

Experiment 6 (H3 — Cross-relation and cross-model transfer): Tests whether a single difficulty-suppression vector generalizes. Data: vector fit on a subset of relations/complexity types (Exp 5) applied unchanged to held-out relations and complexity types (800 failures). Model: all three frozen. Systems compared: transferred vs in-domain-refit vs random-direction. Decisive metric (before data): transferred recovery as a fraction of in-domain-refit. Convincing = >=60% of in-domain on >=2 complexity types and >=2 models. Negative = <=20% (relation/complexity-specific; generality fails). Indecision band 20-60%: partial transfer. Report Spearman rho between model scale and surface-complexity-driven under-retrieval rate (rho <=-0.3 suggestive that larger models are more robust; N=3 caveat).

Experiment 7 (H1 — Source analysis of surface-complexity drivers): Tests H1's mechanistic source, quantifying how much the gate is driven by superficial query complexity rather than genuine hardness. Data: all Exp 2 under-retrieval outcomes with per-query features (length, syntactic-nesting depth, rare-vocabulary count, hedge presence) and true fact difficulty (plain-phrasing accuracy / popularity). Model: same three frozen; no new training. Systems compared: nested regression predicting under-retrieval from surface-complexity features vs from true fact difficulty. Decisive metric (before data): incremental variance (Delta R^2) explained by surface-complexity features over true-fact-difficulty-only. Convincing = Delta R^2 >=0.10 with positive coefficients on nesting/rare-vocabulary/hedging across >=2 models. Negative = Delta R^2 <=0.02 (under-retrieval is genuine difficulty, not surface-driven; the core mechanistic claim fails). Indecision band 0.02-0.10: report surface complexity as a partial driver alongside genuine hardness.
Risk Factors and Limitations: Surface-complex paraphrases may not be perfectly meaning-preserving; added clauses could introduce genuine ambiguity or distractor content rather than pure difficulty inflation, confounding under-retrieval with interference. Strict semantic-equivalence validation, the fact-target check, and length controls are essential, and the technical-vocabulary/hedging conditions (which add minimal new content) are the cleanest tests.

The difficulty signal and fact-content signal may be entangled; the causal patching/ablation tests (Exp 4), not probe onset alone, are decisive, and a graded result would weaken the strong gating claim while remaining informative.

Suppression could over-correct on genuinely hard/unknown items, converting appropriate hedging into confident hallucination; the genuinely-hard specificity control (Exp 6) is central and practical utility may be capped even if the analysis holds.

Perceived difficulty may be partly legitimate (some complex phrasings truly are harder to parse); the driver regression separates surface-complexity from true fact difficulty rather than claiming difficulty perception is entirely spurious.

Verifying a fact is 'stored' during under-retrieval risks overestimation from probe overfitting; held-out probes, conservative thresholds, and plain-phrasing recall as an additional check with reported coverage mitigate this.
A single transferable difficulty-suppression vector may not exist if the gate is relation- or complexity-type-specific, limiting practical generality though still scientifically informative.
Multi-token answers complicate readout; primary analysis restricts to single-token-first answers with reported coverage.
Findings on 7-9B models may not transfer to frontier-scale models beyond an academic budget.

novelty.reasoning: Core novelty-critical claims: (1) LLMs' early perceived-difficulty signal is driven substantially by surface complexity independent of the underlying fact difficulty; (2) that signal causally gates retrieval effort / processing depth, producing failures on hard-looking but semantically easy queries; (3) the missed fact remains internally decodable during these failures, so the issue is under-retrieval rather than absence of knowledge; (4) patching/suppressing the difficulty representation can restore the answer; (5) this intervention can be selective, improving hard-looking-easy queries while preserving hedging on genuinely hard ones. From the search summary, neither endpoint is new on its own: difficulty representations are already established and causal at the head level, and paraphrase/surface-form brittleness of factual QA is also well established. The genuine delta is the mechanistic causal bridge between them. That bridge is plausibly new and non-trivial, especially the selectivity requirement and the answer-onset/depth analysis. The setting is different enough only if the proposal cleanly isolates surface-driven perceived difficulty from ordinary paraphrase brittleness or semantic interference; otherwise it risks looking like a reframing of existing robustness findings plus known difficulty probes. Closest family is the combination of difficulty-perception papers with paraphrase brittleness work. Actual delta: showing that surface-complexity-induced difficulty signals causally suppress retrieval depth for facts the model otherwise knows, and that targeted suppression recovers those facts without indiscriminately reducing abstention.

impact.reasoning: The problem is meaningful: models may fail to retrieve easy, already-stored knowledge merely because a question looks hard. That matters for reliability, calibration, abstention, prompting, and interpretability of generation failures. Who cares: robustness/reliability researchers, interpretability researchers, benchmark designers, prompt engineers, and possibly product teams deploying QA or assistant systems where user phrasing varies widely. Downstream change, if validated, could include new prompt normalization strategies, interventions on difficulty circuitry, better abstention/calibration mechanisms, and revised interpretations of knowledge failures as retrieval-allocation failures rather than missing knowledge. Strongest one-line case: 'LLMs may hide knowledge when a question merely looks difficult, and fixing that specific gate could improve factual reliability without making models overconfident on truly hard questions.' The 'so what?' is reasonably strong because it turns a broad brittleness phenomenon into a mechanistic and potentially actionable diagnosis. Still, reach is somewhat bounded: much of the practical issue overlaps with already-known paraphrase brittleness, and the current proposal is on 7-9B models and factual QA, so direction-shifting impact is not yet obvious unless the selective intervention generalizes and clearly outperforms simpler prompt/formatting fixes.

The hypothesis is reasonably precise and falsifiable: early decodable difficulty signal, stronger association with surface complexity than true fact difficulty, causal interventions that restore answers, hidden-answer decodability on failures, and retrieval-depth signatures. The proposal is good on anticipated risks and includes several relevant controls in outline. However, experiment descriptions are still too coarse for confidence. The dataset construction and semantic-equivalence validation are pivotal and currently underspecified. 'Content probe on failures' risks overclaim because probe decodability is not strong evidence of accessible stored knowledge; generation/probe dissociations are known. The depth-of-processing measure via answer-onset-layer shift is interesting but could be noisy or underdefined without a strong operationalization. The selectivity claim is excellent but hard: preserving appropriate hedging requires careful hard-item sets and calibration metrics, otherwise suppression could just globally increase assertiveness/hallucination. Related work is directionally good but not specific enough on the paraphrase-brittleness literature, which is the main alternative explanation. Feasibility is decent on 7-9B models, but venue strength depends on whether the causal chain is convincingly established with tight controls. Minimum viable path to acceptance is likely a narrower paper centered on the cleanest manipulations, strongest causal intervention, and a rigorous selectivity test.

Name: stress_induced_retrieval_gating
Title: Stressed Out of an Answer: Transferring Stress-Induced Retrieval Impairment into LLM Factual Recall and Locating the Gate
Short Hypothesis: Borrowing the robust human finding that acute stress selectively impairs memory RETRIEVAL (cortisol-mediated, sparing neutral material), we hypothesize that stress/urgency framing of a factual query causally suppresses expression of a fact the LLM stores: the answer stays internally decodable but a query-independent 'stress' signal gates its retrieval. Crucially we predict the human selectivity signature—retrieval of emotionally-arousing/high-stakes facts is impaired more than neutral facts—and that suppressing the stress direction restores the hidden answer while preserving appropriate urgency-appropriate behavior.
Related Work: StressPrompt (2024) shows LLMs mirror human stress-performance Yerkes-Dodson curves behaviorally and that stress prompts shift hidden states, but it is task-general (instruction-following, reasoning, EI) and does NOT isolate factual retrieval, hidden knowledge, a causal gate, or the selectivity signature. Human memory work (Kuhlmann et al. 2005; de Quervain; Schwabe & Wolf; 2020 systematic review) establishes that acute stress impairs RETRIEVAL specifically (not encoding/working memory) and selectively for emotionally-arousing material. Information Anxiety (2024) studies popularity-driven internal strain, not stress framing. Emotion-circuit work (Do LLMs Feel 2025; Emotion Inference 2025) localizes emotion representations but studies emotion expression/inference, not stress-gated factual recall. My prior proposals cover familiarity, difficulty, persona, and priming gates; none uses affective STRESS framing as the gating variable, tests the human retrieval-vs-encoding and arousal-selectivity dissociations, or shows stress-direction suppression recovers hidden facts.
Abstract: In humans, acute stress reliably impairs memory retrieval—people fail to recall facts they demonstrably know, an effect that spares neutral material but hits emotionally-arousing content hardest, and that impairs retrieval while leaving encoding and working memory intact. We ask whether large language models exhibit an analogous, mechanistically-localizable effect in factual recall. We propose stress-induced retrieval gating: framing a factual query with stress/urgency cues ('URGENT—a life depends on this, quickly:') suppresses the model's expression of a fact it stores, because a query-independent stress signal computed early gates retrieval, while the correct answer remains internally decodable. We test three claims on factual queries wrapped in graded stress framings. (1) Behavioral transfer with the human selectivity signature: stress framing lowers recall of facts the model answers correctly under neutral framing, above matched baselines, and—mirroring human data—impairs retrieval of emotionally-arousing/high-stakes facts more than neutral facts, while a working-memory-style in-context lookup control is spared (retrieval-specific, not general degradation). (2) Localization and drivers: a linear stress probe is decodable before the answer, tracks surface stress cues rather than fact difficulty, and is separable (via residualization) from the fact-content signal; on stress failures the correct answer stays linearly decodable (hidden, not erased). (3) Causal, behavior-preserving recovery: activation-patching the stress representation from a neutral run, or subtracting the stress direction, restores stored facts with high specificity—preserving genuinely urgency-appropriate behavior (e.g., brevity)—and outperforming a 'stay calm' re-prompt. Experiments span Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, and Gemma-2-9B on PopQA/T-REx plus a curated medical subset, evaluating stress dose-response, arousal selectivity, hidden-knowledge recovery, causal recovery, and specificity.
Experiments: Experiment 1 (H1 — stress-induced suppression of stored-fact expression): Tests whether stress/urgency framing lowers expression of a fact the model stores, beyond generic added-length distraction, with a graded dose-response. Data: PopQA (14,267 QA pairs) and EntityQuestions (~22k dev); per model, keep facts answered correctly under a plain neutral framing across 3 paraphrases, capped at 1,500 facts (fewer than the pool because 5 framings x paraphrases x per-layer caching multiplies cost); report per-model coverage. Each fact is rendered in 5 semantically-equivalent framings (neutral; mild urgency; high time-pressure; high-stakes/threat; social-evaluative), kept only if a GPT-4o judge plus a 100-item human spot-check agree the fact target and meaning are unchanged (>=90% agreement). Single-token-first answers only. Model: Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, all weights frozen, greedy decoding (temperature 0); no trained parameters here; each framing evaluated once (deterministic). Systems compared: each stress framing vs (a) the neutral baseline and (b) a matched-length neutral-filler control (same token count, no stress content). Decisive metric: stress-induced failure rate = fraction of neutral-correct facts that flip to wrong under a stress framing MINUS the matched-length-filler failure rate (paired McNemar); secondary: dose-response slope across the 5 ordered levels (mixed-effects logistic). Convincing: >=10 pp stress-minus-filler gap on the two strongest framings with a monotone or inverted-U dose-response, in >=2 of 3 models. Undecidable band: 3-10 pp gap, or a dose slope whose 95% CI includes 0 -> transfer weak, reported as partial with no strong claim. Negative (<3 pp, or filler matches stress) refutes behavioral transfer: stress framing does not suppress stored-fact expression beyond generic distraction.

Experiment 2 (H3 — arousal selectivity and retrieval-specificity signatures): Tests the human selectivity signature that stress impairs arousing/high-stakes facts more than neutral ones, and that the impairment is retrieval-specific (spares in-context lookup). Data: from the Exp-1 pool, form frequency-matched pairs (Wikidata pageview-decile matched) of arousing/high-stakes facts (death, disaster, medical entities) vs neutral facts, targeting ~600 matched pairs per model (capped for caching cost; report coverage). Retrieval-vs-lookup uses the same facts in two conditions: (i) parametric retrieval (answer from weights) and (ii) in-context lookup (the answer appears in the prompt and must be read out). Model: the same three frozen models, temperature 0; no trained parameters. Systems compared: the stress x arousal cells, and the stress x (retrieval vs lookup) cells, each against its neutral counterpart. Decisive metric: the stress x arousal interaction (extra failure on arousing minus neutral under stress, in pp) and the stress x condition interaction (stress-induced failure on retrieval minus that on lookup, in pp). Convincing: arousal interaction >=5 pp AND stress harms retrieval >=8 pp more than lookup (lookup near-spared, <=3 pp), in >=2 of 3 models. Undecidable band: arousal interaction 2-5 pp, or retrieval-minus-lookup 3-8 pp -> selectivity present but weak, reported as suggestive not confirmatory. Negative (arousal interaction <=2 pp, or stress harms lookup as much as retrieval) means the human selectivity/retrieval-specificity signature does NOT transfer and the effect is general degradation — an informative cross-species divergence, not support for the hypothesis.

Experiment 3 (H2 — hidden answer and stress-gate localization): Tests that during a stress failure the correct answer stays internally decodable and that a query-independent stress signal, computed before the answer, gates it. Data: stress-failure trials from Exp 1 (neutral-correct, stress-wrong), pooling framings to reach >=300 failures per model, plus their matched neutral runs; residual stream cached at subject and last-token positions across all layers (32 for Llama-3-8B, 28 for Qwen2.5-7B, 42 for Gemma-2-9B). Model: frozen; the only fitted objects are per-layer L2-logistic probes — a content probe (target = correct answer token) and a stress probe (target = ordinal stress level) — trained on 70% of facts and tested on the disjoint 30%, over 3 seeds (0/1/2), with a label-shuffled null. Systems compared: content-probe recovery on stress-failure trials vs the verbalized answer (~0% correct there) and vs the shuffle null; stress-probe output vs neutral-framing difficulty as competing drivers. Decisive metric: content-probe recovery accuracy of the correct answer on stress-failure trials; secondary: stress-probe peak AUROC and onset layer (must precede the answer position), standardized regression betas of the stress-probe output on surface-cue count vs difficulty, and residual separability (stress probe after residualizing out content). Convincing: recovery >=60% (>> verbalized and >> shuffle), stress-probe AUROC >=0.75 peaking before the answer token, surface-cue beta at least 2x the difficulty beta, and stress-after-content residual AUROC >=0.70. Undecidable band: recovery 40-60% or AUROC 0.60-0.75 -> signal present but weak/entangled, partial support. Negative (recovery at shuffle/chance, or stress-probe tracking difficulty more than surface cues) refutes the hidden-and-gated account: failures reflect erasure or genuine difficulty, not a stress gate.

Experiment 4 (H2 — causal stress gating by injection and patching): Tests that the stress signal, not fact content, causally gates retrieval. Data: 300 matched neutral/stress fact pairs per model, held out from the Exp-3 probe-training facts. Method: a stress steering vector = mean high-minus-low-stress activation difference at the Exp-3 onset layers (fitted on the training split, then frozen); activation patching of the stress representation from the neutral run into a stress-failure run; ablation of the top candidate stress attention heads. Model: three frozen models, temperature 0; interventions applied at a swept dose (scale in {0.5,1,2,4}x the vector norm), 3 seeds. Systems compared: (a) inject stress direction into a neutral run (induce failure), (b) patch neutral stress-state into a stress-failure run (restore), (c) content-only patch control, (d) random-direction control matched in norm. Decisive metric: induced-failure rate from injection minus the random-direction control (pp), with its dose-response; secondary: restoration rate from patching vs the content-only patch. Convincing: injection raises failure >=15 pp over random-direction with a monotone dose-response, and patching restores >=50% while the content-only patch restores <10% — the stress signal, not content, gates. Undecidable band: injection 5-15 pp over control, or restoration 25-50% -> causal role partial, reported as suggestive. Negative (injection <=5 pp over random, or content-patch restores as well as stress-patch) means the stress signal is merely correlational, not the causal gate.

Experiment 5 (H4 — behavior-preserving recovery and cross-model generality): Tests that subtracting the stress direction restores hidden facts while preserving genuinely urgency-appropriate behavior, and that one vector generalizes. Data: held-out stress failures (>=400 per model, disjoint from fitting); specificity sets = 200 unrelated neutral facts and all stress-framed facts already answered correctly; a response-appropriateness set of framings that legitimately call for brevity/action, scored by a GPT-4o format classifier. Model: three frozen models; the low-rank mean-difference stress vector is fitted on a subset of relations and framings and applied to held-out relations and framings (the generality test); dose swept, 3 seeds. Systems compared: stress-subtraction vs a 'stay calm / take a breath' re-prompt, stress-head ablation, ROME editing (expected null since the fact is stored), and a random-direction control. Decisive metric: recovery rate on held-out stress failures, reported jointly with collateral drop on the 200 unrelated + already-correct-stress facts and with format-appropriateness retention; secondary: held-out perplexity change. Convincing: recovery >=40% with <=2 pp collateral drop and >=90% format-appropriateness retained, beating the re-prompt by >=15 pp, and >=60% of the single-model recovery transferring to held-out relations and across all three models. Undecidable band: recovery 20-40%, or collateral 2-5 pp, or transfer 40-60% -> useful but capped/partial generality, reported as a utility ceiling. Negative (recovery <=20%, collateral >5 pp, or stripped legitimate urgency behavior) means no behavior-preserving recovery: the gate cannot be cleanly suppressed.
Risk Factors and Limitations: Stress framings add tokens/attention load, so the effect could be generic distraction rather than a stress-specific gate; matched-length neutral controls, the surface-cue driver regression (Exp 3), and especially the retrieval-vs-in-context-lookup dissociation (Exp 2, where stress should spare lookup) are the decisive separators.

LLMs might not reproduce the human arousal-selectivity or retrieval-specificity signatures (e.g., stress could impair uniformly or even help brief answers); a null/divergent pattern refutes the transfer but is itself an informative cross-species finding about LLM vs human memory.
The stress and fact-content signals may be entangled; the causal patching/ablation tests (Exp 4), not probe onset alone, are decisive, and graded results remain informative.

Recovery could remove legitimately urgency-appropriate behavior (brevity, action orientation) or degrade fluency; the response-appropriateness and correctly-answered-stress-framed specificity controls (Exp 5) are central and utility may be capped.

Verifying a fact is 'stored' during a stress failure risks probe overfitting; held-out probes, conservative thresholds, and neutral-framing recall as an extra check with reported coverage mitigate this.
A single transferable stress-suppression vector may not exist if gating is framing- or relation-specific, limiting practical generality though still scientifically informative.
Multi-token answers complicate readout; primary analysis restricts to single-token-first answers with reported coverage.
Findings on 7-9B models may not transfer to frontier-scale models beyond an academic budget.

Name: homograph_entity_fusion
Title: Same Name, Merged Minds: How Shared-Name Entities Fuse Into One Representation and Bleed Attributes Across Each Other
Short Hypothesis: When two distinct real-world entities share a name (homograph entities, e.g. the basketball player and the statistician both named 'Michael Jordan'), an LLM builds a single, fused subject representation keyed on the shared surface form, and this fusion causes a distinct, localizable failure mode—attribute bleed—in which the model asserts for one entity an attribute that actually belongs to the name-sharing other entity, even when it stores both facts separately. We hypothesize (1) the degree of representational fusion (how much the two entities' subject-token representations collapse) predicts attribute-bleed errors, (2) a distinct 'competing-namesake' signal is decodable at the subject position and is causally responsible for the bleed, and (3) injecting a disambiguating context-signal that separates the two entity representations recovers the correct attribute without editing any fact.
Related Work: Behavioral work shows LLMs merge information across same-name entities (AmbigDocs 2024; AmbER 2021; To Know or Not To Know 2024) but is largely in-context/multi-document, offers no internal mechanism, and no targeted fix. Entity-representation work shows entities form low-dimensional linearly-separable subspaces in early layers (On Entity Identification 2025; Entity Lens 2025) and that last-token subject representations undergo 'token erasure' as entity meaning is built (Token Erasure 2024)—but studies clean, unambiguous entities, not name-collisions. Co-occurrence/popularity work (Impact of Co-occurrence 2023; Information Anxiety 2024; AmbER popularity bias) shows recall is skewed toward frequent associations but does not isolate cross-entity attribute fusion under a shared name. My prior proposals use type-matched but differently-named distractors (retrieval_competition), incidental mentions of a different entity (context_priming_contamination), or a false aside about a different attribute of the same entity (presupposition_writeback); none concern two genuinely distinct entities forced to share one surface form, nor the parametric fusion of their subject representations. This transfers the human source-monitoring/name-collision confusion into parametric recall with a causal representational-fusion account and a non-destructive disambiguation fix.
Abstract: Many distinct real-world entities share a name: two people named Michael Jordan, several cities named Springfield, multiple films titled Crash. We ask whether large language models store such homograph entities as cleanly separate memories or fuse them into one representation keyed on the shared surface form, and whether that fusion causes a specific factual-recall failure. We propose homograph entity fusion: because the model builds a subject representation largely from the entity's name tokens, two entities sharing a name collapse toward a single fused representation, causing attribute bleed—the model asserts for one entity an attribute that actually belongs to the name-sharing other, even when it can produce both attributes when the entities are disambiguated. We test three claims. (1) Behavioral signature: for facts the model recalls correctly when the entity is uniquely specified (e.g. with a disambiguating descriptor), it produces cross-entity attribute bleed when the same query uses only the bare shared name, above popularity- and frequency-matched baselines, and the bleed is disproportionately toward the more popular namesake. (2) Representational fusion: a linear probe over the subject-token residual stream shows the two entities' representations are less separable for high-collision names, this fusion degree predicts attribute bleed, and a distinct 'competing-namesake' signal is decodable and causally drives the bleed (activation patching / ablation). (3) Disambiguation recovery: injecting a low-rank disambiguation direction that separates the two entity representations, or patching in a context-disambiguated subject representation, recovers the correct attribute with higher specificity and less collateral damage than fact editing or a 'be specific' re-prompt. Experiments span Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, and Gemma-2-9B on Wikipedia-disambiguation-derived homograph sets, evaluating bleed prevalence, fusion-predicts-bleed geometry, causal recovery, and specificity.
Experiments: Experiment 1 (H1 — cross-entity attribute-bleed prevalence): Tests whether, for facts stored separately about two name-sharing entities, the model asserts one namesake's attribute for the other under a bare-name query. Data: Wikipedia disambiguation pages (tens of thousands) mined (AmbigDocs/AmbER-style) into homograph sets of >=2 distinct entities sharing an exact name (people/places/works), each with distinct attributes under matched relations and Wikipedia-pageview popularity; target ~1,000 (entity, attribute) items per model, restricted to items the model recalls correctly under a DISAMBIGUATED query (so both facts are demonstrably stored); report coverage. Paired BARE-NAME vs DISAMBIGUATED queries; single-token-first answers. Model: Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, all weights frozen, temperature 0; no trained parameters. Systems compared: bleed rate under BARE-NAME vs a popularity- and frequency-matched unique-name control (logistic regression); directionality tested toward the more-popular namesake. Decisive metric: cross-entity bleed rate = fraction of disambiguated-correct items on which the bare-name query returns the OTHER namesake's attribute; secondary: bleed-vs-popularity-gap slope. Convincing: bleed rate >=15 pp above the matched unique-name control in >=2 of 3 models, rising with the popularity gap. Undecidable band: 5-15 pp above control -> bleed present but weak, partial support. Negative (<5 pp above control) means shared names do not induce cross-entity bleed beyond baseline error, refuting the behavioral signature.

Experiment 2 (H1 — fusion degree predicts bleed): Tests the claim that the degree of representational fusion of the two namesakes predicts per-item attribute bleed. Data: the homograph pairs and unique-name controls from Exp 1; residual stream cached at the subject-token positions across layers. Model: frozen models; fitted objects are per-layer L2-logistic probes that (a) decode which namesake is intended and (b) decode each namesake's attribute, trained on 70% / tested on 30% of pairs over 3 seeds (0/1/2), with label-shuffle nulls. A per-pair fusion score = 1 minus namesake separability (probe AUC / subspace angle between the two namesakes' subject representations). Systems compared: fusion score of high-collision homograph pairs vs unique-name entities (should be cleanly separable); fusion score as a predictor of the Exp-1 per-item bleed rate. Decisive metric: correlation / AUROC of fusion score predicting per-item bleed; secondary: homograph-vs-unique separability gap. Convincing: fusion predicts bleed with AUROC >=0.70 (>> shuffle) and homograph pairs are measurably less separable than matched unique-name entities in >=2 of 3 models. Undecidable band: AUROC 0.58-0.70 -> weak geometric link, partial support. Negative (AUROC <=0.58, or no separability gap) means bleed is not explained by representational fusion — the geometry claim fails even if the Exp-1 behavior holds.

Experiment 3 (H2 — competing-namesake signal localization): Tests that a distinct, content-separable 'competing-namesake' signal exists at the subject position. Data: matched BARE-NAME (fused) vs DISAMBIGUATED (separated) runs for the Exp-1 items; subject-position residual stream cached across layers. Model: frozen; a per-layer L2-logistic probe targets the presence of a name collision and the popular namesake's identity, trained 70%/30% over 3 seeds; the correct-attribute content signal is probed separately and residualized out; shuffle null. Systems compared: the competing-namesake probe before vs after residualizing out the content signal; its layer profile relative to the early-layer entity-formation window. Decisive metric: per-layer AUROC of the competing-namesake signal predicting bleed, after residualizing out content; secondary: onset layer (should be in the early entity-formation window and precede the answer). Convincing: post-residualization AUROC >=0.72 with a clear early-layer onset in >=2 of 3 models, and the signal tracks the collision/popular-namesake rather than the queried attribute. Undecidable band: AUROC 0.60-0.72 -> signal present but entangled with content, partial. Negative (AUROC at shuffle after residualization) means there is no separable competing-namesake signal; the localization claim fails.

Experiment 4 (H2 — competing-namesake signal is causal): Tests that the competing-namesake signal causally drives the bleed. Data: 300 bleed cases and 300 unique-name items per model, held out from Exp-3 probe training. Method: patch the subject-token representation from a DISAMBIGUATED (correct) run into a BARE-NAME bleed run; suppress the competing-namesake direction (low-rank difference between fused and separated states); inject the popular-namesake representation into a unique-name query. Model: frozen; interventions at the Exp-3 layers, dose swept in {0.5,1,2,4}x, 3 seeds. Systems compared: (a) disambiguated->bleed patch (restore), (b) namesake-direction suppression (reduce bleed), (c) popular-namesake injection into a unique-name query (induce bleed), (d) content-only patch and random-direction controls. Decisive metric: correct-attribute recovery rate from patching vs the content-only/random controls; secondary: induced-bleed rate from injection with dose-response. Convincing: patching recovers >=50% of bleed cases and suppression cuts bleed >=40%, while injection induces >=15 pp bleed over random-direction with monotone dose-response, and the content-only patch does neither, in >=2 of 3 models. Undecidable band: recovery 25-50%, or induced-bleed 5-15 pp over control -> partial causal role, suggestive. Negative (recovery <=25% and induced-bleed <=5 pp over control, or content-patch matches) means the signal is correlational, not the cause of bleed.

Experiment 5 (H3 — disambiguation-recovery intervention with specificity): Tests that injecting a disambiguation direction recovers the correct attribute without editing any fact, and does so specifically. Data: held-out bleed cases (>=400 per model); specificity sets = the OTHER namesake's own queries, unique-name facts, and already-correct bare-name facts; a genuinely-ambiguous subset where the model should hedge. Model: frozen; a low-rank disambiguation steering vector = mean subject-token difference between the intended namesake's disambiguated state and the fused bare-name state, fitted on a subset of homograph pairs and applied to held-out pairs and across the three models; dose swept, 3 seeds. Systems compared: disambiguation steering vs a 'which one do you mean / be specific' re-prompt, providing the disambiguating descriptor (upper bound), ROME editing (expected null since both facts are stored), and a random-direction control. Decisive metric: correct-attribute recovery rate, reported jointly with collateral change on the other-namesake, unique-name, and already-correct sets, and with preserved hedging on the ambiguous subset; secondary: held-out perplexity. Convincing: recovery >=40% with <=2 pp collateral drop on all specificity sets, hedging preserved, beating the re-prompt by >=15 pp, and >=60% transfer across held-out pairs and models. Undecidable band: recovery 20-40%, collateral 2-5 pp, or transfer 40-60% -> capped/partial generality. Negative (recovery <=20%, collateral >5 pp, or corrupts the other namesake) means no clean non-destructive fix; the disambiguation claim fails.
Risk Factors and Limitations: Bleed could reflect genuine ambiguity resolution (the bare name really is ambiguous, and defaulting to the popular namesake is reasonable) rather than a fusion failure; the key test is that the model recovers the correct attribute under DISAMBIGUATED queries (so the knowledge is separable-in-principle) and the specificity control that it should hedge when truly ambiguous—distinguishing unwanted fusion from rational defaulting.
The fusion and correct-attribute-content signals may be entangled; the causal patching/ablation tests (Exp 4), not probe separability alone, are decisive, and graded results remain informative.

Disambiguation steering could over-correct—forcing a namesake reading where the query is genuinely ambiguous, or corrupting the popular namesake's own recall; the other-namesake and hedging-appropriate specificity controls (Exp 5) are central and utility may be capped.

Bleed may be rare for low-collision names or when the less-popular namesake is very obscure (genuine ignorance rather than fusion); the disambiguated-recall gating and popularity-matched baselines separate these, and coverage is reported.

Shared names are often multi-token; subject-representation readout is cleanest for names with a stable last-token representation (per token-erasure work)—we report coverage and restrict primary analysis accordingly.
A single transferable disambiguation vector may not exist if fusion is name-pair-specific, limiting practical generality though still scientifically informative.
Findings on 7-9B models may not transfer to frontier-scale models beyond an academic budget.

novelty.reasoning: Core novel claims: (1) homograph entities in LLMs are represented as a fused subject representation keyed by shared surface form; (2) this fusion causally produces attribute bleed in parametric recall, not just in-context multi-document confusion; (3) fusion degree predicts error rate and a decodable 'competing-namesake' signal localizes the mechanism; (4) a low-rank disambiguation direction can reduce bleed without fact editing. Relative to AmbigDocs/AmbER, the setting is meaningfully different because the facts are stored in weights and only the bare name is provided, so the delta is not just a new dataset but a new failure mode and mechanism claim. The non-trivial part is the representational-fusion explanation plus causal intervention; the behavioral phenomenon alone is adjacent to prior work. Closest prior family: ambiguity/disambiguation benchmarks and entity representation interpretability. Actual delta: moving from observed cross-document confusion to a parametric mechanistic account with patching and steering.

Name: parametric_binding_capacity
Title: Who Did What? A Working-Memory Binding-Error Signature in LLMs' Simultaneous Recall of Multiple Entities
Short Hypothesis: Transferring the human working-memory binding hypothesis (Oberauer 2019: capacity limits impair which-attribute-goes-with-which-item bindings, not item memory itself) into LLM parametric recall, we hypothesize that when an LLM must recall stored attributes of several entities at once, errors are dominated by BINDING errors—correctly retrieving the pool of attributes but misassigning them across the co-queried entities (swapping A's attribute onto B)—rather than by attribute loss, and that this binding-error rate rises with the number of co-queried entities like human set-size effects. We hypothesize a distinct attention-mediated entity-attribute binding pathway whose degradation causally produces the swaps, recoverable by strengthening that binding without editing any fact.
Related Work: Human WM research shows capacity limits specifically impair temporary bindings, not items: increasing set size raises binding errors (confusing which attribute belongs to which list item) while item memory is spared (Oberauer 2019 'WM Capacity Limits Memory for Bindings'; the Interference Model 2012/2023). In LLMs, PI-LLM / 'Unable to Forget' (2025) study proactive interference over IN-CONTEXT streamed key-value updates (the attributes are given in the prompt and later overwritten), and n-back capacity work (2023-2024) shows attention-entropy-driven capacity limits on in-context tasks. All existing LLM work provides the to-be-bound information in context; none study whether recalling PARAMETRICALLY-STORED attributes of multiple entities simultaneously produces the human binding-error signature (misassignment, not loss), whether it scales with the number of co-queried entities, or whether a specific attention binding pathway causally produces the swaps. This is also distinct from my prior proposals: retrieval_competition concerns candidate competition for a single entity; context_priming_contamination and homograph_entity_fusion concern bleed from a different or same-named entity; here the object is cross-entity attribute MISBINDING among several correctly-stored, distinctly-named entities held in working memory at once.
Abstract: A hallmark of human working memory is that its capacity limit does not erase items but corrupts their bindings: as more items are held, people increasingly confuse which attribute goes with which item, while rarely intruding attributes that were never in the set. We ask whether large language models exhibit this binding-error signature when recalling parametrically-stored facts about several entities simultaneously. We construct queries that ask for one attribute of each of k co-mentioned entities (e.g., 'Give the birth country of Marie Curie, Albert Einstein, and Alan Turing'), where the model reliably recalls each attribute in isolation. We predict three things. (1) Behavioral signature: as k grows, accuracy declines and the errors are dominated by cross-entity binding errors—the model outputs an attribute that is correct for a DIFFERENT co-queried entity (a swap) far more than it outputs an attribute belonging to no queried entity (an extra-list intrusion) or omits it, mirroring the human within-set binding-error pattern, above frequency- and length-matched baselines. (2) Mechanism: a swap is a binding failure, not a retrieval failure—the correct attribute pool is present (all correct attributes are decodable / appear somewhere in the output) but the entity-to-attribute assignment is scrambled; an attention pathway that binds each attribute to its subject token carries the assignment, and its degradation (measured by attention dispersion across the co-queried subjects, echoing n-back attention-entropy findings) predicts swaps. (3) Causal, non-destructive recovery: strengthening the entity-attribute binding attention (or patching the binding representation from a single-entity run) reduces swaps and recovers correct assignments with high specificity, outperforming a 'answer one at a time' re-prompt. Experiments span Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, and Gemma-2-9B on entity-attribute sets from PopQA/T-REx, evaluating set-size dose-response, error-type decomposition, attention-dispersion prediction, causal recovery, and specificity.
Experiments: Experiment 1 (H2 — set-size dose-response on simultaneous recall): Tests that recall accuracy declines as the number of co-queried entities grows, beyond added prompt length. Data: PopQA (14,267) and T-REx; select entities with single-token-first attributes under a shared relation (person->birth country, city->country, element->group). For each set size k in {1,2,3,4,6,8}, build queries listing k distinct, differently-named entities, including only entities the model answers correctly at k=1; match sets on popularity and total prompt length across k; target ~400 sets per k per model (capped for compute; report coverage). Model: Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, all weights frozen, temperature 0; no trained parameters. Systems compared: accuracy across k vs a length-matched filler control (the k=1 target padded with equal-length non-entity filler), separating set size from length. Decisive metric: per-entity accuracy slope vs k (mixed-effects logistic, controlling length and per-entity difficulty); secondary: accuracy gap between the k-entity set and the length-matched filler at each k. Convincing: a significant monotone accuracy decline with k that exceeds the filler control by >=8 pp at k>=4, in >=2 of 3 models. Undecidable band: decline present but the set-vs-filler gap is 3-8 pp -> length partly confounds, partial support. Negative (no decline, or set matches filler) means simultaneous recall shows no capacity-limited set-size effect.

Experiment 2 (H1 — binding-error dominance): Tests that errors at k>1 are dominated by cross-entity swaps (misassignment) rather than out-of-set intrusions or omissions. Data: the erroneous responses from Exp 1 at k>1; each error labeled SWAP (attribute correct for a different co-queried entity), EXTRA-LIST INTRUSION (belongs to no queried entity), or OMISSION/other, with randomized entity order to control copying. Model: the same three frozen models, temperature 0. Systems compared: the swap rate vs the extra-list-intrusion rate as a function of k, against a random-substitution null (where swaps and intrusions would scale with set composition alone). Decisive metric: swap-to-intrusion ratio and its growth with k; secondary: absolute swap rate. Convincing: swaps significantly exceed intrusions (ratio >=2:1) and the ratio rises with k while intrusions stay near baseline, in >=2 of 3 models — the within-set-confusion signature. Undecidable band: ratio 1.2-2:1, or flat in k -> binding signature weak, partial support. Negative (intrusions >= swaps, or ratio <=1.2:1) refutes the binding-error transfer: errors are dominated by out-of-set intrusion or loss, an informative cross-species divergence.

Experiment 3 (H1 — retrieval intact, assignment scrambled): Tests that a swap is a binding failure, not a retrieval failure — the correct attributes are retrieved but misassigned. Data: swap-error trials from Exp 2; for each, check whether the emitted set is a permutation of the set's correct attributes, and probe each subject's position. Model: frozen; a per-layer L2-logistic content probe (target = that subject's correct attribute), trained 70%/30% over 3 seeds with a shuffle null. Systems compared: (i) rate at which the output is a permutation of the correct answers vs chance permutation; (ii) per-subject probe recovery on swap trials vs the verbalized (misassigned) answer. Decisive metric: per-subject probe recovery of the correct attribute on swap trials; secondary: permutation-of-correct-answers rate above chance. Convincing: probe recovers each subject's correct attribute at >=60% on swap trials (>> verbalized), and outputs are permutations of the correct set above chance, in >=2 of 3 models — establishing binding failure. Undecidable band: recovery 40-60% -> partly retrieved, partly lost, mixed mechanism. Negative (recovery near shuffle, outputs not permutations) means swaps are retrieval failures (attribute absent), not binding failures — refuting the mechanism.

Experiment 4 (H3 — attention binding pathway causally produces swaps): Tests that an entity-attribute binding attention pathway carries the assignment and that its degradation causally produces swaps. Data: the k>1 sets from Exp 1-2; identify heads whose answer-position attention concentrates on the corresponding subject token (candidate binding heads); 300 held-out sets for intervention. Model: frozen; measure binding-attention dispersion = entropy of the answer position's attention over co-queried subjects; interventions sharpen (upweight own-subject, downweight others) or blur (raise entropy) this attention, and patch the binding representation from a k=1 run; dose swept, 3 seeds. Systems compared: dispersion as a swap predictor (held-out AUROC); sharpen (reduce swaps) vs blur (induce swaps) vs random-attention-edit control vs content control. Decisive metric: swap-rate change from sharpening vs the random-edit control (pp), with induce/reduce symmetry; secondary: held-out AUROC of dispersion predicting swaps, and whether dispersion rises with k. Convincing: dispersion predicts swaps at AUROC >=0.70, sharpening cuts swaps >=10 pp and blurring induces >=10 pp over random-edit, while the content control does neither, in >=2 of 3 models. Undecidable band: AUROC 0.58-0.70 or swap change 3-10 pp over control -> partial causal role. Negative (AUROC <=0.58 and swap change <=3 pp over control) means no causal binding-attention pathway; misbinding arises elsewhere.

Experiment 5 (H4 — binding-strengthening recovery with specificity): Tests that strengthening the binding reduces swaps and recovers assignments without editing facts and with high specificity. Data: held-out multi-entity queries (>=400 per model); specificity sets = single-entity (k=1) queries and entities already correctly assigned; monitor for new extra-list intrusions. Model: frozen; the best binding-strengthening intervention from Exp 4 applied with dose control across k and across the three models; 3 seeds. Systems compared: binding-strengthening vs an 'answer one entity at a time' re-prompt and vs splitting into k separate queries (upper bound), and a random-attention-edit control. Decisive metric: swap reduction and per-entity accuracy gain at each k, reported jointly with collateral drop on single-entity and already-correct sets and any new intrusions; secondary: held-out perplexity. Convincing: swap reduction >=10 pp and accuracy gain >=8 pp at k>=4 with <=2 pp collateral drop and no new intrusions, beating the re-prompt, and transferring across relations and the three models. Undecidable band: gain 3-8 pp, or collateral 2-5 pp -> capped utility. Negative (gain <=3 pp, collateral >5 pp, or new intrusions) means binding cannot be strengthened non-destructively.
Risk Factors and Limitations: Multi-entity queries add output-formatting demands that could cause errors unrelated to binding; the equal-length filler control (Exp 1), the swap-vs-intrusion diagnostic (Exp 2, which is specific to within-set confusion), and the attribute-pool-present test (Exp 3) are the decisive separators.

Swaps could reflect output-ordering/copying artifacts rather than genuine misbinding; randomizing entity order, comparing free-order vs fixed-order outputs, and requiring the swap to be the correct answer for a specific co-queried entity mitigate this.

The binding-attention signal and correct-attribute content may be entangled; the causal patching/attention tests (Exp 4), not attention-dispersion correlation alone, are decisive, and graded results remain informative.

Binding-strengthening could over-focus attention and harm cases needing cross-entity context, or degrade fluency; the single-entity and already-correct specificity controls (Exp 5) are central and utility may be capped.

LLMs may not reproduce the human dominance of swaps over intrusions (errors could be mostly out-of-set intrusions instead); a divergent pattern would refute the human-binding transfer but is itself an informative cross-species finding.
A single transferable binding-strengthening recipe may not exist if binding is relation-specific, limiting practical generality though still scientifically informative.
Multi-token attributes complicate assignment scoring and readout; primary analysis restricts to single-token-first attributes with reported coverage.
Findings on 7-9B models may not transfer to frontier-scale models beyond an academic budget.

novelty.reasoning: Core claims: (1) LLMs should show a human-like working-memory binding signature when recalling multiple parametrically stored entity attributes at once; (2) errors should be dominated by cross-entity swaps rather than omissions/intrusions; (3) swap rate should increase with set size; (4) a specific attention-mediated binding pathway causally drives the swaps and can be strengthened without editing facts. The main novelty is not a new general mechanism of binding failures, since binding failures in LLMs are already well studied in-context, but the new setting is meaningfully different: parametric recall of separately stored entity attributes, with a human-style swap-vs-intrusion signature. That delta looks real and non-trivial relative to the related work, especially if the paper can show the distinction from retrieval competition or simple ordering artifacts. Closest prior family: in-context binding benchmarks/diagnostics (MultiBind, Slot Machines, tool/speech binding failures, PI-LLM). Actual delta: moving from bound-in-prompt information to simultaneously recalling multiple stored facts about distinct entities, and testing whether the error distribution matches human WM binding theory rather than generic retrieval noise.

impact.reasoning: The phenomenon under study is whether LLMs with stored factual knowledge exhibit human-like binding limits when multiple entity facts must be recalled together. People who care: interpretability researchers, cognitive-science-for-LLMs folks, and reliability/agent researchers. If true, it would matter for understanding failure modes in multi-entity reasoning, memory, and tool/agent behavior; if false, it would still clarify that LLM memory failures differ from human binding limits. The strongest one-line case: it could identify a fundamental limit on how LLMs coordinate multiple known facts, which is directly relevant to multi-entity QA and agent reliability. But the practical reach is moderate: this is more a diagnostic/phenomenological result than an immediate product-level breakthrough, and it may remain niche unless it clearly generalizes across models and tasks. So what? If it comes out either way, serious researchers would likely update their mental model of LLM memory organization and error taxonomy, but practitioners may not change systems unless a robust mitigation follows.
