review.reasoning: The proposal is plausible and testable, but several parts are underspecified or vulnerable to alternative explanations. Main gaps: 'retrieval-intact-assignment-scrambled' is a strong claim that needs a very careful operational test; attention entropy predicting swaps may be correlational rather than causal; and 'strengthening binding' sounds promising but is not yet a concrete intervention. The hypothesis is directionally falsifiable, but the scope is still broad: multi-entity queries, parametric recall, specific swap dominance, set-size slopes, and a causal pathway are all bundled together. Related work is reasonably positioned, though it should cite more directly the closest multi-entity LLM binding failures and distinguish parametric recall from in-context tasks with sharper wording. Experiments are mostly feasible, but some controls are missing: exact matched baselines for output-order bias, random permutation nulls, retrieval-vs-assignment probes, robustness across prompt templates, and tests that separate content similarity from binding failure. As written, the story risks sounding like 'LLMs make binding errors too' without proving the deeper mechanism. If executed well with rigorous controls, this could be a solid conference paper, but in proposal form it needs tighter definitions and stronger causal design.

Name: fluency_as_truth_heuristic
Title: Easy to Read, Easy to Believe: An Internal Retrieval-Fluency Signal LLMs Misuse as a Truth Cue
Short Hypothesis: Transferring the human fluency-as-truth heuristic into LLM factual verification: when judging whether a statement is true, LLMs partly rely on an internal retrieval-fluency signal (how quickly/easily the statement's content is processed) as evidence for truth, rather than solely on stored content. We hypothesize (1) verification errors are systematically biased so that fluently-processed false statements are over-accepted and disfluently-processed true statements are over-rejected, above matched baselines; (2) a linear 'retrieval-fluency' signal, decodable before the verdict and driven by surface/processing ease more than by the fact's actual truth, causally drives the verdict; and (3) suppressing this fluency direction (not editing any fact) selectively fixes fluency-induced verification errors while preserving correct verdicts.
Related Work: Human cognitive science robustly establishes that processing fluency and retrieval fluency are used as cues for truth and confidence, independent of actual validity (Epistemic Status of Processing Fluency 2010; Illusory Certainty / repetition-fluency 2024; Processing Fluency and Judgment 2016; Retrieval Fluency contributes to JoLs 2019). In LLMs, prior interpretability work encodes only truth/correctness-correlated signals: attention-to-constraint predicts factual accuracy (SAT Probe 2023), attention-head entropy predicts correctness (HEADENTROPY 2026), local intrinsic dimension separates truthful from untruthful generations (2024), and entropy/token-frequency neurons regulate confidence (Confidence Regulation Neurons 2024); Information Anxiety (2024) shows popular queries converge early internally. Idiom-recall work (2023) shows memorized content is promoted early (a fluency proxy). Crucially, all of these treat internal ease/confidence signals as (imperfect) indicators of truth; none test the reverse causal misuse — that an LLM treats its own retrieval fluency as EVIDENCE for truth, causing it to accept fluently-processed falsehoods and reject disfluently-processed truths in a verification task. This transfers the human fluency-as-truth heuristic into LLM verification with a causal fluency-signal locus and a non-destructive fix, and is orthogonal to my prior proposals, which all concern retrieval/expression of a target answer rather than verification of a presented statement.
Abstract: Humans judge statements they process fluently as more likely true — a fluency-as-truth heuristic that operates independently of the statement's actual validity. We ask whether large language models exhibit an analogous, mechanistically-localizable bias in factual verification. Existing interpretability work reads internal ease/confidence signals as indicators of truth; we test the reverse causal misuse: that an LLM treats how fluently it can process a statement as evidence for that statement's truth, causing it to over-accept fluently-processed falsehoods and over-reject disfluently-processed truths. We test three claims. (1) Behavioral signature: on true/false verification of factual statements, holding truth value fixed, manipulating processing fluency (via surface cues — rhyme/phonetic ease, high-frequency phrasing, prior in-context repetition, and lexical simplicity) shifts verdicts toward 'true' for fluent framings and 'false' for disfluent ones, producing directional errors above content-matched baselines. (2) Localization and drivers: a linear retrieval-fluency signal is decodable before the verdict, tracks surface/processing-ease cues more than the statement's actual truth (measured by plain-phrasing verification accuracy), and is separable (via residualization) from a content/truth signal. (3) Causal control: activation-patching the fluency representation from a disfluent-but-true (or fluent-but-false) matched run, and suppressing the fluency direction, remove the fluency-induced verdict bias with high specificity — preserving correct verdicts and appropriate uncertainty — whereas a 'ignore how it sounds, judge only the facts' re-prompt does not. Experiments span Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, and Gemma-2-9B on FEVER-style and curated true/false factual sets, evaluating fluency dose-response, verdict-bias geometry, causal removal, and specificity.
Experiments: Experiment 1 (H1 — fluency-induced directional verdict bias): Tests that, holding truth value and propositional content fixed, fluent framings push verification verdicts toward 'true' and disfluent framings toward 'false'. Data: factual statements with known truth labels from FEVER (~185k claims) and curated true/false sets over PopQA/T-REx facts; target ~1,200 statements per model (capped for the framing x caching cost; report coverage), each rendered in 5 meaning- and truth-preserving framings (plain; rhyming/phonetically easy; high-frequency lexical; rare/technical; prior in-context repetition vs first-exposure), validated by a GPT-4o judge plus a 100-item human spot-check (>=90% agreement, truth unchanged). Verdicts via a fixed true/false/uncertain template plus 3 paraphrases. Model: Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, frozen, temperature 0; no trained parameters. Systems compared: each fluency framing vs the plain baseline and a content-matched null (framing that adds equal length but no fluency manipulation); paired McNemar. Decisive metric: signed verdict shift toward 'true' for fluent and toward 'false' for disfluent framings, holding truth fixed (fluency x truth-value interaction), yielding the two diagnostic error types (fluent-false over-acceptance, disfluent-true over-rejection). Convincing: >=8 pp acceptance lift for fluent-false and >=8 pp rejection lift for disfluent-true over the content-matched null, consistent in sign across >=2 of 3 models. Undecidable band: 3-8 pp -> bias present but weak, partial support. Negative (<3 pp, or no consistent sign) refutes the fluency-as-truth transfer — an informative cross-species divergence.

Experiment 2 (H2 — retrieval-fluency signal decodable before the verdict and driven by ease not truth): Tests that a linear fluency signal is decodable before the verdict, tracks processing-ease cues more than actual truth, and is separable from a content/truth signal. Data: the Exp-1 items with residual stream cached at the statement/last-token positions across layers. Model: frozen; per-layer L2-logistic probes — a fluency probe (target = ordinal fluency level; plus, as robustness, self-rated ease and the content-promotion layer) and a content/truth probe — trained 70%/30% over 3 seeds with shuffle nulls. Systems compared: fluency-probe output regressed on surface fluency cues vs actual truth / plain-phrasing verification accuracy (standardized betas); fluency probe residualized on the content probe. Decisive metric: fluency-cue beta vs truth beta in predicting the fluency signal; secondary: fluency-probe peak AUROC and onset layer (before the verdict token), and residual separability. Convincing: fluency-cue beta at least 2x the truth beta, fluency-probe AUROC >=0.75 peaking before the verdict, and residual AUROC (after removing content) >=0.70, in >=2 of 3 models. Undecidable band: cue-to-truth beta ratio 1-2x, or AUROC 0.60-0.75 -> signal partly a truth proxy, partial support. Negative (fluency signal tracks truth more than cues, or is not separable from content) means there is no distinct retrieval-fluency signal; the locus claim fails.

Experiment 3 (H2 — the fluency signal causally drives the verdict): Tests that manipulating the fluency representation flips verdicts in the predicted direction, independent of content. Data: 300 matched fluent-but-false and disfluent-but-true trials per model, held out from Exp-2 probe training. Method: patch the fluency representation from a disfluent-but-true run into a fluent-but-false run (and vice versa) at the Exp-2 onset layers; suppress or inject the fluency direction (low-rank high-minus-low-fluency difference); a content/truth-only patch control. Model: frozen; dose swept in {0.5,1,2,4}x, 3 seeds. Systems compared: fluency-patch/inject vs content-only patch vs random-direction control. Decisive metric: per-item verdict-flip rate in the fluency-predicted direction from the fluency intervention vs the random-direction control; secondary: dose-response monotonicity, and that the content-only patch changes the verdict via truth without reproducing the fluency-bias pattern. Convincing: fluency injection flips >=25% of verdicts toward the bias with monotone dose-response (>> random-direction), while the content-only patch shows a different (truth-driven) pattern, in >=2 of 3 models. Undecidable band: flip 10-25% -> partial causal role, suggestive. Negative (flip <=10% over control, or indistinguishable from the content patch) means the fluency signal is correlational, not causal.

Experiment 4 (H3 — fluency-debiasing intervention with specificity and generality): Tests that suppressing the fluency direction selectively removes the two directional errors while preserving correct verdicts, and generalizes. Data: held-out fluency-biased verification items (>=400 per model); specificity sets = items where fluency and truth already agree, genuinely-ambiguous statements that warrant 'uncertain', and 200 unrelated verification items. Model: frozen; a low-rank fluency steering vector fitted on a subset of cues/relations and applied to held-out cues/relations and across the three models; dose swept, 3 seeds. Systems compared: fluency-subtraction vs an 'ignore how it sounds, judge only the facts' re-prompt, chain-of-thought verification, and a random-direction control. Decisive metric: reduction in fluent-false over-acceptance and disfluent-true over-rejection (verdict accuracy moving toward the plain baseline), reported jointly with collateral change on the fluency-truth-agree, uncertainty, and 200-unrelated sets; secondary: output perplexity. Convincing: >=40% of the fluency-induced error removed with <=2 pp collateral drop and preserved 'uncertain' behavior, beating the re-prompt by >=15 pp, transferring across cues and models. Undecidable band: 20-40% removed, or collateral 2-5 pp -> capped utility. Negative (<=20% removed, collateral >5 pp, or flips fluent-but-true items) means no clean debiasing; the fix claim fails.
Risk Factors and Limitations: Fluency manipulations (rhyme, rare vocabulary, repetition) risk altering meaning or introducing genuine ambiguity rather than pure processing ease; strict truth-value and semantic-equivalence validation, content-matched baselines, and using multiple independent fluency cues (so any shared effect isolates fluency, not one confound) are essential.

LLMs might not reproduce the human directional bias (e.g., verdicts could be insensitive to surface fluency, or the effect could be pure repetition-copying); a null or divergent pattern would refute the transfer but is itself an informative cross-species finding, and the repetition cue is distinguished from verbatim copying by including both true and false repeated items.

The fluency and content/truth signals may be entangled; the causal patching/steering tests (Exp 3), not probe onset alone, are decisive, and a graded/partial dissociation would weaken the strong claim while remaining informative.

Debiasing could over-correct — making the model reject fluent-but-true statements or lose appropriate confidence; the fluency-truth-agree and genuine-uncertainty specificity controls (Exp 4) are central and utility may be capped even if the analysis holds.
The fluency probe target (ordinal cue level / promotion layer / self-rated ease) is a proxy for internal retrieval fluency; we report multiple operationalizations and their consistency.
A single transferable fluency-suppression vector may not exist if the bias is cue- or relation-specific, limiting practical generality though still scientifically informative.
Verification verdicts are prompt-sensitive (true/false/uncertain framing); we use multiple paraphrases and report robustness, since framing itself may modulate the bias.
Findings on 7-9B models may not transfer to frontier-scale models beyond an academic budget.

Novelty rests mainly on the controlled verification task plus causal intervention and suppression.

Name: anchor_selective_accessibility
Title: Anchored Recall: How an Irrelevant Anchor Contaminates Which Stored Facts an LLM Can Access
Short Hypothesis: Anchoring in LLMs is not merely output-level assimilation toward a number; it is a selective-accessibility retrieval-contamination effect. An irrelevant anchor presented before a factual query causally biases which stored values become accessible in the residual stream, so that on anchored trials the correct value the model otherwise recalls is out-competed by an anchor-consistent value even though it remains internally decodable. We hypothesize a transient, anchor-driven accessibility signal that gates recall, and that suppressing it recovers the model's un-anchored answer without editing any fact.
Related Work: Behavioral work now firmly establishes anchoring in LLMs (Anchors in the Machine 2025; CBEval 2024; AnchorBench 2026; anchoring meta-analysis 2023) and some mechanistic touches: Shapley attribution shows anchors reweight log-probs, authority-bias steering (Trust Me I'm an Expert 2026) subtracts a residual-stream bias vector, and Anchoring Depends on Confidence (2026) shows susceptibility tracks distributional certainty rather than accuracy. Numerical-attribute work (Interpreting Multi-Attribute Confounding 2025) shows irrelevant numeric context perturbs magnitude subspaces. Crucially, none test the classic human selective-accessibility account: that the anchor contaminates *which stored fact is retrieved* rather than only shifting the output distribution, none show the correct value remains internally recoverable during an anchored error (hidden knowledge), and none localize a transient anchor-accessibility signal that gates recall and can be suppressed to restore un-anchored recall. This is distinct from my magnitude_prior_regression proposal (a query-independent category-typical compression prior, no external anchor) and from context_priming_contamination (a semantic distractor entity, not a numeric comparison anchor).
Abstract: Large language models assimilate their answers toward irrelevant numeric anchors, a robust behavioral cognitive bias. But the leading human account of anchoring is not distributional imitation: it is selective accessibility, where comparing a target against an anchor makes anchor-consistent information more retrievable. We ask whether LLM anchoring is likewise a retrieval-contamination phenomenon in factual recall, and whether the model still holds the correct value it fails to report. We study anchored factual queries (e.g., 'Is the population of Riga greater or less than 9,000,000? Now, what is the population of Riga?') for facts the model answers accurately when un-anchored. We test three claims. (1) Retrieval contamination: on anchored trials that produce a wrong, anchor-shifted answer, a linear probe recovers the correct value from intermediate activations at rates far above the verbalized answer, showing the fact is hidden, not overwritten, and the emitted answer is an anchor-consistent competitor. (2) Accessibility locus and drivers: a transient anchor-accessibility signal, decodable before the answer and separable (via residualization) from the fact-content signal, predicts and scales with the anchor's magnitude and its plausibility, tracking selective-accessibility rather than only distributional certainty. (3) Causal recovery: suppressing the anchor-accessibility direction, or patching the pre-anchor representation, restores the un-anchored correct value with high specificity, whereas fact editing does not, and outperforms a 'ignore the previous number' re-prompt. Experiments span Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, and Gemma-2-9B on numeric-fact sets from Wikidata, evaluating hidden-knowledge recovery, accessibility-signal prediction, causal recovery, and specificity, plus a safety transfer to clinical numeric facts.
Experiments: Experiment 1 (H1 — anchor-driven retrieval contamination with hidden correct value): Tests that an irrelevant anchor shifts the emitted value toward an anchor-consistent competitor while the correct value the model otherwise recalls stays internally decodable. Data: from Wikidata, single-numeric-answer facts (city population, elevation, area, founding year, drug dosage), restricted to facts the model answers within a tolerance band when un-anchored; target ~1,000 facts per model (capped; report coverage). Matched conditions per fact: no-anchor; high anchor; low anchor, introduced via the comparative pathway ('Is X greater or less than [anchor]? What is X?') at controlled log-distances, with both implausible/random and plausible anchors. Model: Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, frozen, temperature 0; the only fitted object is a per-layer log-magnitude linear probe (held-out facts, 70%/30%, 3 seeds, shuffle null) reading the internal value on anchored-error trials. Systems compared: probe recovery of the true value on anchored-error trials vs the verbalized (anchor-shifted) value vs the un-anchored run. Decisive metric: probe recovery accuracy (within tolerance) of the true value on anchored errors; secondary: signed assimilation magnitude vs anchor log-distance (dose-response), and whether the emitted value aligns with an anchor-consistent competitor. Convincing: probe recovers the un-anchored value on >=60% of anchored errors (>> verbalized, comparable to the un-anchored run) with a monotone assimilation dose-response, in >=2 of 3 models. Undecidable band: recovery 40-60% -> value partly hidden, partly shifted internally, partial support. Negative (recovery near verbalized/chance) means anchoring is output-distribution imitation with no hidden correct value — refuting the selective-accessibility framing.

Experiment 2 (H2 — anchor-accessibility signal scales with anchor properties, not just certainty): Tests that a transient anchor-accessibility signal, separable from fact content, is decodable before the answer and scales with anchor magnitude/plausibility (selective accessibility) rather than only un-anchored distributional certainty. Data: anchored vs no-anchor runs for the Exp-1 facts; residual stream cached at subject/last-token across layers. Model: frozen; a per-layer L2 probe targets the accessibility signal, trained 70%/30% over 3 seeds; residualized against the fact-content/magnitude probe; shuffle null. Systems compared: accessibility signal regressed on anchor log-distance and plausibility vs the model's un-anchored distributional certainty (competing drivers). Decisive metric: standardized betas of anchor magnitude/plausibility vs un-anchored certainty in predicting the accessibility signal; secondary: per-layer AUROC of the signal predicting anchored error, onset before the answer, and residual separability from content. Convincing: anchor-property betas dominate the certainty beta (>=2x) and the signal predicts anchored error at AUROC >=0.72 after residualizing out content, in >=2 of 3 models. Undecidable band: anchor-to-certainty beta ratio 1-2x, or AUROC 0.60-0.72 -> the selective-accessibility and certainty accounts coincide, partial support. Negative (certainty dominates, or no separable signal) favors the distributional-certainty account over selective accessibility.

Experiment 3 (H2 — the accessibility signal causally gates recall): Tests that the accessibility signal causally produces assimilation. Data: 300 anchored-error and 300 no-anchor facts per model, held out from Exp-2 probe training. Method: patch the pre-anchor (no-anchor) representation into an anchored-error run; suppress the accessibility direction; inject the accessibility direction (or a synthetic anchor signal) into a no-anchor run; a content-only patch control. Model: frozen; interventions at Exp-2 layers, dose swept {0.5,1,2,4}x, 3 seeds. Systems compared: patch-restore, suppression, injection-induce, content-only patch, random-direction control. Decisive metric: induced-assimilation magnitude from injection vs the random-direction control (with dose-response); secondary: recovery rate of the un-anchored value from patching/suppression vs the content-only patch. Convincing: injection induces assimilation >=15 pp of the anchor gap over random-direction with monotone dose-response, and patch/suppression restores >=50% of un-anchored accuracy while the content-only patch does not, in >=2 of 3 models. Undecidable band: induced 5-15 pp, or recovery 25-50% -> partial causal role. Negative (induced <=5 pp over control, or content patch matches) means the accessibility signal is correlational, not the gate.

Experiment 4 (H3 — de-anchoring recovery with specificity and generality): Tests that suppressing the accessibility direction restores the un-anchored answer without editing facts and specifically. Data: held-out anchored queries (>=400 per model); specificity sets = no-anchor facts, cases where the anchor is legitimately informative, and 200 unrelated facts. Model: frozen; a low-rank anchor-accessibility steering vector fitted on a subset of relations/anchor types and applied to held-out ones and across the three models; dose swept, 3 seeds. Systems compared: de-anchoring steering vs an 'ignore the previous number / answer independently' re-prompt, chain-of-thought, authority-bias-style residual steering, ROME editing (expected null), and a random-direction control. Decisive metric: reduction in assimilation / recovery of un-anchored accuracy, reported jointly with collateral change on no-anchor, informative-anchor, and 200-unrelated sets; secondary: held-out perplexity. Convincing: >=40% assimilation reduction with <=2 pp collateral drop, beating the re-prompt by >=15 pp, transferring across relations and models. Undecidable band: 20-40% reduction, or collateral 2-5 pp -> capped utility. Negative (<=20% reduction, collateral >5 pp, or harms legitimately-informative-anchor cases) means no clean de-anchoring.
Risk Factors and Limitations: Anchoring could be pure output-distribution imitation with no retrieval contamination; the hidden-knowledge probe (Exp 1) and the induce-on-demand causal test (Exp 3) are the decisive separators, and a null here would refute the selective-accessibility framing while remaining informative.

The anchor-accessibility and fact-content signals may be entangled, especially since both live in numeric-magnitude subspaces (per Multi-Attribute Confounding 2025); the causal patching/steering tests, not probe AUROC alone, are decisive, and graded results remain informative.

Distinguishing selective accessibility from the distributional-certainty account (Owusu 2026) is subtle; the driver regression (Exp 2) that separates anchor-property scaling from un-anchored certainty is the key test, but the two may partly coincide.

De-anchoring could over-correct on cases where the anchor is legitimately relevant, or degrade fluency; the informative-anchor and no-anchor specificity controls (Exp 4) are central and utility may be capped.
Multi-token numeric readout complicates probing/logit-lens; primary analysis uses log-magnitude probes and tolerance-band accuracy rather than exact-digit recovery, with reported coverage.
A single transferable de-anchoring vector may not exist if accessibility is relation- or anchor-type-specific, limiting practical generality though still scientifically informative.
Findings on 7-9B models may not transfer to frontier-scale models beyond an academic budget.

novelty.reasoning: Core technical claims that need to be novel: (1) anchoring in LLMs is a selective-accessibility retrieval contamination effect, not just output-level bias; (2) during anchored errors, the correct value is still internally decodable ('hidden knowledge'); (3) there is a transient anchor-accessibility signal separable from fact content that causally gates recall; (4) this signal scales with anchor magnitude/plausibility and can be distinguished from a confidence/certainty account; (5) suppressing/injecting that signal can de-anchor answers without editing facts. This is a real and defensible delta, but it sits in a very crowded anchoring/interpretability space and is narrower than it first sounds. The closest prior work family is anchoring-in-LLMs behavioral and mechanistic analysis (especially Localizing Anchoring Pathways and Anchoring Depends on Confidence). The actual delta is the human selective-accessibility framing plus a hidden-knowledge probe and a causal gate test that adjudicates anchor-property vs model-certainty. That is non-trivial, but also an obvious next step once one has observed anchoring and wants to localize it mechanistically.

Name: abstention_momentum
Title: Abstention Is Contagious: How One 'I Don't Know' Suppresses Knowledge on the Next Question
Short Hypothesis: Abstention in LLMs carries session-level momentum: once a model abstains ('I don't know') on one query, it becomes more likely to abstain on a subsequent, unrelated, and easily-answerable query in the same conversation, hiding knowledge it demonstrably holds. We hypothesize this is a distinct behavioral phenomenon—abstention hysteresis—carried by a transient, query-independent 'abstention-mode' signal imprinted by the prior abstention act, and causally suppressible so a prior abstention no longer contaminates later recall.
Related Work: Prior work treats each query's abstention/refusal decision as independent: entity-recognition directions gate knowledge refusal on the current entity (Do I Know This Entity, 2024), sparse ambiguity-encoding neurons control answer-vs-abstain for the current question (AENs, 2025), over-refusal benchmarks measure per-prompt refusal rates (OR-Bench, 2024; Do RALMs Know When They Don't Know, 2025), and abstention frameworks estimate per-query knowledge boundaries (ABCA, 2025; Know Your Limits survey, 2024). None test whether the *act of abstaining on one query causally biases the abstention decision on a later, independent query* within a session, whether this hides knowledge the model would otherwise express, or whether a transient abstention-mode signal carries this contamination. This transfers the human response-set perseveration / decision-hysteresis phenomenon into LLM knowledge expression, and is orthogonal to my prior single-turn gating proposals (familiarity, difficulty, stress, persona) which all manipulate the *current* query rather than a *prior abstention act*.
Abstract: Large language models increasingly operate over multi-turn conversations, deciding on each turn whether to answer or abstain. Existing work treats these abstention decisions as independent per-query events. We ask whether abstention is instead contagious: does the act of saying 'I don't know' on one query causally increase the model's propensity to abstain on a subsequent, unrelated, easily-answerable query in the same session—thereby hiding knowledge the model demonstrably holds? We call this abstention hysteresis. We first document the behavior: for facts a model answers correctly in a fresh context, we compare later-query abstention rates between a condition where the model first genuinely abstained (on an unanswerable prior query) and matched controls where it first answered a question or saw equal-length filler. We predict elevated abstention (and reduced accuracy) after a prior abstention, above baselines, scaling with how many prior abstentions occurred and their recency. We then test the mechanism with a Location plus Causal Intervention strategy: a transient 'abstention-mode' signal imprinted by the prior abstention should be linearly decodable, separable (via residualization) from the current-query content signal, and—during a contaminated failure—the correct answer should remain internally decodable (hidden, not lost); activation patching from an answer-first run and suppression of the abstention-mode direction should restore correct answers with high specificity, while preserving genuinely appropriate abstention on truly unanswerable follow-ups. Experiments span Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, and Gemma-2-9B on PopQA/T-REx plus a medical subset, evaluating hysteresis prevalence, dose-response, hidden-knowledge recovery, causal recovery, and specificity.
Experiments: Experiment 1 (H1 — abstention hysteresis prevalence and dose-response): Tests that abstaining on one query raises abstention on a later unrelated, answerable query, beyond conversational drift. Data: PopQA (14,267), T-REx, EntityQuestions; per model select target facts answered correctly in isolation; target ~1,200 facts (capped; report coverage). Two-stage sessions holding total length equal: ABSTENTION-FIRST (a genuinely unanswerable prior query on which the model abstains, verified), ANSWER-FIRST (an answerable prior it answers), and FILLER (equal-length neutral text). Dose variants: 1/2/3 consecutive prior abstentions and varied recency (turns to target). Single-token-first targets. Model: Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, frozen, temperature 0; no trained parameters. Systems compared: target abstention rate / accuracy across the three conditions (paired McNemar; mixed-effects logistic), and across dose. Decisive metric: target-query abstention-rate increase (and accuracy drop) in ABSTENTION-FIRST vs the ANSWER-FIRST and FILLER controls; secondary: dose-response with number and recency of prior abstentions. Convincing: >=10 pp higher abstention (or >=8 pp lower accuracy) in ABSTENTION-FIRST than both controls, rising with dose, in >=2 of 3 models. Undecidable band: 3-10 pp -> hysteresis weak, partial support. Negative (<3 pp, or a protective/opposite effect) refutes the hysteresis transfer — an informative behavioral finding either way.

Experiment 2 (H1 — hidden knowledge under contaminated abstention): Tests that on contaminated failures the correct answer remains internally decodable (hidden, not rationally discarded). Data: contaminated failures from Exp 1 (target abstained/wrong in ABSTENTION-FIRST but correct in isolation), with their ANSWER-FIRST counterparts; residual stream cached at the target-query positions. Model: frozen; a per-layer L2-logistic content probe (target = correct answer) trained 70%/30% over 3 seeds with a shuffle null. Systems compared: content-probe recovery on contaminated failures vs the verbalized accuracy (~0) and vs the ANSWER-FIRST run. Decisive metric: content-probe recovery of the correct answer on contaminated failures; secondary: comparability to the ANSWER-FIRST recovery. Convincing: recovery >=60% (>> verbalized and >> shuffle), comparable to ANSWER-FIRST, in >=2 of 3 models — the knowledge is hidden, not lost. Undecidable band: recovery 40-60% -> partly hidden, partly a genuine competence downgrade, partial support. Negative (recovery near verbalized/chance) means the contaminated abstention reflects rational recalibration or loss, not hidden-knowledge suppression.

Experiment 3 (H2 — abstention-mode signal localization): Tests that a transient, content-separable 'abstention-mode' signal imprinted by the prior abstention is decodable at the later query. Data: matched ABSTENTION-FIRST vs ANSWER-FIRST runs at the target query for the Exp-1 facts; residual stream cached across layers. Model: frozen; a per-layer L2-logistic probe targets the presence/recency of a prior abstention, trained 70%/30% over 3 seeds; residualized against the current-query content probe; shuffle null. Systems compared: the abstention-mode probe before vs after residualizing out content; its layer/position profile and attention over the prior-abstention tokens. Decisive metric: per-layer AUROC of the abstention-mode signal predicting target abstention, after residualizing out content; secondary: onset before the answer, and tracking of prior-abstention presence/recency rather than the specific fact. Convincing: post-residualization AUROC >=0.72 with a clear onset before the answer, in >=2 of 3 models. Undecidable band: AUROC 0.60-0.72 -> signal entangled with content, partial. Negative (AUROC at shuffle after residualization) means there is no separable abstention-mode signal; the locus claim fails.

Experiment 4 (H3 — abstention-mode signal is causal): Tests that the abstention-mode signal causally contaminates later recall. Data: 300 contaminated failures and 300 answer-first facts per model, held out from Exp-3 probe training. Method: patch the target-query residual stream from an ANSWER-FIRST run into a contaminated ABSTENTION-FIRST run; suppress the abstention-mode direction; inject the abstention-mode direction into an ANSWER-FIRST run to induce contamination; a content-only patch control. Model: frozen; interventions at Exp-3 layers, dose swept {0.5,1,2,4}x, 3 seeds. Systems compared: patch-restore, suppression, injection-induce, content-only patch, random-direction control. Decisive metric: induced-abstention increase from injection vs the random-direction control (dose-response); secondary: recovery rate of the correct answer from patch/suppression vs the content-only patch. Convincing: injection induces >=15 pp abstention over random-direction with monotone dose-response, and patch/suppression recovers >=50% of correct answers while the content-only patch does not, in >=2 of 3 models. Undecidable band: induced 5-15 pp, or recovery 25-50% -> partial causal role. Negative (induced <=5 pp over control, or content patch matches) means the abstention-mode signal is correlational.

Experiment 5 (H3 — recovery with appropriate-abstention specificity and generality): Tests that suppressing the abstention-mode signal restores correct answers without forcing hallucination on genuinely unanswerable follow-ups, and generalizes. Data: held-out contaminated failures (>=400 per model); specificity sets = truly-unanswerable follow-ups (must still be abstained, not hallucinated) and 200 unrelated answerable facts. Model: frozen; a low-rank abstention-mode suppression vector fitted on a subset of relations and applied to held-out relations and across the three models; dose swept, 3 seeds. Systems compared: suppression vs a 'treat each question independently' re-prompt, re-querying the target in a fresh context (upper bound), refusal-tuning, and a random-direction control. Decisive metric: recovery rate on contaminated failures, reported jointly with the false-answer rate on truly-unanswerable items (must not rise) and collateral on the 200 unrelated facts; secondary: held-out perplexity. Convincing: recovery >=40% with <=2 pp rise in false answers on unanswerable items and <=2 pp collateral drop, beating the re-prompt by >=15 pp, transferring across relations and models. Undecidable band: recovery 20-40%, or unanswerable false-answer rise 2-5 pp -> capped utility. Negative (recovery <=20%, or induces hallucination on unanswerable items >5 pp) means suppression cannot separate contamination from appropriate abstention.
Risk Factors and Limitations: The effect could be generic conversational drift or output-format entrainment rather than an abstention-specific momentum; the answer-first control (same prior-turn structure, no abstention) and equal-length filler control (Exp 1), plus the induce-on-demand test (Exp 4), are the decisive separators.

LLMs might not reproduce the hysteresis effect (per-query independence, or prior abstention could even prime helpfulness); a null or opposite result refutes the transfer but is an informative cross-species / behavioral finding.

Contaminated abstention could reflect rational recalibration (the model updates downward on its own competence) rather than hidden-knowledge suppression; the content probe (Exp 2) and fresh-context recovery separate hidden from lost knowledge.
The abstention-mode and content signals may be entangled; the causal patching/steering tests (Exp 4), not probe AUROC alone, are decisive, and graded results remain informative.

Suppression could break genuinely-appropriate abstention on unanswerable follow-ups (inducing hallucination); the unanswerable-item false-answer specificity control (Exp 5) is central and utility may be capped.
A single transferable suppression vector may not exist if hysteresis is relation-specific, limiting practical generality though still scientifically informative.
Multi-token answers complicate readout; primary analysis restricts to single-token-first answers with reported coverage.
Findings on 7-9B models may not transfer to frontier-scale models beyond an academic budget.

Name: ordinal_access_chain
Title: Stored as a Chain, Queried by Position: Why LLMs Know the Sequence but Fail to Retrieve Its Nth Element
Short Hypothesis: LLMs store ordered real-world sequences (rankings, chronologies, alphabetical/positional lists, taxonomic orders) as a linked chain accessible primarily by neighbor-traversal, not as position-indexed slots. A distinct failure mode is ordinal-access failure: a model that reliably knows 'what comes after Y' and can recite the whole sequence nonetheless fails to answer 'what is the Nth element' by direct positional query, even though the element is internally recoverable. We hypothesize (1) whether a query is answered via a decodable neighbor-chain signal vs a position-index signal is separable, (2) ordinal-access errors concentrate on mid-sequence, high-N elements where chain traversal must span many steps, and (3) injecting a decoded 'running-position' signal (or patching from a recitation run) recovers the correct element without editing any stored fact.
Related Work: Beyond Memorization (2024) shows LLMs access parametric memory sequentially but struggle with RANDOM access, mitigating via recitation and training-time sentence permutation on SYNTHETIC data; it offers no inference-time mechanistic locus, no test on real-world ordered knowledge, and no steering fix. Your-Context-Is-Not-an-Array (2024) locates in-CONTEXT random-access failure in attention on algorithmic tasks, not parametric ordered knowledge. Serial-position / temporal-bias / SORT / listwise-ranking work (2022-2025) all concern IN-CONTEXT ordering, positional bias, or episodic order recall, not positional access to sequences stored in weights. Structure-Development-in-List-Sorting (2025) studies training-time head specialization on synthetic sorting. Crucially, none isolate ordinal-access-by-position as a distinct parametric-recall failure on real ordered knowledge, none contrast a neighbor-chain vs position-index representation causally, and none show a non-destructive intervention that recovers the Nth element. This is orthogonal to all my prior single-fact retrieval/gating proposals; here the object is the internal representational format of ordered knowledge (chain vs index) and how query type gates access.
Abstract: Large language models memorize ordered sequences from pretraining: the order of US presidents, the alphabet, chart rankings, the periodic-table order, a book's chapter order. Prior work shows LLMs can recite memorized content sequentially but struggle to access it randomly, mitigating this only at training time on synthetic data. We propose an inference-time mechanistic account for real ordered knowledge: LLMs store sequences as a neighbor-linked chain accessible by traversal, not as position-indexed slots, so positional queries fail while neighbor queries succeed. We call this ordinal-access failure, and predict it is not a storage failure: the Nth element is internally recoverable even when the model cannot answer 'what is the Nth element'. We test three claims on curated ordered-knowledge sets. (1) Behavioral signature: for sequences the model can fully recite and whose neighbor relations it answers correctly, direct positional queries ('what is the Nth X?') fail at rates far above neighbor queries, and failure grows with position N and with mid-sequence location, above frequency-matched baselines. (2) Chain-vs-index dissociation: a linear probe recovers a neighbor-chain signal (predicting adjacent elements) and, separately, a running-position/index signal; whether a query is answered by chain traversal vs index lookup is decodable, and on positional failures the correct element remains decodable while the position-index signal is weak/absent. (3) Causal recovery: patching a 'running-position' representation from a recitation run into a direct-positional-query run, or injecting a decoded position-index direction, recovers the Nth element with high specificity, whereas fact editing does not, and outperforms a 'recite then answer' re-prompt. Experiments span Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, and Gemma-2-9B, evaluating positional-vs-neighbor accuracy, position dose-response, hidden-element recovery, causal recovery, and specificity.
Experiments: Experiment 1 (H1 — ordinal-access failure with hidden Nth element): Tests that direct positional queries fail where neighbor queries succeed on the same elements, and that the Nth element is nonetheless internally recoverable. Data: sequences with authoritative order from Wikidata/reference sources — ordinal succession (US presidents, monarchs, Olympic hosts by year), canonical fixed orders (alphabet, months, periodic-table order, planets), ranked lists (chart-topping songs, champions by year); restrict to sequences the model recites in full correctly and to single-token-first answers; target ~200 sequences with ~3,000 elements per model (capped; report coverage). Three query forms per element: NEIGHBOR, POSITIONAL, FULL RECITATION. Model: Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, frozen, temperature 0; the only fitted object is a per-layer L2-logistic probe (held-out sequences, 70%/30%, 3 seeds, shuffle null) reading the Nth element on positional-failure trials. Systems compared: POSITIONAL accuracy vs NEIGHBOR accuracy on the same neighbor-correct elements (paired McNemar); probe recovery vs verbalized on positional failures. Decisive metric: positional-minus-neighbor accuracy gap on the same elements; secondary: probe recovery of the correct Nth element on positional failures vs verbalized. Convincing: positional accuracy >=15 pp below neighbor accuracy AND probe recovers the Nth element on >=60% of positional failures (>> verbalized), in >=2 of 3 models. Undecidable band: gap 5-15 pp, or recovery 40-60% -> weak/partly-hidden, partial support. Negative (gap <5 pp, or recovery near verbalized) refutes the ordinal-access-failure and hidden-element claims.

Experiment 2 (H3 — position and mid-sequence dose-response): Tests that positional-query failure grows with N and is worst mid-sequence (longest chain traversal). Data: the positional-query results from Exp 1, indexed by position N and distance from both endpoints; controls for element popularity and sequence length. Model: the same three frozen models, temperature 0. Systems compared: positional accuracy as a function of N and mid-sequence location vs a null where accuracy is independent of position (mixed-effects logistic). Decisive metric: the accuracy-vs-position curve shape — a significant decline with N and a U-shape (endpoints easy, middle hard) after controlling popularity/length; secondary: mid-sequence-minus-endpoint accuracy gap. Convincing: a significant monotone N effect and a mid-sequence dip >=15 pp below endpoints, robust to popularity controls, in >=2 of 3 models. Undecidable band: dip 5-15 pp, or an N effect present only without popularity control -> traversal-cost account weak, partial support. Negative (flat accuracy in N/position) means access is not traversal-cost-limited — evidence against the chain account.

Experiment 3 (H2 — chain-vs-index representational dissociation): Tests that a neighbor-chain signal and a running-position/index signal are separately decodable and that the index signal is weak/absent during positional failures. Data: residual stream from recitation, neighbor, and positional runs over the Exp-1 sequences. Model: frozen; two per-layer probes — a neighbor-chain probe (predict the adjacent element / adjacency) and a running-position/index probe (predict the current element's ordinal position during recitation) — trained 70%/30% over 3 seeds, residualized against each other, shuffle nulls. Systems compared: index-signal strength during recitation/neighbor success vs during positional failures. Decisive metric: index-probe accuracy during positional-query failures vs during recitation (the diagnostic drop); secondary: per-layer AUROC of each probe and their residual non-redundancy. Convincing: both probes decode above shuffle and non-redundantly, and the index signal is >=20 pp weaker during positional failures than during recitation, in >=2 of 3 models. Undecidable band: index drop 8-20 pp -> partial dissociation. Negative (index signal equally strong in both, or chain and index inseparable) weakens the chain-vs-index account; a genuine absence of any index signal is itself informative about a chain-only format.

Experiment 4 (H4 — recovery of the Nth element by injecting a running-position signal): Tests that patching a running-position representation from recitation, or injecting a decoded index direction scaled to N, recovers the Nth element without editing facts and specifically. Data: held-out positional-query failures (>=400 per model); specificity sets = neighbor queries, already-correct positional queries, and 200 unrelated non-sequence facts. Model: frozen; the running-position vector and index direction from Exp 3 (fitted on train sequences) applied to held-out sequences and across the three models; also an ablation of the index signal during recitation (should remove positional access); dose swept, 3 seeds. Systems compared: recitation-patch / index-injection vs a 'recite then answer' re-prompt (upper bound), chain-of-thought counting, ROME editing (expected null), and a random-direction control. Decisive metric: correct-Nth-element recovery rate, reported jointly with collateral change on neighbor, already-correct, and 200-unrelated sets; secondary: whether index-ablation during recitation removes positional access (reverse causal check), and held-out perplexity. Convincing: recovery >=40% with <=2 pp collateral drop, ablation removing positional access, beating the re-prompt by >=15 pp, transferring across sequence types and models. Undecidable band: recovery 20-40%, or collateral 2-5 pp -> capped utility. Negative (recovery <=20%, collateral >5 pp, or ablation has no effect) means position access cannot be causally injected — refuting the recovery claim.
Risk Factors and Limitations: Positional-query failure could reflect arithmetic/counting incompetence (the model cannot map N to a step count) rather than a chain-vs-index storage format; the hidden-element probe (Exp 1) and the recitation-patching recovery (Exp 4) separate storage-format failure from counting failure, and the neighbor-vs-positional contrast on the same elements controls for element knowledge.

The neighbor-chain and position-index signals may be entangled or the position signal may be genuinely absent (no index representation at all); the causal patching/ablation tests (Exp 4), not probe AUROC alone, are decisive, and a graded result remains informative. A genuine absence of any position-index signal is itself an informative finding about the chain-only format.
Recitation itself may be imperfect or the model may recite a wrong order, confounding storage verification; we restrict to sequences with verified-correct full recitation and report coverage.

Position injection could over-correct (produce a plausible but wrong element at the target position) or degrade fluency; the neighbor-query and already-correct specificity controls (Exp 4) are central and utility may be capped.
Endpoint elements (first/last) may be trivially accessible for reasons unrelated to indexing (salience/frequency), inflating the U-shape; popularity controls and mid-sequence focus mitigate this.
A single transferable position-injection recipe may not exist if position encoding is sequence-type-specific, limiting practical generality though still scientifically informative.
Multi-token elements complicate readout; primary analysis restricts to single-token-first answers with reported coverage.
Findings on 7-9B models may not transfer to frontier-scale models beyond an academic budget.

novelty.reasoning: Core technical claims that need to be novel are: (1) real-world ordered knowledge stored in model weights is represented primarily as a neighbor-linked chain rather than directly position-indexed slots; (2) ordinal-access-by-position is a distinct parametric recall failure mode, separable from simple fact ignorance or in-context positional bias; (3) chain and running-position/index signals are representationally dissociable and separately decodable, with index signal selectively weak/absent on positional-query failures; (4) the failure has a position-dependent profile, especially a mid-sequence/U-shaped pattern consistent with traversal cost; and (5) inference-time recovery is possible by patching/injecting a running-position signal from a recitation trajectory, with reverse ablation impairing positional access. Relative to the cited prior family, especially Beyond Memorization, the broad phenomenon that sequential access is easier than random access is not new. The genuine delta is the move from synthetic tasks to real memorized ordered knowledge, the stronger mechanistic representational claim (chain vs index), and the causal inference-time steering/patching story. That is meaningfully different from in-context position-bias work and from synthetic random-access studies. Still, some parts are close to an obvious next step: once prior work shows sequential-easy/random-hard and recitation helps, testing real ordered lists and trying recitation-based interventions is a natural extension. The most novel component is not the behavioral gap itself but the claimed representational dissociation plus causal position injection. From the proposal text alone, that novelty is plausible but not yet airtight because 'running-position signal' may be a relabeling of generic progression/counting state unless carefully ruled out.

impact.reasoning: The phenomenon under study is a failure of parametric retrieval for ordered knowledge: models may know a sequence and local successor relations but still fail to retrieve the Nth item by position. The main audiences are researchers in LLM memory/knowledge representation, mechanistic interpretability, and retrieval/reasoning. If the claim holds, it would change how people think about what 'memorized knowledge' means in LLMs: correct recitation would no longer imply indexable access, and some benchmark failures would be seen as representational-access failures rather than missing facts. The strongest one-line case is: 'LLMs can store real-world sequences in a form that supports traversal but not direct ordinal lookup, and that missing access key can be causally restored at inference time.' The proposal passes the so-what test for the ML research community, especially interpretability and knowledge retrieval, because it isolates a concrete failure mode and suggests a non-destructive fix. However, the likely real-world reach is moderate rather than broad: many practical systems already avoid relying on parametric ordinal recall by using search/tools, and the direct application domain seems narrow unless the authors connect it to broader retrieval or reasoning failures. Citation potential is decent if the mechanistic evidence is strong, but it is more likely to influence a specialized subcommunity than shift the whole field. Its impact depends heavily on whether the result generalizes beyond a handful of canonical sequences and whether the steering method is robust enough to matter beyond the paper's setup.

review.reasoning: The proposal is promising but currently under-specified in ways a strict senior reviewer would flag. The main hypothesis is fairly precise and falsifiable in spirit, but some key terms are loose: 'stored as a chain', 'running-position signal', and 'internally recoverable' need operational definitions independent of the chosen probes. There is a risk of over-claiming mechanism from linear decodability and activation patching: probe-recovered position information may reflect correlated progression/counting features, and patching from recitation may simply transfer a richer task state rather than isolate an index variable. The proposal acknowledges arithmetic/counting confounds, but the current controls are not enough from text alone. Experimental design has several strengths: frozen models, multiple model families, held-out probes, specificity controls, reverse ablation, and comparisons against reprompting/CoT. But important details are missing: dataset construction criteria, exact sequence families and sample sizes, how 'fully-recitable' is verified, how popularity/length controls are operationalized, how hidden-element prompts avoid lexical leakage, how multi-token entities are handled beyond being deferred, and how probes are residualized to separate chain from index without target leakage. The causal intervention is the most exciting piece but also the least clearly feasible: 'injecting index direction scaled to N' assumes a stable geometry that may not exist across sequences, layers, and models. Missing controls include synthetic counterfactual sequences, shuffled or reverse-known sequences, adversarial aliases, and tests that distinguish generic counting competence from sequence-specific positional access. Venue-readiness is moderate: the story is coherent and potentially publishable, but it needs tighter operationalization, stronger falsification logic, and a more defensible causal analysis before top-tier acceptance.

Name: credibility_ungated_illusory_truth
Title: Believing the Distrusted Source: LLMs Show an Illusory Truth Effect That Fails to Gate on Source Credibility
Short Hypothesis: Transferring the human illusory-truth effect and its recently-established source-credibility moderation (repetition raises belief only for trusted sources) into LLMs: in-context repetition of a claim raises an LLM's belief that the claim is true, but—unlike humans exhibiting adaptive rationality—the LLM largely FAILS to gate this repetition-induced belief inflation by the claim's source credibility, so repeating a claim attributed to an explicitly distrusted/unreliable source still inflates the model's endorsement. We hypothesize this is because a repetition-familiarity signal and a source-credibility signal are computed as separable representations that are only weakly causally coupled at the verdict, and that strengthening this coupling (steering the credibility signal to gate the familiarity signal) restores human-like source-sensitive belief without editing any fact.
Related Work: Human cognitive science establishes the illusory truth effect (repetition increases perceived truth even for implausible claims; Fazio; repetition-frequency studies 2021) and, critically, its source-credibility moderation: repetition does NOT increase belief in claims from distrusted politicians (Repetition Does Not Increase Belief in Claims From Distrusted Politicians, 2024) and source reliability modulates epistemic vigilance (2015; 2025) - the adaptive-rationality refinement. In LLMs, prior work covers confidence-regulation and token-frequency neurons (2024), credibility-aware attention modification for EXTERNAL RAG documents (CrAM 2025), repetition/knowledge-conflict durability during TRAINING (Learning and Unlearning of Fabricated Knowledge 2024; Layer of Truth 2025), and fluency-as-truth in humans (2010). Crucially, none test whether LLMs exhibit the inference-time illusory-truth effect as a belief-verification bias, whether it is MODERATED by source credibility as in humans (the key adaptive-rationality signature), or whether a repetition-familiarity signal and a source-credibility signal are separable-but-uncoupled such that repetition bypasses credibility gating. This differs from my prior proposals (all about retrieval/expression of a stored answer) and from my fluency_as_truth_heuristic proposal (surface processing ease within a single exposure, no repetition and no source manipulation): here the object is repetition-driven belief inflation and its failure to gate on source trust.
Abstract: Humans judge repeated claims as truer - the illusory truth effect - but recent work shows this is adaptively gated by source credibility: repeating a claim from a distrusted source does NOT increase belief. We ask whether large language models exhibit the illusory truth effect and, decisively, whether they inherit the human source-credibility gating or instead let repetition inflate belief regardless of who said it. We first document the behavior: for factual claims (true and false) presented in a multi-turn context, we measure the model's endorsement of a claim as a function of how many times it was repeated earlier and the credibility of the source attributed to those repetitions (trusted expert vs. explicitly unreliable/distrusted source vs. no source). We predict LLMs show a robust repetition-induced endorsement lift but that this lift is largely UNMODERATED by source credibility - repetition from a distrusted source still inflates belief - a departure from human adaptive rationality, above matched baselines. We then test a mechanistic hypothesis with a Location + Causal Intervention strategy: a repetition-familiarity signal and a source-credibility signal are separately decodable from intermediate activations, are only weakly coupled at the verdict, and the credibility signal fails to suppress the familiarity signal's effect on the endorsement. Activation patching and steering that strengthen the credibility signal's gating of the familiarity signal should restore human-like source-sensitive belief (repetition stops inflating belief for distrusted sources) with high specificity, whereas a 'consider the source' re-prompt does not. Experiments span Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, and Gemma-2-9B on curated true/false claim sets plus a health-misinformation subset, evaluating repetition x credibility dose-response, signal separability, causal gating, and specificity.
Experiments: Experiment 1 (H1 — in-context repetition raises endorsement): Tests that repeating a claim in context increases the model's 'true' verdict, holding truth value fixed. Data: factual claims with known truth labels from FEVER (~185k) and curated true/false statements over PopQA/T-REx (including plausible-but-false items); target ~1,000 claims per model (capped; report coverage). Multi-turn contexts vary REPETITION (claim appears 0/1/3/5 times earlier as neutral, paraphrased non-verbatim mentions) with source neutral; verdict elicited via a fixed true/false/uncertain template plus 3 paraphrases. Model: Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, frozen, temperature 0; no trained parameters. Systems compared: endorsement rate vs repetition count for true and false claims, against a no-repetition equal-length control (separating copying from belief change). Decisive metric: endorsement ('true') lift per added repetition, holding truth fixed (repetition x truth-value mixed-effects logistic); secondary: monotonicity across 0/1/3/5. Convincing: a monotone endorsement lift of >=8 pp from 0 to 5 repetitions for both true and false claims, over the equal-length control, in >=2 of 3 models. Undecidable band: 3-8 pp lift -> illusory-truth effect weak, partial support. Negative (<3 pp, or only via verbatim copying) refutes the LLM illusory-truth effect.

Experiment 2 (H2 — repetition inflation fails to gate on source credibility): Tests the decisive cross-species signature: whether source credibility moderates the repetition effect (human) or leaves it largely unmoderated (hypothesis). Data: the Exp-1 claims, now crossing REPETITION (0/1/3/5) with SOURCE CREDIBILITY of the mentions (high-credibility expert; low-credibility/distrusted; no source), with a manipulation check that the model can rate each source's reliability when asked directly (items failing the check are dropped; report coverage). Model: the same three frozen models, temperature 0. Systems compared: the repetition-induced endorsement lift under high- vs low-credibility sources (repetition x credibility interaction), against the human benchmark (near-zero lift for distrusted sources). Decisive metric: the repetition x credibility interaction — specifically the distrusted-source repetition lift; secondary: the high-source lift as a positive-control anchor. Convincing (for the ungated hypothesis): distrusted-source repetition lift remains >=6 pp (i.e., the interaction is small, less than half the human-benchmark moderation) in >=2 of 3 models. Undecidable band: distrusted-source lift 3-6 pp, or interaction roughly half the benchmark -> partial gating, ambiguous. Negative for the hypothesis (distrusted-source lift <=3 pp, strong human-like moderation) refutes the 'ungated' claim — an informative positive cross-species finding that LLMs gate as humans do.

Experiment 3 (H3 — familiarity and credibility signals are separable but uncoupled, and familiarity causally drives the lift): Tests that a repetition-familiarity signal and a source-credibility signal are separately decodable, that the credibility signal fails to reduce the familiarity->verdict pathway, and that the familiarity signal causally produces the endorsement lift. Data: verdict-position residual stream over the Exp-2 items; 300 held-out repeated-claim trials for ablation. Model: frozen; two per-layer L2-logistic probes — familiarity (target = repetition count) and credibility (target = source level) — trained 70%/30% over 3 seeds, residualized against each other, shuffle nulls; ablation of the familiarity direction. Systems compared: decodability of each signal; whether higher credibility-signal activation predicts a reduced familiarity-to-verdict slope (mediation); familiarity-ablation vs random-direction control. Decisive metric: endorsement-lift change when the familiarity signal is ablated vs the random-direction control (should remove the lift); secondary: both probes' AUROC and residual non-redundancy, and the (predicted near-zero) coupling between credibility activation and the familiarity->verdict pathway. Convincing: familiarity ablation removes >=50% of the repetition lift (>> random-direction), both signals decode non-redundantly (AUROC >=0.70), and credibility activation does not reduce the familiarity->verdict slope, in >=2 of 3 models. Undecidable band: ablation removes 25-50%, or credibility shows partial coupling -> partial support. Negative (ablation has little effect, or credibility strongly gates familiarity internally) means the separable-but-uncoupled account fails.

Experiment 4 (H4 — restoring source-sensitive belief by strengthening credibility gating): Tests that steering the credibility signal to gate the familiarity signal restores human-like moderation without editing facts and specifically. Data: held-out repetition x credibility items (>=400 per model); specificity sets = claims where credibility and repetition already align, genuinely-true trusted-source claims (must stay endorsed), and 200 unrelated verification items. Model: frozen; a low-rank 'low-credibility -> discount' steering vector (activation difference between runs that correctly withhold belief from a distrusted repeated claim and runs that do not) fitted on a subset and applied to held-out source types/relations and across the three models; dose swept, 3 seeds; plus a reverse control that suppresses the credibility signal (should make repetition inflate belief uniformly). Systems compared: credibility-gating steering vs a 'consider the reliability of the source' re-prompt, chain-of-thought verification, CrAM-style credibility attention modification, and a random-direction control. Decisive metric: restoration of moderation = elimination of the distrusted-source repetition lift, reported jointly with preserved trusted-source endorsement and collateral on the aligned and 200-unrelated sets; secondary: held-out perplexity. Convincing: distrusted-source lift cut to <=3 pp with <=2 pp collateral drop and trusted-source endorsement preserved, beating the re-prompt by >=15 pp, transferring across source types and models. Undecidable band: lift cut to 3-6 pp, or collateral 2-5 pp -> capped utility. Negative (lift unchanged, collateral >5 pp, or over-suppresses trusted-source belief) means credibility gating cannot be restored by steering.
Risk Factors and Limitations: LLMs might actually show human-like source moderation (strong credibility x repetition interaction), refuting the 'ungated' hypothesis; this would be an informative positive cross-species finding rather than a failure, and the design measures the interaction either way.

Repetition manipulations could act via verbatim in-context copying rather than genuine belief inflation; including both true and false repeated claims, using paraphrased (non-verbatim) repetitions, and comparing to a no-repetition-but-equal-length control separate copying from illusory-truth belief change.

Source-credibility framings may not be genuinely understood or may add confounding content; the manipulation-check (model can rate source reliability directly) and matched-length source framings mitigate this, and the neutral-source condition anchors the baseline.

The familiarity and credibility signals may be entangled; the causal patching/steering tests (Exp 4), not probe separability alone, are decisive, and a graded/partial dissociation would weaken the strong claim while remaining informative.

The gating intervention could over-suppress (making the model distrust trusted-source repeated claims) or degrade fluency; the trusted-source and aligned-condition specificity controls (Exp 4) are central and utility may be capped.
Verdicts are prompt-sensitive (true/false/uncertain framing, source phrasing); we use multiple paraphrases and report robustness, since framing itself may modulate the effect.
A single transferable credibility-gating vector may not exist if gating is source-type-specific, limiting practical generality though still scientifically informative.
Findings on 7-9B models may not transfer to frontier-scale models beyond an academic budget.

novelty.reasoning: Core claims that would need to be novel are: (1) LLMs show an inference-time illusory-truth effect as a belief-verification bias when objective truth is held fixed; (2) unlike humans, this repetition effect is not properly moderated by source credibility, i.e., repetition from explicitly distrusted sources still raises endorsement; (3) repetition-familiarity and source-credibility are represented as separable internal signals that are only weakly coupled at the final verdict; (4) causal intervention on the familiarity signal reduces the repetition lift; and (5) a low-rank steering intervention can restore human-like credibility gating better than prompting or CrAM-style attention modification. From the search summary, claim (1) is only partly novel because direct investigations of illusory-truth vulnerability in LLMs already exist or are strongly adjacent. The strongest genuine novelty is claim (2): the source-credibility moderation test as the decisive human/LLM signature of adaptive rationality appears meaningfully different from prior repetition, accommodation, or source-conflict work. Claims (3) and (4) are moderately novel as a specific mechanistic account, but they rest on familiar interpretability templates (decoding separable signals + causal ablation), so the framework is less new than the exact hypothesis. Claim (5) is somewhat novel in applying steering to restore credibility gating at inference time, though this is also an understandable next step once the behavioral failure is posited. Closest prior family is the cluster of illusory-truth-in-LLMs / epistemic-vigilance / source-preference works, plus CrAM for credibility-aware document weighting in RAG. The actual delta is not 'credibility matters in LLMs' generally, but specifically that repetition-induced endorsement should fail to be gated by distrust, and that this failure can be explained as separable-but-uncoupled familiarity and credibility signals. Overall: clearly differentiated from CrAM and from generic source-conflict work, but only partially new on the basic behavioral phenomenon and somewhat incremental on the intervention methodology.
revision_notes: State explicitly which prior LLM illusory-truth papers already test repetition-induced false-belief increases, and narrow your novelty claim to the source-credibility moderation signature plus mechanism.
Clarify why the proposed setting is not just another knowledge-conflict/source-preference benchmark but a distinct belief-verification paradigm holding truth fixed.
Make the mechanistic novelty precise: what would count as evidence for 'weak coupling' beyond separate probe decodability?
Differentiate the steering fix from standard activation steering or attention edits by specifying what is uniquely being restored: interaction structure, not overall skepticism.
Avoid implying that no prior work studies inference-time repetition effects unless you directly cite and distinguish those papers.

impact.reasoning: The phenomenon under study is not a new method but a potentially important epistemic failure mode: repetition can inflate LLM endorsement of claims even when the source is explicitly unreliable. Who cares: misinformation/factuality researchers, LLM safety and evaluation groups, alignment teams working on epistemic vigilance, product teams building assistants that summarize user claims or multiple sources, and interpretability researchers interested in belief formation heuristics. What would change if it holds: the field would need to treat repeated user assertions as a distinct inference-time bias, separate from training-data memorization or retrieval credibility, and safety mitigations would need to explicitly gate familiarity/repetition effects by source reliability. Strongest one-line case: 'If repeated claims from distrusted sources still raise model endorsement, then LLMs can be manipulated by sheer repetition in a way humans often are not, creating a concrete, actionable safety and misinformation vulnerability.' On the so-what test: yes, there is a real answer—this would identify a deployment-relevant failure mode and suggest an interpretable mitigation target. That said, the impact is not obviously field-redefining because (a) some form of repetition/accommodation vulnerability is already expected from nearby work, and (b) the proposal uses relatively small open models, so external stakeholders may question generality to frontier assistants. If replicated on strong models and linked to realistic conversational settings, it could get good uptake across factuality/safety/evals; if confined to synthetic source labels and narrow prompts, it may land as a neat but niche bias study.

review.reasoning: The proposal is sharper than average and has a falsifiable main hypothesis, but as a strict ML reviewer I see several weaknesses. Positives first: it has a clean behavioral interaction test, acknowledges an informative null/opposite outcome, includes controls for paraphrased repetition and equal-length non-repetition exposure, and proposes both mechanism and intervention. However, several claims are under-justified. First, 'endorsement' is underspecified: exact prompting, output format, calibration method, and whether endorsement is measured from logits, verbalized probabilities, or forced-choice judgments matter a lot. Second, the key manipulation of source credibility is vulnerable to confounds: distrusted sources may differ in style, sentiment, or political valence; a manipulation check alone does not prove source reliability rather than generic negativity is driving effects. Third, the criterion 'interaction < half human moderation' imports a human benchmark without establishing comparability of scales or tasks. Fourth, the mechanistic section overclaims: separate decodability from L2 probes does not establish distinct computational signals, and 'credibility activation does not reduce familiarity->verdict slope' is not yet a well-specified causal test. Fifth, the proposed familiarity ablation removing >=50% of lift may be difficult to interpret because many interventions damage general semantic processing; stronger controls are needed. Sixth, comparison to CrAM is only loosely relevant unless you instantiate a fair inference-time analogue, since CrAM operates over external retrieved documents. Seventh, feasibility is mixed: cross-model transfer, layerwise probes, causal interventions, and preserving trusted-source endorsement all in one paper is ambitious for three small models and three seeds. The narrative is close to venue-ready as a focused workshop/short paper idea, but not yet robust enough for a top-tier main-track submission without much more methodological detail and tighter claims.
